Commentator: Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha Commentator: Aghoraśiva Editor: Śāstrī Kṛṣṇa

Notes: Transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, with provisional corrections by Dr. Dyczkowski. Revision 1: Reformatted on 02/06/2006.
Publisher: Śivāgama Siddhānta Paripālana Saṅgham Year of Publication: 1928 City of Publication: Devakottai
Country of publication: India. Homage to Śiva and Śivā. The Mṛgendra.
The Vidyāpāda, adorned with the commentary accompanied by the Dīpikā. The Dīpikā.
I bow to that Supreme Lord, the ordainer of all knowledge, whose power—consisting of both wisdom and action—bestows liberation upon the earth. (1)
In this commentary on the *Śrīmṛgendra* composed by the venerable Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, I shall today elucidate the intended meaning, which is not contradicted by either reasoning or scripture. (2)
Whatever meaning is explained by the author of the commentary himself most clearly in this Śāṅkara scripture, I perceive nothing therein that needs to be stated by me;
yet, whatever has not been spoken by him for fear of prolixity, or whatever was indicated unclearly—
On this very point, I shall now also state something that is consistent with both scripture and reasoning. (3)
Following in the footsteps of Rāmakaṇṭha, Mahākaṇṭha, and Kaṇṭhīrava, I do not fear the roars of the elephants that are the bad logicians. || 4 ||

In this regard, first of all, our venerable teacher, in order to conform to the conduct of the learned and to ensure the completion of the treatise without obstacles, bows with the first half-verse to the author of the treatise, the materials employed for its composition, and the teachers who introduced it.
With the second half [of the verse], however, he promises the exposition of the treatise: "Candrārdha," and so forth.
Among the twenty-eight Āgamas, this *Mṛgendra* is a subsidiary scripture (*upāgama*) of the *Kāmika*, which is the first.
The reason for its designation as *Mṛgendra* will become clear in the introduction.
The commentary: Having prostrated before the pair of lotus-feet of the one who bears the crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
and before Vāgīśvarī, Gaṇapati, and the gurus in succession;

I shall now clarify, according to my understanding and in accordance with the scriptures, the profound ultimate truth of the venerable Mṛgendra, which is hidden by the subtle traces of thought and other obscurations. || 1 ||
*Dīpikā*:

The "half-moon" (*candrārddha*) refers to the digit of the moon; because it illuminates and bestows joy, it is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) itself that is spoken of as the lunar digit. He is one whose crest-ornament (*cūḍā*) is that very [power].

According to the scriptural statement, "adorned with the digit of the moon of knowledge," the two feet of that Supreme Lord—by which He is moved, approached, known, practiced, performed, and enacted—are His powers of knowledge and action (*jñāna- and kriyā-śakti*), which serve as the instruments for the composition of the scriptures. As he will state: "And the instrument is not other than power."
Because they possess the nature of blooming and are stainless, these two alone constitute the "pair" (*yugam*), which is their collective form.

Although power (*śakti*) is one, it is called a "pair" by means of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), with the intention of distinguishing between the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and its effect (*kārya*). Having bowed down—having become prostrate—with body, speech, and mind; [to] Vāgīśvarī, who is the material cause of the treatise.

The power (śakti) whose nature is Great Illusion (mahāmāyā), who abides as the possessor [of the universe], and whose essence is supreme knowledge (paravidyā). As it is stated in the venerable Pauṣkara: "The supreme knowledge is Vāgīśvarī; the lower knowledge is known as Māyā. And as he will state later: "From the power arises the primordial sound (nāda)," and so forth. Likewise, Gaṇapati, the leader of the hosts...

Having prostrated before Paramaśiva— the Lord of the Vidyeśvaras, the Vidyās, the other Mantreśvaras, and the multitudes of bound souls (paśu), and the author of this scripture— [the author proceeds], for the instrument is mentioned first because it is the most effective means (sādhakatama) in the agent's performance of an action.
Since even that which possesses an instrument requires a material cause (*upādāna*), the material cause of the material cause follows after the material cause of the agent;

[this occurs] sequentially, in due order. Having prostrated before the gurus—the introducers of the Tantras, namely Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, Śakra, Bharadvāja, and Hārīta—and others down to one's own immediate teacher.

The connection [of the sentence] is: "I shall manifest the supreme reality of the illustrious Lord of Beasts (Mṛgendra). By this, he demonstrates the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the scripture because it was composed by the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), and the authenticity (*āptatva*) of himself because he has come down through an unbroken tradition (*avichinnasampradāya*). "From a fragment" (*leśāt*) means from a summary (*saṃkṣepāt*).

"According to my intellect, according to my understanding. For even by Brahmā, the supreme teaching of the Lord cannot be fully comprehended in its entirety. If, being so, he were to state whatever came to mind through mere personal fancy, he would indeed be unreliable. Therefore, he says: "according to scripture and reasoning."

The meaning is: "without transgressing scripture (āgama) and inference (anumāna). "Gūḍham" means extremely profound. And this is the reason for engaging in the commentary by way of a qualification; the sense is that because it is profound, it must be explained. [Regarding the phrase] "the supreme reality of the venerable Mṛgendra," "śrīmat" [is used].

Because it possesses sovereignty over all, it is the Supreme Lord; and since that "Śrī" exists within this scripture as its author, it is both "Śrīmat" and "Mṛgendra. Now, one might object: among the ten and eighteen divisions of the Śiva-scriptures, nothing is heard by the name "Mṛgendra. This is true; for this very reason, it is called the "Kāmika."
This *Jñānaśāstra* is called *Mṛgendra* because it was resorted to by Śakra, who has assumed the form of the king of beasts (*mṛgendra*).
As he will state in the conclusion: "Thus this *Kāmika-jñāna* was obtained from the Supreme Lord.
Likewise: "And this supreme secret knowledge is clearly manifest throughout the three worlds."

"Because the listener has the form of a lion (mṛgendra), he is called 'Mṛgendra' by the wise," so it is said. "I shall manifest"—that is, I shall make clear—"his ultimate reality," which is the true nature of the object. Thus [ends] the *Dīpikā*.

He rebukes both types of commentators with the second verse: those who, as commentators, prattle on at great length about whatever is irrelevant to the subject at hand; and those who, considering themselves learned, neglect to clarify the meaning of the text that is to be explained.
Regarding the [three] modes of conduct:
some indeed roar excessively for the sake of proclaiming the power of their own realization, yet it is certainly not applicable to the subject at hand.
Others, however, though possessing sharp intellects, do not discern that this is of clear meaning; thus they disregard it. || 2 ||
Dīpikā: By means of the third [verse], indicating the correctness of his own commentary— Vṛtti.
In brief, those who explain the subject at hand— which is not yet clear— by means of a systematic connection of words and their meanings,
are generally respected here by those of sharp intellect.
And by those who fear fruitless prolixity, the authors of commentaries [have likewise refrained]. || 3 ||
The *Dīpikā* states the characteristics of a correct commentary with the three verses beginning with "sākṣāt. [The] *Vṛtti* [explains]:
Having heard this from Śrī Rāmakaṇṭha— who, like Śrīkaṇṭhanātha himself, descended for the sake of favoring virtuous people—
the venerable Vidyākaṇṭhabhaṭṭa, a mature sun for the blossoming of the lotus of the Śiva doctrine, taught this very [work] while instructing him in it.
O child, compose here a concise commentary of clear meaning that is useful for all.
Indeed, various treatises on different philosophical systems have been composed by some one after another;
yet until this very day, this [work] has not had its seal broken.
Therefore, my guru instructed me in this manner. || 5 ||
Therefore, I have set about this commentary,
for the command of a guru is not to be transgressed.
Who, by his own whim, would [venture to explain] that which possesses exceedingly profound terminology?
One would attempt to challenge this lord of beasts. || 6 ||
The *Dīpikā* states the reason for engaging in the explanation of the scriptural tradition:
just as in the case of study and listening, it is the command of the guru alone that prompts one to the exposition of the scripture.

The intended meaning is that it is the cause of engagement. As it has also been stated by the Teachers: "From the very moment of approaching the Guru, one must proceed everywhere solely on the basis of the Guru’s word. Regarding the term *mṛgendram*: it refers both to the *Mṛgendra* scripture and to a lion. Regarding the phrase *gabhīraśabdam*: the profundity of the scripture is due to its profound subject matter.

"And as a mantra" means that by the words "whatever [it may be]," and so forth, he resolves what has been left unsaid, what is poorly expressed, and what is doubtful. This is the commentary (*vṛtti*).
Whatever has not been stated here, whatever has been poorly expressed, or whatever I have said that does not appear clearly, [may it be forgiven],
for those whose sole intent is the concealment of faults are like the sun.
Therefore, may the foremost of the wise, making this clear, forgive [me].
From this point forward, let further stages of conduct proceed,
like a continuous succession of lamps expanding from a lamp that has been kindled.
*Dīpikā*:

Regarding the word "doṣa," it means "night. It also refers to the reversals of the *guṇas*. He says, "From this point forward," etc., so that other commentaries (*vṛtti*) may also proceed by means of this very same matrix (*mātṛkā*).

Commentary: Now, the statement "free from beginningless impurity" constitutes the *tantra* (the body of the work). Furthermore, the introductory section (*upoddhāta-prakaraṇa*) beginning with "having paid homage to the Supreme Lord" [serves] as the connection (*sambandha*), the subject matter (*abhidheya*), and the purpose (*prayojana*).

For the purpose of demonstrating the sequence of the introduction to the Tantra: formerly, indeed, there was a sage named Hārīta, a disciple of Bharadvāja, who had realized the true essence of the meaning of all the Vedas and Śāstras;

his mind was directed toward the power of Śiva (Śiva-śakti), and he had received initiation from those whose minds were likewise oriented toward Śiva’s power through the paths of knowledge, action, and conduct.

Having seen those dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest, whose wealth was their austerity, who were desirous of knowing Yoga, and who stood with palms joined in salutation, [he] was questioned by them regarding this glorious division of the Kāmika, known as the Mṛgendrottara, which has spread through the upward stream (ūrdhvasrotas). He [then] looked upon those disciples endowed with the requisite qualities.
Having first offered salutations to Parameśvara and others, the disciple of Hārīta— or his grand-disciple— imitating dispassion, spoke this to his own disciples.
[Root Text]
Having paid homage to the Supreme Lord and then to the sage Bharadvāja,
[the teaching] which descended from Hara through Indra in succession.
Listen to this knowledge, O you of excellent vows.

Commentary: O you of excellent vows (*suvratāḥ*). Because they possess an excellence of splendor nourished by the preeminence of devotion to the Supreme Lord, those whose vows—namely, the performance of scriptural injunctions—are beautiful are [called] *suvrata*. And those who...

The listeners have been awakened, as he will state in the conclusion: "This which I shall speak to you, who are as white as the moonlight of Śiva’s cool-rayed moon, has been spoken by my own will. The connection is:
"Listen"—that is, hear—the knowledge that has come down from Hara through the succession [of teachers] starting with Indra. He removes... [the darkness].

"From the bound souls (paśu) [he removes] the fetters; from the individual soul (puruṣa) also, he [leads them] to the state above—thus is Hara. Although this name is etymological and common even to Ananteśa and others, nevertheless, due to the proximity of the word "Indra," the word "Hara" here should be understood as referring specifically to Umāpati. As they say:
"Meaning, context, indicative mark, and the proximity of another word—
these are declared to be the causes for the specific determination of general terms. If it is asked why this is so,
it is because in this *Kāmika-bheda* of the *Aindra* [tantra], the Blessed Lord Umāpati is the speaker and Indra is the listener.
The relationship [of the text] with the listeners is indeed understood; for it will be stated here by Indra himself to the sages immediately prior:
"This knowledge was vomited forth by Śiva [and received] by the Mantras, the Mantreśvaras, and the Mantreśvara-īśvaras."
Because it grants desires, it is celebrated at great length as "Kāmikā."

"Having received it from them, the Lord of Umā, who has licked the tree of Smara with the flames of the light of his vision, gave it to me. Therefore, it has descended and been transmitted through the sequence beginning with Dhareśvara and ending with the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, arriving in the order starting with Indra. By this [scripture], things are known.

The knowledge of the *vidyā*, *caryā*, *kriyā*, and *yoga* is the scripture (*śāstra*). Having done what? Listen: having paid homage to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). He is the "Lord" (*īśa*) because he rules over the universe characterized by consciousness and the unconscious through [the acts of] emanation, maintenance, withdrawal, and so forth. Since even Ananteśa and others possess lordship (*īśitṛtva*), he is qualified by the term "Supreme" (*parama*). And he is supreme...

Because the state of Śiva is manifested in others through His grace, He is the Lord (Īśvara); and because He performs creation and other acts by His own autonomy, He is the Supreme Lord (Parameśa). Having paid homage to Him—having become bowed before Him with body, speech, and mind—thereafter [one pays homage to] the sage Bharadvāja, the introducer of the Tantra; for the root *ṛṣ* means "to go."
Since the verbal root *ṛ* and all roots meaning "to go" also carry the sense of "to know," the Seer (Ṛṣi) is, in the ultimate sense, [the one who knows].
Having paid homage to him, [the author says] "listen"—this is an instruction for the listeners to perform a salutation.
For those who have not paid homage to the Supreme Lord and have not bowed to their Guru, [there will be no] obstacle-free [attainment].

Because it is impossible to acquire the Saṃhitā [otherwise], it is understood that whoever instructs the audience in this manner does so by virtue of having himself already performed such [preliminaries]; therefore, just as I have set out to teach after bowing to the Supreme Lord and my gurus, so too should you proceed to listen.

This is established. Although this very matter was taught by Umāpati to Indra and exists in the text itself at its conclusion, nevertheless, something is stated here because the relationship and other such factors must necessarily be expressed at the commencement of an exposition.

Once, he beheld the Lord who sports in the seventh ocean— a sea enchanting with its golden floor inlaid with heaps of exceedingly beautiful jewels; the Lord who possesses the luster of a blue lotus, has four arms,
and supports two necks with two faces that simultaneously perform the recitation of the Vedas and the drinking of wine.
The Lord of the Thirty-three beheld the evil-minded great Asura surrounded by hosts of Asuras. Then,

Śatakratu, accompanied by a multitude of sages agitated by anger born from witnessing such wicked conduct, realized that the Asura was invincible through weapons because he had obtained a boon, and thus could not be restrained.

With a thunderbolt concealed within foam, he severed the two heads of the asura. Fearing the sin produced by the killing of a brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) due to that act, and desiring its pacification, he praised the Lord Acyuta with a thousand names and with the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas. By Hari, being thus pleased—

As he was bestowing the Narasiṃha armor—which is radiant like the newly risen sun and capable of overwhelming all destroyers—he said: "With your body thus armored, perform austerities while propitiating the Lord who wields the Pināka bow;
at the end of a thousand years, however, [propitiate] him."
Having said, "Upon seeing me, you shall attain your desire," the Lord Murāri vanished; then Indra performed all that [was commanded].

When the Blessed One, the wielder of the Pināka bow, appeared before his eyes, the end of all his suffering occurred. Furthermore, the Supreme Lord taught him the venerable scripture known as the Kāmika, because it belongs to Indra.
This was taught by Umāpati to Him who has the form of Nṛsiṃha; therefore, because the King of Beasts (Mṛgendra) was the listener, it became renowned by the name Mṛgendra.
Furthermore, the relationship here is of six kinds, beginning with the "Supreme" (parā). For instance, at the beginning of creation, the Supreme Lord...
Knowledge, which is divided into five streams—upward, east, south, north, and west—is manifested immediately after the awakening of the eight Vidyeśvaras who are favored by His own will;
having become manifest, He taught it to the Mantreśvaras and others as will be described hereafter. Thus it is stated in the *Kiraṇa*:

Immediately after creation, the Lord Śiva, having created ten sons who were auspicious, quickly divided the single knowledge into as many parts as there were sons and taught it to them, beginning with [the scriptures] named Kāmika, Praṇava, Yōgaja, and so forth. Here, the term "sons" (ātmajān) refers to those born from his own self.
The intention is that they were favored by a grace that is without basis [in prior merit]. Umāpati received it from them;
Śakra from him; Bharadvāja from him; and Hārīta from him. We shall clarify later how he, in turn, imparted it to his own disciples. Furthermore, the subject matter (*abhidheya*) here is as follows:

[The topics are] knowledge, action, yoga, and conduct; and the purpose here is the realization thereof. That purpose, in turn, is enjoyment and liberation. Although the presentation of the means of valid cognition that establish the existence of the Supreme Lord and the refutation of objections against Him are for the sake of proving the authority of the scripture composed by Him, [the following is stated].

It is employed right from the very beginning. Nevertheless, since this has already been deliberated upon by the author of the treatise itself, we shall discuss it there. We shall state here only this much: as it has been said—"He is accepted as authoritative because he has mastered Ayurveda, mathematics, and the mantras along with their phonology, as well as the extensive secret doctrines (upaniṣads) of alchemy."
Thus, that quality of being an authority (āptatva) belongs only to their respective domains for the founders of other systems, who possess eyes with cataracts and thus do not perceive all objects;
however, it belongs eternally to [the Lord], who possesses the power of knowledge and action regarding all objects, which is ever-pure and unsurpassed.

Because he is engaged in the act of bestowing grace upon all, and because he is the Supreme Lord and the presiding authority over all, his [teaching] pertains to every object. Since it is impossible for a speaker endowed with such qualifications to be a deceiver, there is no lack of authority (aprāmāṇya). We shall explain this in its proper place. Thus, being of such a nature—

The Blessed One is the author of the scripture, while the scripture makes him known. Therefore, since the two perform distinct functions, there would be no fault of mutual dependence here. It is just as when someone says, "I, Devadatta, have arrived," and upon hearing those words, others understand it.
"This is Devadatta who has arrived. Nor is it logical for there to be mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) between Devadatta and his statement in this instance.

Furthermore, having observed that his tradition is fruitful in cases where the objects are perceptible—such as his statements regarding the taste of poison and the like—it is inferred that his teaching regarding imperceptible objects is likewise productive of results.
Enough of this; let us return to the subject at hand. || 1 ||

*Dīpikā*: He shows the nature of the treatise with the words beginning "Now, beginningless... and so forth. He states the purpose of the introductory chapter (*upodghātapaṭala*) with the words beginning "As for that which... and so forth. As they have said regarding *cintā*...
They say that an introduction (*upodghāta*) is stated for the sake of establishing the subject at hand.

He provides the introduction to this chapter on the introduction with the words "In former times," and so forth. By the phrase "by those who have received initiation," the meaning is that those who are uninitiated do not have the authority to hear [this]. The phrase "the upward stream" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) and so forth refers to the form of the Siddhānta, and not to the Vāma and other [streams].

Regarding the phrase "known as Mṛgendrottara," he spoke to Mṛgendra about that which is called Mṛgendrottara, and not merely a portion of Mṛgendra; this is because it possesses the fourfold division of knowledge (jñāna) and the other limbs. Regarding the phrase "endowed with the qualities of a disciple," it is as stated: "One who is desirous [of liberation], capable, learned, and not excluded by the scripture is qualified for the Tantra."

Regarding the phrase "from Parameśvara and others," the inclusion of the word "others" (ādi) refers to Bharadvāja and so forth, because the teacher is to be honored and saluted at the beginning of the exposition. The statement "a disciple of Hārīta," etc., means that the very words of Hārīta are being restated by his disciples and others. "Vrata" refers to the performance of scriptural injunctions.

This is established by both general and specific scriptures. Regarding the *Śrīmadbhārgava*: "One should not transgress, even in thought, the conduct prescribed for one's caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramācāra*). Whosoever, abiding in whatever stage of life, has received initiation whose essence is Śiva, he should remain steadfast in that very stage and protect the Dharma of Śiva."
In the venerable *Svāyambhuva* [Tantra] as well, it is stated: "Householders who abide by the path of the world should not transgress worldly norms;

likewise, those initiated into the conduct [of the tradition] should act accordingly. Here, by the word *Hara*, which means "he who removes the bonds from the bound souls (*paśu*)", the disciple of Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, is intended. He states the reason for this here:

"Because of the proximity of the word 'Indra'" means that he alone possesses the authority over the center of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). To elaborate on this very point, he asks: "Whence is this? and so forth. He provides the answer: "Since... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "transmitted from Hara through the lineage of Indra," he states that the word "Indra" is also an elliptical designation for Bharadvāja.

Regarding the phrase "by the sequence of Indra," he explains the term *jñānapada* (the word for knowledge) with the words "it is known by this," and so forth. Here, by the word *vidyā*, the meaning of the Lord (*pati*) and others, which is expressed by the *vidyāpāda* (the section on knowledge), is intended. This is because the manifestation of the state of Śiva occurs through His grace; that is, the omniscience of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) and others is manifested solely through the grace of Śiva. As he will state:

In that regard, first he forms an octad of pure, qualified atoms, joined with the powers beginning with Vāmā and surrounded by seventy million attendants. Therefore, it is said that the word "Lord" (Īśa) has its primary application to Him alone; as for Ananta and the others, they exist only through His impulsion, as expressed in the passage beginning with "by His sovereignty."

The meaning is that although they possess omniscience due to performing acts such as creation, their status as agents is inferior in comparison to Śiva. Anticipating the objection that the word "ṛṣi" is redundant given that Bharadvāja is already well-known as a seer (*ṛṣi*), he provides a rebuttal beginning with the statement, "the root *ṛṣ* means 'to go,'" and so forth.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "of the connection, etc.," both the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) are understood.

In that regard, he relates a historical narrative (*itihāsa*) for the sake of illuminating the connection, beginning with "Once upon a time... and so forth. The term "one who indulges in sport" (*viharaṇabhoginam*) refers to one who is addicted to play. The phrase "the end of all his suffering has occurred" is used because [his state] is the cause of the cessation of all suffering.

The meaning is that the end—the disappearance—of all suffering, which is impurity (*mala*), has occurred at that very moment; for, by virtue of the ripening of that impurity, his initiation into *nirvāṇa* was accomplished, preceded by the descent of power (*śakti-nipāta*).
Precisely because of this qualification, the Supreme Lord taught him the venerable scripture known as the *Kāmika*.

The word "treatise" (*śāstra*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. He states the types of relationships with the words "the relationship, however," and so forth; [these are] the "supreme and so on," namely:

the supreme (*para*), the great (*mahān*), the intermediate (*antarāla*), the divine (*divya*), the semi-divine (*divyādivya*), and the non-divine (*adivya*). He demonstrates these very [types] with the words "for instance," and so forth. "Divided into five currents" refers precisely to this form of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
It is called the form of the five currents (*pañcasrotas*) because it is embraced by the five mantras, because it accomplishes the fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtya*),

and because it manifests as the body of Śiva whose nature consists of the five mantras. Nor is [the system] consisting of Vāmā and the others [to be excluded], for even though they act as non-Śiva (i.e., as impure agents), how could they not nonetheless be Śaiva?

In some cases, the established tradition [of scripture] exists through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), because it was composed by another self presided over by Śiva. If this is so, one might argue that since the Supreme Lord is bodiless, the teaching of scripture would be untenable.
This is not so; for just as in the case of the creation of the world and so forth, the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) and others are made aware of the scripture by His mere will alone.

He says that very thing in the passage beginning with "graced by His own will," and so forth. Now, it is heard that the divisions of Śiva, such as the *Kāmika* and others, are taught to Praṇava and the rest; how then can there be an instruction for the Vidyeśvaras?
To this he replies: "immediately after the awakening of the eight Vidyeśvaras"—this refers to the first [stage].
The instruction for the lords of the *vidyās* comes first, followed by that of the *praṇava* and the others. From them [the lords of the *vidyās*], Umāpati received it;

immediately after them, Śrīkaṇṭha obtained it from the venerable Ananta, and not from Sūkṣma and the others, because he is renowned specifically as the disciple of Ananta. And it is said in the *Śrīmadraurava*: "The cause of the world..."
[He taught] the god Ananteśa, the supreme guru. It was said by him [to Śiva]: "O Supreme Lord, [it was taught] to the high-souled Śrīkaṇṭha. Thus, there is a supreme bond between Śiva and Ananta;
a great one between Ananta and Śrīkaṇṭha; an intermediate one between Śrīkaṇṭha and Śakra; and [another] between Śakra and Bharadvāja.
[The lineage] of Divya; [the lineage] of Bharadvāja and Hārīta is both divine and non-divine; [the lineage] of Hārīta and his disciple is non-divine.

Regarding the terms "knowledge, action, yoga, and conduct," here the word "knowledge" (jñāna) refers to the objects of knowledge (jñeya), namely the Lord (pati), the individual soul (paśu), and the bonds (pāśa);
and the purpose here is realization (jñapti). For this very reason, the relationship here is characterized as that between the means (upāya) and the goal (upeya).

Thus, the supremely authoritative person has indicated that [the Veda] is of such a nature. Regarding the phrase "of both," since one acts as the agent and the other as the indicator, their functions are dissimilar; therefore, there is no fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). He clarifies this very point by means of an example, beginning with "Just as someone," and so forth. || 1 ||

Commentary: Thus, having promised the instruction on knowledge to his own disciples, the sage Hārīta spoke the following in order to demonstrate that [the tradition] has descended through the lineage of Indra.
In the meritorious hermitage of Nārāyaṇa,
the twice-born Bharadvāja and others performed austerities after having installed Śiva.
With their minds fixed solely upon that. || 2 ||

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: at the hermitage named Badarikāśrama—which is purifying precisely because it is a hermitage of Viṣṇu—the sages, beginning with Bharadvāja, performed austerities. The qualifier "twice-born" (*dvija*) is applied because the status of being twice-born is well-established for the seers (ṛṣis) such as Bharadvāja and others; it is not [used] because of their association with the power of Vāgīśvarī (the Goddess of Speech).

By means of the rites beginning with the *sañjanana* (the rite of generation), it is for the purpose of establishing his excellence through having received initiation (*dīkṣā*). At that time, mere re-initiation (*punarupanayana*)—as understood by the term "twice-born" (*dvija*) in the Smṛti tradition—is not intended; for those who have not been initiated lack the qualification to hear the Tantras and so forth, and on the contrary, there is a scriptural teaching of sin (*pratyavāya*) [for doing so]. [The phrase] "having installed Śiva" [is used].

The intention is that one should conceive of the installation of the Supreme Lord upon a support such as an iron arrow or a *liṅga* by means of general mantras and so forth; otherwise, it would be illogical for there to be a subsequent question regarding the subject of installation and other rites for those who already know the respective procedures exactly as they are. It is deposited within that very same [support].
Those whose minds were made one-pointed, being of such a nature, performed austerities; the meaning is that they practiced penance characterized by the worship of Śiva.
The *Dīpikā* connects the second sūtra with the words "tadevam" and so forth.
Since there are many hermitages of Nārāyaṇa, in response to the inquiry "in which one?", he says:

Regarding the phrase "named Vadarī-āśrama," he explains the term *dvija* with the words "of Bharadvāja and others," and so forth. As for what was stated: "The first birth of Māyā is from Vidya, and after that [is the next]," and so on—how then can Bharadvāja and the others be considered initiated (*dīkṣita*) prior to their direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of Indra? It is not [so].
At that time—specifically at the time of Hārīta’s statement—it is indeed so. "Like the Smṛti" means like the word *dvija* as used in the Sūtra.

As Devala says: "When a boy has been consecrated by his mother and father with the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*, he becomes eligible for initiation (*upanayana*) in the eighth year from conception; therein, the teacher (*upādhyāya*) is the father, and the mother is Gāyatrī. Thus initiated...

"A twice-born man may have two fathers," it is said; [this is because] he lacks the qualification for hearing the Tantras and so forth. Here, by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the Mantras is intended. As it is stated in the venerable *Kālottara*: "The Mantra and the Tantra have been proclaimed by You.
Furthermore, only those who have received initiation (*dīkṣita*) possess the qualification for hearing the Mantras and Tantras, as it has been said:
"In the venerable *Parākhyatantra*, it is stated: 'One who has been initiated shall be an authority, fit for [performing] bathing, worship, and so forth.
And it will be stated in the section on study: 'Standing upon purified ground, avoiding the hearing of [the scriptures meant for] the bound souls (*paśu*).
This is because of the scriptural mention of transgression (*pratyavāya*). As it is said in the venerable *Rauravatantra*:"

"It has been declared that for transgressing His command, one becomes a flesh-eater for a hundred years. Alternatively, by the word "twice-born" (dvija), their excellence is expressed through their connection with the knowledge of the Lord— which results from their pervasion by the status of being twice-born—
and because omniscience and other such qualities are not observed even in the absence of self-knowledge and the like within the non-self and so forth.

For those who fear that they might be bound by another bond, the propitiation of Śiva— who knows the means for their liberation— is appropriate, occurring through the power of the descent of grace (*śaktinipāta*).
This is what is meant by "the characteristic of the propitiation of Śiva," [which occurs] because of the transformation of their impurity (*mala*).

By the power of the descent of grace (*śaktinipāta*), [the soul] consists of the nature of Śiva’s qualities (*śivadharmādi*) and so forth. As it is said in the *Kiraṇatantra*: "When equal karma has arisen, again, by the force of the descent of intense grace (*tīvraśaktinipāta*) at another time.
Also in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*, it is said: "That primordial grace descends upon the person..."

"In this final birth, through the convergence [of causes], his impurity—the cause of saṃsāra—flows away; but when that has been exhausted by means of wisdom, he shall attain supreme beatitude. || 1 ||
Then, perceiving that they had become spiritually cultivated,
the Lord of the Thirty-three once visited their hermitage.
He himself assumed the garb of an ascetic.
Commentary: Subsequently, having recognized that they were cultivated and possessed faith in the Tantra, Śakra, assuming the form of a sage at a certain time, frequented their hermitage. (3)
Dīpikā: In that context, regarding the reading "śraddhālūn," the meaning is "those who have faith in Śiva. || 3 ||
Honored by them and having inquired after the welfare of all of them,
he spoke regarding the dharma of exhortation.
For what reason is it not followed? || 4 ||

Having been honored by Bharadvāja and the others with hospitality appropriate for a hermitage, Indra asked each of them, Bharadvāja and the rest, about their welfare and said: "What is it? He then stated the question:
"Why is the dharma of *codanā* not followed? By *codanā*, he means that which impels one toward action.

They say that the word [of the Veda] is the authority; why then is the Dharma taught therein not practiced? For the injunction alone is the means of valid knowledge regarding Dharma, and the injunction alone is indeed the means of valid knowledge—thus, by excluding both non-connection and connection with another, there is no contradiction regarding the fruits, whether of this world or the next, for those who proceed according to it. Likewise:
And it has been said:
"For a human being who practices the duties proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti attains fame in this world and, after death, the unsurpassed state."

Thus [it is said]. Conversely, however, that which consists of the worship of emblems external to the *trayi* and so forth is, precisely because it is external to the *trayi*, for the most part worthless. As Bhaṭṭa has said:
"Likewise, for those who conduct themselves by transgressing the boundaries prescribed in the Vedas..."
Even in the case of statements that are consistent with experience, their status as a means of valid cognition is not accepted.
Manu also says: "Those Smṛtis which are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—all of them are fruitless after death, for they are declared to be of the nature of darkness. (4)
The *Dīpikā* explains the meaning of the word "all": "He spoke of each one" means that, from the perspective of the Mīmāṃsakas,
he urged [them]— the intention being that by the word "codanā" (impulsion), here injunctions and prohibitions are denoted.

Thus he says, "codanā," and so forth; for it is accepted that the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of injunctive sentences (*codanāvākya*) pertains only to a task to be accomplished (*kārya*), and not to an already established fact (*siddha*). Now, one might object: since the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers, as mere suffixes, possess the capacity to impel action by having the injunction (*vidhi*) as their meaning, why is the word "sentence" (*vacana*) introduced? True; the meaning of the injunction belongs to the suffix alone. However—

It is only with regard to the cultivation [of the means] that the [injunctive suffix] impels the person. This is the meaning: when it is said "one should do," there arises an expectancy as to what, by what means, and how; it is the sentence itself—such as "one should do this in this manner"—that possesses the power to impel.
As they say: "The injunctive suffix is capable of enjoining only when it is complete through the requirements beginning with 'what'."

By the word "dharma" here, a quality of the intellect (buddhiguṇa) in the form of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is not intended, because that is not accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas. Nor is it the essential nature (*bhāvasvabhāva*) [of things], because that is something produced (*kāryatva*). Nor is it the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) called *apūrva*, because that arises at a time subsequent to the performance [of the action]. Rather, [it refers to...]

He states that [dharma] consists precisely in the performance of sacrifices and so forth, saying: "Dharma is that which is enjoined in scripture. He says it is not [simply] that which is performed, because "injunction alone is the means of valid cognition regarding dharma. This is because even if dharma, in its form as performance, were perceptible, [the means of cognition would still be required for] its result—namely, the *apūrva* (unseen potency) produced by that performance—and for that result, such as heaven, as well as for the relationship between them.
Since it is beyond the reach of the senses, it is not possible for means of valid cognition such as perception to have authority regarding it.
If this were so, then because it would not be included among the means of valid cognition, even *codanā* (Vedic injunction) would not be a means of valid cognition; therefore, he says:
"Injunction alone is indeed a means of valid cognition," because of the eternality of the injunction.

Because there is an absence of defects such as deception on the part of an author, its status as a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) by virtue of making known supersensible objects is indeed unavoidable. As they say: "A means of valid cognition is that which makes known an object not already apprehended. Thus, the restriction that the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is "exclusively" a means of valid cognition is established through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*).

It excludes the possibility of invalidity. The restriction "only the injunction" (codanā), however, excludes the possibility of validity for perception and other means of knowledge. Regarding the phrase "because the result is non-contradictory":
[an objection is raised]—"But in some cases, such as the *putreṣṭi* sacrifice, a discrepancy with the result is observed; how then [can it be said that the result is non-contradictory]?"

The authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is established because its results are not deceptive. It is replied: in some cases, as in agriculture and the like, there may be a discrepancy regarding the result due to defects in the action, the agent, or the means; however, such a discrepancy does not prove a lack of authority. [The term] *phalguprāyam* means having little purpose or utility. (4)
Commentary: Having heard these words of his, who followed the doctrine of Jaimini— Root Text: They said, "But surely this is Dharma..."
O Sage,
the means for propitiating the deity, as prescribed by the injunctions, is austerity for the sake of attaining one's desired goal. (5)
Those [sages], Bharadvāja and the others, having addressed Indra by the word "muni" because of his ascetic form,

spoke the words beginning with "nanu": "This dharma, characterized as the means for propitiating the deity named Rudra who is desired by us, which is being practiced by us for the sake of accomplishing our goals through austerity— "

For it is by *codanā* alone that [the dharma] is enjoined and established. To explain: *codanā* is defined as a statement that impels one toward actions such as sacrifice, which take the form of injunctions and prohibitions established by words such as the optative (*liṅ*), imperative (*loṭ*), and gerundive (*tavya*). For example: "One who desires heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and so forth. And that...
Primarily, it is based on the Śruti; and because it is rooted in that, it also includes the Smṛti. Thus it has been said:

"Therefore, the Śruti and the Smṛti alone are the authoritative means regarding the sphere of Dharma. Likewise: "The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as well as the Smṛti and the conduct of those who know it."
Let it be, then, with these Puranic compendiums that are not in contradiction with the meaning of the eternal scriptures such as the Śruti, and with certain other Śrutis, whose purport is as follows,
for instance, in the Mahābhārata and elsewhere:
"Those devotees who worship Śiva, Rudra, the Lord of Umā, the boon-bestowing God,
attain happiness in this world and go to the supreme goal. Thus,
having known Bhava as possessing all forms, the master who worships Him in the *liṅga*—
"In him the Bull-bannered One (Śiva) bestows excessive affection.
Likewise:
"The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the sages of great luster..."
"Having worshipped the *liṅga* according to the prescribed rule, they have attained their most desired state.
Likewise:
"The *liṅga* may consist of earth, ashes, cow-dung paste, molasses, sugar-candy, and so forth."
"One who worships with faith attains the goal of his installation.
Even granting this, we say: according to the intention with which this is stated by you, let the meaning of the Veda itself first be remembered. || 5 ||

The *Dīpikā*: It introduces the subsequent sūtra with the words "In this way," and so forth; and with the words "This which has been [stated] by us," and so forth, [it means]: let injunction alone be the authority (*pramāṇa*) regarding dharma; we too shall practice only that dharma which is based on injunction. This is the meaning.
"For the sake of accomplishing what is desired. And what is desired by them is the removal of impurities and so forth.

He establishes that the nature of dharma consists precisely in being an injunction (*codanā*) with the words "For it is thus," and so on. It has been stated that only an injunction is that which prompts action. Now, it may be objected: "We do not accept as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) merely any sentence that prompts action; rather, [the means of valid cognition] must be specifically one in the form of Vedic revelation (*śruti*)."
[This is] an objection. To this, he says: "Even granting [your point], we say," and so forth. (5)
For it is said: "In the Veda there is a Raudrī Saṃhitā; Rudra is the deity to be addressed."
Even for the purpose of bringing about his presence,
this ritual procedure prescribed for the Kalpa has been ordained.
Commentary: That which has Rudra as its deity is the Raudrī Saṃhitā; it exists in the Veda characterized by Ṛk, Yajuḥ, and Sāman, as well as in the Atharvaṇa Veda.
For in the Yajurveda, the Rudraikādaśinī Saṃhitā is heard, in which the Blessed Ones...

The Rudras are recited as the accomplishers of all desired goals. Even in the Ṛgveda, there exist such mantras as "We worship Tryambaka," "These [offerings] for Rudra, the ascetic with matted hair," and "These songs for Rudra, the wielder of the firm bow," which yield specific results through the particular injunctions prescribed in the Ṛgvidhāna.

For it is heard even in the Sāmaveda, in the injunction regarding the Sāmans: "The hymn beginning with 'ā vo rājānam' belongs to that class; this Saṃhitā is dedicated to Rudra (raudrī). One who employs this [Saṃhitā] pleases Rudra. Likewise, in the Atharvaveda as well, there are methods for the propitiation of Rudra and the Saṃhitās of his mantras.

They arise; and it is not merely the *saṃhitā* that exists there. For in that context, Rudra alone is heard as the deity in the form of the expressed meaning (*vācyarūpa*), according to the Śruti: "This is your portion, O Rudra, together with your sister Ambikā;
accept it, Svāhā! Nor is this merely ritualistic (*kālpika*); for the *Kalpa* is a limb of the Veda (*vedāṅga*), and what is stated therein [is authoritative].

A rule is heard for the purpose of conceiving the presence of the Blessed One. For instance, in the Rudra-kalpa of the Sūtra-pariśiṣṭa in the Kāṭhaka, after stating that one should perform ablutions three times a day, it is said:
"Sitting upon *darbha* grass and holding a handful of *darbha*, one becomes unrecognizable even by demons."

"One who subsists on vegetables, barley-gruel, milk, and almsfood beholds the Blessed Lord Pinākin becoming manifest within six months. Thus, even for those whose minds lack faith and who follow the shadow of Jaimini's school, this [deity] is indeed well-known as being demonstrated by the Vedic injunction (codanā).
[This is] the path. How much more so for others whose vision is clearly restored by the destruction of the great darkness of delusion through the illumination of the Supreme Lord? (6)
The Lamp (Dīpikā): "But what [more]?
means that by virtue of the descent of power (śaktipāta), there occurs the destruction of doubt and erroneous knowledge regarding the Lord (Īśvara).

The meaning is: "of those for whom the certainty of its existence has been revealed. However, one should not explain "great delusion" (*mahāmoha*) here as being the impurity (*mala*), because it will be stated later that its destruction occurs through initiation (*dīkṣā*) alone.
Even when this was said, the Lord, desiring to know their supreme disposition, laughed and said to them: "Your knowledge is false— "
For the deity is indeed mere sound. || 7 ||

Commentary: Even though this had been said, the Lord—who, by virtue of possessing supreme sovereignty as Indra, is characterized by the power of manifestation—desiring to know the excellence of their devotion, spoke with a smile to those sages. What did he say?
This false knowledge belonging to you—namely, that scripture which propounds the worship of Śiva through the veneration of his *liṅga* and so forth—is false and not true;
for there is no logical possibility of such a deity as its author. Since the fruit [of action] arises solely from the performance of ritual acts, and not...

Regarding the deity: the deity is indeed nothing more than sound. We certainly do not maintain that the deity is non-existent, as the Cārvākas—those of wicked conduct who are intent on denying all means of knowledge other than direct perception (pratyakṣa)—would have us believe; rather, the deity truly exists.
That deity, however, does not transcend the word;

rather, like fire in a red-hot iron ball, it is the word itself, being inseparable from the denoted object which is not perceived. It does not enter into the state of being a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) in those specific ritual actions.
It receives the designation of a specific deity who is the recipient of the sacrifice. As it has been said:
"One should meditate on the Lord as the syllable Om, wherein word and meaning are inseparable. Nor can it be asserted here as a rule that there is only one single Lord of All.

This is because one hears of many distinct deities, well-known in their manifold forms; and this is the manifestation of that very Word-form (Śabdarūpa) of incomparable majesty, which, though being one, serves as the cause for the cognition of each of those various specific deities as well as the cause for the cognition of itself. Thus says the Śruti:
"They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni; and he is the divine, fair-winged Garuḍa.
The sages speak of the One Being as many—calling him Agni, Yama, and Mātariśvan.
Thus, it is well established that the deity consists of the Word (Śabdātmikā). || 7 ||
*The Lamp* (*Dīpikā*):

Even when [the objection] has been stated thus, he explains the sūtra beginning with "even so" (*evam api*) and so forth. He explains the phrase "the supreme state" (*paraṃ bhāvam*) as "the excellence of his devotion" (*tadīyaṃ bhaktiprakarṣam*). Devotion is precisely that fitness for the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), which consists in being established in Him.
It is a specific type of knowledge characterized by the penetration of *yogyatā* (spiritual fitness). As it has been said:
"Another [state] is also described as being characterized by the penetration of *yogyatā*;
furthermore, even a portion of higher realization (*vijñāna*) is designated as 'devotion' (*bhakti*). For this very reason, now...

"Endowed with the perfection of the transformation of impurity. He said this with a gentle smile, rather than out of a habit of derision, thinking: "Since the power of the Supreme Lord exists there as the sign of the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*), I shall once again challenge these [Mīmāṃsakas] from the perspective of the Mīmāṃsaka in order to ascertain the excellence of that [power]. Thus he spoke.

The fruit arises solely from the performance of the ritual action, not from the deity; for that deity is unestablished by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through the various words—such as Rudra, Īśa, and so forth—which are accepted as its designators, because it is impossible to grasp a relationship with such [words]. Therefore, it is likewise unestablished even by scripture (*āgama*). And for that very reason...

Because the relationship [between word and meaning] must be grasped through mutual dependence, there is indeed a lack of establishment [of the deity]. Consequently, even in such cases as "one should offer a *caru* oblation to Rudra," since the specific action is understood as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) by way of being the object of reference (*uddeśya*), it is that very word denoting the deity which is perceived [as the cause];
thus, the fruit arises from the ritual act itself and not from the deity. Here too, he will state later: "And..."
"Something that establishes this [existence] appears as an uncontradicted means of valid cognition.
Therefore, he says "And not here," etc., meaning that even if one accepts [the existence of something] other than sound, the specific deity you intend is not established,
because even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others are heard of as being the lords of all.
Nor is such an admission tenable; thus he says, "This is well-established," which means it is certain. || 7 ||
Commentary: Having thus stated [the matter] through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he speaks in order to strengthen that very same point by means of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Root Text: Since sound is distinct from other things, it does not attain proximity simultaneously to multiple objects situated in different locations.
Because it possesses corporeality, like ourselves and others. || 8 ||

If a deity exists as distinct from sound, is it embodied, disembodied, both, or neither? If it were neither, it would be a non-entity because it lacks any form. Furthermore, its reality [as such] would not exist. If it were both, there would be a superimposition of contradictory attributes.
There is the acceptance of the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda), which contradicts one's own established tenets;

and there is the consequence of the faults arising from both alternative positions when considered individually. If [the deity] is bodiless, what wrong has sound committed? But if [the deity] possesses a body, then [how could it attend] sacrifices commenced simultaneously at different locations?

Because she possesses form, her presence among the sacrificers is impossible. [Objection: Even though they possess form, the presence of the solar and lunar orbs is observed when they receive worship from people situated in distant places; therefore, possession of form is an inconclusive reason.

It is not inconclusive. For you, proximity appears to be merely the state of being situated in a location perceivable by all people due to the high elevation of the sun and moon orbs—which are radiant with their own light—and residing in a place accessible to many observers; it is not a real [proximity].
Just as a dancer standing upon the expanse of a very high stage,
though being watched repeatedly by spectators situated at a great distance, does not manifest her presence before each individual through the power of omnipresence (*prākāmya-śakti*); and just as...

It has never been observed that those of us who are invited by many hosts at the same time can eat in multiple houses simultaneously because we possess physical form. Likewise, it is not possible for a deity, due to its corporeality, to be present at sacrifices located in different places at the same time.
It would be more appropriate that it be merely a word. || 8 ||

The *Dīpikā* states the connection of the sūtra beginning with "other than sound" (*śabdetara*) as follows: "In this way, by positive concomitance," and so forth; for there is no other category possible besides those possessing a composite structure (*vigrahavattva*) and those lacking a composite structure (*avigrahavattva*), such as that which is "neither of the two forms" (*anubhayarūpa*).

The sense is that [the phrase] "in the case of having both forms," etc., refers to the fact that the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anaikāntavāda*) will be refuted by such statements as "that very same thing is existent and that very same thing is non-existent. Regarding the phrase "of the two separate positions," etc., it refers to the faults that may be conceived regarding the two positions of possessing a body and not possessing a body.

The states of being a knower of only a little and so forth, as well as the states of being a non-agent and so forth—both of these sets of attributes would thus result here [for the individual soul]. || 8 ||
Commentary: Furthermore, there is nothing whatsoever that establishes that.
Indeed, that [knowledge] shines forth as an uncontradicted means of valid cognition,

for it belongs to a particular deity whose nature is supremely non-sensory, who is devoid of any state of such [ordinary] reversal, and who is endowed with the greatness of knowledge and bliss characterized by the highest excellence of sovereignty.

Some proof appears to be effective. To explain: first of all, this [Self] is not within the scope of the means of perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is the eldest among all means of knowledge due to its being immediate; for it is impossible for perception to possess the capacity to grasp that which transcends the senses. Now, [if one asks...]
If it is argued that yogic perception, which has as its object things that are obstructed or remote, is the means for ascertaining their existence— that is not so.

For the claim that there are yogis who perceive objects beyond the senses of those such as ourselves, that their perception has subtle objects as its domain, and that through this perception God is directly perceived— all of this is untenable due to a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*).

Someone who is beyond the senses and who perceives objects beyond the senses is intended to be established. Why is it not shameful for you, even though you are a seeker of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), to attempt to prove such a person by means of a perception that is unestablished? Surely there exists here an inference whose capacity is unimpaired; for instance:
This world—having as its subject (dharmin) the earth, mountains, rivers, oceans, and so forth—is an effect (kārya); this is the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma).

Because it possesses parts (sāvayavatvāt). Whatever possesses parts is an effect, such as a palace, a rampart, a lotus pond, and so forth; and this reason is excluded from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa). Where...

Indeed, since the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) does not exist in the Self (*ātman*) and so forth, the property of having parts (*sāvayavatva*) likewise does not exist there. Nor is this reason (*hetu*) inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the body of the Lord (*īśvara*), as the followers of Jaimini have said: "And your reason would be inconclusive on account of His body and so forth. This is because even that [body]...

Because we maintain that it is an effect produced by His will. And once the world's status as an effect is established, whatever is an effect is invariably concomitant with a creator endowed with specific knowledge and action, like effects such as pots and cloth. This world is an effect; therefore, this too—

It establishes a creator endowed with unsurpassed knowledge and agency. And as for that creator here, he is Īśvara; why is this not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? This would be a valid means of knowledge if it were uncontradicted;
however, since the state of being composed of parts (*sāvayavatva*) is unestablished for portions of the world such as atoms and sense organs.

This reason (*hetu*) is "partially unestablished" (*bhāgāsiddha*). For while you maintain that atoms, being insentient, must necessarily be effects because they possess multiplicity— just like a jar or similar objects—
even the examples you have cited, such as the city walls, moats, and lotus ponds, [are not established].

The state of being composed of parts (*sāvayavatva*)— which consists of a configuration that is either existent or non-existent, produced by the adequacy or inadequacy of the primary and auxiliary causes directed toward that [object]— is indeed different from anything else; for the state of being composed of parts residing in the earth, mountains, and so forth, is entirely dissimilar to those various configurations.

It is logical that one proceeds by means of valid cognition for the sake of establishing the probandum (sādhya) and the probans (sādhana) in accordance with that [inference], based on the latent impression (saṃskāra) produced by the observation of pervasion (vyāpti), which is preceded by the apprehension of a similarity between real entities (vastu). However, it is not the case that "possessing parts" (sāvayavatva) is [established] by relying merely on the generality of the word. As Dharmakīrti said:
That which is established as being endowed with an arrangement and so forth, and which follows the presence or absence of a presiding agent, is that from which [the agent] is inferred.
Even when a difference between entities is established, an inference based on the identity of words for things that are not identical is improper,
just as one would not infer fire from a white substance.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, since Valabhī and other such things are included within the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*), they cannot serve as valid examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). Nor is it reasonable to postulate another cause called Īśvara while setting aside an observed cause. For if that were the case, the relationship between cause and effect would collapse everywhere. As it has been stated:

"When X exists, Y necessarily comes to be; if one were to postulate something else as the cause of that [Y], there would be an infinite regress of causes in every case. Furthermore, it is not reasonable to accept a specific deity who is a creator without a body. Regarding him...

Because it is impossible for the world to accomplish its characteristic effects [if it were bodiless]. As it has been said: "Since every effect is always pervaded by an agent endowed with a body, it follows that because the world is an effect, its creator must possess a body."
Consequently, the probans "being an effect" (kāryatva) proves the opposite of the nature of Dharma.

Furthermore, [the opponent argues] that because [the Lord] possesses a body, like ourselves and others, he is subject to birth and dissolution; therefore, his body must be either self-created or created by another agent. If it were self-created, was he possessed of a body at the time of creation, or was he bodiless?
If [the agent] is devoid of body and senses, it has already been stated that no effect whatsoever is ever observed in such a case.
If, on the other hand, he possesses a body and creates a body, then by what was that body of his itself produced?
Whether it were created by himself or created by another—
1. This means the essential nature of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
Alternatively, because of the existence of such subverting arguments (*bādhaka*) as infinite regress (*anavasthā*), no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes it is tenable.
Dīpikā: Thus, having established in general that the deity is a mere word,
there is no lack of evidence for the existence of its specific instance known as Īśvara.

He states "it is said" by means of the passage beginning with "that which establishes it," and so forth. Regarding the passage beginning with "not indeed," he first states that God is not an object of perception by means of the passage beginning with "by way of being immediate," and so forth, as well as the passage beginning with "for not," citing what they have said:
"When there is contact [of the senses], the arising of cognition for a person is the cause of perception."

"Because it is the apprehension of what is present," and so forth. With the words "Now," etc., the perception of the yogin is raised as a possible means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He refutes this with the words "That is not so," etc.; since there is an absence of any means of valid cognition, the yogin himself is not even established. How much less, then, can God be established by his perception? [The opponent then presents] the inference for the existence of God:

He raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*) and so forth, [arguing] that [the scripture] would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is because Bharadvāja and others have not mastered the treatises on established tenets (*siddhānta-śāstra*). According to the view of the Paurāṇikas, it is stated [in reference] to the very body of the Lord (*īśvara*); [this is expressed in the passage] beginning with "of that too" (*tasyāpi*) and so forth. He states the sublation (*bādhā*) of that as well.

"‘This might be so,’ and so forth. In that regard, he states the sublation (*bādhā*) of the reason ‘because of having parts’ with the words ‘of atoms, sense-faculties, and so forth. ‘Your own admission’ means: for those such as you—the Sāṃkhyas and others—who maintain the non-eternality of atoms. In that case, by that very [reason], for them..."

If it is argued that [the world] possesses the nature of being an effect, we say no; for it can also be stated that atoms are eternal because they are substances devoid of parts, like the self (*ātman*), and so forth. Since, for this very reason, the fact that the worlds are effects is unestablished, their being preceded by a creator is also refuted. Now, regarding the world...
Having accepted [the position] that it is an effect, he states the refutation beginning with "Furthermore," and so forth. The commentary:
Now, it may be argued that there exists a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) characterized as scripture (āgama), which is [in the form of] a sentence.
Because it is observed that for one who proceeds on the basis of that which ascertains an object absolutely beyond the senses, there is the attainment of the intended goal;
this is the meaning of "of inference" (anumānasya) as well.
Regarding this, they say: "The meaning [of the scripture]—that the eyes, marks, and so forth are hidden from men—is shown by the śāstra. To refute this very point, he says:
"That statement is established otherwise."
Wherein are the worldly sayings virtuous? || 9 ||

As sung in the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and other texts—for instance, in the Mahābhārata and elsewhere—the venerable sage Vyāsa has said: "O dear one, that radiant Śiva shines forth through his grace; even among the gods, including Indra and the rest, it is his sovereignty alone that is proclaimed. Go for refuge to him, the primordial God of gods."

"Bhuvaneśvara," and so forth; even in the Śruti: "The Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants—the Rudra who has entered all worlds—to that Rudra let there be obeisance. Likewise: "We worship Tryambaka," and so forth.
This [objection] is established otherwise; for here, upon careful consideration of the preceding and following context, [it is seen that...]

The meaning of a sentence is not produced merely by what has been heard; rather, those whose intellects are deceived by mere cognition cultivate the conviction that it is so. For example, in the case of the statement, "Eat poison, but eat at another's house," there is an apparent permission for eating poison.

Even though it is heard [in the text], it is not the meaning of the sentence; rather, the intended purport (tātparya) is precisely the prohibition against eating at the house of an adversary. Likewise, in the *Mahābhārata* and other works, through the medium of narratives, the pacification of enemies by one who is agitated and desirous of victory occurs without obstacle; and for the Kṣatriyas as well—

"The performance of one's own duty leads to prosperity"— this is the meaning. In the Śruti, however, the remainder is that the words of the mantras and arthavādas constitute a statement (*vākya*) that makes known a specific excellence of the action to be performed (*kāryātiśaya*).

Since the activity of those [who lack direct experience] is a means for generating faith and various types of sacrificial knowledge, it does not possess objective reality in its own nature; thus, mere verbal description does not establish the existence of a specific deity. As they have said: "The cognition produced by hymns of praise is a delusion..."

"A word, when its prior and subsequent context is not considered, produces a different understanding. Now, there exists a well-established consensus proven by the entire world that cannot be denied: for every person here, from the learned down to the infant, proceeds impelled by the command of the Supreme Lord's will. Thus, one who says "destiny alone is the cause" [is refuted].

And it is indeed seen. Furthermore, various narratives composed concerning the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the subduing of Kāla, the burning of Madana, the slaying of Andhaka, the conquest of the three worlds, and so forth, are found being read, recounted, and heard by many. With reference to these, here—
Human beings follow a course of action that involves hardships such as yoga, ritual observances, recitation, and austerity;
they do so because of the worldly saying, "There are specific deities," and so forth—
a mere popular report propagated by foolish people who have not reflected upon the sequence of what precedes and follows.

O, alas! Desiring to establish the reality of a thing based on the fact that it has been repeatedly proven to be inconsistent, you have indeed fallen into a state of mere wretchedness. If, on the other hand, this is a report set in motion by a trustworthy person, then it is simply scripture (*āgama*). And by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is his trustworthiness established?
Furthermore, the establishment of that [deity] would depend on the authority of the scripture promulgated by him, and the authority of the scripture would depend on the establishment of that [deity];

thus, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). If, however, the scripture were eternal, its authority would apply only to what is to be accomplished (*kārya*) and not to what is already established (*siddha*); therefore, the specific deity you favor cannot be established by any means whatsoever. (9)

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: He states the doubt in order to explain that the statement is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*). "Now it is said" (*athocyate*) means that the answer is stated by this portion of the sūtra. "This very [point]" (*etadeva*), etc. [is the response].

The phrase "sung in the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth" is intended to refer to the general category of statements that incite action, while "even in the Śruti" is intended to refer to specific instances. To refute both types of statements, he explains that they are established otherwise (anyathāsiddha), saying: "This very [scriptural authority] is established otherwise. This is because the Vedic injunctions (codanā) pertain exclusively to matters that are to be accomplished (kārya).

The intended meaning is "validity. He establishes that very point with the words "for here," and so forth. [Objection: In that case, there would follow the consequence of invalidity for sentences such as the *arthavādas* in the Veda. To this he replies with the words "but in the Śruti," and so forth.
Now, since comparison (*upamāna*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) are included within inference (*anumāna*), setting those aside, there are worldly sayings (*lokavāda*).

In order to explain where the virtuous are, he raises an objection based on the Purāṇic view regarding the establishment of God through the authority of tradition (*itihāsa*), beginning with the words "Now, [the existence of God] is established for all the world," and so forth. This means that he states the reply. He cites that very fragment of the Sūtra:

He explains [the passage] beginning with "not having reflected," and so forth. The sense is that the validity of tradition (*aitihya*) is not possible, because deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed. Now, one might object: "No deviation is seen in a report that has been set in motion by a reliable person. To this he raises the doubt beginning with "Now" (*atha*), and here too he states the refutation beginning with "Then" (*tarhi*). As for scripture (*āgama*), however...

"This very thing is called a defect. Furthermore, the authorship of those respective sentences is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus he says, "and reliability," etc., referring to that author of the scripture. Now, one might object:
"In the Veda it is stated that there exists the *Raudrī Saṃhitā*, and Rudra is the deity to be addressed"; to this he replies: "in the case of eternality..."
"Tvityādi" and so forth; and this has been stated previously. || 9 ||
Commentary: Having thus related the words spoken by Śakra, the sage Hārīta addressed his own disciples with these words of his own.
Thus, like the ocean driven by the tide of the waters of the words of one who lacks mastery, he [was overwhelmed];
"from where is the authority?"— this is a variation in the reading.
Even by Śakra, the mountain of their intellect did not waver, owing to its weight of essential substance.

In this sequence, although the mountains of the intellect belonging to Bharadvāja and others were impelled and urged by the surging tide of their waters— the words refuting the existence of Īśvara— following the downward path, they did not [submerge] because of their solidity and weight.
He did not waver (*cacāla*) nor tremble (*cakampe*). By whom was he impelled? The text says: by Śakra, as if by the ocean.

Just as the ocean, though struck forcefully by the waves of water, does not move from its own foundation because it is the "shore-mountain" (*velācala*), so too the sage’s intellect—conceived as a mountain due to its common characteristics such as having a sharp peak—did not [move] from its own steadfastness.
He moved forth. || 10 ||

The *Dīpikā* introduces the sūtra beginning with "it is not independent" (*anīśa*) and so forth, stating: "Thus [is] the speech of Śakra," and so on, because of its essence and its weight. The essence of the intellect (*buddhi*) is its capacity to grasp subtle objects; its weight is...
And stability; the meaning is: the non-abandonment of an object once it has been grasped. || 10 ||
Commentary: Thereupon, they spoke this again to Indra:
"Never [is there a perception] of the form of a deity..."
Like the bodies of ourselves and others;
therefore, that [example] is not a valid illustration because it is endowed with distinguished sovereignty. || 11 ||
1. "The apprehension and grasping of objects" is the reading [preferred].

The gradation of the yoga of sovereign power (vibhūti) is observed to reside in ordinary persons possessing bodies that are within the range of vision for people like us; however, this is not seen in one whose form is invisible.

Since it infers that a particular deity possesses the perfection of sovereign powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and so forth, how can you consider the simultaneous presence in multiple locations produced by the power of *prākāmya* (irresistible will) to be impossible? For the form of a deity is never— unlike the bodies of those like us— subject to the ripening of afflictions and karma, nor is it non-pervasive.

Or rather, because He is endowed with a distinguished sovereignty capable of effecting the creation, maintenance, and destruction of ourselves and others by mere will; for His corporeality, arising from the protection of unconscious atoms, is indeed distinct from the corporeality of ourselves and others. And therefore—

The reason (hetu) termed "corporeality" (*mūrtatva*), which was adduced to refute [the opponent's claim of] simultaneous presence in multiple locations, is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*). Furthermore, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is untenable because the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is unestablished;
for here, the property to be proven is characterized by the non-presence in multiple locations at the same time in its entirety.

It is not non-existent because, even in the present day, it is not impossible for those such as ourselves who possess physical bodies— even while existing in the midst of this world— to simultaneously be present in many locations through the excellence of their attainments such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and so forth;
and this is even more so in the case of the Supreme Lord, who possesses unsurpassed and complete excellence.

For those who are dogmatically attached to their own philosophical systems, a delusion of false conceptual constructions enters regarding the creation of the world— polluted by such examples as that of the potter and so forth— as to how much [the creator] there is, what his basis is, and what his instruments are. And thus it has been said:
By Siddhacūḍāmaṇi: "What is his desire? What is his body? Indeed, what is his means? What is the support of the three worlds? What does the Creator create, and what is the material cause?"
While Your sovereign power is beyond the reach of logic, this faulty reasoning— ill-placed and out of its time— only serves to silence the intellect of some and delude the world.

Thus it is said. And just as the possibility of a specific bodiless deity is sublated by its impossibility, so we shall explain in the section on Īśvara. Even though he is propounded in various ways, he will not serve as a purpose for those skilled in refuting him. As it has been said:
King Ajātaśatru Utkaladeva said:
"Even that which is brilliantly illuminated and established by a thousand logical arguments does not attain success for those of deluded minds."
"Even though Maheśvara stands in the palm of his hand, the excellent jewel of one struck by fate flees away. (11)
The *Dīpikā* states:
"By the words 'never' (*na jātu*), he explains the connection to the Sūtra; thus, etc.
Herein lies the intention of the proponents of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*): if it is admitted that the deity is merely sound (*śabdamātra*).

In such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," even a result consisting of heaven and the like would be a mere word, because it is not established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Now, if it is argued that the word "heaven" refers to a specific object because it is well-known from the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth; [the response follows:]...

It is said that [the word] denotes [the deity] as its fruit; since this is the same here as well, the distinctness of the deity from the word is established. And therefore, regarding the deity's distinctness from the word, there arise these alternatives: is she embodied, unembodied, both, or neither?

The refutation of the objections raised by the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) regarding the latter two positions is achieved through their non-acceptance. He demonstrates that the refutation of the objection stated against having a physical body— namely, the impossibility of being present in multiple locations simultaneously— is expressed by the words beginning with "na jātu" (never indeed), as well as by the passage beginning with "vibhūtiyogatāratamyam" (the gradation of the possession of [divine] powers).

"Endowed with an excellence of afflictions, karma, and maturation" means that the bodies of deities such as Brahmā and Indra are not, like those of ourselves and others, abounding in suffering and non-pervasive; rather, they possess the sovereign powers (aiśvarya) such as atomization (aṇimā) up to the limit of their own respective offices. "By mere will" [means...]

Regarding the power of irresistible will (*prākāmya-śakti*), as it has been said: "Having created numerous bodies for himself by means of his own [will], the yogin enjoys thousands of women simultaneously through the power of irresistible will. For corporeality (*mūrtatva*) arises from the protection of the coagulated atoms (*mūrcchita-aṇu*). That is, of the atoms—meaning the elements—which are coagulated, that is, abounding in ignorance.
