"Because of protection" (*trāṇāt*) is an elliptical expression meaning "because of performing [actions] such as maintaining [the world]"; since the powers beginning with *aṇimā* arise from the body consisting of the effects and instruments [of the senses], it is precisely therein that these powers and their effects, such as creation and so forth, are superposed. As it is said in the third [chapter] of the *Mataṅga*:

Sovereignty, consisting of the powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth, is established through its effects; the five qualities beginning with *prāpti* are born from the instruments (*karaṇa*) of the yogins.

Regarding the phrase "of the yogins": it should not be argued that yogins are unestablished for us, for it is heard in scripture: "Having made the Self the lower fire-drill and the *praṇava* the upper fire-drill..."

"By the practice of churning with knowledge, one may see the God as if hidden. For this very reason, the existence of the deity is established even through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of yogis. Having thus established the general existence of the deity, he shows its specific form, known as Īśvara, with the words "And not," etc., [even] in the state of being bodiless.

Because the deity possesses immeasurable power independent of a physical body, it is the actualizer of results. Therefore, being inseparable from the word, the deity manifests its presence in various instances; however, the word alone, being insentient, is not capable of bestowing fruits and the like, nor is karma, because of its inertness, [capable of acting] without a presiding agent.

We shall explain later that [an action] does not produce a result without [an auxiliary cause]. As for what was stated—that the creation of the world is not possible if God is bodiless—the author replies: "And just as the existence of a particular bodiless deity is sublated by its impossibility. The sense is that even for one who is bodiless, agency is observed in relation to the movement of one's own body and so forth.
The Teacher says that this will also be established later, stating, "We shall explain it in the same way in the section on Īśvara.

The implication is that the existence of Īśvara is thus established even by inference. We shall explain later how atoms possess the nature of being effects. [This refers to those for whom the world, up to the primary elements, has him as its cause.]
In the passage beginning with "paramāṇavaḥ" (atoms), etc. Thus [ends section] 11.
Commentary: He states that if one accepts the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) through such reasons and examples, this same logic would necessarily apply elsewhere as well.
Now, let it be that the same logic applies to the word "jar" as to the word "Indra," because both are words;
yet the word "jar" does not denote water.
The word "moon" does not shine [there]. || 12 ||

Indeed, you have asserted that the deity is merely sound; therefore, since a deity distinct from sound is not admitted, this consequence follows: namely, the impossibility of a denoted object existing apart from its designator. Just as there is no other [denoted object] for words such as "Indra" [besides the sound itself].
The expressed meaning exists in this way because there is no distinction in their being "sound" (*śabdatva*); this same logic applies even to the case of a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth.
Yet, this is not tenable, because it contradicts experience. For instance, [the word] "jar" does not take up water;

rather, it is called a "jar" because it is capable of action (*ceṣṭate*) for the sake of purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*). Similarly, it is called "moon" (*candra*) because it gladdens (*candati*), delights, and shines. Thus...
According to the method of linguistic convention (*śabdavyutpatti*), since no denotable object exists apart from the word itself,

it would follow that the act of fetching water belongs to the word "jar" alone, and the act of delighting and so forth belongs to the word "moon" alone; yet this is not the case for these two words, but rather for their denoted objects.

It is observed that two things possessing the nature of a luminous disc—one with a broad base and belly, and the other [a reflection]—are both capable of performing their respective functional activities (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, there is no identity between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*).
Consequently, it is established that the deity is not the mere word, but rather that which is signified by it. || 12 ||

Dīpikā: Now, [the author] introduces the sūtra with the words "Let it be so" (*athāstvevam*), beginning with "And by such [reasons]" (*īdṛśābhyām ca*) and so forth, namely by these two reasons and examples: "because of having form (*mūrtatvāt*)" and "like ourselves and others" (*asmadādivat*).
The meaning is that even if one accepts that the deity is merely sound, there is still a contradiction with experience. || 12 ||
Commentary: Now, having restated the opponent's view that the sentence is established otherwise, he refutes it: "Now, [if] the sentence has another object..."
If [the word] *mastu* were to denote Śakra and so forth,
how could words such as "action," "form," and the like possess any meaningful significance? (13)

As for what you have stated— that the indicative marks (liṅga) of deities such as Śakra, found in passages beginning with "Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the golden one," are intent upon the explanatory portions (arthavāda) of mantras and do not convey their own literal meaning— let that be so. However, regarding those [passages] which are intent upon conveying their own primary meaning:

How could words for action, form, and so forth, when being heard, possess meaningfulness? In this regard, "action-words" (karmaśabda) are those that denote an activity, such as "he threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*) and others; "form-words" (*rūpaśabda*) and "genus-words" (*jātiśabda*) are likewise included. For example, in the injunction "one should sacrifice a white goat" (*śvetacchāgam ālabheta*), there is the word "white" (*śveta*).

Since there is no distinction in their being words between a term like "goat" which denotes a form and a term like "Śakra" which denotes a genus, and since it is impossible for them to correspond to their own literal forms, they would be meaningless. Consequently, the injunctive sentences (*codanāvākya*) would be ineffective. Or else:

If a sentence denoting Śakra and others were assumed to have a different referent, then those action-words referring to him— such as "Indra slew Vṛtra" and so forth— as well as words like "thousand-eyed" and "thunderbolt-handed," which denote his form and other attributes, [would become inconsistent].

How could words possess meaningfulness? Furthermore, the logic of the "half-old woman" (ardhajaratīya) cannot be established here, by which it might be claimed that only words of injunction possess correspondence with their own forms, while words such as "Indra" do not. || 13 ||

*Dīpikā*: Now, he states the connection for the sūtra beginning with "atha anyaviṣayam" (now, regarding another object), starting with the words "idānīm" (now) and so forth. For the word "tathāstu" (let it be so), insofar as it primarily conveys meaning for one who has already understood the relationship between words and their referents...

It is established for you as well. Therefore, since the cognition produced by those [words] would otherwise be untenable, the fact that words such as "Indra" correspond to their own literal forms (svarūpa) is indeed unavoidable; nevertheless, the meaning is that we speak while provisionally accepting this view.
Or rather, there is another explanation. But how, then, can statements such as "Eat poison" have a different purpose?
We say that this is because of the force of the subsequent statement, "Eat in the house of the teacher.
Thus, even by means of scripture (āgama), the existence of a specific deity is established. || 13 ||
Commentary: As for what was said— that "where are virtuous worldly sayings?"— that is incorrect,
because even every popular tradition is false.
Because it is rootless, it is not logical; if that [root] were absent, all activities of living beings would be destroyed. (14)

Even a groundless report, such as "a cart of molasses has overturned on the riverbank," is not necessarily false, because it may occasionally be corroborated. Therefore, the claim that "every report is untrue" is neither logical nor supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), provided that the report possesses a basis.

Because falsity is unestablished; and its root is scripture (*āgama*). Thus they say: "That which has attained renown through scripture is called 'the world' (*loka*). Now, if it were argued that a tradition devoid of a root is false, that too is incorrect, because if this were assumed, all activities of living beings [would likewise be false].

[Otherwise,] they would be contradicted. For everyone who desires what is beneficial or wishes to avoid what is harmful does not generally engage in worldly activities— whether those with visible results such as service or agriculture, or those with invisible results such as *iṣṭāpūrta* sacrifices— by first establishing and prioritizing a formal system of epistemic instruments (*pramāṇa*),
but rather mostly by following the path of others.

One whose mind is permeated by mere rumor—what kind of root for that rumor must you seek? If it is its long-standing existence and its being proclaimed by many people, then that is indeed appropriate;
otherwise, it would not even be a rumor. That being the case, it cannot be false.

Even though [this tradition] has been renowned among many people for a very long time, why is its origin investigated in such a manner? Rather, this is an investigation of scripture (*āgama*) itself; it is not an inquiry into popular rumor. And it is not as you suggest, because even by you, that which is practiced by the virtuous is held to be distinct from scripture in the form of *śruti*.

Since worldly convention, known as the conduct of the cultured (*śiṣṭācāra*), is accepted as being rooted in *dharma*, enough with this hostility toward it. Thus, by means of popular tradition together with its foundation, the existence of a specific deity called Īśvara has been established.
Upon seeing Hara, the sage Upamanyu became free from anger. Is this indeed not universally known? For it is well known how the sage Upamanyu was set in motion by the Supreme Lord.
(The word "pravartata" is understood as the remainder of the sense.)
He was favored by the granting of a boon; and thus, in the Anuśāsana Parva of the Mahābhārata, the words of the venerable sage Vyāsa regarding Upamanyu are shown:
"The Lord Īśvara Śaṅkara, having arrived here, spoke with a smile."
"O child Upamanyu, I am pleased; behold me, O best of sages!
You are firm in devotion, O brahmin-sage, and you have been tested by me.
Because of this devotion of yours, my son, I am exceedingly pleased."

"Therefore, I shall grant all the boons that reside in your mind. To this it is replied: "This statement by Upamanyu was spoken for the purpose of describing his own power; for what proof is there here that he was indeed favored by the Blessed One? That is incorrect, because how [could that have been] for him...

How could the word of one whose command the ocean obeys—indeed, the Ocean of Milk, visible to the eyes of all the sages, being under his control—possibly be false? This is the intention: "I have obtained a boon from the Supreme Lord."

If his speaking of falsehood were to occur now, it would be so unless the subjugation of the Ocean of Milk had been witnessed by a multitude of eminent sages. Furthermore, if even those words that are consistent with reality were false,
then no word whatsoever could be true— especially not those of those whose passion and hatred have been stilled.

If you admit that even the sages—who have directly perceived the facts of the past and the future—are capable of speaking falsely, then Manu and the others are also rendered as those to whom you have paid the sacrificial fee (dattadakṣiṇā)! Oh, what skill in your philosophical vision!
Furthermore: "One who is ensnared by the noose that emits rows of poisonous flames..."
Having been released by her husband with a roar of "huṃ," Śveta was seen by the crowds of people.
Śveta was rendered helpless by a noose of venomous serpents, terrifying due to the successive hurling of flames from poisonous fire;
yet he was liberated by his protector— the Supreme Lord, whose nature is to protect— who, uttering a mere *huṃ* sound,
reduced that noose to ashes with the fire of his wrath— thus [it was done] repeatedly and without interval.

It has been seen by people of our own kind, as well as by sages and others; and even regarding this matter, if there is no confidence in the tradition established by the gods who perceive the three times with stainless vision, then it must be said that you do not tolerate scripture at all. And such being the case, even the Śruti [is rejected] by you, who are so intolerant.

Since they look upon his face with trembling fear out of wretchedness because they have not attained validity, let this extreme rashness be abandoned out of compassion for them. [Objection: But surely, since the defects that cause falsity reside in the agent, and since the scripture is eternal due to its being uncreated, therefore, for the sake of its validity—
What kind of mockery is this? It is nothing at all; rather, we do not perceive any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for ascertaining the absence of an author.

On the contrary, because it possesses a composition—just like the sentence beginning with "Having paid homage to Svayambhū"—we infer that it is invariably connected to the activity of an author. Enough of this; let us return to the subject at hand.

*Dīpikā*: Regarding the phrase "in the case of *iṣṭāpūrta* and so forth": *iṣṭa* refers to that which is obtained through gifts in sacrifices; *pūrta* refers to such things as wells and tanks. Regarding the phrase "by you" and so forth: "The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the Smṛtis and the conduct of those who know it."

It has been stated [that this is] "with its root," meaning by way of worldly tradition established through the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth. He demonstrates that very fact of having a root with the words "for as... and so on. [The objection is: "In that case, you do not even tolerate scripture (āgama). The word "you" (bhavān) is to be supplied. The sense is that [scripture is accepted] because the Āgamas were composed by gods and others.
In this context, he demonstrates that the Vedas (*śrutis*) also possess authority because they were composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*).
Thus, beginning with the words "And so," the opponent who raises the objection says, "But surely," and so forth. The Teacher says, "No one at all";
the meaning is that this is not intended as a derisive joke. For this very reason, he speaks according to the facts, beginning with "But rather," and so forth.
He introduces the subsequent sūtra with the words: "We follow the subject at hand. || 14 ||
Thus, as they were delighted by the praise of Hara during the course of their discourse,
their voices became choked with tears.
Upon seeing this, Hari became pleased.

Having seen Bharadvāja and the others, whose voices were indistinct due to the influence of bliss arising from the joy of praising the Supreme Lord who had arrived as the Prastāva, Indra addressed them further.
"Thus he was gratified," said the sage Hārīta to his own disciples. || 15 ||
Dīpikā:
"He was pleased with them" means that, perceiving them to have been permeated by the intense power (tīvra-śakti), he set his mind upon bestowing grace upon them. || 15 ||
The wielder of the thunderbolt, the god Śatakratu, revealed his own form,
resembling the rising sun.
Being praised by the hosts of Maruts. || 16 ||

Commentary: The god Vajrapāṇi, Śatakratu, manifested his own form, which was intensely radiant and being praised by hosts of gods. He is called "Vajrī" (the wielder of the thunderbolt) and "Śatakratu" (the performer of a hundred sacrifices) because of his possession of an extraordinary intensity of splendor.

Indeed, these two qualifications of the thunderbolt are its very nature: its wondrous luminosity, and its state of possessing a vast mass of radiance produced by the power of the merit generated from being the performer of a hundred sacrifices. || 16 ||

Dīpikā: There are two meanings for the rule beginning with *svaṃ rūpam*. Of these, one has already been demonstrated by the Teacher; the other is now being demonstrated. [The word] *śatakratuḥ* refers to the Teacher who has performed infinite Śaiva sacrifices (*kratu*).

This is the meaning. Since others lack the qualification for the instruction of the scriptures and so forth, [the subject] is the Lord of the Thirty-three (Indra), who was introduced in the preceding sūtra. The term "Vajrī" (the Wielder of the Thunderbolt) is an elliptical designation; having become characterized by such attributes as holding a vajra in hand and possessing a thousand eyes, and so on.

With the departure of the darkness of impurity, [the Lord], who resembles the rising sun and is being praised by the hosts of Maruts, Brahmā, and others, including the Vidyeśvaras, manifested His own innate and non-accidental nature, which consists of omniscience and omnipotence, to Bharadvāja and the others.
This is what is meant: immediately after the certainty of the descent of power (śaktipāta),

the Lord of the Gods, having manifested his own body as the basis for his authority, removes their bondage of impurity (mala) and the rest through the activity of the Self known as initiation (dīkṣā), and [bestows] the state of Śiva.
"It makes [the soul] manifest. But if this were so, would it not follow that the body would fall immediately?

No, because in the initiation for liberation while still in an impure womb (*asadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*), that [falling of the body] is impossible due to the obstruction of the experience of the fruits of karma that has already begun to bear fruit (*prārabdhakāryakarman*).
As it is said in the *Kiraṇatantra*: "For that by which this [body exists] is indeed through experience. And regarding this point:

The Master [Vācaspati Miśra] has disregarded this because it is established by implication through the subsequent sūtra, which sets forth salutation and praise, and because it would otherwise be impossible for the instruction of the treatise to have occurred. || 16 ||
Bowing down, they praised him with Ṛg verses, Yajus formulas, and Sāman chants.
He said, "Let your desire be stated."
For he is indeed the most excellent in the worlds. || 17 ||
They chose the auspicious knowledge,
saying, "Let it be heard! He replied, "But let there be only one questioner for me."
Agreed upon by all the listeners. || 18 ||

Commentary: Bharadvāja and the others, bowing low, praised Indra—who had manifested his true form—with Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman verses. He, the most excellent boon-granter in all the worlds, said: "Let a boon be requested by you."
He said to them; having been addressed thus, they chose the supreme Lord’s knowledge and scripture.
To those who requested the instruction of that knowledge, he spoke this reply:
"But let only one among you, who is approved by all the people listening here, [come forward]."
"Let him be the questioner regarding matters not yet mentioned as the occasion arises; and let all of you listen as well. (17–18)
The *Dīpikā* [comments]:

For this very reason, it says, "the humble and virtuous ones praised him. And he [Śiva], who is the foremost of the entire world, is the lord of all realms; thus he explains [the word] "kāma" as "let a boon be requested by you. Let a boon be entreated from you.
Or rather, that Indra is the most excellent boon; the meaning is that you should request it from him.

"The knowledge of the Supreme Lord" (pārameśvaraṃ jñānam) refers to that which is more exalted because it was imparted by the Supreme Lord, and not something such as the Vāmā-kalā and so forth. (17–18)
Commentary: When Śakra, the Blessed One, had spoken thus,
then among them, Bharadvāja—
The Blessed One became the leader.
Eloquent and bold, he questioned the one honored by the gods in accordance with what is right.

Immediately thereafter, from among them, the sage Bharadvāja was the most eloquent due to his possession of qualities such as sovereignty and the like, and because he was endowed with speech praised for its refinement through the study of various scriptures; furthermore, he was bold, being free from any lack of skill or hesitation when the occasion for questioning arose.
"In accordance with logic" means by way of reasoning, by the method appropriate for a disciple, and by formulating a prima facie argument supported by logical arguments;
thus he questioned Indra. || 19 ||
*Dīpikā*:
He states the connection of the sūtra beginning with "atha" (now) with the words "evam" (thus), etc., [explaining] "due to the possession of qualities such as sovereignty," as they have said:
"Of complete sovereignty, heroism, fame, prosperity, and dispassion..."

"Consciousness (bodha) is said to be the sixfold Bhaga"—this is the Śruti. By the phrase "due to the absence of lack of skill, non-comprehension, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes [faults] such as lack of concentration. "By the method appropriate for a disciple" refers to [qualities] such as humility; as stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "Well-disciplined and with a well-peaceful mind, neither too far away nor too close," and so on.

Regarding what was stated beginning with "established by reasoning," students should inquire about that very point again and again for the sake of clarification, whenever doubt arises, and so forth. || 19 ||
The commentary says: What did he ask? It says:
"How [did this come] from Maheśvara?"
The supreme knowledge has arrived;
moreover, having established it within his mind, the Blessed One fashioned this.

Regarding this knowledge which the Blessed One has begun to teach to us: since it yields a fruit far superior to other forms of knowledge, it is the most excellent knowledge. How, then, has it issued forth from Maheśvara—Śiva, who is of a tranquil nature and devoid of parts? For knowledge is indeed of two kinds.
It consists of the nature of consciousness and the nature of sound; that nature of consciousness, having ascended onto the form of sound, operates upon objects.

In this regard, one might first ask: how has this nature of consciousness, originating from the Supreme Lord, come to possess such [extent], and how, having attained the form of sound, has it become divided into so many different varieties? Furthermore, having reflected upon this...
The Blessed One did this; for no agent is ever seen performing any action without having a purpose in mind. The meaning is: what was the reason for that Blessed One to perform this? || 20 ||
The *Dīpikā* explains the term "supreme state" (*uttamapada*) with the words "from other cognitions," and so forth; for,
preceded by a demonstration of the state attainable through all other scriptures, it brings about the realization of meanings not previously understood.

It is the embodiment of valid cognition (*pramāṇabhūta*). As they say: "Valid cognition is that which apprehends an object not yet apprehended. Furthermore, the fruit—consisting of perfection and liberation—is characterized by excellence due to its purity and its non-return [to saṃsāra]. As he will state in the *Śiva-sūtra*: "The perfected one shines at the head of others; the liberated one, the best of men, enters [the supreme state] in creation and does not go downward."
The phrase "attaining the nature of sound" means that it attains the state of being manifest to a cognition whose essence is sound.
This is the sense of the question here: cognition is indeed twofold—having the form of pure awareness (*avabodha*) and having the form of sound (*śabda*).
Even that which has the form of pure awareness functions only when mounted upon the form of sound; therefore, it is that [cognition] which has the form of sound.

How could [this state] have been attained by the Vidyeśvaras and others from Śiva, who is devoid of cause and effect? Furthermore, with what purpose in mind did He compose this scripture? This very point is the answer here:
knowledge, which consists of pure awakening, exists at the very commencement of creation in the form of experience (bhoga) and liberation (mokṣa).

For the sake of accomplishing the goals of human existence, the Supreme Lord first manifested [the knowledge] in the form of sound (*nāda*), and subsequently, having entered the state of a qualified teacher, taught it to the Vidyeśvaras and others as it was established in the form of words. Furthermore, it has already been stated previously that this teaching at the beginning of creation is accomplished by mere volition (*saṅkalpa*).
Commentary: Here is the reply: At the time of creation, Maheśāna...
For the sake of accomplishing the goals of human existence, he bestows pure knowledge characterized by the five streams. || 21 ||

At the beginning of creation, for the sake of accomplishing the goals of human existence— consisting of enjoyment and liberation— the Supreme Lord [emanated] as the "Immaculate" (Vimala), because it first issued forth in the form of *nāda* from the nature of pure consciousness, and thus its distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) were not yet grasped.
But from the other side, it is characterized by the five streams—above, east, south, west, and north—which extend outwards on all sides;

thus, through the vision of the form of Sadāśiva, knowledge is brought to the state of being the very essence of perception, and this is the sequence. Furthermore, the purpose has been described as that which was previously questioned. || 21 ||

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: "By way of being the nature of resonance (*nāda*) within the self that is awakening. [It says] "But the supreme," and so forth; and that knowledge, because it consists of the grasping of the five mantras and because it is manifested as the body of Śiva which consists of the five mantras.

It has been stated that [the Lord] is characterized by the five currents; however, it is not logical to accept the existence of a *bindu*-body for the Lord here, as is the case for the Vidyeśvaras and others,
because that would entail the consequence of his being non-supreme due to being subject to origination and dissolution, and because it would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress.
We shall explain [this]. || 21 ||
Furthermore:
"And from the multitude of expressive words residing therein,
[arise] the Great Lords who are the objects of expression."
And he [taught] mantras numbering seventy million on the supreme path.

The eight Vidyeśvaras, Ananta and the others, who are the objects denoted by the group of mantras— which constitute the collection of expressive words situated within the knowledge to be described in the section on the extraction of mantras (mantroddhāra)—
are likewise [to be understood] because the impure path belonging to Māyā has not yet manifested at that time.

The connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: the Supreme Lord ordains the mantras, numbering seventy million, which have taken their station in the world of Śuddhavidyā. Although time is generally uniform, because the first instrument [of action] is intended here, the meaning is that he "ordained" them at the time of creation; or else, he acts in this manner at every time of re-creation.

It is precisely their state of being present. In that regard, for the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras), the instrument (*karaṇa*) is called the manifestation of their own sovereign power through union with powers such as Vāmā;
for the mantras, however, it is the state of having vision and action made manifest through the removal of veils. For both of these, [this occurs] from the Supreme Lord.

The awakening of the powers of knowledge and action is what should be understood here; it is not, however, a process of purification like that of a liberated soul (muktāṇu), because this liberation is distinct from that due to the presence of the impurity of office (adhikāramala), as we shall explain later. || 22 ||
*Dīpikā*: Now, in order to demonstrate the sequence of instruction, he says "mantroddhāra," etc., stating that the sequence of grace (*anugrahakrama*) follows from that [sequence of instruction].
"Because it possesses the nature of reflecting (*manana*) and protecting (*trāṇa*), it is called 'mantra'—this being the established rule.
According to this principle, the word *mantra* here applies primarily to Śiva, Śakti, and those favored by them; however, it is used figuratively [in other cases].

He says that [the power] operates within the expressive words: "those which are the objects of expression (vācya) of the collection of expressive [words], namely the group of mantras," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the eight Lords of Knowledge" (vidyeśas), this is possible both in the category of the individual soul (aṇupakṣa) and in the categories of Power (śaktipakṣa) and Śambhu.
And it has been said:
"The Śruti declares that 'Śiva is the mantra for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world';
thus, that power which is gracious has attained the state of being a mantra here.
For this very reason, together with Śiva and Śakti, who are distinguished by the differences of their respective substrates and limiting adjuncts (upādhi)...
There are twenty-four [deities]. Even the mantras, numbering seventy million, possess these same three forms. As it has been said:
"The supreme lords of mantras are declared to be twenty-four;
likewise, there are other millions of mantras consisting of the Āṇava, Śāmbhava, and Śākta [powers]."
And he says that these mantras are indeed pure and not impure, with the words "of the Māyeya.
It is also stated in the venerable *Raurava*:
"Other mantras, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and so forth, belong to Pradhāna and are inferior."
"Those consisting of *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* [qualities] abide in the midst of *sañjana* and *stenḍa*.
Regarding this, he states "they ordain" (*vidhatta*) and so forth, indicating that the connection with the preceding action must be supplied here.
He further explains that their ordainment occurs at the very beginning of creation, which is indicated here as being in the present tense.

The meaning of "even though there is a commonality of time," and so forth, is that although the instrument (karaṇa) of creation is connected to all three times, since the first [time] is intended here, a transposition of the verbal suffix (lakāra-vyatyaya) must be made. He states another resolution with the words "or at the time of each dissolution" (pratisargakālam), and asks: "But how is the instrument possible for these [entities], given their eternity? He replies:
Regarding the passage beginning with "there," for this very reason the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) perform the fivefold activity. As it is stated in the *Raurava*:

"They effect maintenance, protection, bestowal, manifestation, and grace. Furthermore, we shall explain that mantras are also the cause of grace. He states that grace belongs specifically to these [beings] who are liberated through pure knowledge (vijñānakevalins):

"By the removal of obstructions" means by the removal of impurities (*mala*). If this is so, then because they have attained equality with Śiva, they must have become formless; to this he replies with the words "of both," and so forth. [He states that] they do not possess equality with Śiva because a portion of the impurity pertaining to their office (*adhikāra-mala*) remains. || 22 ||
Commentary: Having thus described the Mantramaheshvaras and the Mantras, he speaks in order to describe the Mantreshvaras:
"And another [group] consisting of eighteen more..."
An umbrella belongs to those who hold office over Māyā,
as well as to the Lords of Mantra (mantreśvara), whose splendor is equal to that of the Lord situated on the upper path.

Regarding those who hold authority over *māyā*— the *māyādhikāriṇaḥ*— the connection with the preceding [text] is that one hundred and eight [deities] are ordained for them, whose status is equal to the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) residing on the higher Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*). Among them, the eight *maṇḍalinaḥ* will be described [later].
The meaning is that the eight [deities] beginning with Krodha, the hundred Śatarudras who support the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
and Śrīkaṇṭha and Vīrabhadra— thus one hundred and eighteen— are appointed by Śiva to the status of Mantreśvara, as previously described. || 23 ||

The *Dīpikā* states that there is grace for all [beings] by means of their status as subordinate Mantreśvaras, beginning with the words "those who hold authority over Māyā" and so forth. For those [who arise] from Śiva himself...

He states that because of the manifestation of omniscience and other qualities, even though they possess all [powers], there is no subjection to bonds (pāśavaśyatva) as there is for bound souls (paśus); thus he says: "of those whose abode is equal to that of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara) residing in the higher pure path (śuddhādhvan). As it has been said: "Even when conjoined with the limited powers (kalā), they are not subject to those powers, unlike the multitude of bound souls. For this very reason...
Because they are presided over by Śiva and Śakti, these too possess three forms, just as before. As it has been said:
"Thus, the supports of the Egg are indeed those headed by Vīrabhadra, namely Śrīkaṇṭha and Vīrabhadra."

And this Śrīkaṇṭha resides in the worlds situated above the principle of *guṇa*; he does not, however, dwell within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), because he is well-known as a disciple of Śiva. Nor is he included among the Vidyeśvaras, because he lacks the connection with *kalā* and the other [principles]. || 23 ||
Among those who are fit for accomplishment, the Blessed One makes himself manifest to them; therefore,
he reveals [the teachings] to others as well.
Whatever meaning is logically consistent [is to be accepted]. || 24 ||

Commentary: The Lord manifested as these Mantramaheśvaras, such as Ananta and others, and as these Mantreśvaras, such as Maṇḍalī and others; this refers to the knowledge introduced immediately above as "this."

He reveals it. Regarding this matter, he asks for what purpose he reveals it, and says: "To those who are fit"—meaning to those who, because their mental faculties (*añjana*) have reached maturity, desire the unsurpassed good (*niratiśaya-śreyaḥ*) for the sake of enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). "To others than these" means to those other than those worthy of this scripture, who, due to the immaturity of their mental faculties, [are not fit].

For those who follow the scriptures of the bound (paśu), whatever object is attainable through the systems of Kapila, Pāñcarātra, and so forth, is established as "correct" in accordance with their respective fitness; [the Lord] reveals that which is appropriate for them.
Furthermore, by presiding over the authors of those various scriptures, He brings about the revelation of each respective system through a traditional lineage.
"Perform [it]," so much is meant. || 24 ||

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: "In them, Ananta and the others," and so forth. Having thus favored these lords of the worlds (*viśveśvara*) and others, this knowledge was revealed to them; and having directly or indirectly presided over them through speech, [it was transmitted] to those who were fit.
He explains that the word "siddhis" (accomplishments) here is an elliptical expression, stating: "for the sake of enjoyment and for the sake of liberation. || 24 ||
Commentary: Now, he states what the name of this knowledge being taught to us is:
"This knowledge was vomited forth by Śiva."
Because it grants all desires, it is celebrated at great length by the lords of the lords of mantras as the "Kāmika" (the Wish-fulfilling). || 25 ||

This knowledge, which is the scripture, has issued forth from the Supreme Lord according to the sequence [he] proclaimed; it was taught in great detail through many divisions because there were numerous individual listeners— such as Skanda, the Goddess, and others— and because the teachers of mantras [taught] by way of the *Kāmika* [tantra], since it grants all desires (*kāmadatva*).
And it was taught by the Lords of Mantras, namely the Great Lords of Mantra (Mantramaheshvaras) such as Ananta and others. || 25 ||

The Dīpikā: Having thus established, by way of digression, the sequence of instruction concerning the object of all knowledge, [the author] now explains the knowledge to be taught to Bharadvāja and others, beginning with the words "the knowledge vomited forth by Śiva."
He says "then his" and so forth in order to specify [the subject]. || 25 ||
Having understood from them [the lineages], he states to whom, by how much text, and who gave it:
"Having understood from them, Dṛgjyoti..."
The Lord of Umā, whose intoxicated elephant licked [the offering] with his straight trunk,
gave it to me along with thousands of attendants equal in number to Bhava.
From those [sages] beginning with Ananta, the Lord Umāpati— the tree of Smara having been consumed by the flames of fire from his third eye— received it and,
condensing it into eleven thousand verses counted as *bhavas*, bestowed it upon me.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tebhyaḥ" (from them): immediately after [receiving it] from Ananta and the others, Umāpati obtained it from the god Ananta and bestowed it upon me; for he is renowned precisely as the disciple of Ananta. He states that the word *mada* refers to the Madana tree because it is the cause of intoxication (*mada*). || 26 ||
Therefore, I shall now— therein also omitting the detailed exposition—
speak with sūtras that express the essential meaning.
I shall explain the unconfused knowledge,
for the most part by means of what has already been stated.
The commentary: Even there, having discarded the extensive portions consisting of explanatory eulogies (*arthavāda*) and restatements (*anuvāda*),
[this work] is composed in a manner that is sometimes crowded with meanings expressed by others in abundance and sometimes with those of my own.
"Indra said to the sages, 'I shall declare the scripture of comprehensive knowledge'; thus Hārīta speaks to his own disciples. (27)
Thus ends the first chapter, the Introduction (*upodghāta-prakaraṇa*), in the *Mṛgendra-vṛtti* composed by Śrī Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, son of Śrī Bhaṭṭa Vidyākaṇṭha.

*Dīpikā*: In passages such as "In some places by my own [disciples]" (*kvacic cātmīyaiḥ*), which refer to the *Mahātantra* consisting of three subjects and four feet, the meaning is that I too possess the status of an author. If this is so, then here [in the *Tantrāloka*], by virtue of Bharadvāja being the speaker—

It is not the case that those who will be mentioned hereafter do not possess the status of being Supreme Lords (Pārameśvara). It is not so; for even in the present day, such a thing is observed in the composition of scriptures. The teachers maintain that the scripture was indeed composed by Śiva in the form of a dialogue consisting of prima facie arguments and their refutations, and that terms such as "Bharadvāja" were introduced into the questions by way of grace. || 27 ||
Thus ends the first chapter, the Introduction (*upodghāta-prakaraṇa*), in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā* composed by Aghoraśivārya.
Now begins the chapter on the Refutation of [Other Views regarding] Supreme Liberation (*paramokṣanirāsa-prakaraṇa*).
Then, free from beginningless impurities, the omniscient and omnipotent Lord [acts] upon the individual soul who was previously cast into a state of inversion.
He dispels the net of snares. || 1 ||
Commentary: The connection (*sambandha*), subject matter (*abhidheya*), and purpose (*prayojana*) have already been analyzed at the very beginning;
now, following this incidental discussion of the connection and so forth, the section known as the *Vidyāpāda* is commenced.

And in this scripture, there are three categories of entities known as the Lord (pati), the bound soul (paśu), and the fetter (pāśa). Because the bound souls lack autonomy and the fetters lack consciousness, the Lord—who is distinct from them—possesses the performance of the fivefold acts; his instruments, which consist of his own powers such as Māyā and the rest, as well as the action itself, are also included.

Initiation and its fruit consist of the attainment of supreme liberation (*parakaivalya*) through the rite known as "grace" (*anugraha*) for bound souls (*paśu*); this is what will be explained hereafter. This root aphorism contains that very meaning within it. In the phrase "free from beginningless impurity" (*anādimālāpeta*), the word "beginningless" (*anādi*) is an adverbial modifier, meaning "because it is beginningless."

The Supreme Lord is free from impurity and is pure by nature. Likewise, the multitude of liberated souls is beginningless and free from impurity, having had all its stains destroyed through His grace. Furthermore, being freed from beginningless impurity and having its innate impurities torn asunder, its power of vision and action (*dṛkkriyā*) is manifested by the Supreme Lord.
Because something remains to be accomplished, the class of Mantras and Mantreśvaras is joined with the impurity of office (*adhikāramala*) which has a beginning;

thus, by means of these three compounds, the category of the Lord (*pati*) is indicated here as being accompanied by both liberated souls (*muktāṇu*) and those such as the Vidyeśvaras. And for all three of these, there exists omniscience and omnipotence.

It exists. However, although liberated souls possess the capacity for perceiving all objects and acting upon them, their "removal" (apohana) consists solely in the power to cast off the net of bonds (pāśajāla). Therefore, because there is nothing further to be accomplished, they do not engage in activity; thus, through union with the supreme good within their own self, such is their state of Śiva-hood. This is the case for the Vidyeśvaras as well.
Because he is the cause for attaining the state of Śiva; because the Blessed Lord is engaged in bestowing grace upon all;

and because liberated souls lack such activity, while the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) are dependent on the Supreme Lord—[the author] says what the independent Blessed Lord does: "He removes the net of bonds from the individual soul."
Of that which possesses a threefold nature— consisting of the *vijñānākala*, the *pralayākala*, and the *sakala*—

as well as of each of the two types (*vijñānākala* and *pralayākala*) which are distinguished by the difference in their transformation due to the governance of the Lord’s power over residual impurities (*mala*),
and of the *sakala* who is bound by the three fetters; each of these is of two kinds.

By some means, through the exhaustion of karma, one becomes endowed with the pure creative power (*kalā*) and so forth; thus, for this very [liberated soul] which is of two kinds, each being further divided into the *videha* (bodiless) and *sadeha* (embodied), and for each of these subdivisions— whether devoid of the influence of impurity (*mala*) and so forth, or still possessed of it— [the following applies].

And thus, the connection is that the Supreme Lord removes the net of bonds (pāśajāla) for the eightfold self—which is divided in this way into many sub-divisions—as far as possible. And we shall explain everything regarding for whom and how He removes them in due course further on. To the question "Of what kind of individual soul (aṇu)? he says:

"Of one who has been previously displaced" means: of one who has been made dissimilar to the Supreme Lord, brought to a state of non-conformity with Him, impelled by Him, and joined to other bonds; that is, of one who has been displaced by those factors existing as causes—namely, beginningless impurity (*mala*), karma, *māyā*, the Supreme Lord, and the power of obstruction (*nirodhaśakti*)—as they apply respectively.

This is the meaning: due to impurity (*mala*), the power of obstruction (*nirodha-śakti*) of the Lord, and both existent and non-existent karmas, the individual soul (*aṇu*) possesses a state of non-Śiva-hood;

from that follows its connection with other forms of bondage. But upon the removal of those [obstructions], there is Śiva-hood. Thus, while these very [impurities] are the beginningless causes for the soul's dissimilarity to Śiva, Śiva himself possesses the power of unimpeded and unsurpassed causal efficiency regarding all objects.
Engaged in bestowing grace in accordance with [the disciple's] capacity, he removes the multitude of bonds (*pāśa*).
The word *apohati* is used because of the rule: "The root *as* (to throw) may optionally be substituted by *ūh* after a prefix.
Thus, because it indicates the meaning of the entire system (*tantra*), this is the root aphorism (*mūlasūtra*). And so it is here:

He will explain this at the occasion of the commentary: "That in which the great tree of the meaning of the Tantra is mounted like a seed, beginning with the root-sūtra 'Āḥ' and adorned by the word 'atha' and so forth. (1)

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: He recites the opening sūtra of the treatise beginning with "Now" (*atha*). If it is the case that the relationship (*sambandha*) and other factors must be stated at the commencement of a treatise, he says "the relationship," etc., and "manifested in them," etc.

The meaning is "those which were taught in the preceding section. Now, the word *atha* does not mean "after the statement of the connection and so forth," because it has no syntactical connection with the verb *vyapohati*. Nor does it serve as a marker of a new topic (*adhikāra*), since that purpose is already established by the very phrase "I shall explain the unconfused knowledge. How, then, is its meaning here? It is said:

The meaning is that immediately after the state of the bound soul (*bhavin*)—who has brought about the cessation of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) and is facing the exhaustion of his status as an agent—is reached, Śiva removes the net of bonds (*pāśajāla*). Now, one might ask: why is this word *atha* not interpreted as having the sense of "auspiciousness" (*maṅgala*), since it is precisely when there is no possibility of immediate succession (*ānantarya*) that it is used in the sense of auspiciousness and so forth?

It is established through the proof of the conceptualization of non-existence (*abhāvavikalpa*). But how so? [The answer is: "Now, furthermore... and so forth, beginning with the statement of the incidental connection (*anuṣaṅgika-sambandha*) and other elements; this is the text of the *vṛtti*. However, this is not the text of the *vṛtti*, but rather an interpolation by those ignorant of the treatise; thus there is no fault. The nature of the first aphorism (*ādisūtra*) is as follows:

He demonstrates this here with the words beginning with "and here," which he will state immediately thereafter: "The Lord of the World, having condensed the Great Tantra—which consists of three categories and four feet—into a single aphorism. The meaning is that there are three categories (*padārtha*);
*padārtha* refers to masses of objects, in which all other entities are included.

"Because of the lack of autonomy in bound souls (*paśu*)," [it is said]. Bound souls, being independent of the Lord (*pati*), are not capable of releasing themselves from their own fetters (*pāśa*) due to their lack of autonomy, like domestic animals such as rams. Furthermore, the fetters themselves, being independent of the Lord, do not release the bound soul by their own power, because they are insentient, like iron shackles.
Now, it may be argued that those learned in the Vedānta maintain that the self will be liberated from itself through the knowledge of the self alone; however, that is incorrect.

Since impurity is a substance, its removal cannot occur through knowledge alone—just as a cataract or other defects of the eye are not removed by mere knowledge—but rather through the agency of the Lord, specifically through the rite known as *dīkṣā*, just as a cataract is removed by the action of an oculist.

"Having their own powers as their form" is said with reference to the powers that are inherent [in them]. But how can there be multiplicity for a single power? It has been stated that this is due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). And we shall explain later that "that one [power], through the infinity of objects, attains an infinity of distinctions. "Māyā and so forth," etc.

This is with regard to the capacity for maintenance (*parigraha-śakti*). By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the *bindu* is also included. The mention of "action" (*kriyā*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes both yoga and conduct (*caryā*) as well. Regarding the phrase "initiation and so forth" (*dīkṣā-ādi*):
by the inclusion of "and so forth," the subsidiary elements of initiation—such as bathing, worship, and other rites to be performed after the time of initiation—are also included.
The phrase "the attainment of supreme isolation" (*parakaivalyāsādana*) is an elliptical expression that also includes the attainment of enjoyment (*bhoga*).
Thus, this root aphorism contains [all of this] by way of internalizing it;
the meaning is that it internalizes the entire subject matter of the treatise together with its three categories (*padārtha*). In this regard, first, Śiva...

By this, the summary of the category of the Lord (pati) is stated as consisting of the Mantra, Mantreśvara, Mantramaheśvara, the liberated soul (muktātman), Śakti, and Śiva. Thereafter, by the phrase "from the atom" (ataḥparamaṇoḥ), the category of the bound soul (paśu)—distinguished by the various types such as the Vijñānākala—is indicated. By the phrase "the net of bonds" (pāśajāla),...
The fetters (*pāśas*), which consist of impurity (*mala*), the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*), and *karma-māyā*, are indicated; the word "apohati" implies that they are "grasped.
Furthermore, [the category of] action (*kriyā*) and the other three feet (*pādas*) to be described later are included within the category of the Lord (*pati*).

The means to both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) are thus subsumed. Now, one might ask: how can there be a subsumption of both the category of the Lord (*pati*) and the category of the fetter (*pāśa*) within a single power of the Lord? True; the power is indeed included within the category of the Lord.
However, we shall explain that it is designated as a "fetter" only figuratively, by virtue of its conformity to the characteristics of a fetter.
"Among them, the power of Maheśvara is Śivā, who bestows grace upon all;
it is only because she follows [the individual's] dharma that she is metaphorically designated as 'bond' (pāśa).
Furthermore, impurity (mala) is indeed one, yet possesses many natures, is endowed with multiple powers that conceal [the self], and is eternal and pervasive.

Karma also is distinct for each individual, consisting of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), and is eternal by way of its continuous flow. Furthermore, *māyā* is of two kinds—pure and impure—each accompanied by its own respective effects; all of this we shall explain in due course. Having accepted this very [system], he explains the root aphorism, beginning with "free from beginningless impurity," and so forth.

"Pure by its own nature" means that it is not [purified] through the operation of another Lord, for that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor is the position of a perpetually flowing Lord possible here, because sovereignty consists in the attainment of the manifestation of one's own essential nature, and thus its destruction is impossible. "By His grace, all impurities are destroyed" does not mean as the Sāṅkhyas maintain.
He is pure by nature. Furthermore, we shall explain that he is not liberated through his own power alone, as the Vedāntins maintain.

He explains the two terms "the doer of all" (*sarvakṛt*) and "the knower of all" (*sarvavit*) with the words beginning "Of him... and so forth. In that regard, omniscience is common to all; however, the status of being the creator of all belongs to the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*s) only partially, in comparison to the Supreme Lord.

"Inferior": we shall explain that this is even more inferior than the Mantras and Mantreśvaras. It expresses the connection of all three types with the activity of *apohana* (removal) and their denotability by the term "Śiva.
Regarding the phrase "but for the liberated souls," and so forth: it is because they are the cause for the Vidyeśvaras to attain the state of Śiva.

[This is] by virtue of being the bestower of grace upon the higher and lower Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*s), and by virtue of being the instrument for the *mantra*s indicated by them. [It is so] because it is engaged in the grace of all, and because it is the bestower of grace even upon the Lords of Knowledge. "Of the limited soul" (*aṇoḥ*)—this is the statement of the Sūtra.
He says "of the atom" (*aṇoḥ*) and so forth, using the singular number to denote the class. He says "by some means" (*kutaścid upāyāt*) and so forth:

"By means of knowledge, yoga, renunciation, or from the exhaustion of karma through experience, he remains with the body sustained by the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), like the whirling of a potter's wheel."
Because it is possible for one to exist even while joined with the impurity of *mala* and *māyā*; this is due to the distinction of being "bodiless" (*videha*).

Here, by the word "body" (*deha*), the physical bodies born of the worlds (*bhuvana*) are meant. Therefore, "with body" (*sadeha*) means joined with that [physical body]. However, "bodiless" (*videha*) means having a body consisting solely of the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*). The phrase "as far as possible" refers to [the state] through the two: the obstruction of *mala* and the power (*śakti*).

[The state] of the *vijñānākala* [is produced] by those two together with *karman*; [the state] of the *pralayākala* [is produced] by those two alone. Regarding the phrase "of that which is reversed":
for this very reason, it refers to "that which is impelled by Him," meaning that which is impelled by that Supreme Lord through the power of obstruction (*rodha-śakti*).
And "possessing connection with another bond" means that which has a connection with another bond, such as *kalā* and so forth.

"Of the *sakala* [individual], who is joined with the impurity of *māyā* and karma, and impelled by the power of obstruction"—this very point he elaborates upon with the words "this is the meaning," etc., up to "having regard for fitness. And having perceived that [the individual] is worthy of grace along with his substratum (*sādhikaraṇa*), he "removes the multitude of fetters" (*pāśavrāta*); as it has been said: for some, the two [impurities of] *mala* and *karman*; for others, all three.
First, it excludes [the object] according to its possibility. || 1 ||
Commentary: Now, the subsequent sūtra is for the purpose of illuminating the meaning indicated by this [preceding one]:
"It consists of three categories and four feet."
The Lord of the World, having condensed the Great Tantra into a single sūtra, spoke it again in full detail. (2)
For it is only when the *pāśa* (the bond) exists that the Lord becomes the agent of birth, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace for souls; thus,
there is no other ontological category whatsoever distinct from the *pati*, the *pāśa*, and the *ātman*.

Since all other [categories] are included within those that possess a purpose, it is said that there are only three categories (*tripadārthatva*). Furthermore, by the phrase "it removes the net of bonds" (*pāśajālam apohati*), the *kriyā-caryā-yoga-pāda* (the section on ritual action, conduct, and yoga) is implied through the act of removal;

and by the mention of the Lord (*pati*), the individual soul (*paśu*), and the bonds (*pāśa*), the *vidyā-pāda* (the section on knowledge) is implied. Thus, the presentation of the four sections (*pāda*) is accomplished.

It is called *Mahātantra* because it is "great" (*mahat*) due to its superior fruit compared to other systems of philosophy, or because it is supreme as a differentiator of Śiva; and it is a "tantra" because it extends (*tantrita*) various objects of knowledge. Having condensed this very object of knowledge within this single aphorism, the Lord of the Universe, the venerable Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, has then explained it again in detail. 2.
*Dīpikā*: Now, explaining [the system] as consisting of three categories (*tripadārtha*), he states the reason for its being threefold,
beginning with "For when the *pāśa* exists," etc., because the Lord (*pati*) acts as the benefactor and the bound souls (*paśu*) are the objects of that beneficence.

In this context, the nooses (pāśas) are primary because they are raised as the bow; it has been stated that other factors are included within them, either as their subsidiaries or as their causes. Furthermore, he states that their fourfold nature was already indicated in the very first aphorism, beginning with "Moreover" (kiñca), on the grounds that [this system] yields a superior fruit compared to other philosophical systems (darśanas).
This is because, by first demonstrating the points established in all other scriptures, it reveals meanings not previously understood therein and bestows liberation that surpasses all others.
"The Lord of the World, Śrīkaṇṭhanātha": here, by the word *jagat* (world), the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ are meant.
The meaning is that his husband was a disciple of Ananta. || 2 ||
Commentary: From the root sūtra, he explains the two qualifiers "the creator of all" and "the knower of all. [The world's] birth, maintenance, and destruction...
The concealment and liberation [of the soul]—
this alone is to be known as its activity, along with its instruments and its fruit. || 3 ||
Therefore, the creator of the world must be established by way of intrinsic nature;
for if it were established through something posterior, there would be an infinite regress.
Or liberation may be without cause. || 4 ||

Birth (*janman*) is the repeated arising of the wheel of living beings (*jantucakra*), together with the equipment necessary for their enjoyment, within various successive wombs. Abiding (*sthiti*) is the establishment of all the world, restrained by His will, in its respective sphere of activity. Destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is the withdrawal [of that wheel] into the womb of the universe (*jagadyoni*).
Concealment (*tirobhāva*) is the non-falling away from experience corresponding to one's [past] actions; it is described elsewhere by the name "protection" (*saṃrakṣaṇa*).

As the author of the *Vārttika* said: "The non-falling away of embodied beings from experience appropriate to their own latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), which is the preservation according to the rule, is declared to be what is called 'protection'."

By the word "liberation" (vimukti), what is meant here is grace in the form of contemplation; this constitutes the fivefold activity belonging to the Supreme Lord. It should be understood—that is, known—together with the causal factors such as the powers (śakti) and so forth, as well as the fruit consisting of enjoyment and liberation. || 3 ||

And this [world] cannot be produced by means of illusions or other such actions, because they lack consciousness; nor can it be produced by the individual soul (*puruṣa*), because its powers are obstructed by impurity (*mala*). Furthermore, it is not logical that a non-omnipotent being should be the agent here.
And whoever is capable of performing such creation and so forth must necessarily possess knowledge regarding that object.

Because if there were even a partial deficiency in the specific cognitions regarding the objects of the actions one intends to perform, those respective actions would not be accomplished. Therefore, that creator of the world must be an omniscient and omnipotent being, established by his very nature. This is established as being from the beginning, starting with the word "arvāk" (prior).

If that [omniscience] is accepted, then if its favor toward him arises from some cause, one must seek the cause of that [cause], and the cause of that cause yet another cause; thus there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Alternatively, if such sovereignty belongs to him by his very nature without any cause, then it has arisen spontaneously; in that case, it would be without a cause (*nirhetuka*).
Liberation would either belong to everyone, because of the lack of dependence on anything else, or it would not belong even to that [specific person]. As they say:
"Existence or non-existence must be eternal, because of the lack of dependence on any other cause;
for it is through dependence that the occasional occurrence of entities is possible."

Therefore, the category of Pati, which was previously mentioned as having eternally established, unsurpassed, and pure perception and action regarding all objects, has now been defined; it shall be examined hereafter. || 4 ||
The *Dīpikā* [comments]:
"Accompanied by the equipment for enjoyment" means together with that which is for the purpose of enjoyment,
whether it be internal or external, uncommon, and subtle in form, consisting of the worlds (*bhuvana*) and so forth.

The meaning is: "of that which is joined, as the case may be, with a multitude of principles (tattva-vrāta) consisting of both pure and impure forms, along with common and uncommon adjuncts, having as its essence the body and so forth born of the world.
Birth (janma) is the arising in various such wombs. In that regard, concerning those things of pure and impure form—

Birth (*janma*) is the arising of the principles (*tattva*), whether directly or through a succession, from the material cause consisting of the *bindu* and the *māyā*; [this occurs] preceded by the production of omniscience and omnipotence in the Vidyeśvaras and others.

[It consists of] the conjunction with a *baindava* body appropriate for their respective offices; and the joining of the multitudes of bound souls (*paśus*) to world-born bodies located in objects present [to them], which are projected by their respective karmas;
and [the joining] of the lower Mantra-lords through the production of omniscience and so forth, as well as through the conjunction with *kalā* and the other [categories].

We shall explain that this consists in the appointment [of beings] to their respective offices. And it has been stated that this activity of the Supreme Lord concerns both pure and impure objects, occurring both directly and through a succession:
"In the pure path, Śiva is said to be the agent; in the dark [impure path], the Lord Ananta."
"Of the entire world restrained by His will" means of the aforementioned universe restrained by the power of the Lord (*īśvara*).

"In the womb of the world" refers to *māyā* and the *bindu*. We shall explain that therein, the group beginning with *kalā* resides in *māyā*, while the group beginning with *śuddhavidyā* resides in the *bindu*. And there is the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) of the multitudes of bound souls (*paśu*).
It is precisely the state of being devoid of the *pālaya* (the sustaining power). As he will say:
"Having withdrawn the means of enjoyment and having made them rest upon the Cause, and having taken possession of that [Cause] along with the Self, it remains for the sake of repose."

It has been stated that for the Vidyeśvaras and others, liberation occurs at the time of universal dissolution when their office comes to an end. As it is said in the venerable Raurava: "Upon the cessation of Ananta, those great sovereigns [attain liberation]."

"The supreme state is established as the cause of all agency. Thus, there is no contradiction, as concealment (*tirobhāva*) and grace (*anugraha*) have been demonstrated by the passage beginning with "according to the corresponding experience" (*yathānurūpād bhogāt*). By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "by power and so forth" (*śaktyādibhiḥ*), *māyā* and the rest are understood. || 4 ||
Commentary: Now, in order to define the category of the bound soul (paśu), he says:
"Consciousness consists of the nature of perception and action."
Therefore, that [liberation] exists in the self at all times and in every respect,
since liberation is heard of as being "all-facing" (sarvatomukha).
Even though it exists, because it does not appear, it is perceived as ceased;
[this is so] for one whose vigor is unobstructed and under control.
The ear [is to be used] until liberation. || 6 ||

We shall explain in the refutation of the Cārvākas that consciousness, which consists of knowledge and action, resides in the Self and is not inherent in the body. Furthermore, that [consciousness] exists at all times; there is no absence of consciousness in liberation as is maintained by the Vaiśeṣikas, nor is there such a thing as a state of delusion.

Because liberation will be refuted [later]. Furthermore, that consciousness of the Self consists of knowledge and action and is all-pervasive; it is not non-pervasive like that of the Jainas (Kṣapaṇakas), who maintain the restriction that the soul is the size of the body, because pervasiveness will be stated in the section concerning the category of the bound soul (paśu). He states the reason for this here:

The meaning is that because it is heard [in scripture] that liberation is "all-facing" (*sarvatomukha*), there is the hearing of the all-facing consciousness of the selves in the state of liberation. Nor should it be said that this [consciousness] arises for them only at that time, because the existence of that which has already arisen will be explained in the section on the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). Now, [as for the phrase] "only in liberation"...

To dispel the doubt as to how consciousness can be "all-pervasive" during the state of transmigratory existence— given that such consciousness is not perceived prior to its being heard of in scripture, and based on the method of agreement and difference— he says: "Even though it exists, because it does not manifest."
It is true that such consciousness is not perceived during the state of saṃsāra;

however, that non-perception is established otherwise. For a non-perception caused by the absence of a manifestor does not prove non-existence, but rather [proves it] only when a manifestor is present.

And this non-perception, which is caused by the absence of a manifesting agent, does not therefore establish non-existence. Furthermore, since that all-pervasiveness, though existing, is not manifested, it is determined to be obstructed by something; and for this reason, prior to liberation, [the soul] possesses its own power unobstructed.
"The self is to be controlled. || 6 ||
The *Dīpikā* states:

"Because of the arising of the existent," and so forth. Now, if this were the case, then—just as with the *kalās* and other categories—the state of being in the form of power (*śaktirūpatva*) would apply during the period of transmigratory existence (*saṃsārāvasthā*), while the state of being in the form of manifestation (*vyaktirūpatva*) would apply upon liberation; thus, there would follow the defect of [the Self] being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) and the like. That is not so.

This has been stated merely on account of the similarity in the nature of manifestation; however, in the ultimate sense, consciousness is all-pervasive and is simply made manifest through the removal of impurity—thus there is no fault. He states this very point, preceded by an objection, in the passage beginning with "Now, [if it is] only in liberation," etc. (verse 6).
Commentary: Having thus explained the second category (padārtha), he speaks in order to define the third category, that of the fetter (pāśa).
The fourfold activity of Māyā, consisting of the powers of Prāvṛti and Śabalī,
is in brief the net of bonds.
Phenomena are proclaimed by their names alone. || 7 ||

"Prāvṛti" means that which covers or conceals intensely; thus, it refers to the obscuration of the vision and action of the selves, meaning innate impurity or "mala. "Īśaḥ" means one who rules with sovereignty; the word "of the Lord" (īśvarasya) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.
His power (*bala*), which is the capacity for obstruction, is the second *pāśa*; for he will state further on:
"The power of Māheśvarī, which is Śivā, bestows grace upon all;
it is designated as a *pāśa* solely because it follows after [the influence of] *dharma*."

It is called *karma* because it is performed by those who desire its fruit. Its beginninglessness (*anāditva*) is established because no initial limit (*ādyakoṭi*) can be perceived. Since the performance of action belongs to one possessed of a body, and that body is itself originated by action, and those actions were likewise performed with another body, and that [body] was born of action—this is the cycle.

The third bond is *māyā*. It is called *māyā* because, in the form of power (*śakti*), the entire universe merges into it during dissolution and emerges into manifestation during creation. As it is stated in the venerable *Saurabhreya*:
"At the time of the great dissolution, all effects are merged within her in the form of power."
In the transformation, they manifest through their own effects, such as the *kalās* and so forth.
This fourth [category], which is accompanied by its effects and is beginningless, is called a "jāla" (net) because, like a net, it acts as an obstruction to the innate power of the selves;
this has been stated in brief, that is, in summary. Furthermore, their functional activities are evident from their very names.
They have been shown and indicated by their own names according to their meaning; nevertheless, they will be explained in due course. || 7 ||
The *Dīpikā* states:

"Impurity (*mala*) is natural impurity. Thus, impurity is beginningless, like the husk or the chaff [of grain]; it is not the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the Self, as are knowledge and action. It is [attributed] to power (*śakti*) only figuratively (*upacāreṇa*), because it conforms to the properties of the fetters (*pāśa*).

That it is not primarily a "noose" (pāśa) is shown by the explanatory passage beginning with "tathā hi" and so forth, as well as by the statement "and its beginninglessness," which refers to its beginninglessness as a continuous flow. He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "yataḥ" and so forth. [Objection:
But surely even bondage in the form of the pure path (śuddhādhvan) exists; how then can it be established by its own effects, such as *kalā* and the rest?

Thus it has been said. Although that conjunction constitutes bondage in relation to supreme liberation (*paramukti*), there is no contradiction [in not including it as a *pāśa*] because it will be described as "inferior liberation" (*aparamukti*) since it is the cause for attaining the status of a Vidyeśvara and so forth. This is because it acts as an obstruction to innate capacity (*sahajasāmarthya*).
Because it brings about the cessation of omniscience, omnipotence, and the power of all agency. "In brief" means that since the impurities (*mala*),
the powers (*śakti*) fixed to each individual soul, the karmas, and the effects of *māyā*— which exist in both common and uncommon forms— are infinite, a detailed exposition is impossible.
The activities of the dharmas consist in producing the result of concealing the manifestation of their own essential nature, as well as the production of the body, sense organs, and so forth. (7)
Commentary: Now follows the summary of the three categories;
thus, of these three entities...
Prior to the establishment of the preceding section,
the application [of the tantra] will be explained through the sections on conduct (caryā), yoga, and ritual action (kriyā).

Thus, the application—that is, the distribution—of these very three categories established in the *Vidyāpāda* by means of the other three sections beginning with the *Caryāpāda* will be described; it will be stated that by such a procedure, the Lord, having brought about the pacification of the fetters (*pāśa*), becomes the bestower of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) upon the bound souls (*paśu*). This is the case for each of these [sections].
The meaning is that seclusion will be explained [in the following]. || 8 ||
To state the fruit of that application, he says: "The fruit of the application is liberation, and enjoyment as a secondary consequence."
These two, however, are divided in many ways according to the distinction between the higher and the lower.

The commentary: The fruit of that application (viniyoga), which is the distribution [of the sacrificial portions], is enjoyment (bhukti). This follows as a secondary consequence; enjoyment also arises as a byproduct. It is conjoined with the material initiations (bhautika-dīkṣā) and so forth that will be described hereafter.
Beyond the perception of enjoyments and objects of enjoyment, there arises the manifestation of the deficiency of others. Thus it is said in the Rudrasaṃhitā:
"Those purified by initiation, having taken birth within the maṇḍala of Gaṇapati, the Guru..."

"Having become perfected through mantras, their bodies radiant as the orb of the rising sun, they enjoy pleasures for a very long time accompanied by throngs of celestial nymphs; then, with their longing subsided, they become partakers of the supreme sovereignty of the state of Śiva. Thus it is said.

Enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*) are divided in many ways according to the distinction between the higher (*parā*) and the lower (*aparā*). Among these, higher enjoyment consists in the sovereignty over various worlds (*bhuvana*), endowed with diverse powers, situated along the path from the netherworlds (*pātāla*) up to the *kalā* level; while lower enjoyment is merely residing in those respective worlds. Likewise, higher liberation is equality with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
But another [attainment] is the state of being a Mantra and a Mantreśvara. We shall explain how these possess many subdivisions later on. || 9 ||
The *Dīpikā* states:

"Liberation is the fruit of the distribution [of the sacrificial materials]. Thus, through the sequence of knowing the application [of the ritual] and performing it, there is liberation. Furthermore, enjoyment also occurs as a secondary result; however, this is the case in the material initiation (*bhautika-dīkṣā*).
Since liberation is accomplished immediately after [the experience of] enjoyment (*bhukti*), enjoyment is also called a fruit. This is what is meant:

liberation alone is the primary fruit of initiation (*dīkṣā*); enjoyment, however, like the satiating of birds by one who has set out to water a tree, is established as a secondary consequence (*anupaṅga*) resulting from the fitness (*arhatva*) inherent in initiation. He states that very point:
"Regarding 'to be described,' and so forth... || 9 ||
Commentary: Now, the Sage asks in order to inquire what the distinction of this Pārameśvara knowledge is compared to other systems of philosophy.
In the systems of Vedānta, Sāṅkhya, and those asserting the reality or unreality of creation,
liberation along with its means exists.
What is the distinction in the Śiva-āgama? || 10 ||

In the systems of those who know the Vedānta, in the scriptures such as the Upaniṣads; in the Sāṃkhya systems, such as the sixty-four Tantras; in the systems of the Ārhats who maintain the doctrine of existence and non-existence, beginning with the three stainless ones (Akalanka); and in the scriptures of Kaṇāda and others who propound categories such as substance.

Because liberation and its means are also heard of in the systems of the Sugatas and others due to the inclusion of the word "etcetera," the sage’s question arises from a desire to know the specific distinction— since he has not yet reached a definitive conclusion as to what that distinction in the Śiva-āgama might be—
and not because of doubt. This is because he proceeded to listen only after having already ascertained the possibility of such a distinction.

Nor did they choose the knowledge of Śiva because they were deluded; for it is evident that they were not biased toward other systems of philosophy, as they proceeded with their request [for instruction]. Furthermore, the liberation and the means thereto taught in those various scriptures will be restated by the author himself at the appropriate occasions and subsequently refuted.
We do not present them through any separate effort of our own. || 10 ||
The *Dīpikā* states: He explains the connection of the sūtra beginning with "Vedānta" by saying "Now, from others," and so forth.

Because of the context of enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), there is a question arising from a desire to know their specific distinctions; for this very reason, the word "liberation" (*mukti*) is used here.
It should be understood that "eating" is also intended as an illustration [of other such acts]. || 10 ||
Herein is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). The commentary (*vṛtti*): Because the author is all-seeing—
The summary of the reality is not yet clear;
however, since the means are fruitful,
all this is supreme within Śaivism.

For the authors [of those systems] are Hiraṇyagarbha and others, as well as Kaṇāda, Patañjali, Kapila, and so forth; and they are not omniscient, being regarded as inferior because they do not comprehend the entire range of objects of knowledge—including that which exists beyond their own specific subjects of inquiry—as established by both reason and scripture. As it has been said:

"By those who propound the doctrines of primordial nature (svabhāva), the person (puruṣa), the unmanifest (avyakta), karma, and time as the self, liberation has been falsely imagined without even having seen the Supreme Lord. Likewise:
"If Sugata is omniscient, what proof is there that Kapila is not?"
"Now, if both are omniscient, how can there be a difference of opinion between them? [To this we reply:
Since the treatises were composed by them, for that very reason the compendium of reality within them is not clear;
the meaning is that their knowledge regarding bondage and liberation is indistinct. And as for the means [taught] therein...
The discernment between the self and primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the cultivation of selflessness (*nairātmya*),

the practice of the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaita*), the knowledge of the reality of the sixteen categories, and so forth, as well as their fruits characterized by heaven and liberation— all that is likewise unclear in that very same way.
Because it cannot be sustained in the manner that will be explained later, this scripture possesses a distinction from those [other systems].
