Or rather, it is entirely superior, because it was taught by the Supreme Lord— who transcends the sphere of both *paśu* (the bound soul) and *pāśa* (the bond)— and whose nature consists of unsurpassed knowledge and action regarding all objects.

The supremacy of the means, such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth, also consists in their being derived from a supreme author, because their efficacy has been observed to correspond with reality. For instance, it is observed that even those burdened with great sins such as the killing of a Brahmin become freed from those sins through initiation and other such means; therefore, [the means] are supreme. As for poison...
Just as the power of killing is removed, the binding nature of the fetters (pāśas) is established to be eliminated.
As it has been said:
"Through initiation, one attains purification on the scale [of the soul] even from the primary sin of Brahmin-slaughter."
"One should know the cessation of bondage through [this] means, like the destruction of poison.
Thus, the fruit here is superior to the fruits characterized by enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*) seen in all other philosophical systems.
For it is said in the *Mataṅga*:
"By means of the Agnihotra and other such works of public utility (pūrta), as well as the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances,

the illustrious ones rejoice even in the three worlds, stationed in celestial chariots. Furthermore, "Having performed a hundred sacrifices according to the rule, they may attain the station of Śakra."
"O best of sages, that state which is attained by high-souled devotees of Śiva even through deceit cannot be reached by a thousand sacrifices. Furthermore,
in this system, liberation (apavarga) is supreme because it lies beyond the scope of all other scriptures.

Because the authors of those respective scriptures are possessed of impurities and are therefore not omniscient, the liberation taught by them is merely a semblance of liberation. And it is said in the *Śrīmad-Bhārgavottara*:
"Those men who are liberated in other systems through the exhaustion of merit and demerit..."
"These are declared here to be the Rudrāṇavas, devoid of the three qualities. (11)

The *Dīpikā* explains the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) with the words "the authors," and so forth. Now, one might object: since treatises such as those of Kaṇāda and others are preceded by an author, and because there is the possibility that their authors were untrustworthy, it is conceivable that these works may lack clarity.

But since no author is observed for these [Vedas], and since their validity does not depend upon that [author], how can there be any lack of clarity? To this he says: "Hiraṇyagarbha and others... The intention is as follows:

because it is established that a composition, such as a cloth and so forth, is preceded by an author, the human origin of the Vedas is also established; and by the establishment of that [human origin]...
And there is the possibility that [the meaning] is not clearly manifest. Furthermore, Hiraṇyagarbha alone is the author of the Vedas, as it has been stated by the Teachers as well:
"Hiraṇyagarbha, Kapila, Matsyendra, and others [are the authors] of the Vedas, Sāṃkhya, Kaula, and other Tantras."

He explains [the reason] "because they are not all-knowing" by stating, "and those [others] are non-omniscient. [The claim that] "knowledge of bondage and liberation regarding the person (puruṣa) is indistinct" is because the person is endowed with attributes such as momentariness, non-pervasiveness, and purity, and because [the Lord] is characterized as the master (pati) in the form of the material cause (upādāna) and so forth.

This is because bondage is admitted to be incapable [of liberation], and liberation is admitted to consist in the attainment of the principles of nature (*prakṛti-tattva*) and so forth, as well as the destruction of knowledge and so forth. The phrase "characterized by heaven and liberation" means having the form of enjoyment and liberation. Furthermore, one should not suspect that the word "liberation" (*apavarga*) is redundant here.

It was stated previously that the nature of liberation (*mokṣasvarūpa*) is indistinct, whereas here it is said that there is disagreement regarding its attainment. Now, one might object: since even the Śaiva [system] presupposes an agent, and because of the possibility that such an agent might be untrustworthy (*anāpta*), how is it not indistinct? To this, he says: "Therefore, from them..."
Because the Supreme Lord is the ultimate authority (*paramāpta*), deception is impossible for him.
This has been stated in the *Upodghāta* itself; therefore, the liberation taught by him cannot be a semblance of liberation (*muktyābhāsa*). As it has been said:
"The Buddhists are established in the principle of consciousness (*buddhitattva*); the Jainas (*Ārhata*) are established in the qualities (*guṇa*) alone."
"The knowers of the Vedas abide in the unmanifest Person; the Pāñcarātrikas [abide in Him]," and so forth. 11.
Commentary: Now, what is this lack of clarity in other philosophical systems? To this, he says:
"In the Vedāntas, there is only one Self."
Characterized by the manifestations of consciousness and unconsciousness. || 11½ ||

"The Self alone is all this universe; there is no diversity whatsoever here. Likewise: "The one Controller, the inner Self of all beings, who makes the single universe manifold. By such scriptural passages, it is established that the Supreme Self alone is the primordial material cause (*prakṛti*) for the manifestation and dissolution of all sentient and insentient entities.

The knowers of Vedānta maintain that although He alone is independent and possesses the full majesty of the six divine attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*), He undergoes transmigratory existence; following the nature of various internal limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) characterized by diverse mental states, He becomes known as He truly is for the sake of spiritual prosperity. For He alone is indeed...

When the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the self of sentient beings is predominantly *rajas*, it remains as if tranquil; when its nature is *tamas* and full of passion, it remains as if deluded by ignorance. Yet nothing else exists separately from that. Because the appearance of duality is unreal—being merely the manifestation of that very [self] in various diverse forms—it is like the cognition of two moons and so forth.
Because it is erroneous. Thus the venerable Bhartṛhari has said:
"Just as a person afflicted by cataracts perceives the pure sky as if it were filled with various specks."

"Thus, this immortal Brahman, which is changeless, appears to undergo impurity through ignorance and proceeds in the form of differentiation. And so, this supreme Brahman, characterized as the Supreme Self, is indeed non-different from the minds [of individual beings].

There is a conjunction with the phenomena of saṃsāra, such as pleasure, pain, and so forth. But the Supreme Self, like the sun, although undivided by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) which are like diverse reflections in water, appears as if divided. And thus says the Śruti: "Just as this light, the sun, though one, enters into the waters that are divided, so does He."
"By means of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), the Lord, whose nature is non-differentiation, is made to appear as differentiated; thus the Self has immersed itself in the fields (kṣetra). || 11½ ||
The Lamp (*Dīpikā*):

Now, in order to illuminate the lack of clarity in other systems of thought, the author first indicates the lack of clarity in the position of the Vedāntins with the half-verse beginning with "In the Vedāntas... and so forth.
That view is set forth. He demonstrates it with the words "This is indeed the Self," and so on. The intention is as follows:

since the Self is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), there is no possibility of anything else—even a supreme atom—that is not pervaded by it. If such a thing were possible, then because its own nature and attributes would be non-pervasive, the pervasiveness of the Self would remain unestablished.

Furthermore, because other pervasive selves (*ātman*) would necessarily exist, even the coexistence of multiple pervasive entities within a single world-system is impossible; for the presence of one cloth obstructs the presence of another cloth in the same spatial location. Thus, there is only one Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This is precisely what [the author] expresses with the words "The Supreme Self alone," and so forth. How then...
Since there is an occasion for distinctions such as Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and so forth, he says:
"conforming to the internal nature of the various distinctions of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) characterized by the respective minds," and so on.
He elaborates on this very point with the words: "for that very [Self]," and so on. Regarding the phrase "of the appearance of duality," and so forth:

Due to the persistence of ignorance (*avidyā*), this [world] is perceived by individual souls (*jīvātman*) in many ways through the infinite variety of bodies such as those of animals and deer, even though it is unreal in nature. For, like a dream within a dream, an infinite manifestation of persons, lights, and so forth is seen; and thus, it is like the appearance of two moons.
Even the appearance of duality is unreal; thus, the Self alone is established by both scripture and reasoning.
And it has been stated that when this Self is understood as it truly is, it leads to exaltation. || 11½ ||
Commentary: This is not tenable,
because this is merely a thesis.
What is the basis for certainty?
If it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the self (*ātman*) therein becomes an object of cognition (*prameya*). (12)

If this is accepted simply by setting aside the consideration of whether it is logically possible or impossible—well, let it stand as you wish. However, it cannot be established according to the method of valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*), because this is merely a thesis (*pratijñā*) alone;
for here there is no possibility of a reason (*hetu*), an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and so forth. In the absence of these, what basis could there be for certainty?

For what basis does a certainty, which is grounded in a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), possess the capacity to establish its respective objects of knowledge? Not otherwise. Now, one might object: "In this case, the means of valid cognition has already been shown to be scripture (*āgama*) in the form of the revealed word (*śruti*.
To this he says: "Now, as for the means of valid cognition"—if [that] means of valid cognition is, in the ultimate sense, of an unreal nature, [then it cannot establish anything].

Because the Supreme Self alone is reality, that which is being cognized by such a means of knowledge is primarily like the discernment of objects situated in deep darkness by means of a lamp fashioned by the mind. Now, if scripture— specifically the Śruti— is indeed a true means of knowledge, then in that case, that Supreme Self [is established].

It exists as an object of cognition (*prameya*). For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) attains the status of being a means of valid cognition only by delimiting its object of cognition; otherwise, it would not even possess the nature of a means of valid cognition.
(Dīpikā)

He introduces the *siddhāntasūtra* with the words "That which is this... and so forth, [stating] that neither the oneness of the Self nor liberation through the knowledge of the Self is tenable. He says this with the words "Om" and so forth. Now, it may be argued: "But a reason has been stated here, namely 'because of its all-pervasiveness' (*vyāpakatvāt*); that is incorrect, because it is contradictory (*viruddha*) due to being pervaded by the opposite."

For the pervaded—such as the earth, mountains, and so forth—is established by that which pervades it, like the light of the sun and other luminaries; it does not abide within itself alone, for that would entail the fallacy of infinite regress. Thus, the refutation of duality is already answered by the very establishment of pervasiveness. As for what was also said—that when the world is pervaded by one [entity], there is no room for a second, just as in a space already occupied by a cloth—[that too is refuted].

"It is impossible for that which is all-pervasive to have a localized state. This is true for material things, but not for immaterial ones, because no contradiction is established [in their case]. It is like coldness, smoke, light, and so forth, which pervade the interior of a house; thus there is no fault. As for what was also said regarding "having ignorance as its cause":

As for the claim that there is the appearance of duality (*dvaitapratibhāsa*), that is not so; for since ignorance (*avidyā*) is admitted to be removable by knowledge (*vidyā*), and knowledge is distinct from it, this contradicts non-duality (*advaita*). [Objection: But surely only knowledge is real, not ignorance.
[Response: If that were the case, then because ignorance would be a non-entity (*avastu*), like the horn of a hare and so forth, it would be eternally ceased.
In that case, such means for its cessation as "the Self must be known, reflected upon, and meditated upon" would be entirely useless,

like a means for the cessation of a hare's horn and the like. If it is argued that this will be a means for the realization of the Self, that is not so, because there is an absence of that bondage which consists of ignorance and is ultimately real.

The nature of knowledge is indeed already attained, just as light exists when darkness is absent; thus, the sense is that the means [of attaining it] in that case would be useless. The unity [of the self] through reasoning has been refuted. Now, in order to refute the unity [of the self] through scripture, he raises the point regarding the unity of the self by way of scriptural authority (*āgama-pramāṇa*) as a consequence: "But here..."

"Valid means of knowledge," and so forth. "He says" means he states the reply. He explains the aphorism of the established doctrine (*siddhānta-sūtra*) beginning with "If," and so on. The intention is as follows: since there exist scriptural texts (*śruti*) that establish difference, and because the texts concerning unity have other purposes, even for that [unity] which takes the form of scripture...

Even if one accepts its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) on the grounds that it possesses an object, that cognition must be either true or false. If it is true, that very same fault of contradicting non-duality (*advaita*) remains. If it is false, then it lacks the status of a means of valid cognition. || 12½ ||
Commentary:
What follows from this? Nothing else.
Wherever these two [conditions] exist, there...
If all four were to exist [simultaneously],
there would be a loss of non-duality; otherwise, it would result in a lack of any means of valid cognition.
And there would be equality of enjoyments and lack of liberation—two things which are not desired by the proponents of the self. (14)
Wherever this dyad characterized by the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) exists,

there another dyad consisting of the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the act of knowing (*pramiti*) is also necessarily present, because they are mutually dependent. Indeed, without a knower, the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge could never perform any function whatsoever.

Since the instrument and the object depend upon the agent for the accomplishment of the action, valid cognition (*pramiti*)—being itself an operation in the form of an action—is perceived through positive and negative concomitance as distinct from them; thus, these four factors are necessarily present. As Akṣapāda said: "And within these four, every worldly transaction [is contained]."

"It is concluded. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "The loss of non-duality (advaita-hāni). For when the conventional usage of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*) is admitted, there is indeed the loss of non-duality; therefore, there is a contradiction with one's own accepted doctrine. But if that [usage] is denied, there is a lack of any basis for knowledge (*niṣpramāṇakatva*). Regarding "equality of enjoyment" (*bhoga-sāmya*): [the text continues as follows:]... Furthermore, two defects—namely, the equality of enjoyment and the absence of liberation—are entailed [for those who deny the self].
All proponents of the self, fearing contradiction with direct perception, must necessarily accept the observed diversity of experience. Moreover, the liberation of selves must be admitted.

Since treatises are composed solely for the sake of attaining the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), the All-pervading Lord (*vibhu*) here does not take upon himself anyone’s sin nor their merit; likewise, because it is accepted that there is neither agency nor actions [belonging to Him],
[the Lord] does not act as the bestower of diverse fruits, since those [actions] are performed by specific individual beings.

Since there would be an absence of those very karmas that determine specific enjoyments, the consequence of an equality of enjoyment would be unavoidable. For it is only when there is a plurality of selves that the diversity of enjoyment—such as one being happy and another being miserable—is logically established; otherwise, it would not be so. And it is precisely from this [plurality] that the origin of transmigratory existence arises.

If liberation (*mokṣa*) were dissolution into that very same partless Supreme Self (*paramātman*), then there would be a reappearance from that very source, followed again by liberation; thus, this would be merely following after what has already gone, and not true liberation. For instance, the venerable Avadhūta Ācārya [states]: "In your view, even those liberations accomplished through supreme knowledge [are subject to recurrence]."
"Nor do they enter into communion, like raindrops with water.

Consequently, because liberation would be non-existent, the means to that liberation—such as "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be heard, to be reflected upon, and to be meditated upon"—would be rendered purposeless. Furthermore, of this [Self]...

If the Supreme Self were the cause of the origin of the universe of both sentient and insentient things, then the effects would necessarily possess sentience and insentience, because of the inherence of the nature of the cause within the effects. As they say:
"Entities possessing such-and-such a form arise from causes possessing such-and-such a form."
And for this reason, since two contradictory things can only come into existence through mutual suppression—

just as existence and non-existence cannot coexist at the same time— it is not possible for the natures of consciousness and unconsciousness to reside simultaneously in the Supreme Self. As the venerable Kheṭakanandana has said:
"Two contradictory properties, existing at the same time and residing in a single substratum,
bring about their own annihilation through their mutual destruction.
Furthermore, because this [Self] is partless, it is not logical for it to possess insentience in any respect.
If, however, one accepts that [the Supreme Cause] possesses parts, then because it would be an effect—like a wall or a granary—it would forfeit its status as the ultimate cause.

Furthermore, whatever is a material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) is insentient, such as clay and so forth; and this Supreme Self is insentient because it is a material cause. If it were sentient, it could not be a material cause.

If it is argued, "Let it be insentient; what is the fault?", this statement is truly strange: that [the cause] is itself insentient while being the cause of sentient things. Furthermore, if its lack of sentience is admitted, it lacks the capacity to produce its own effects, just like a lump of clay or similar materials unless presided over by an intelligent agent. And as for those who [hold it to be] a grasper...

If it is argued that the selves, established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), are enjoyers because they are produced from Him, then—since they would be produced—they would follow as being insentient like jars and other such objects; thus, the non-duality of the Supreme Self, which is the locus of many such defects, is untenable. || 14 ||

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: He states another objection with the words "Furthermore, what of this? (*kiñcātaḥ*), and he further confirms the consequence of the equality of experience with the words "In that case... (*tadiha...*) and so forth. And he says that by accepting the diversity of experience, the plurality of selves (*ātman*) is established.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "If there were a difference between the self [and experience]" (*ātmanānātve hi*) is as follows: Experience (*bhoga*), it has been stated, consists of the perception of pleasure and pain; as it is said, "Experience for this person is sensation characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth. Consequently, the self is established as distinct from experience, which consists of perception. This is what is being expressed.

Just as the oneness of the Supreme Self is established by its nature as consciousness and its being of the essence of self-awareness, so too the difference among individual selves (jīvātman) is established by their own distinct self-awareness. Whatever is established by self-awareness is indeed true, just as the oneness of the Supreme Self is.

Furthermore, this distinction between individual selves (*jīvātman*) is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); therefore, it too is indeed real. Thus, non-dualism (*advaita*) is refuted.
Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*), because it manifests itself as the cognizer of both its own self and the other self. [Objection:
But surely, since difference is preceded by the apprehension of mutual negation (*itaretarābhāva*), it cannot be grasped by perception whose object is a positive entity (*bhāva*).

Apprehension is simply not possible. As for what was said—that "the wise declare perception to be a means of affirmation, not of negation"—that is incorrect. For this [concept of] mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is established only when difference is established; otherwise, one seeking milk might even run after fire, and everything would become incoherent. This leads to the undesirable consequence of never being liberated (*avimokṣaprasaṅga*).

And he confirms this with the words "precisely because of that," and so forth. Furthermore, since liberation is not authentic, the means to it are also not authentic; thus he says "therefore," and so forth.
Moreover, he states that such knowledge is not authentic with the words "moreover," and so forth. And this expression is manifold regarding effects.
The meaning is: "because of the continuity of the cause. He states another refutation with the words "And those who... and so forth. || 14½ ||

Commentary: Now, when the position of the Vedāntins has been thus refuted, it may be argued that the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) will result from the knowledge of the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, as stated by the followers of Kapila. As they say:

Thus, through the practice of reality, by means of the realization "I am not, nothing is mine, there is no 'I'," one attains both the certain and the absolute liberation without remainder. The Śruti also says: "The unborn, one, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form; for there is one unborn [male]..."
"Enjoying it, the other, the unborn one, lies along with it; having experienced its enjoyment, he abandons it. To refute this as well, he says:
"Even in Sāṃkhya knowledge, there is falsity."
Because one perceives the cause within the effect. || 14½ ||

Even in the Sāṃkhya system, there is this same lack of correctness: the notion that the *pradhāna*—which is an effect produced from *māyā* and generated by the *kalās*—is the ultimate cause, which is a delusion regarding its status as the supreme cause. For they maintain that the *mūlaprakṛti* (root-nature) is unevolved (*avikṛti*), whereas the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with *kalā* are effects.

This is because we do not accept a world-ground consisting of *māyā*—which serves as the cause for those various purposes that are perceived individually—as being itself the repository of the universe. And it has been said elsewhere:
"Since no karma exists to be experienced beyond the level of the *guṇas*, even the *kaivalya* (isolation) of the Sāṃkhyas [is merely a state of latent impressions]."

"It is not at all logical because of non-exhaustion. This is the meaning: regarding this *prakṛti*—which is postulated by the followers of Kapila as the supreme cause and consists of the equilibrium of the three qualities (*guṇa*) characterized as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—it has been established through arguments that it is not distinct from the qualities; indeed, the qualities themselves are *prakṛti*. Given that it is not other than the qualities...

Furthermore, it must necessarily be manifold; and whatever is manifold while lacking consciousness is preceded by other causes, just as threads or lumps of clay [are preceded by their own parts]. And if it is preceded by other causes, it cannot be the ultimate cause.
This is what you must be asked: namely, that the conjunction of the seer and the seen is the cause of saṃsāra.
Regarding the statement that disjunction preceded by that [conjunction] is the cause of liberation:

first of all, the conjunction between the Puruṣa and Pradhāna consists solely in their relationship as the seer and the seen; it is not of the nature of mutual physical contact. Since both are formless, such [physical contact] is impossible.

Furthermore, the *pradhāna* is not perceptible in itself, as it is accepted that it is beyond direct perception (*apratyakṣa*). Nor is the seer able to perceive it when it has transformed into the forms of the *mahat*, *ahaṅkāra*, and so forth.
Consequently, how can there be an initial conjunction between these two? And in the absence of that, how can there be a disjunction preceded by it? Thus, and so on...

Because conjunction and disjunction are impossible, the primary cause (pradhāna) lacks causality with respect to the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha); and for this reason, the knowledge concerning it is false. 14½.

*Dīpikā*: Now, in order to explain the sūtra beginning with "atha sāṃkhyajñāne'pi," [the author] first presents the Sāṃkhya doctrine briefly, even outside the formal sūtras, starting with "athaivam" and so forth. Thus, then, the followers of Kapila...

They believe that the Puruṣa is indeed a non-agent and naturally pure; because prior to the arising of discriminative knowledge, he is not independent when engaged in activity for the sake of another, Prakṛti alone—the supreme cause—presents herself as an object of enjoyment through her own effects, consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, in the form of Mahat and the rest. It is she who does so.

This is called *saṃsāra*. Nor should it be argued that the activity of an insentient entity is not logical, for we observe activity in things such as magnets in the drawing of iron and so forth. Consequently, when there arises in him—preceded by the knowledge of the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*—the realization of the difference between the intellect (*sattva*) and the self (*puruṣa*), then [he attains liberation].
Prakṛti ceases [its activity] toward each individual because it has been experienced as an object of enjoyment; that itself is his liberation. As the Sāṃkhyas say:

"Just as a dancer, having exhibited herself on the stage, withdraws from the stage, so too does Prakṛti, having manifested herself to the Puruṣa, withdraw. And likewise: "There is nothing more subtle than Prakṛti."
This is my opinion: that once a person has seen [the Self] as it truly is, he does not come to see it again.

He explains the passage beginning with "even in the knowledge of Sāṃkhya" by saying "this is also the case even in the knowledge of Sāṃkhya," and so forth. To the question, "How, then, is there error on the part of the Sāṃkhyas?", he says "of the *kalās* and so forth," and so on. And those are the *tattvas*.

We shall explain later that these [entities] are established through their respective effects, as well as by means of inference and scripture. He demonstrates the very fact of being an effect with the words "this, therefore, is the meaning," and so forth. He states another refutation with the words "and this," and so forth. He says "therefore" and so forth in order to refute what was stated, namely, that "the person is indeed not an agent. || 14½ ||
Why is this so? He says:
"Because the enjoyer lacks the state of being an agent, and because [the object] possesses independence from the insentient. (15)

What purpose would there be for a non-enjoying *puruṣa* in having a body as the locus of enjoyment, sense-faculties as the instruments of enjoyment, sense-objects as the things to be enjoyed, and enjoyment itself as the fruit consisting of the experience of pleasure and pain? And since this is so...

Experience exists together with its locus and its instruments; therefore, the state of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtva) cannot be discarded. And how can he who is an enjoyer be a non-agent? For in one who is not an agent, the connection with instruments and so forth would be purposeless.
Since the very nature of consciousness consists in the essence of seeing and acting, then, by the rejection of agency, cognition (jñatva) is also rejected.

This [objection] is refuted because even for cognition, which is of the nature of an action, its status as an agent has not departed; for indeed, cognition is not possible for one who is not an agent. And for this reason, he states that the knowledge of the Sāṃkhya is false: "Because of independence, even though it is insentient. Thus, even the non-sentient *pradhāna*...

How could it proceed toward the performance of its effects independently, without being impelled by an intelligent agent? For even for an intelligent being, an activity such as that of a wood-boring insect in carving letters is not logical if devoid of conscious deliberation; how much less so for an insentient entity subject to transformation? And as for the sentient person in this case, he—
Since the agent is not independent [but dependent on material nature], this liberation is not desired for those abiding in primordial nature (prakṛti). || 15 ||
The *Dīpikā* [comments]: First, he states "not an enjoyer," and so forth, because the self's status as an enjoyer is directly perceived.
He then states "and since," and so forth, because agency is established precisely from being an enjoyer. This is because [agency] is never dissociated from consciousness (*caitanya*).
He states that agency is established through consciousness in the passage beginning with "consisting of vision and action," and so forth. This is the intended meaning:

the *puruṣa*, being of the nature of consciousness, is the agent; for it is he alone who is perceived as the cause of the engagement and disengagement of all other factors of action (*kāraka*). Regarding both engagement and disengagement, he is the sovereign of the factors of action, remaining himself unengaged.

"Or rather, that agent is called a 'doer' because he is engaged [in action]. Now, an objection: if agency were the soul's immersion in action, then it would be subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitā*), like the wind and so forth. To this we reply: no, for agency is not the immersion in action, by which there would follow the consequence of its being subject to transformation; rather, [agency consists] in [the soul's] relation to action...

It is simply the possession of power, as in the case of the magnet-stone and similar objects. For there is no entry of activity into the magnet-stone; rather, by its power, it is observed that the iron itself [is moved]. Likewise, there is no activity on the part of the Self, but by its power, experience is perceived in the body and so forth—thus there is no contradiction. If this is so, then [activity belongs] to Nature (prakṛti) alone, which consists of the body...

"Let there be its agency. To this he says: "That is incorrect," as expressed by [the words] "due to independence" (*svātantryāt*) and so forth; namely, "even though it is insentient," and so on. This is the meaning: for the body, which has the nature of *prakṛti*, cannot possess agency because it is insentient, like a jar or similar objects. [Objection: But surely even the insentient *pradhāna* possesses agency?

It is logical that the activity [of Nature] is directed toward the goal of the Puruṣa, just as in the case of milk. For it is observed that the milk of a cow and other animals proceeds spontaneously for the sake of the growth of its calf and so forth. As the Sāṃkhyas say: "Just as the activity of insentient milk is for the purpose of the growth of the calf, so [the activity of Nature] is for the purpose of the liberation of the Puruṣa."

"Thus is the activity of the Pradhāna. If this is so, since it is observed that insentient milk proceeds only when presided over by a sentient being such as a cow, then because the Pradhāna is likewise insentient, there must be a sentient impeller for it; therefore, the Pradhāna possesses no independence. [This applies] to the Puruṣa as well.

Since it is accepted as being inherently pure, activity directed toward it is not logical. Or, if there were such activity, it would have to proceed toward all [puruṣas] because there is no distinction;
thus, for the Sāṃkhyas, there would be no liberation at all. Furthermore, we shall explain later that inherent purity is not tenable for the puruṣa. || 15 ||
Commentary: Now, in order to refute the proponent of non-absolutism (anekāntavādin), the following is stated to present the Sāṃkhya position as the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
In this system, there are seven categories:
the living being (jīva), the non-living (ajīva), influx (āsrava), as well as restraint (saṃvara) and dissociation (nirjarā).
Both bondage and liberation as well. || 16 ||
And all these are adorned by the doctrine of manifoldness (syādvāda), because they are not characterized by absolute exclusivity. || 16 ||

In that regard, first, the category of the soul (*jīva*) is designated by the term *jīvāstikāya* (the ontological category of souls). It is threefold, distinguished as the eternally perfected, the liberated, and the bound. Here, the eternally perfected is the Arhat, known as the *jīvāstikāya*. One whose bonds of delusion and so forth have been removed is the liberated (*mukta*). One who is enveloped by those [bonds] is the bound (*baddha*).
The category of non-living entities (ajīva-padārtha) is also divided into four types: matter (pudgala), space (ākāśa), the principle of motion (dharma), and the principle of rest (adharma).

Among these, the first consists of the sixfold division: the four great elements beginning with earth, and the stationary (sthāvara) forms such as grass, shrubs, and creepers, along with the mobile (jaṅgama) forms consisting of those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from sweat, and those born from sprouts.
The category of souls (pudgalāstikāya). The category of space (ākāśāstikāya) is of two kinds:
the category of worldly space (lokākāśāstikāya) and the category of non-worldly space (alokākāśāstikāya).
The intermediate space within the worlds is known as the category of worldly space.
And that which is outside of them is proclaimed to be the body of the space of the non-world (alokākāśa).
The *dharmāstikāya* is distinct from the *pudgalāstikāya* and is the cause of upward movement (*abhyudaya*).
The *adharmāstikāya* also acts as its counteragent. This is the category of non-living entities (*ajīva*), which is of four kinds.
*Āsrava* is the functioning of the five sense organs, such as the eyes, each according to its own nature. Thus they have said: "Functioning..."

"The five fluctuations of the group beginning with the eye are constant and inconstant; this [stream] flows incessantly, and therefore it is called an 'influx' (āsrava) here. Thus, because meditation that has attained stability through the restraint of the senses consists in the cessation of influx (āsrava-nirodha).
It is called *saṃvara* because it restrains (*saṃvṛṇāti*) the influx (*āsrava*).

The accumulation of ascetic practices (*tapas*), such as climbing heated stones or plucking out one's nails and hair, which has exhausted its potency, is designated by the term *nirjarā*. The eightfold [karmic categories], beginning with delusion (*moha*), are the causes for wandering through various transformations (*saṃsāra*).
Bondage is so called because the qualities (guṇas) cause the obstruction of one's independence. And it has been said:
"This bondage of the soul, consisting of delusion and the other qualities, is imagined;
it is like [a bird] cast into a body of water while bound by an iron cage."
Just as the gourd sinks downward, so too does the living being with its bonds.
Thus, because all obscurations have been completely destroyed, liberation (*mokṣa*) is the attainment of sovereignty and the reaching of the supreme state. As they say:
"Just as a gourd floats when the iron cage [weighing it down] is severed."
"Likewise, through the destruction of delusion and the other [passions], the soul ascends to liberation;
endowed with qualities such as eternal consciousness and bliss, it remains [there].
These are the seven categories, which follow the doctrine of *syādvāda*. For instance:

To one who inquires whether the *jīva* exists prior to the assumption of a body or not, the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*) must be accepted: it may exist; it may not exist; it may both exist and not exist; it may be inexpressible;
it may exist and be inexpressible; it may not exist and be inexpressible; it may exist and... [and so forth].

"Nor is it both existent and inexpressible. For in this context, whatever is subject to inquiry must be resolved by way of its existence or non-existence. Therein, the resolution of contradictions—whether through expressibility or inexpressibility—must be effected by those who possess the unfailing Brahmāstra of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*).
What is it that is "unconquerable" here? It is that by which the entire world is made to wander through the speech of the *pudgala*, thinking "it exists" or "it does not exist.
Now, since a proponent of non-absolutism (*anaikāntavādin*) does not accept absolutism, he must necessarily accept the doctrine of non-absolutism; and thus—
[Objection: "In that case, since there is only one-sidedness (*ekānta*), how can there be the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) everywhere? [Response: This is not a fault.

For even in the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*), one-sidedness is not asserted. Thus: it may be non-absolutist; it may be absolutist; it may be both non-absolutist and absolutist; it may be inexpressible; and it may be both absolutist and inexpressible.
It may be manifold and inexpressible; it may be both absolute and manifold and inexpressible.

The *Dīpikā* introduces the commentary on the sūtra beginning with "here" (*iha*) with the words "now," and so forth. It explains that very [sūtra] with the words "therein," and so forth. [An objection: But why is there a description of the seven categories (*saptapadārtha*) here, when [the author] is intent upon refuting the proponents of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*)?

"It is improper [to say] that for one desiring to go to the ocean, going to the Himalayas is like [the goal]; that is not so. There is no fault, because after first demonstrating the incorrectness of the summary of the subject matter already stated, this is said in order to demonstrate the incorrectness of the proof for that [summary] which follows upon it. (16½)
Commentary: To refute this point even briefly, he says: "That very thing is existent, that very thing is non-existent..."
By what means is this [duality] measured? || 17 ||

The statement that "it may exist" and "it may not exist" is inconsistent; for no one with an unerring mind, when perceiving any given object as existent by virtue of its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), could at that very same moment understand it to be non-existent in an absolute sense. Indeed, who with a deluded intellect would perceive what is manifesting before them as "existent"?

One should form the cognition that "this [existence] does not exist" in the case of things such as a jar which serve as counter-examples; for when that [existence] is absent— being devoid of both manifestation and description— the determination of existence cannot arise,
since affirmation and negation, in the form of presence and absence, acquire their own nature only through mutual exclusion.

For even non-existence, though its birth is obtained through the impossibility of that [existence], would not be non-existence at all if it were accompanied by that very existence; for its own nature is established only by the sublation of that [existence]. Likewise, existence too would not be existence if it were non-different from the non-existence that negates itself. 17

The *Dīpikā* explains the sūtra beginning with "that very [thing]" (*tadeva*) by means of the passage beginning with "it might exist" (*syādasti*). To the question "Why would it be improper?", he says "for not... (*na hi*), and so forth. He elaborates on this very point with the passage beginning "who indeed... (*kaḥ kila*), and so forth. || 17 ||
Commentary: Now, it might be argued that a jar exists in its own nature as a jar, but does not exist in the nature of another, such as a non-jar;
thus, its being both existent and non-existent has been stated. But that is not tenable. What exactly would be established by this much? That the jar—

It exists as the nature of a jar; [it is said] that "there is no cloth in the jar. This is exactly what is intended. Since it does not exist there by virtue of not having that nature, this jar—which is distinct from the cloth—is established as being indeed other.
Thus he says:
If it is something other than existent and something other than non-existent, then in this way there is the fallacy of proving what is already established.

Now, one might object: just as a jar performs its own function by means of its own nature (*svātmanā*), so too it should perform that same effect by means of the nature of a cloth (*paṭātmanā*). Yet it does not do so; therefore, it does not exist as the nature of a cloth. If it did not exist even as its own nature, then it would not perform its own function either. Therefore, it both exists and [does not exist].

And it has been stated that "it does not exist. Thus, in this way, pot-ness and non-pot-ness are mutually non-different; for if there were a distinction between them, the persistence of their respective cognitions and designations would not occur. Furthermore, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "the pot and the non-pot. Since this [coreferentiality] does exist, this entity possesses both natures sequentially.
"Carrying the denotation of that word [‘pot’], it would be both a pot and a non-pot; thus there is no contradiction.

This too is incorrect, because there is no such thing as non-difference. To explain: the word "non-pot" must be either a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), meaning "it is not a pot," or an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*), meaning "something other than a pot, such as a cloth."

In the first alternative, when it is said that "it would be both a jar and a non-jar," because the jar and the non-jar are not distinct, the intended meaning is that the very absence of the jar is the jar itself. If this were accepted, even the absence of the sun would be the sun itself; and that being the case, there would be fear even of its absence, just as one fears a snake.

In both cases—where there is a snake or where there is no spreading [of poison]—the perception would be exactly the same. Even on the view of relative negation (*paryudāsa*), "non-potness" is said to be something distinct from potness, such as clothness and so forth;
for that is indeed different from the pot. For if there were no difference, then even in the case of pots and the like, there would be the cognition and designation of "cloth."
[Otherwise] there would be a contradiction; furthermore, even in the case of a jar and the like, the cognition "this is a jar" would not occur when [the jar] is clearly perceived.
Therefore, there is no identity between the jar and the non-jar, and thus existence and non-existence do not have a single substratum. || 17½ ||
The objection that "one thing is existent and another is non-existent" constitutes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*); thus he says, "But surely," and so forth.
He explains the passage beginning with "In this way" as being the response to that. Regarding the phrase "the persistence of the cognition and designation of that":
it refers to the persistence of the cognition and designation of a jar. Furthermore, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
The meaning is that the co-referentiality of existence and non-existence pertains only to the object, such as a jar. || 17½ ||
Furthermore,
the wise also say that the non-existent is the lowest and the existent is the best.
Because of their mutual dependence, neither exists in isolation; therefore, both are established [only in relation to one another]. || 18½ ||

Commentary: Furthermore, even that object which is denoted by the words "existent" and "non-existent," and which takes the form of the superior and the inferior, is not designated as being in one and the same place by those who know it; for its objects are distinct. Indeed, that which is inferior...
It can indeed be said that "this alone is superior," for this is precisely what constitutes the distinction between entities:

namely, the attribution of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*). Now, it might be thought that this quality of being superior or inferior is possible in a single thing by virtue of relative dependence (*apekṣābalāt*), just as this Devadatta is handsome in comparison to Yajñadatta.

"But in relation to Caitra, he is formless. If that is so, then both Yajñadatta’s inferiority and Caitra’s superiority are obtained as distinct [only] through that very relativity. Furthermore, since that pair is relative, it is unreal; for relativity itself is not real. Indeed, if it were real in substance...

What is the purpose [of dependence] regarding that which already exists? Because its existence is already established, it has no need for anything else. As they have said: "How can every existent entity, being independent, require anything? Furthermore, there is nothing to be done by dependence with respect to an object whose existence has not yet been attained.
Because that [non-existence] is itself non-existent, dependence upon it is untenable. This has been stated:
"Dependence does not belong to existing things, because they are already established; nor does it belong to non-existing things, because they are not yet established.
Thus, in no way whatsoever is the identity of existence and non-existence possible. (18½)

The *Dīpikā* explains the passage beginning with "asajjaghanyām" and so forth by means of the passage beginning with "yadapi" and so forth. It explains the passage beginning with "atha matam" and so forth as the response to the objection raised by the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) in the phrase "tadapekṣāt" and so forth; thus it is [explained] in this manner.
"If that is so," and so forth. || 18½ ||
If, moreover, the existence of both the existent and the non-existent is considered always more logical, then [one must accept this] for fear of the confusion of karma.
And they declare that it is all-pervading. || 19½ ||
Because the insentient [matter] lacks the knowledge of the relationship between the universal and its particulars. || 20 ||

Commentary: Since that [self], which is considered to be both existent and non-existent prior to the body, is all-pervasive, a confusion of karmas with other individuals is possible; for if it were all-pervasive, there would be a commingling of scattered karmas.

What is the basis for the restriction regarding the enjoyers? Since those [enjoyers] are non-pervasive, the very category of bondage—consisting of delusion and so forth—is established individually as their regulator.
Out of fear of the confusion of karma, those mindless ones of poor intellect proclaimed that they are non-pervasive. Why?
He states that these [beings] possess dull intellect because they lack knowledge of the relationship between the universal and its opposite:
the relationship of the self with the universal— which is beginningless and all-pervasive—
is common to all times due to its existence at every moment, whereas the relationship with the other occurs only upon liberation.

For those proponents of the person (pudgalavādins), there is no correct understanding—that is, no right realization—of that connection which exists between such [a self] and those [aggregates]. For if they possessed such realization, they would not conceive of it in such an irrational manner.
This is because [they fail to understand] the nature of the self as being innate, pervasive, and obstructed by the snares of delusion and the like.
The admission that the mind is non-pervasive by its very nature is a contradiction [of the opponent's position]. || 20 ||

The *Dīpikā* explains the passage beginning with "that action" (*tatkarma*) and so forth by means of the passage beginning with "of that" (*tasya*) and so forth. What is meant is this: since the all-pervading self (*ātman*) is present everywhere, it would follow that it is joined not only with the fruit of its own actions but also with the fruit of the actions of others.
Thus, even that [external object] would become something to be experienced; and consequently, the rule that one is the experiencer of the fruits of one's own karma would be untenable.
Therefore, since that [rule] cannot otherwise be established, this *pudgala* must be accepted as being all-pervasive (*vibhu*).
Furthermore, because there is no perception even of an atom’s worth outside the body, it is established that the self is coextensive with the body alone.
Thus it has been asserted by the proponents of non-absolutism (anekāntavādins). He states that what they have said is indeed incorrect, beginning with the words "of the insentient" (*acetasaḥ*).
And he states the reason for their speaking incorrectly, beginning with the words "the universal" (*sāmānya*), etc. This is the intended meaning:

for if the self were not all-pervading (*avibhu*), then how could an action performed in one place—such as by someone residing in Kaśmīr—produce a result in another location, such as the Deccan (*dakṣiṇāpatha*)?

That [the soul] is seen being enjoyed is not tenable, because, being formless, movement is impossible for it, just as it is for space. Now, it might be argued: "In some way the *pudgala* is indeed both material and immaterial. How so?
In this philosophical system, there may be the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda), by which [the world] is established.

That is incorrect, because corporeality and incorporeality exist by way of mutual exclusion. As they say: "Two contradictory properties, residing in a single locus at the same time, bring about their own annihilation through their mutual destruction. But how is there no perception [of the self] outside the body? To this, he says:

"Due to delusion and so forth," etc.: because it is obscured by impurities, it is manifested only where there is the presence of a manifestor such as the body. "Because that is contradictory": because it contradicts [the property of] non-pervasiveness. || 20 ||
For instance: how could that which was previously non-pervasive become otherwise at the end?
If it possesses properties such as expansion and so forth,
then there follows a succession of faults.

Commentary: How can that which was previously non-pervasive during the state of saṃsāra become pervasive in liberation? Furthermore, it is improper to accept its non-pervasiveness at that [earlier] time.

For in this way, there would be no distinction between the transmigrating soul and the liberated one. Now, if it is admitted that such a nature of expansion and contraction belongs to it—namely, that it undergoes contraction in the state of transmigration and expansion in the state of liberation—even from that, a succession of many defects, such as mutability and insentience, would follow; therefore, [this view is not tenable].
In no way whatsoever can the doctrine of those who maintain that things are either existent or non-existent be established.
The *Dīpikā*: Demonstrating the very contradiction, he explains the passage beginning with "prāk" (before) and so forth.
[Objection: But was it not stated that there is a confusion of fruits due to the confusion of actions? [Response: That is not so; for each individual person...

The cause of action is indeed distinct from the desire to act; since that [desire] differs, the difference in actions and the difference in their results are established—thus, this [objection] is trivial. || 21 ||
Now, in order to refute the liberation demonstrated by the school of the Six Categories (Ṣaṭpadārthika), he says: "From the thorough knowledge of the six categories,
false knowledge ceases."
Attachment, aversion, and the sense of "mine-ness" are its specific qualities; therefore [it is distinct]. || 22 ||
Since those [qualities] born from contact with the body gradually cease,
that liberation is of the nature of insentience.
Then why is the corpse not released?

Because it is accepted that the knowledge of the true nature of the similarities and differences among substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*),
there follows the cessation of ignorance through the correct knowledge of the six categories, beginning with substance.

Liberation is that state which occurs when, through the subsiding of defects such as passion and the rest, there is a gradual cessation of the nine qualities of the self— namely, intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression— due to their being produced by conjunction with the body.

When the intellect and other faculties cease, since the self—deprived of them—ceases to possess limited knowledge, it is admitted to assume the state of insentience (*jaḍatā*). Consequently, why is even a corpse not considered liberated? The point is that the corpse, too, is devoid of qualities such as the intellect and lacks desire, cognition, and so forth.

Dīpikā: But then, having conceived the incorrectness of that liberation called the attainment of the "upper state" as taught therein, as well as its means such as lying on heated stones and so forth, [one concludes] that its obscuration is *mala*.
If you postulate that, then it is better that he himself be inert; for in this way, one does not postulate many unseen things.
It might be argued: "Consciousness is his very nature as a quality, just as luminosity is a quality of fire.
That too is not correct, because that consciousness is observed in him only when there is the presence of the collection of causes such as the body and the sense organs.

And since it is not observed in the absence of that [activity], it is established that [the self] is produced by that alone—just like a jar or similar object produced by the causal complex of a potter and so forth—and thus the self is inherently insentient (*jaḍa*). Furthermore, as long as the body exists, there is no absolute cessation of pleasure and pain for it. As it is heard: "Indeed, not..."

"For one who possesses a body, there is the presence of the pleasant and the unpleasant; however, for one who is indeed bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch him. And since that [bodiless state] results from the cessation of false knowledge through the realization of reality (tattvajñāna) supported by the means of liberation, there is an absolute cessation of suffering due to the separation from the body and so forth. This very point is stated in the verse beginning with "substance" (dravya), etc.

He states the refutation with the words "tataḥ" and so forth. For here, at the time of the cognition of objects such as the body, does that which illuminates them—the nature of the cognition consisting of joy, sorrow, and so on—manifest or not?
First of all, it is not tenable to say that it does not manifest, because that would contradict one's own experience. Now, suppose it indeed manifests.

If it is argued that this is merely Buddhist cognition (*bauddha-jñāna*), that is incorrect. Because it manifests as the illuminator of various objects at all times and because it is the enjoyer of pleasure and so forth, this is indeed the Self (*ātman*), since such is its nature. For this very reason, even when there is a succession of different objects, it remains stable by virtue of always apprehending those respective objects, as if they were simultaneous.
Manifesting [itself], its cognition is not produced by the respective causal complexes of the sense organs and so forth; rather, it is simply the very nature of consciousness itself.

However, by virtue of those respective causal complexes, it possesses a specific nature for the apprehension of this or that object. Thus, always manifesting as the conscious self alone, it is non-inert (ajaḍa).
Thus the Self is established; however, because its consciousness is veiled by impurity (*mala*), it does not function toward objects without the body and so forth. As it is said in the *Mataṅga*:
"The innate attribute of consciousness is that [consciousness] itself, yet it is veiled by beginningless impurity."

Consequently, even in that system, the lack of clarity regarding the collection of entities (*vastu-saṃgraha*) is established. Furthermore, since they are devoid of cognition and other faculties, even wood and such things—which are insentient by nature—would find the state of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) more preferable than liberation (*mokṣa*). Thus, the liberation described by them is incorrect. For this very reason:
The means for that [liberation] is also incorrect. || 23 ||
Commentary: Now, with the desire to refute the liberation of the Buddhists, he first sets forth their doctrine and then refutes it:
"Of the karma and so forth that manifest consciousness..."
Because it is momentary, it is manifested again and again; thus, it is considered by others to be "momentary" as if it were being born anew at every instant. (24)

Consciousness is knowledge in the form of the grasper, that very consciousness which arises from the connection with the operation of the manifestor— the cause of manifestation— such as action or the act of grasping; or else, it arises from the object of perception, such as a jar or a cloth, and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," [it includes] the instrument, such as the eye.
Because the manifestors, such as light and so forth, lack extreme stability, [the effect] appears—that is, becomes manifest—as if being produced anew at every moment.

The meaning is this: from the perspective of the doctrine of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*) which will be explained hereafter, for entities that undergo manifestation and concealment, [this occurs] through a distinction in their functional activity (*vyāpāra*) and through distinctions of place, time, and so forth.

Others maintain that because it lacks stability, even that respective cognition is momentary, being manifested again and again through the distinctions of its respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and that this alone constitutes valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As they say:
"There is no eternal means of valid knowledge, because validity arises from the correspondence with a real object."
Because it is impermanent due to the impermanence of its objects of cognition, it lacks stability and arises sequentially. Thus [it is said].
Indeed, this very consciousness alone is momentary, consisting of the manifestation of various objects, and is established by experience;
however, no self exists apart from this, because nothing distinct from cognition appears as a separate entity.
As they say: "This single nature of consciousness is a transformation into manifold forms such as joy, despondency, and so forth."

"We see that we may apply designations there as we please. Thus, within consciousness itself—which is momentary like the flow of a stream of water—the notion of stability is superimposed by conceptual construction due to the delusion arising from the production of a continuous succession of similar moments. This is the view of a self produced by ignorance. As it has been said:
"Your effort for the sake of false superimposition [occurs] even though there is no experiencer.

When there is grasping at a self (*ātmagraha*), because one conceives of "otherness" in that which is other than it, there is the distinction between self and other. And from that, since harmful states such as attachment and aversion arise, the Blessed One, the Sugata, taught that grasping at a self is bondage.
The cultivation of selflessness has been taught. As it has been said: "When there is a notion of self, there arises the conception of 'other';

from the division between self and other, attachment and aversion arise. Bound by these two, all defects are produced. Furthermore, the permanence of a self that is accepted [as existing] is not tenable; for whatever exists is momentary.
Because for that which is not momentary, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is impossible either successively or simultaneously, existence itself is unestablished. As they say:
"That which is capable of causal efficiency is here the ultimately real (*paramārthasat*)."
"Therefore, non-momentary things are non-existent, because of the contradiction with [the possibility of] succession and simultaneity.
Likewise, would an eternal entity perform a causal function (arthakriyā) successively or simultaneously? First of all, its successive performance is not tenable.
Since this [entity] is unchanging, unarisen, stable, and of a single nature,

why does it not perform at that very moment the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) that is to be accomplished at a later time? For it cannot perform what is to be done at another occasion by means of a different nature.

Because intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is of a single form. For if there were a change in intrinsic nature, that which possesses it would also perish, since it is not distinct from it; and thus, it would be impermanent. Now, if it is argued: "That entity certainly performs its causal function provided its auxiliary causes (sahakārin) are present; it does not perform it when they are absent."

"It is not subject to censure"—this is not so. If its auxiliaries (sahakārin) do nothing for it, why does it depend upon them? If, however, they do something, is that which they produce distinct from it or non-distinct? If it produces something distinct, what need has it for those [auxiliaries]? If it produces something non-distinct from it, then that [effect]...

Thus, it follows that what is done by these auxiliary causes? Furthermore, the production of this permanent entity is not tenable, because that which exists with such an inherent nature arises solely from its own causes, and it is impossible to produce again what has already been produced.
Now, [it might be argued that] these auxiliaries produce an excellence (*atiśaya*) in this entity which possesses a stable nature, by means of which...
"It performs causal efficiency at a later time"—this too is incorrect.
Because that which possesses an enhanced nature is necessarily distinct from that which does not possess such an enhancement, the very notion of a single, stable nature is destroyed.
For instance, if an enhancement arises from auxiliary causes, then...
One must admit that what has arisen previously, possessing a nature in which no excellence has been infused, perishes by its very own nature;

for since its nature is non-perishable, even a cause of destruction would be incapable of acting upon it. Alternatively, if its nature were to arise as perishable, then [a cause of destruction] would be redundant, because there would be no difference in that nature itself.

"Every moment" refers to momentariness. Thus, in this way, there is no causal efficiency for a permanent entity either sequentially or simultaneously. For even if it were to perform causal efficiency simultaneously, it would not cease from that nature, because its very nature is exclusively stability; [otherwise] there would be a cessation of that nature.

The "loss of intrinsic nature" (svabhāvahāni) is precisely momentariness. Now, if it is argued that this [entity] does not possess another intrinsic nature, but rather simply does not act, and that this is indeed the maturation (vipāka) of the effect—namely, the impossibility of performing an action once it has been performed—that too is incorrect. For, insofar as it does not perform any purposeful activity (arthakriyā), its very existence (sattā) is difficult to establish.

Since it has been stated here that "that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is what is ultimately real," and since its nature is defined by the performance of causal efficiency, its nature as non-performance would be entirely different. How, then, could this not involve a connection with another nature? Furthermore, even if it were performing [actions] simultaneously and incessantly...

If it were to act [only at that time], then because there would be no difference in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would follow that it must perform all purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*) at all times; therefore, it is logical that this cognition is strictly momentary. Thus, the proof of an eternal self distinct from that [cognition] is not established—this is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). || 24 ||

The *Dīpikā* introduces the sūtra beginning with "cidvyañjakasya" [and so forth]. The meaning is that by the words beginning with "atha" and ending with "paraiḥ," it introduces the refutation, stating "it refutes. [This refers to the phrase] "yogasaṃgrahaṇādeḥ."
"Yoga" is the contact between the sense organ and its object. "Comprehension" (*saṃgrahaṇa*) is the reflective awareness of that [object] through cognition and so forth.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "of action, etc.," the objects and so forth mentioned in the sūtra are included. For this very reason, he explains it in another form with the words "or rather," and so on;
he clarifies this very point with the words "this is the meaning," and so forth. Now, as for the Buddhist...

The momentariness belongs only to cognition, whose nature consists in the apprehension of the object (*grāhya-parāmarśa*), and not to the self, which is of the nature of the subject (*grāhaka*). For this very reason, he says "For consciousness alone... and so forth. The meaning is that there are not two perceptions: one of the object and another of the self. But how, then, does the appearance of stability arise for that [consciousness]? To this [he replies]:

Thus he says: "In perception," and so forth. He states that even if one accepts a self distinct from cognition, its stability is not tenable: "And not of that which is accepted," and so forth. He elaborates on this very point with:
"For instance," and so forth. || 24 ||
Commentary:
As for the established conclusion (siddhānta), that [is not so], because of the experience of that non-existent karma.
Because there is recollection of past experience. (24½)
Therefore, this momentariness of cognition and the acceptance of the doctrine of selflessness (nairātmyavāda) are not tenable;
for there is the manifestation of a self that is established through self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), which is of a stable nature and directly perceived. [Objection:
But surely, because one is deceived by the production of a continuous succession of similar successive moments...

It was stated that stability is superimposed; however, that is incorrect, because superimposition is untenable due to the contradiction of action within itself. Furthermore, for the purpose of proving momentary destruction, since the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—whether successive or simultaneous—is contradictory for that which is non-momentary, existence itself is unestablished; therefore, whatever exists...

The formulation of the inference that "everything is momentary" is incorrect because it is sublated by the direct perception characterized by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Furthermore, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since the experience of all existing things as non-momentary is established through direct perception; for everything that exists is [perceived] as being momentary.

When pervasion has been demonstrated, because a heterogeneous example (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) that is non-momentary and ultimately real is impossible, and because a purely positive reason (*kevalānvayin*) lacks probative power due to the failure to demonstrate its exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*), this reason called "existence" (*sattva*) is also contradictory (*viruddha*).

This is because the pervasion is established with respect to things such as jars, which—by virtue of being non-momentary, the opposite of the probandum—are always performing causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Furthermore, there is this other reason for establishing that pervasion: "because for a permanent entity, causal efficiency is incompatible with both succession and simultaneity."

That too is untenable because its locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*). For you do not accept any eternal entity upon which this reason (*hetu*) could be established. Nor is it possible for a non-momentary object, such as a jewel, to manifest various objects situated in multiple locations sequentially.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction whatsoever in [consciousness] simultaneously illuminating jars, cloths, and so forth located within a single house. Moreover, momentary consciousness is not capable of performing a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) that is to be accomplished over multiple moments;
for it is impossible for that which perishes immediately after arising to perform such an action. Nor can stability be superimposed [upon it].
Capable of accomplishing its respective functions.

1. The meaning is that this is the reason [for its non-existence], because for that which is eternal, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is contradictory whether it occurs successively or simultaneously.
And because it has already been stated that such superimposition upon itself is untenable, [the object] to be superimposed—

Furthermore, because it is not a real entity (*avastu*), it lacks any connection to causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). And if it were a real entity, there would be no difference [between us], since we also accept that cognition in its stable form is identical with the nature of the self (*ātman*). Moreover, a continuum of existence (*sattāsantāna*) distinct from the momentary is not perceived in any way whatsoever.

Therefore, the stability of this conscious self (*cidātman*) is established as a matter of fact, because otherwise the observed connection with the performance of actions would be inexplicable. For this reason as well, its momentariness is untenable;
for if consciousness were not continuous into subsequent moments, the experience of the results of action would be impossible, since the action [would perish] through its fruition. By whomsoever...
For we observe that actions such as service, agriculture, and so forth, once performed, have a specific experiencer;

and it is logical to infer the unseen (adṛṣṭa) in accordance with what is seen. If it is accepted that there is one and the same undivided experiencer even when the body and other factors differ between two births, then indeed the enjoyment of the fruits of action remains uncontradicted. Otherwise, [it would not].

If an action known as the *caityavandanā* were performed by one person, yet another person were to experience its fruit, such as rebirth in heaven, then the unavoidable consequence of "attaining what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and "the loss of what was done" (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*) would follow. As it is said in the *Mataṅga*: "How could another experience the maturation of an action performed by someone else?"

"One attains [the result] due to the weakness of reasoning. Now, it might be argued that this is not a fault, because the experience of a worldly action can occur in another life through a continuum of cognition (*jñāna-santāna*) even when no body has been obtained. That is incorrect, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of a continuum of cognition that is devoid of a body.

The proof of the continuum of consciousness (*vijñānasantāna*) through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the experience of the fruits of karma, and the experience of the fruits of karma through the proof of that [continuum]—this is untenable if cognition is unstable. Therefore, the claim that "cognition is momentary" is incorrect. Why? He says: "Because of the recollection of past experience. [That is,] because that which has passed away...

Memory arises from the recollection of that which was experienced. For when a self of stable nature is accepted as the one who synthesizes both times, then memory—in the form of the non-forgetting of an experienced object—is logically possible; but not if [the self] were momentary.

For it is not possible for a present moment, or a moment occurring at another time, to remember the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth that was experienced by a previous moment, because that [present moment] is distinct from it— just as a son does not remember what was experienced by Devadatta. And yet, it is observed that what was experienced in childhood and so forth [is remembered].

That which is remembered across states such as youth and old age—this very recollection of past experience refutes the momentariness of consciousness, but it does not infer a self (*ātman*) of a stable nature;
for that [self], being established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), has its own experience as its sole means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, in this way:
Because of the experience of the results of karma and because of the recollection of past experiences, momentariness is not tenable for consciousness. (24½)

The *Dīpikā* explains the sūtra beginning with "That is not so" (*tadasat*), etc., starting with "This very [point]," etc. Regarding the phrase "of cognition" (*saṃvedanasya*), it refers to that which has the nature of a grasper, and not to the Buddhist [cognition], because the latter is admitted to be precisely unstable. That very [point]...
"He shows that it is established by self-awareness" means that,

distinct from the unstable Buddhist cognition which consists of the reflection upon the object (grāhya), the subject-aspect (grāhaka) in the form of synthetic unification (anusandhāna) is indeed established by self-awareness as something stable.

He states the refutation regarding momentariness with the words "Moreover" (*apica*) and so forth; the meaning is this: if the self were momentary, then the study of the scriptures and the performance of the actions prescribed therein, such as the worship of caityas, would be impossible.
[Objection: But even if consciousness is momentary...
1. The meaning is that [the effect] is experienced in a single moment.
He states, "And [an entity] distinct from momentariness," etc., because causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is possible for its continuum.
Consequently, if there is a connection between the subsequent moment and the preceding moment, there is indeed stability; if there is no connection, [there is no causal efficiency].

"Because purposeful action is otherwise impossible. Having established the stability of the self through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and because the performance of ritual acts would otherwise be impossible, he says "and for this reason as well," etc., to establish its stability because the experience and enjoyment of the fruits of those acts would otherwise be impossible. Furthermore, the phrase "because of the recollection of past experience" introduces another supporting reason.

Therefore, beginning with the words "ataśca" (and thus), he demonstrates that very point by means of a question, starting with "kutaḥ" (why?), and clarifies that same point with the words "yadā hi" (for when), and so forth. || 24½ ||
He states that very point: "Persistence [of the self] would not exist if there were destruction without residue; neither from memory nor from karma. (25)

Since moments of consciousness perish without pause—like mustard seeds falling upon the point of a needle—and do not endure, the occurrence of memory cannot be established as explained above; nor can that of karma.
Enough, then, with this obsession with momentary destruction, which confounds one's position with such baseless imaginings.
The *Dīpikā* says: "He explains this very point with the half-verse beginning with 'sthitir' (the state)," thus stating: "tadevāha" (he says that very thing). || 25 ||
Commentary: Furthermore, there is this other defect here, namely:
that which is characterized by destruction departs.
There is no affliction even in liberation;
nor is there any experience whatsoever [of it].
Therefore, the state of worldly existence is better than that.

Would your liberation consist in the arising of a continuum of pure consciousness, or would it be of the nature of the extinguishing of a lamp? In the first case, there would be no cessation even in liberation of the affliction characterized by momentary destruction as you have imagined it. But in the second case...
Since it is of the nature of the extinction of a lamp and because consciousness is impossible, there is no experience whatsoever;

therefore, for the Buddhists, the state of cyclic existence is better than such a liberation—which consists in the destruction of consciousness and is as easily attained by pieces of wood or walls. Thus, enough with the desire for such a liberation!
*Dīpikā*:

Having thus demonstrated the lack of clarity regarding the summary of the subject matter (*vastusaṃgraha*), he introduces the sūtra beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiṃca*) and so forth, in order to show the lack of clarity regarding the liberation described therein. "In this regard" (*atra*).

In the Buddhist view, it is established precisely by the proof of the stability of the self that the lack of clarity regarding the means to liberation, such as the meditation on selflessness (*nairātmya-bhāvanā*), is proven. || 26 ||
Commentary: Thus far, regarding the systems of Vedānta, Sāṃkhya, and those based on the categories of existence and non-existence,
