because they were composed by those who do not perceive the whole of reality, there is a lack of clarity and coherence in their summary of the actual state of things.

Having raised this point, he says [the following] in order to state that since this same situation applies even to other philosophical systems, those who are dogmatically attached to them do not possess unsurpassed liberation (*niratiśaya-niḥśreyasa*).
Relying on such views held by those deluded by ignorance, the evil-minded long for liberation.
Like one who seeks fire from a firefly. || 27 ||

Those of unrefined intellect, who— based on the doctrines and scriptures of other systems of thought propounded by those deluded by ignorance— lack any understanding of the reality that, from the perspective of ultimate truth, consists of Śiva, Śakti, Vidyeśvara, and so forth as things to be accepted, and of karma, mala, māyā, and so forth as things to be rejected; [they are thus described].

They are like those who desire fire from a firefly or those wishing to obtain light from a glowworm; just as their efforts are in vain, so too theirs become fruitless labors—this is the meaning. || 27 ||

The *Dīpikā* introduces the sūtra beginning with "ityādi" (and so forth) with the words "tadiyatā" and so on; the phrase "of other systems as well" refers to the Pāñcarātra and others included by the word "ādi" (etcetera). || 27 ||
The functions [of the intellect].
For instance:
that which is the isolation (*kaivalya*) resulting from the discrimination between the Spirit (*puruṣa*) and Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*).
Or rather, having realized that all is Brahman, one attains cessation;
for whatever liberations are born of bondage, they all return to differentiation upon creation. (28)

This includes that liberation which Kapila conceived as resulting from the discernment between the Spirit (puruṣa) and Primordial Matter (prakṛti); that attainment of Brahman which occurs when the conceptualization of duality is abandoned by realizing "all this is indeed Brahman"; and those liberations produced by the fetters which are accepted by certain followers of the Pāñcarātra and other systems. As they say: "They are masters..."
"Kṛṣṇa, Aniruddha, the one whose banner bears the makara, and the son of Rohiṇī were born from the Supreme Prakṛti.
Or as it is said by those who maintain that time alone is the sole agent:
"Time creates all beings; Time destroys all creatures."
"When others are asleep, he remains awake; for time is indeed difficult to overcome.
Or as some say:
"The mind itself is saṃsāra when it is defiled by the afflictions such as passion and the like."
That very same [reality], when liberated from that [conditioning], is designated as "liberation."

These, indeed, because they take the form of bonds (*pāśa*) by acting as the binders of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), time (*kāla*), intellect (*buddhi*), and so forth, are called "liberations born of bonds" (*pāśajā muktyaḥ*); at the beginning of creation, they undergo differentiation, meaning they perish. As it is said in the *Mataṅga*:
Therefore, by the word "Pradhāna," the insentient reality has been described;
for those whose conviction is established, there exists nothing beyond it, nor anything inferior to it.
"O tiger among sages, those who are liberated do not return to a downward state.
Likewise:
"For those who are attached to the objects of grasping, rebirth is certain. But for them...

For those who possess such practice, the continuous darkness of ignorance does not perpetually shroud the internal organ; rather, through the gradual expansion of discernment, they will at some point become recipients of the Supreme Lord’s grace.
And so it has been said in the venerable *Pauṣkarapārameśvara*:
"Men never attain liberation through their own power alone, except by the grace of the Lord Śiva, the remover of all inauspiciousness. (28)
The *Dīpikā* says: "By the sūtra beginning with 'That which is kaivalya' (YS 4.34), he clarifies this very point," and so on, starting with "tathāhi.

Therein, by means of the first half [of the verse], [the author] speaks of the aforementioned liberations characterized by absorption into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*) and the attainment of Brahman.

The conclusion of the refutation: with the latter half [of the verse], the refutation of the liberations of the Pāñcarātra and other systems is presented. He demonstrates that these liberations of the Pāñcarātra and so forth, as well as those of certain supersensuous theists, are produced by fetters, in the passage beginning "these, it is said," and so on; therein, it is indeed said of her named Nārāyaṇī...

It has been stated that [the Pradhāna] is indeed not independent because it is accepted as the material cause (*upādāna*) of another nature and because it is insentient (*acetana*). Furthermore, since time (*kāla*) also possesses a threefold form consisting of the past and so forth, it is insentient; thus, due to its multiplicity, it is non-eternal and therefore lacks causality. As for the mind (*citta*), its insentience is likewise established because, like the elements and so forth, it is manifest (*vyakta*).

For those who have attained that respective [level], liberation consists solely in the limit of the dissolution of that respective [state]. Consequently, because impurity (*mala*) and karma persist at the time of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), there is again transmigration; this is the meaning. If this were so, the possibility of their liberation would never occur. He says "no," beginning with "But for them" (*teṣāṃ tu*); when the ripening of impurity occurs, even for them...
Liberation is accomplished through the grace of Śiva. || 18 ||

Commentary: Now, if liberation as described in other systems is unreal—as previously stated—then what is its distinction from that [unreality] here? To explain this, he speaks regarding the establishment of these two: [the nature of] bondage and liberation.
1. There is a variant reading: *saṃjñāvadhireva*.
When Śiva has attained perfection, he shines at the summit; others [shine] below that.
Once liberated, the foremost of men ascends during the process of emanation and does not descend again.
Having supported all things by his own power, he remains forever impelled as the Lord of All.

In this scripture, he who has attained perfection becomes a partaker of those various enjoyments brought about by the diverse sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*) inherent in the manifold worlds, and thus possesses supreme excellence. As it was said by the venerable Bṛhaspati:
"Whatever majesty exists in Paramaśiva—unparalleled, imperishable, and inconceivable—that [majesty]..."

"Thus, when the circle of bonds has been destroyed, the majesty [of the Self] becomes perfected. Furthermore, it has been stated that liberation—which consists of the dissolution of consciousness into Brahman as accepted by other systems, or the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, and so forth—does not possess such qualities. However, he who is liberated according to this system...

The meaning is that because the authority (*adhikāra*) of the binding causes—namely, impurity (*mala*), karma, *māyā*, the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), and the power of obstruction (*nirodhaśakti*)—has ceased, he does not descend again at the commencement of creation, nor does he become a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*). What, then, does he do? He says: "all misfortunes" (*viśvānarthān*), meaning those [misfortunes] whose manifestation has ceased.

Because he possesses the capacity for omniscience and omnipoience, and because his majesty is equal to that of Śiva, that liberated soul (muktātmā), although presiding over all objects by his own splendor, does nothing, as there remains nothing further to be done. If it is argued that he was incapable of action prior to liberation and remains of that same nature even when liberated, then what is his [attainment] in liberation?

This is the distinction, this is the distinction: because he is not impelled—that is, not urged—by the Supreme Lord, the Ruler of All, at that time, he remains so. One might ask: "Is he unimpelled only for some period of time? No; it says "always" (*sarvadā*), meaning that the venerable Śiva is forever one who does not urge him.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Mṛgendravṛtti*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Vidyākaṇṭha.
[The] Dīpikā.

"In the Śaiva [system], it is established," and so forth. He states "here" and so on to provide a summary of what was previously mentioned—that all this is supreme—namely, the clarity regarding enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) as established in this scripture. Now, one might object: even for the liberation pertaining to this [system], there is the possibility of returning once again at the conclusion of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).

Therefore, he says "of the causes of bondage," and so forth; the meaning is that because this liberation consists in the complete severance of all fetters, there is no returning [to worldly existence] again.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā* composed by Aghoraśivācārya.
The Chapter on the Refutation of Ultimate Liberation is completed.
The Chapter on the Examination of the Characteristics of the Lord. Commentary.

Thus, it has been stated that in this scripture are expounded both the most excellent fruits known as worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*), as well as the means for their attainment, which are observed in other philosophical systems. Now,

that which was indicated by the term "Lord of All" (*sarveśāna*) in the concluding summary of the preceding section— namely, that [this system] is "proclaimed by the Lord of All"— [is further elaborated].

Establishing [the subject], he says this in order to demonstrate the category of reality known as Īśvara: "In this context, at the commencement of another section, a fivefold relationship must be stated. Thus it has been said in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"That which proceeds as a *sūtra* within a *tantra*, following upon a *paṭala*..."
Its connection should be stated as established in five ways:
from the subject matter of the tantra (*tantravastu*), from the aphorism (*sūtra*), from the sentence (*vākya*), from the section (*prakaraṇa*), and likewise from the chapter (*paṭala*).
Regarding the "subject matter of the tantra," which consists of the three categories of *pati*, *paśu*, and *pāśa*, there are three categories and four sections.

Because of the introduction with the word "thus" (*iti*), the present connection is characterized by the examination of the Lord (*pati*). However, the connection expressed in the Sūtra is stated by the words "Śiva is the maker of all and the knower of all. The connection consisting of the sentence, moreover, is established by such sentences as "He must be the creator of the universe by virtue of His innate nature," and so forth. The topical connection, furthermore, is established by that which is called the *Vidyāpāda*.
By way of context: however, the connection for the *Pāṭalika* [chapter] was indicated at the end of the preceding *paṭala* by the word "Sarveśāna.
In this very sequence, the fivefold relationship (*saṃbandhapañcaka*) is to be traced up until the end of the *Vidyāpāda*.
Now, having perceived the body and so forth...
The object possesses the property of being an effect;
we know its agent to be distinguished by means of inference. (1)
Now, the word "atha" (then/therefore) serves the purpose of introducing the topic; for here, the examination of the individual categories of existence is undertaken—this is the meaning.

And herein, having understood through inference that entities such as bodies, organs, and worlds possess the nature of being effects because they are characterized by a specific arrangement, like a jar, one establishes that these are preceded by an intelligent agent.

The intended meaning is that [the body] is perceived [as such]. Now, it may be argued that the fact that the body itself is an effect is unestablished; for nowhere and at no time has a body ever been seen being created by anyone. True. However, while it is true that the body being created by someone has not been seen, it is not tenable to deny the existence of an agent on that basis, since the agent is something to be inferred.

Since the body is not an object of [prior] perception, how is it that its being produced is not seen? For indeed, "being an effect" consists precisely in coming into existence after not having existed; and this is certainly perceived in the case of the body, because it arises from the material causes of semen, blood, the *kalala*, and so forth, according to the meaning of the verbal root *diha* (to increase).
Since the body residing in the womb is perceived to grow incrementally month by month, how could it transcend the status of being an effect?

Furthermore, because the body and such possess a specific configuration and are perishable, their nature as an effect cannot be denied; for whatever possesses a specific configuration and is perishable [is an effect].
Every such effect, such as a jar and so forth; and these entities, beginning with the body, are likewise [effects]. Therefore, these too are indeed effects.

This being the case, the class of objects beginning with the body is the subject (*dharmin*); "having an intelligent agent as its cause" is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Because they are effects. Whatever is an effect, that has an intelligent agent as its cause.
It is observed, as in the case of chariots and the like. That which is not of this nature is not an effect, as in the case of the self and so forth. [Objection:

But even in the case of "worm-eaten letters" (*ghuṇākṣara*), which are effects, there is no prior agency by an intelligent creator; thus, the reason "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). [Reply: It is not so, because in that case there is no actual status of being an effect (*kāryatā*) at all; it is merely a matter of occurring by chance.
It is said that the wood-boring insect possesses agency, but not in the creation of letters with a specific configuration;

rather, that configuration occurs as it does simply by the very nature of the insect as it crawls along. [Objection: But surely, because the letters exist when the insect is present and do not exist when it is absent, the letters must indeed have the insect as their agent. [Reply: If this were so, then in its acting in such a manner—

Since a letter is not manifested when there is an absence of such activity, and since the "worm-eaten letter" (ghuṇākṣara) is immediately preceded by an intelligent agent, how could the reason of "being an effect" (kāryatva) be inconclusive? Nor is this [reason] inconclusive on account of rice growing without being sown, wild trees, and the like; for in those cases...

Because the non-existence of an agent is not certain, and because those [examples] have been made into the subject (*pakṣa*) of the argument. Now, if the status of being a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) were removed merely by making something a subject whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished, then there would be no reasons at all that could be considered fallacious. This would be the case if this reason of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) were one whose pervasion was unestablished.

To whatever extent there exist entities such as bodies, instruments, and worlds within the belly of the three worlds— which are distinct from pots and the like that have been cited as examples and whose makers are perceived— these are preceded by a maker, because they are effects,
just like pots and the like whose makers are observed. When this inference is formulated, what else remains [to be proven]?

In this case, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the property of being an effect would not be established. Now, one might object: "In this very inference, the subject (*dharmin*) is the pot and so forth, which have a visible maker; therefore, it is not accepted that [the world] is produced by God (*īśvara*), as that would be unproven. Furthermore, because such things are effects of potters and the like, it would follow that God is not the maker of everything."

If the state of having God as the creator is intended for the subject of the example, such as a jar, then that example is deficient in respect to the probandum (*sādhya*). Furthermore, it is contradicted by common experience; for no one perceives an object such as a jar—which follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the potter and other factors—as having God as its creator.

Furthermore, this reason is contradictory; for just as the maker of a jar or similar object, such as a potter, is subject to afflictions and is neither sovereign nor eternal, so too would the maker of the universe necessarily be. As it has been stated by the followers of Jaimini:

If it is claimed that the potter and others exercise superintendence over the jar and so forth, then there would be no superintendence by God; yet if such superintendence does exist [in the case of the jar], then the example is devoid of the probandum.
1. There is a variant reading: *siṣādhayiṣita*.

Likewise, if the example were established [as proving the opposite], the reason would become contradictory (*viruddha*), for it would entail that [the world] has a creator who is non-Īśvara, perishable, and so forth.
This opening for every objection might exist if we were to admit that the presiding of God has a non-universal scope;
however, even those who are the makers of jars and the like, such as potters and others, [are likewise...].

We maintain that their potencies, when supported by the act of observation (*pratyavekṣaṇa*), become capable of accomplishing their respective effects. But where has this been observed—that because a collection of effects such as jars exists when a potter, a weaver, and so forth are present, and does not exist when they are absent, the entire range of effects is presided over by Īśvara? Where?
Or have you not seen it, or has it not been heard by the Blessed One himself, even as it is proclaimed in the scriptures well-known to all people?
"Entering into all beings, I sustain them by my own power."

"Becoming Soma, whose essence is nectar, I nourish all herbs. And: "There is nothing, whether moving or unmoving, that exists without me. Also in the Śruti: "Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the herbs—Rudra who has entered all beings. For this very reason:
The contradiction with common experience pointed out by you has also been refuted:
"This ignorant creature is not its own master over pleasure and pain;
impelled by God, it goes either to heaven or indeed to hell."
Since this very kind of cognition is,

on the contrary, established— nor is this reason contradictory, because there is no pervasion by the opposite— and because its pervasion with the probandum, namely being preceded by an intelligent agent, is established in the subject of the example, such as a jar.

Because it is excluded from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa), such as the self (ātman) and so forth, which lack the property of being preceded by an intelligent agent; that [reason] is called "contradictory" (viruddha) which is absent from the similar instances (sapakṣa) and pervades only the dissimilar instances. For example: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced. And [the property of] being preceded by an intelligent agent exists in the case of a jar.

Since it is established by virtue of being the product of a potter, what deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyabhraṣṭatā*) could there be? Furthermore, not all properties of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharma*) are ever present in the subject of the inference (*sādhyadharmin*), such that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the world] having a non-omniscient, perishable, and so forth, as its creator. For instance: "Sound is impermanent..."

Regarding the argument "because it is produced, like a jar," you must explain why the properties of a jar—such as being the product of a potter, its redness, or its roundness—do not also apply to sound; therefore, this [objection] is nothing. Now, these [properties], such as being an effect, possessing a specific configuration, and so forth—
Causes also establish that an effect has multiple agents; therefore, they are "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because they prove the opposite of the nature of the subject (*dharmin*). Thus Maṇḍana said:
"Although everything possessing arrangement and so forth has an intelligent cause..."
How can there be a single cause for the well-known arrangement [of the world] and so forth?
"Even chariots and the like, though fashioned by various craftsmen,
are generally seen in the world as being both benefactors and beneficiaries"—
this too is incorrect, for even in the case of effects such as chariots, which are constructed by many craftsmen...

Because completion is never observed without following the will of a single architect, it is thus established by the reason of "being an effect" that the world is preceded by an intelligent creator. That creator,
who is endowed with the powers of will, knowledge, and action for the accomplishment of its various diversities, is [the Lord].

Thus, it is logical to infer a specific cause that produces a specific effect, such as the earth and so forth, which is distinct from effects like those produced by us and others. Nor is this unestablished; for a distinction [in the cause] is observed from a distinction in the effect, even within the worldly condition and in common worldly practice, where one perceives a specific cause precisely upon seeing a specific effect.

A cause is inferred just as, upon observing the manifold variety of the world and other objects— the entire range of artistic skills such as painting and plastering— including their excellence, their intermediate state, and their possession of incomparable beauty, one infers the existence of their creator as well.
Its distinctness is determined from its difference from that [ordinary cognition]. || 1 ||
The Lamp. Now begins the section on the examination of the characteristics of a husband.
Now, with the words "atha" and so forth, he introduces the chapter beginning with "tadevam" and so on.

At the conclusion of the dialogue between Śiva—the subject matter of the scripture mentioned incidentally—and [his interlocutor], concerning the Lord (pati), the individual soul (paśu), and the bonds (pāśa) previously mentioned, the category of the Lord is first examined. But why is this?

The purpose of explaining the fivefold relationship is stated as follows: it is for the sake of demonstrating the authority of the chapters (*paṭala*) by virtue of their being composed by the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). For those chapters that lack such a relationship, however, there is no status of being authored by the Supreme Lord. By this aphorism (*sūtra*), two types of inference are encompassed.
Thus he says, beginning with "And here," etc. First, even though the body is impermanent, one might object that its being produced by someone is not perceived;

thus he raises the objection with "But surely," etc., and answers it with "True," etc. [The opponent objects: "But surely the world was never otherwise than it is now"—according to this principle, the fact that the world and such things are effects is unestablished, since they did not come into being [after not having existed]..."

1. Regarding the variant reading *śāstrotkarṣaviṣayaprativacana*, [it is argued that] their state of being produced (*bhāvitva*) is not observed; therefore, that is not [the case]. This is because the argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to old monasteries, wells, and so forth, since even those are not observed to be currently being produced. Furthermore, this position is refuted by inference (*anumāna*).
To this he says, "Furthermore," and so forth. [Objection: But since it has been stated that the world is never otherwise than it is, its perishability is unestablished.

[Reply: That is not so, because the perishability of the worlds will be explained by such statements as, "Having seen death millions of times," and so on. If this is so, then regarding the instruments...

Since they are accepted as being merely of the nature of potentiality (*śakti*), their state of possessing an arrangement (*sanniveśavattva*) is unestablished; how, then, can there be the perception of their being an effect (*kāryatva*)? We reply: because they are instruments (*karaṇa*), like swords and other tools, they possess the state of being an effect.
If this is so, how can the atoms (*paramāṇu*) denoted by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) be effects?
We say that [the elements] possess form (mūrtatva) like dust and other such things. Furthermore, since they are insentient and manifold, they must be effects; as he will state:
"That which is manifold and insentient is observed to have the property of origination. It is also stated in the venerable Parākhyatantra:
"Whatever is insentient and manifold must necessarily be led [to its cause]. Thus, by means of these three inferences, the status of these [elements] as effects is perceived. For example:
whatever is corporeal is an effect, such as dust and the like; where there is no state of being an effect, there is also no corporeality.

Just as the self (*ātman*) and so forth [are not composed of parts]. Furthermore, atoms (*paramāṇu*) are established by both disputants as being corporeal (*mūrta*). Therefore, they too must be effects; this is the first formal argument (*prayoga*). The second, however, is: whatever possesses parts (*sāvayava*) is an effect, such as a jar and the like. Where, on the other hand, there is no possession of parts, there is also no state of being an effect, as in the case of the self and so forth.

This collection of worlds, beginning with the earth, possesses parts; therefore, it too is an effect. As for the third [reason]: whatever is an instrument is an effect, such as a pen and so forth. Where there is no state of being an effect, there is also no state of being an instrument, as in the case of the Self and so forth. And this eye and so forth are instruments; therefore, they too...
"An effect," he says. Having thus established that the body and so forth are effects, he demonstrates that they have an intelligent agent as their cause.

By the passage beginning with "And this being so" and continuing with "this [world]," the point is that because they possess constituent parts (*sāvayavatvāt*), their having a creator prior to them is proven, just like a jar and other such objects. As for those who say "of jars and so forth," [the agents] are the potters and others.

These are the indirect agents (prayojyakartṛ). The meaning is that God, however, is the instigating agent (prayojakakartṛ). Now, one might object: "Even if it is established that the body and so forth have an agent as their precursor, not even a single creator of the universe is thereby established. To this he says, "But these [beings]," and so on. If it is argued, "In that case, let there be many creators," that is incorrect; because, due to their multiplicity...
Just as in the case of kings whose agency has been observed, no sequential order is possible regarding the action;
if simultaneity were admitted, the action itself would be impossible. This is what was said:
"Where there are many leaders, all of whom consider themselves wise..."
"Likewise, they desire greatness [for the Creator], yet that manifest [world] perishes.

To this he states the established conclusion (siddhānta): "That too is incorrect," and so forth. The meaning is as follows: since it is certain through the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that an effect cannot exist without a maker, the status of being its maker is established by the occurrence of that effect.

It is perceived by someone; moreover, this world characterized as an effect is established through mutual dependence. Just as in the case of a palace and the like, its constituent parts cannot function as mutual supports without a single architect; likewise, for the world as well, there must be a single creator.

"It is established. And therefore, we shall explain that the production of effects by a single universal creator, both successively and simultaneously, is logically consistent—specifically in the context of the statement:

"Because of the arising [of effects] in succession and non-succession, [the cause] possesses the power for successive and other types of arising. For this very reason, from the specific nature of the effect, there follows the specific nature of the agent.

He says "siddham" (it is established). Regarding the passage beginning with "tadevam" (thus, in this way), he says "yasmāt" (because) and so forth [verse 1], stating that this is not unestablished; rather, the inference of a specific agent from the specificity of the effect is expressed by the half-verse beginning with "etadeva vaiśiṣṭyam" (this very specificity).
Commentary: And therefore:
whatever, in whatever manner, of whatever kind, and to whatever extent—
That which is the effect is likewise the cause.

The effect, such as smoke and so forth, is that which has been perceived in a certain manner— namely, by its being located in a mountain cave, situated within its interior, or existing on its other side— and in whatever specific form it is characterized,
such as by being composed of grass or leaves, and to whatever extent its magnitude extends.
Its cause—characterized by fire and so forth—is either in the form of very thin lines or dense like a mass of clouds;
likewise, it may be situated on the slope of a mountain, or located upon its peak, or found on its rear side;
and it is of such a nature as to consist of grass, leaves, and the like, and of such a magnitude, whether small or large.
Just as it is inferred [in the case of a potter], so too, having observed the manifold variety of forms and structures in the effect characterized as the universe,
one infers a cause endowed with unsurpassed power of knowledge and action regarding those various specific objects. || 1½ ||
The *Dīpikā* states: "This very point is elaborated by the second half [of the verse]," and thus says "Therefore, etc. (1½).
The commentary.
And that [space] is eternal because it is not delimited by time; due to its all-pervasiveness, it does not occupy a specific location.
Because it arises both successively and non-successively,
it possesses the power for successive and other types of production.

That which, having not existed, comes into being, and having existed, ceases to be, is impermanent because it is delimited by time. That, however, which—due to the absence of both prior and posterior limits—is not delimited by time, is therefore eternal. Furthermore, it does not abide anywhere, but rather [pervades] due to its all-pervasiveness (*vaitatya*).
Because of its greatness and because it is not limited by direction or space, it is all-pervading (*sarvaga*). And because its effects are perceived everywhere, it is omnipresent (*vibhu*).
Likewise, because it produces the effects of bodies, organs, and so forth, both successively and simultaneously, it is endowed with the power to produce [effects] both in sequence and at once. (2½)
*Dīpikā*: He introduces the sūtra beginning with "eternal" (*nitya*) and so forth with the words "And that," etc.; the remainder is that the definition of the agent is the cause of the world.
Regarding "of whom," etc.: the sense is that if the creator of the world were non-eternal, there would be instability [in his agency]. Regarding "furthermore," etc.

The meaning is that [the soul's] omnipresence is established by means of inference and scripture. The intention of the passage beginning with "tathā" (likewise) is as follows: for the reason that, when a single agent such as Devadatta moves simultaneously to various places, multiple effects are observed, such as eating, conversation, and the carrying of loads.

Since bathing, eating, sleeping, and so forth occur both simultaneously and sequentially, for that reason, because we observe the production of certain things like bodies simultaneously and others sequentially, the agency of their creator, Īśvara,
is also perceived as being simultaneous in some cases and sequential in others; thus, it is by way of sequence.
And it is endowed with the power of the material cause simultaneously. || 2½ ||

Commentary: Now, it might be argued that the activity consisting of the creation, maintenance, and so forth of the world cannot be without an instrument, because it is an action, like the act of cutting; therefore, it must also have an instrument. To this, he says:
It has an instrument by which it is seen, for no action exists without an instrument;
and that [instrument] should be known as non-returning.
Because the establishment of the effect is beginningless. || 3½ ||

Since an action without an agent is impossible, that Blessed One necessarily possesses some instrument; and because his creative activity (kṛtya), such as emanation, exists without beginning, that instrument is non-coming and non-arriving. || 3½ ||
The *Dīpikā*: He states a doubt in order to explain the sūtra beginning with "tasya" (of that), saying "nanu" and so forth.
The sense is that, due to the absence of instruments, it would follow that God is not an agent; but that is not so, because...
He states that by the very fact that agency would otherwise be inexplicable, it is understood that He also possesses an instrument (*karaṇa*), beginning with the words "because" (*yasmāt*).
He will state immediately thereafter that this [instrument] is of the nature of power (*śakti*). Furthermore, the instrument is not something other than power.
This is the meaning: the power of action itself is the Lord’s instrument, because He is the agent of all things.

Like yogins, other yogins are established by all disputants; they cannot be refuted even by the Cārvākas on the grounds that they perform the treatment of poison and possession, just like gems, medicinal herbs, and so forth. As they say: "The power of gems, mantras, medicinal herbs, and the like is indeed inconceivable. And for this reason, [the capacity] inheres in God.

In this context, it is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) alone that is to be accomplished, not the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), because the latter is established through the efficacy of the former;
as we shall explain:
"The omniscient one [is so] because of his being the agent of all, together with the means, the auxiliaries, and the fruits."
"It is well established that whatever one knows, one performs that very thing.
Nor is it the case that the power consisting of Mahāmāyā exists as a separate entity (*parigrahavartinī*), because she is the material cause (*upādāna*).
Therefore, he says that He performs that effect, such as the worlds and so forth, by means of that very inherent power which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
And that [is] "of the task," and so forth. || 3½ ||
Commentary: Now, what is that instrument? It is said: and the instrument is not other than power (śakti).
The power of consciousness is not insentient; [the word] "instrument" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. It is one because there is no restriction regarding its objects.
Likewise, it is so regarding the act of awakening and the duty. || 4½ ||

Power alone is the instrument of this Lord of the Universe, since by that very power he accomplishes those various actions. We shall explain later that this power consists of will and the rest. And it is said in the *Kiraṇatantra*:
"Will itself is considered his instrument, just as it is for a yogin in the present moment."
And power (*śakti*) has the nature of cognition; for that which is of the nature of consciousness cannot have a power that is non-conscious in form.

And this instrument, which consists of power, is "one" because there is no restriction regarding its objects. Since the objects of knowledge and the things to be accomplished are infinite, the instruments of that [consciousness] must also be infinite.

Furthermore, the knowledge and activity of the Supreme Lord have an infinite range, as will be stated beginning with the words "the Śāṅkara knowledge": "That [knowledge], being one, attains an infinity of divisions due to the infinity of its objects."
Because it is non-different from that [consciousness], agency is likewise attributed to it figuratively.

Therefore, since the object— whether as something to be known or as something to be accomplished— is unrestricted and undivided, that single form of its power functions in that same way toward both the object of cognition and the object of action.
The meaning is that it is indeed uninterrupted and infinite. || 4½ ||
The *Dīpikā* explains that this very point is elaborated upon by the passage beginning with "And that [very thing] is the instrument," stating: "His power alone... and so forth.
Now, one might object: God cannot be an agent because he is devoid of instruments in the form of sense organs; for whoever is an agent...
[The opponent argues: "He must be endowed with sense organs and instruments, just like a potter and others. This is not so;
because He possesses specific powers, the Blessed One produces effects by His mere presence, like a magnet.
[The opponent objects: "If this is so, then the Lord would be insentient, just like the magnet. [The author replies: It is not so, because [the Lord] is by nature [sentient].

Furthermore, [the argument] is inconclusive because of [the case of] the sun and so forth. Due to being endowed with a specific power, it produces its effect through mere proximity, just as the conscious self does in the case of the movement of its own body.
Moreover, just as the sun is the agent of the opening and closing of lotuses and water-lilies by means of instruments consisting of its own powers alone, and not...
[This is] by means of a separate instrument; so too is this Lord [said to act]. Now, one might object: "The Sun indeed possesses a body and so forth.
True;
however, there is no contradiction, because he is cited here as an instance of non-inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) on the grounds that his instruments consist solely of his own powers.

For it has been stated that [an unseen agent] cannot be established by being seen in every respect. And this being the case, since there would be no distinction between the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), it would be impossible to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason;

consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total abolition of all inference. Now, one might object: "In the case of an agent who is seen, such as the sun and so forth, [the capacity is indeed perceived]."

Let it be [the cause] by way of being an instrument (*karaṇa*). However, since the agent (*kartṛ*) is unperceived, both of those powers must be postulated because the effect would otherwise be inexplicable; and since the postulation of the agent itself suffices for that explanation, how can the power be postulated otherwise? This very point has been stated by the Prābhākaras: "It is to be postulated..."

"Furthermore, [the opponent] says, 'It obstructs conceptual construction. To this it is replied: even by you, who stand on the position of the Jaiminīyas, since another [organ]—characterized as a specific part of the skin—is to be postulated because the perception of form would otherwise be inexplicable, [conceptual construction is indeed obstructed]."
Since the perception of objects such as the polar star, which are separated by many hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*, is established as vast,

the capacity of even that which is imagined [as the cause] is postulated; just as it is postulated through the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too, by means of the aforementioned inference, a supersensuous capacity is postulated for that imagined agent who is himself beyond the senses.
Since this determination based on logical proof is identical with the object to be established, the aforementioned defect does not apply. Now, one might argue:

"Since even for Īśvara, agency is impossible without power (*śakti*), let power alone be postulated as the cause of the world. That is not so; because power, being a quality (*dharma*), cannot exist without a substratum (*dharmin*).
As it is said in the Mataṅga:
"The qualities (guṇas), depending upon the possessor of qualities (guṇin), exert themselves each in its own respective object; they do not exist without a substratum."

Therefore, just as heat is inseparable from fire, so too is power (śakti) inseparable from the Lord. Having thus established that the instrument is of the nature of power, he states—beginning with the words "And that which..."—that its infinity is merely figurative, due to the diversity of its objects of knowledge and its effects. || 4½ ||
Commentary: Now, by not restating the views of other schools, he further confirms the very existence of God:
"The effect consists of persistence, birth, and so forth."
By the process of elimination, he is indeed Śiva— the seed, the primordial nature, the atom, the Supreme Lord, and the liberated one. || 5½ ||

Now, what is the use of postulating an Īśvara who depends upon instruments, since we do not admit his agency when he is independent of karma? The followers of Jaimini maintain that the very actions performed by him serve as the cause for creation, maintenance, and so forth. As they say:
"If no presiding deity is accepted for any mere cause,
then since that [presiding deity] is established through the actions of all living beings, it is a proof of what is already proven (*siddhasādhana*).
Alternatively, [the Lord] is the material cause (*upādāna*) of effects such as the *kalās*, just as a seed is the material cause of sprouts and the like."

Let Māyā alone, independent of anything else, be the creator of the world and so forth; let Prakṛti, known as the Unmanifest (avyakta), be the agent of this [creation]. Without her, even that Lord (Īśvara) is observed to be incapable of accomplishing those effects. Independent of others and acting for the sake of another in the form of earth and other elements, it is Prakṛti alone. Therefore:

The followers of Kapila (the Sāṃkhyas) ask: "What is the use of a Lord? For it is thus: whatever has a specific nature of transformation, it becomes exactly so, independent of anything else, just as the causal complex of a seed and so forth [produces] a sprout.

"Because its nature consists of the evolution of the flood of transformations beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), and because it is the Pradhāna composed of the three guṇas, Sāṃkhya is 'without a Lord' (anīśvara).
Or else: "The Person alone is all this, whatever has been and whatever is to be"—thus [it is said] of the subtle atom (aṇu).
To claim that the manifestation of the universe, characterized by both the conscious and the unconscious, will proceed from the Puruṣa alone and that there is no need for an Īśvara, is incorrect;

for it has already been stated that the activity of creation and so forth is only possible for insentient factors— such as karma and Māyā— which serve as external seeds, provided they are presided over by an intelligent being.
Furthermore, the engagement of even *prakṛti* in effects for the sake of satisfying its own longing is utterly illogical,
because it is insentient (*acetana*), whereas longing is a property of sentient beings; moreover,
this would entail numerous defects such as the transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) of the *puruṣa*, who is [otherwise] independent.

Since there is no independence regarding the loss of what is desired and the occurrence of what is undesired— given that the agency of persistence, birth, and dissolution has been refuted— it follows by the method of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*) that the Great Lord alone is the agent of those effects, such as their persistence and birth.
This inference by elimination (*pāriśeṣyānumāna*) is faultless; it is thus a means of comprehension. Now, this is being analyzed:

if the Supreme Lord engages in the maintenance, creation, and so forth of the worlds out of compassion, with the desire to uplift transmigrating beings, then for what purpose does he, on the contrary, [act] toward those caught in saṃsāra?

1. "Let it be so by way of agency"—this connects with what precedes. [If one asks: "Does he not employ these wretched living beings in sufferings? Or, if it is argued that his very nature is such, why does he not cause even a liberated being to transmigrate? To this he says: "For the liberated one, he is indeed Śiva; this is the truth."

It is solely out of compassion that the Blessed One engages in favoring living beings. As for the fact that he connects them with suffering, delusion, and so forth, or with the experience of hells and other realms, this occurs by virtue of the power of their own corresponding karma. Nor should it be suspected that the Lord’s sovereignty is compromised by his dependence on karma, for such dependence pertains only to the instruments [of action].

Because no contradiction to the agent's sovereignty is observed, just as a king who relies on his treasurer may grant favors and so forth through that intermediary. As it was said by the Siddha-gurus:
"Sovereignty is the state of not being impelled by another, and it consists in being the instigator of the instruments and other factors."
"For this is indeed the sovereignty of the agent, not a disregard for karma and other factors.
Nor does there occur the destruction of karma that has not been experienced;
rather, it occurs through the exhaustion of various karmas by means of experiencing them within the bodies of their respective wombs.

Or, due to the similarity with that [liberated soul], for a living being whose impurities have been removed by the descent of power (śaktipāta) proceeding from the maturation of extremely intense impurity,

who has obtained grace, and whose omniscience and agency regarding all objects have manifested because all fetters (pāśa) have been cast off— the cause of his state as a transmigrating being [is removed].

Due to the absence of the state of being a bound soul (paśutva), the Blessed Lord becomes the very nature of Śiva; the sense is that, unlike a bound soul, He does not become a cause for the enjoyment of the wretched experiences of worldly existence. || 5½ ||
The *Dīpikā* introduces the aphorism concerning the effects, such as persistence, birth, and so forth, with the words "Now," etc. To explain this,
it first states the various forms of objection with "But surely," etc., and then refutes them with "That is incorrect," and so on.
He states that "by the word 'seed,' action is meant," referring to "actions which have become external seeds.

This is the intended meaning: furthermore, as for the argument that—just like the actions of plowing and so forth—the cause there must be action itself because it is insentient and thus requires an instigator, that is not [valid], because this inference is based on a contradiction with the actual nature of things (*vastu-pratibandha*).

Because it has been stated that [the inference] is like the inference of fire from smoke, just as smoke is an effect of fire, so too an effect cannot possibly exist without an agent. Furthermore, like the act of agriculture and so forth, [the body] requires an intelligent instigator and arranger due to its own insentience; for this person (the soul) is incapable of producing the body and its organs.

Since the status of being an ordainer (*saṃvidhātṛtva*) is established, the existence of a Lord (*īśvara*) distinct from that [nature] is proven. Regarding the phrase "of Māyā and so forth," the meaning here is that by the word *prakṛti*, the triad of natures consisting of *bindu*, *māyā*, and *pradhāna* is intended. The phrase "presiding over the intellect" means that the fetters (*pāśa*), such as Māyā and the rest, [act] toward the person (*puruṣa*).
It proceeds only as presided over by the power of consciousness (*cetanā-śakti*), because it is insentient (*acetanatva*), like a rope and so forth; this has already been stated previously.

Now, if it is argued that whatever has transformation as its sole nature must be such [insentient], just as the causal complex of seeds and so forth is independent of anything else in the case of a sprout—as has been said—then it follows that Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) alone [is the cause].

It has been stated that [the primordial matter] proceeds toward the Puruṣa because it exists for the sake of another through its nature as the Great One (mahat) and so forth; therefore, he says "of Prakṛti also," and so on. Since Prakṛti is insentient like clay and other such things, agency is inappropriate for it. This is because sentience is invariably concomitant with being the cause of the commencement and cessation of the activity of instruments belonging to an agent. As they say:

"He who is the lord of the causal factors (kārakas) in both their engagement and their withdrawal—whether he himself is inactive or active—he alone is called the 'agent' (kartṛ), the causal factor. Now, it might be argued that even insentient things, such as magnets and the like, are seen to act spontaneously. That is not so.
For it has been stated that even this magnet functions only by depending upon an operator. [Objection:
But even an insentient substance, such as milk, is seen to function spontaneously for the sake of the growth of the calf and so forth of cows and other animals.
As the Sāṃkhyas say: "Just as the flow of milk, though insentient, occurs for the purpose of the calf's growth..."

"The activity of Pradhāna proceeds for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa. If this is so, then this reason (hetu) is contradictory (viruddha), because its pervasion (vyāpti) is observed in the example to be with the opposite of that which is to be proven (sādhya-viparyaya). For milk, being insentient, proceeds only when presided over by a sentient cow.
"Established. Since the Pradhāna is insentient, there must be a sentient being as its instigator; thus, God is established.
(Note: This additional reading exists in another manuscript.)

It has been stated that if the *puruṣa* were also the material cause (*upādāna*), it would entail defects such as being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*); thus he says, "Of the *puruṣa* also," and so forth.
Furthermore, because it is observed that [the *puruṣa*] lacks independence and other qualities, its status as the creator of creation and so on is untenable;

thus he says, "Because of the loss of what is desired," and so forth. And therefore, he states that the existence of God (*īśvara*) is established even by means of the inference of elimination (*pariśeṣānumāna*).

"By way of elimination," and so forth. To explain that "for the liberated one, he [the Lord] alone is Śiva," he raises a relevant objection with the words "Now this," and so forth; therein lies the resolution of the first objection.
With the words "True," and so forth, [he says]: "If it is thus, then because the Lord depends upon karma, there is a loss of his sovereignty. Therefore—

He says, "And not by depending on karma," and so forth. For this very reason, he states that the second objection is also refuted with the words, "from those respective wombs," and so forth; the connection of this compound word is immediately after the word *jantoḥ* (of the living being), because the destruction of all karma is accomplished through initiation (*dīkṣā*), even that which is produced from knowledge (*vijñāna*), yoga, and the like.
Because the cause consists solely in the state of being pure consciousness alone. As it has been said: "Initiation is that which brings about the destruction of merit and demerit.

Likewise, in other Tantras: "Those men who are liberated through the destruction of merit and demerit are here called *rudrāṇavas*. And because of that similarity, this absence of karma is the cause of liberation.
This should be disregarded as something interpolated by [certain] disputants, because that [impurity] exists even during the state of saṃsāra;

and because it has fulfilled its purpose merely through the destruction of contrary karma, we shall explain later that it cannot be the cause for the ripening of impurities and so forth. The phrase "of one whose impurities have been removed" means: of one whose impurities are on the verge of being removed by the power of ripening.
Withdrawal from that [bondage] occurs through initiation alone; therefore, he says "of one who has obtained grace," meaning precisely of one who has received initiation.
As it is stated in the *Svāyambhuva*:
"Initiation alone liberates and leads [the soul] upward to the abode of Śiva."

And thus, this is the meaning: through initiation, by means of the ripening of impurity (*mala*) and the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), there occurs the destruction of all karma. By that very [initiation], the binding nature of impurity (*mala*), *māyā*, and the obstructive power (*rodha-śakti*) ceases; for one who has attained the state of Śiva, the Supreme Lord will no longer be the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). || 1½ ||
Commentary: Furthermore, he raises an objection in order to refute the inference intended to establish that the world indeed has God as its creator.
For some, sublation of the cognition occurs due to the non-apprehension of the relationship; that [sublation] would apply to another person as well in the case of smoke and fire.
On the mountain, [the practice] begins with the kitchen and so forth. || 6½ ||

Now, if someone should think: "Surely, if this relationship characterized by invariable concomitance between this effect—namely persistence, birth, and so forth—and some creator of the world were ever apprehended, then this inference would be established;
but since the relationship itself is not apprehended, how could there be no sublation of this [inference]?"

He says that this too must be cross-examined by him: "It applies to others as well. This very sublation follows for every proponent of inference. For instance, if the relationship were grasped only between specific instances of smoke and fire occurring in particular places and times, such as in a kitchen and so forth, [the inference would fail].

Furthermore, since one infers merely fire from merely smoke on a mountain and the like, how could a particular instance of smoke that has not had its relationship [with fire] grasped cause one to understand a corresponding particular instance of fire? Thus, the objection regarding the necessity of grasping the relationship is the same [in both cases]. And therefore—
"In a matter where both [parties] would incur the same fault, or where the rebuttal is likewise equal, neither should be subject to censure in determining such a point.
This objection is not directed at us alone; for instance, regarding mere smoke...
Just as the relationship characterized by the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with fire alone has been grasped, so too here the inference of an agent from the mere effect is observed. (Note:
There is a variant reading, *vicāraṇe*.)

Otherwise, there would be the total destruction of all inference. As it has been said: "Inference proceeds because of the ascertainment of invariable concomitance through the universals of the probandum and the probans; otherwise, that [inference] would be absent."

And thus, by another inference, a creator is inferred who knows the specific distinctions of the enjoyer, the enjoyment, the means of enjoyment, and their material causes, all of which are perfumed by the excellence of various respective karmas; therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. This has been stated as follows:

Regarding this, the venerable Bṛhaspati has said: "This world does not exist without one who knows the states of existence, the experiencer, the means of experience, their material causes, and so forth, as well as the ripening of the latent impressions of human karma. (6½)
*The Lamp* (*Dīpikā*):

Having thus refuted the two incidental objections, [the author] states "again" (*punarapi*) and so forth, using the phrase "of someone" (*kasyacit*) to introduce the actual inference (*anumāna*) which was previously raised by the words "the relation," etc. (*sambandha*, etc.).

He states that even by means of the consideration of the instrument of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is a consideration of its proponent, saying "it might be the opinion of someone," and so forth; for,
having established that the apprehension of the relation between any effect in general and an agent in general is proven in the case of a potter and the like,
one would then have to accept the apprehension of the relation within the very subject (*dharmin*) of the thesis.

"The consequence would be that all inferences are sublated. To this he says: "That [sublation] belongs to the opponent," and so forth; and "This too is that," and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "of smoke in general," for this very reason, what was stated—that the arrangement of mountains and such is dissimilar to the arrangement of buildings and the like—is also incorrect.
Because the pervasion of mere arrangement by mere effect is established; this very point was stated by us in the *Pāṣaṇḍāpajaya*:
"Mere arrangement and so forth are connected with mere effect."
Thus, it is certain that every effect alone is pervaded by an agent alone. || 6½ ||

Commentary: Let it be, then, that God is the agent. However, He cannot be understood as being bodiless. For, according to such [principles] as "An effect is always pervaded by an agent endowed with a body," one who is devoid of a body [cannot be an agent].
Because it has already been stated that agency is impossible [for such a being]. To explain:
in the world, action is observed only in those who possess a body; such a being would also be like us and others.

"In the world, it is seen that [an agent] possesses a body"; that is to say, in the world, it is observed that effects such as pots and cloths are produced only by one who possesses a body, and not by one who is bodiless.
What follows from this? "He too, like us and others, is possessed of afflictions and the like, and is not omniscient."

The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that even such a Lord, being limited in power and delimited by space and so forth, would necessarily become possessed of a body because He possesses a body. || 7 ||
The *Dīpikā* introduces the question-sūtra beginning with "In the world" (*loke*) and so forth, stating: "Let that be so, then," and so forth. The *Vṛtti* [comments as follows].
The established conclusion, however, is: "O Lord, because of the impossibility of [the body] having roots and so forth, the body of the Śakti is not of such a nature. (7½)

Even for one who is bodiless, agency is observed with respect to the movement of one's own body and so forth. Having provisionally accepted the claim that an effect is pervaded by an agent endowed with a body, we say this: even if you possess a body, the previously mentioned fault does not necessarily follow. Why? He says:
Regarding the phrase "due to the impossibility of the root and so forth": the "root" (*mūla*) is impurity (*mala*), because it is the root of all misfortune.
This is because it will be described by synonyms such as ignorance (*avidyā*), covering (*āvṛti*), disease (*ruj*), languor (*glāni*), sin (*pāpa*), and the destruction of the root (*mūlakṣaya*).

By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), actions (*karma*) and the power of obstruction (*rodhaśakti*) are also intended. Because these are impossible [in the case] of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*): [he is free from them].
The web of fetters such as impurity (*mala*) and karma arises; it is for this reason that the *prakṛta* (natural) body is fashioned.
However, the *śākta* [body] is fashioned by one's own will through the five mantras, Sadyojāta and the others, which are of the nature of Śakti.
It possesses limited capacity, is delimited by direction, space, time, and form, and is incomparable and desired.
It is a body, but not one similar to the bodies of those such as ourselves. 7½.
The *Dīpikā* states: Even in the world, it is not only one possessed of a body who possesses agency; thus he says, "even for one without a body," and so forth.
This has already been stated previously. Even if one were to accept that agency belongs only to one who possesses a body, [the question remains] regarding that very body...

Because [the Lord] possesses power (*śāktatva*), he does not have the quality of being a cause of affliction and so forth like the bodies of those such as ourselves; thus he says, "even though possessing a body.

This is the meaning: because the powers (*śakti*) of those such as ourselves are veiled by impurity (*mala*), there is a dependence on a body and so forth for certain activities. But for the Blessed One, because his power is unobscured—his power...

Because it performs all functions through the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of being "active," it is called the "body" (*śarīra*). Furthermore, it has already been stated previously that power (*śakti*) is what brings about an effect. In other cases as well, such as with smoke and its like, it is the powers of fire and so forth that are the causal agents (*kāraka*), not the substance itself;
for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the effect would arise merely by the presence of that substance.
He shows this very point preceded by a question, beginning with "Why? and so forth, stating that it is elaborated upon by the passage starting with "Because of the impossibility of a root," etc.:

"For this very reason, because he is endowed with the powers (śaktis) such as Īśāna and others—which are differentiated by the various functions of creation and so on, and which consist of the nature of both contemplation (manana) and protection (trāṇa)—the Blessed Lord is said to have the five mantras as his body."
He is called "sakala" (with parts) because he is endowed with its thirty-eight kalās. || 7½ ||
For this very reason:
"That body [is constituted] by five mantras, which are applicable to the fivefold activity."
The head and other parts [of the body] are assigned to Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jyeṣṭha. (8½)

The ellipsis to be supplied is as follows: "the body of the Lord is said to consist of those five mantras, Īśāna and the others, which necessarily have utility in the fivefold functions characterized by grace (*anugraha*), concealment (*tirobhāva*), withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), protection (*rakṣaṇa*), and manifestation (*utpatti*), respectively. By means of these [mantras], which are the "boons" (*varaiḥ*).

The word *vapuḥ* (body/form) possesses an etymological significance (*anvarthatā*) because it "nourishes" (*puṣṇāti*) those who meditate; for it is taught in the Āgamas that [the Lord] assumes various forms in order to bestow grace upon his devotees. Thus it has been said in the Pauṣkara:
"This form of His is remembered as being for the sake of the goal perceived by the practitioner. (8½)
The *Dīpikā* states:
By means of the sūtras beginning with "That body" (*tadvapuḥ*), this very point is shown both individually and collectively;
figuratively, it demonstrates that those [faces], Īśāna and the others, constitute the nature of the head and other limbs.

He says, "It is stated," meaning "it is being said. Therefore, he says "for this very reason" and so forth; the sense is that for this very reason, the existence of God (Īśvara) is established even by oneself.

Furthermore, the fact that [God] is accessible through the direct perception of yogis has already been demonstrated in the introduction. But how is the body of the Lord (Īśvara) described as having five faces and ten arms by the passage beginning with "gold, beryl, and gems"?
Since this will be explained later, he says: "He nourishes the meditators with boons," and so forth.
The conceptualization of the form of the Lord is for the sake of meditation alone;
the phrase "in the meditation on Sadāśiva" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence] in the Kriyāpāda.
Not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because meditation, worship, and so forth are impossible in the case of that which is formless (*nirākāra*). As they say:
"You, possessing form, are necessarily the object of worship; the intellect does not reach an entity devoid of form.
And he will state this later as well.
"Because of the existence of the body (vapuḥ), whatever action he performs,
in each instance his body is imitated by the body of that agent.
For this very reason, the word *vapuḥ* here— just like the word *dīkṣā* according to that principle— means "that which nourishes the excellent" (*varaṃ puṣṇāti*).
It should be understood that [the word] is used by means of mentioning only a part of the term. || 8½ ||
Commentary: Now, [the author] explains how the Blessed One possesses the state of being the head, beginning with Īśāna: "By means of which he rules over the entire universe."
By virtue of being situated above;
it is called the "summit" (mūrdhan) because it is at the highest point, not because it is a physical part of the body. 9½.
By virtue of which mantra, because it stands above all currents— both those following the stream and those against it— and because it is the cause of universal grace,
it rules over the entire universe, consisting of both consciousness and the unconscious, as if it were its own head. It is that [mantra].
Because it stands at the very top of all, it is called the "crown" (mūrdhan) like the head; it is not, however, a physical part of the body in the ultimate sense. || 9½ ||
The commentary explains the *tatpuruṣa* face:
"Of that [face], the body is *yā pū*..."
He dwells within that [lotus] by means of which he exists;
because of protection therein and because of its manifestation, he has the face of that Puruṣa. || 10½ ||
Whatever city or body belongs to each respective immortal or human being, that person (tatpuruṣa) dwells within that city as its presiding subject, in the form of the sacrificer. As it has been said:
"This very Self, the Lord of all living beings, dwells within them"—thus he is called Tatpuruṣa. For this reason, He manifests [the world].
Because it protects knowledge and action from the fear of birth and so forth, it is the "Face of Puruṣa" (tatpuruṣavaktra);
for according to scripture, it is called a "face" (vaktra) because its nature is to protect (trāṇa) the phonemes (vyañjana). || 10½ ||
Commentary: He explains the "Aghora-heart.
Heart is a synonym for consciousness.
Since Śiva is the one who will consume [all things] and is non-terrible (aghora),
the term "terrible" (ghora) is applied to his "grasping" (parigraha) only figuratively, because that grasping is indeed terrible. || 11½ ||
1. In the *Mātṛkās*, the reading "he approaches her" (*tasyām upaiti*) is found.

Heart (*hṛdayam*), intention (*āśayaḥ*), and awakening (*bodhaḥ*) are synonyms. Since Śiva is non-terrible (*aghoraḥ*) awakening for the Blessed One, he is therefore "one whose heart is non-terrible" (*aghorahṛdayaḥ*). Now, one might object: that which is called "terrible" (*ghoram*) is of the nature of what is not conducive to welfare; how then can there be "the state of being terrible" (*ghorarūpatā*)?
To the question "How is it so for the Lord?", he says: "Because of the dreadfulness of his appropriation.

This statement regarding the terrible form of the Supreme Lord is not literal; rather, it is because of the dreadfulness of his appropriation—that is, of the multitude of those presiding over the impure path whose power is intensified by his own *śakti*.

The Lord is called "Ghora-śakti" (the Terrible Power) by way of metaphorical designation. Thus it has been said: "Those other powers known as Ghoratarīs stand embracing the Rudra-aṇus, causing them—who were previously absorbed in sense objects—to fall downward."
Thus [ends the section]. 11½.
The commentary explains the secret nature of Vāmadeva,
because he is opposed to the threefold group of the left (vāma-trivarga).
And he is secret by his very nature;
he whose supreme abode is the left and is most hidden is Vāmaguhyaka. 12½.

He is called *vāma* because he entices with the three aims characterized by virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*), and then vomits them out—that is, casts them down. By his very nature, he is said to be secret and hidden.
1. There is a variant reading: *ghoroktiḥ* (terrible speech) instead of *deve*.
2. "And he whose abode is the Left (vāma) would be the god Vāmaguhyaka"—this is a variant reading.
Having thus demonstrated the meaning of these two words separately, he provides the compound analysis (*vigraha*). Regarding the phrase "the Left abode" (*vāmaṃ dhāma*):
because the verbal root *div* has the sense of "shining," the word *deva* is intended to mean "splendor" (*tejas*). By that [meaning]...
The Supreme Lord is called Vāmadeva-guhya because that splendor of His, which has the nature of vomiting forth on the lower path (adhvā) to the left, is secret and not manifest. || 12½ ||
Commentary: It defines the state of having the form of Sadyojāta. The forms of the atoms arise immediately.
By His will, He is immediately designated as such;
or rather, He instantly assumes forms for yogins,
for it is due to the swiftness of His action that He is called "Sadyomūrti," not because of a physical body.

Indeed, by the will of the Lord, various forms of the selves have arisen for the swift exhaustion of karma; thus the Lord is the Sadyojāta form. As he will state in the section on initiation (dīkṣā-prakaraṇa): "By means of Sadyojāta, one should instantly generate [the disciple] whose body has not yet been fully formed."

Alternatively, it is called "Sadyomūrti" because it instantly—that is, at that very moment—assumes for yogins who possess various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) a form resembling its own mantra-constituted body, as previously described; thus, it possesses the state of being "instantaneous form" due to manifesting itself immediately through their *samādhi*. It is not, however, [the case that...]
The meaning is: because of the state of having quickly produced one's own body. || 13½ ||
This very point is further confirmed:
thus, while Śakti performs the functions of the body,
she is designated by the word "body" due to the absence of a [separate] body.
Even those divisions of hers, such as Vāmā and the others,
have been declared by the wise according to the distinction of their functions.

From the ultimate standpoint (*paramārthataḥ*), because the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is bodiless, it is his power (*śakti*) alone that performs the functions of a body; thus, she is designated by the name "body. And although she is one, she is divided into distinctions such as Vāmā and others due to the diversity of her activities. Alternatively, just as the power of fire (*vahni-śakti*) is distinguished by its performance of burning, illuminating, and cooking with respect to objects that are to be burned, illuminated, or cooked.
The plurality is figurative, because in reality it is one. || 14½ ||
Thus ends the third chapter, "The Proof of the Category of the Lord," in the *Mṛgendravṛtti* composed by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Vidyākaṇṭha.

*Dīpikā*: With the first half-verse beginning with "In this way, Śakti," he states the conclusion regarding Śakti— who was described as the body [of the Lord] and who is divided into the distinctions of Īśāna and so forth— by saying "In ultimate reality," and so on.
With the second half [of the verse], however, he provides a summary of what was previously stated regarding the division into Vāmā and the others, by way of its instrumental form;
thus he says, "And of that," and so forth. If it is asked, "How can there be multiplicity for that which is indeed one?

it has been stated that this is due to metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) based on the distinction between the objects of knowledge and their functions. He confirms this very point with an illustration, beginning with "Just as," and so forth.
Thus ends the third chapter, "The Proof of the Category of the Lord," in the *Śrīmanmṛgendravṛttidīpikā* composed by Aghoraśivācārya.
Now begins the fourth chapter, "The Definition of the Nature of the Lord."

Commentary: Thus, having established the meaning of the word *pati* through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [the author] now employs the term *sarvakṛt* (the maker of all), which was introduced in the root aphorism, in order to define its essential nature.
He begins another chapter (paṭala) in order to elaborate upon this [subject]. Since this [chapter] has the purpose of defining the functions indicated in the immediately preceding chapter,
and because it is connected to the section known as the Vidyāpāda, there exist both a chapter-level (pāṭalika) and a topical (prākaraṇika) relationship.
These two are to be understood. The relations between categories and so forth, however, are to be inferred as before.
Thus, with this instrument whose power has been struck down, he possesses such a physical form.
It always performs its function whenever it is appropriate to do so. || 1 ||

"In this manner"—by this phrase, [it means] "one whose body consists of mantra in the manner described"; thus he is the Blessed One (bhagavān) whose body is such. Furthermore, as for the instrument (karaṇa), it is not other than Śakti; thus, by means of that instrument which is of the nature of Śakti and possesses unimpeded power, as previously stated, the entire collection of effects such as maintenance (sthiti) and so forth is [accomplished] at all times.
It brings everything about; it does not merely produce [effects] simultaneously. Rather, whatever is appropriate at whatever time, that it produces at that time;
the meaning is that it performs all effects even sequentially. As it was stated previously:
"Because of the production [of effects] both successively and non-successively, [the Lord] possesses the power for successive and other types of production. (1)
The Lamp (Dīpikā): Now begins the fourth chapter, the "Description of the Nature of the Husband" (Patisvarūpanirūpaṇa).
With the words "tadevam" and so forth, he connects this chapter with the preceding one beginning with "sa itthaṃvigrahaḥ."

Regarding the passage beginning with "But the relations of categories and so forth," therein, the relation of categories (*padārtha-sambandha*) consists in [the Lord] being the subject of each individual category;

this is indicated by the word "all-creator" (*sarvakṛt*) in the Sūtra. The relation consisting of sentences (*vākya-ātmaka*), however, is manifold, such as [His] body [being described] by the five mantras that are applicable to the fivefold cosmic functions (*pañcakṛtya*), and so on. By the phrase "in this way" and so forth, [the author] refers to the Lord in a general sense.

He says "it is said that he performs the fivefold activity," beginning with the words "in this way" (*ittham*) and so forth. "Brings everything to completion" means the fivefold [activity]; "all effects" refers to emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and the others. || 1 ||
Commentary: Now, [the author] states what the Supreme Lord does first;
therein, initially, regarding the isolated individual souls (aṇu):
He makes the desired [offering] for those who are worthy,
joined with the powers beginning with Vāmā, and accompanied by a retinue of seventy million.
"Thus" (tatra) means this being the case. It has been stated that a single power itself is divided into the distinctions of Vāmā and so forth by virtue of its functions such as Vāmā.
And that power, consisting of all knowledge and action, exists in all individual souls (aṇu) just as it does in Śiva. Of them—
And because they are obstructed by beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), they do not become equal to Him without the grace of Śiva; thus,

there is a group of eight [souls] who are *vijñānakevalas*— whose bonds of karma and māyā have been exhausted and who are fit for that state according to the ripening of their *añjana* and other factors.
He makes [it] accompanied by a retinue of seventy million mantras and joined with the nine powers (śakti), beginning with Vāmā. || 2 ||
The *Dīpikā*: In that regard, he introduces the aphorism beginning with "tatra" (therein) in order to demonstrate the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).

As for the passage beginning with "atha" (now), it refers to what was stated previously: "Because there is no restriction regarding objects, the one [consciousness] is likewise [present] in both cognition and action."
In the venerable *Parākhyatantra* as well, after beginning with the statement, "The division [of Śakti] is due to the difference in functions; there is no division in ultimate reality," it continues:

"Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikariṇī, Parā, Balavikariṇī, Balapramathinī, Damani, and Manonmanī. By that [power] through which [the universe] is quickly emitted in three ways during creation, she is called Vāmā."
"It is established; she is designated as Vāmā in this [system]," and so forth. Regarding "she" and so on, it was stated previously:

"Consciousness, whose nature is seeing and acting, exists eternally in the self. He explains "of the isolated individual souls" (*kevalāṇūnām*) with the words "whose [impurities] have perished," and so on. Precisely because this is established by scripture, those who are "isolated through knowledge" (*vijñānakevalinaḥ*) do not [possess it].

They are to be rejected, for they are established by reason. Even those who have transcended the bondage consisting of karma and māyā can only be considered irrational [if they were still bound]. This is because a *mala* distinct from those two is accepted as a form of bondage.
For when a certain thing is the bondage of some beings, even in the absence of that specific bondage, their state of being bound is nonetheless established [by the presence of another cause].
"Like shackles and so forth. Now, one might object: "Is this manifestation of omniscience not simply a particular form of grace? As it will be stated:

'Those whom he liberates during the sleep [of cosmic dissolution] become Śivas immediately; or, whether at the time of withdrawal or emergence, they become Aṇavas or Lords. This is also stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*: [The text continues: "In the *Mataṅga* as well..."

"It is true that this liberation is of seven kinds. For this very reason, it is stated here that creation consists precisely in the production of the bodies and so forth—which serve as the substratum—for the Vidyeśvaras and others, preceded by the production of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*);
it does not refer merely to the manifestation of omniscience and other such qualities. This is what is meant by the phrase "surrounded by seventy million mantras."
1. There is a variant reading: *māyātmikā bandhitā*.

Since formless selves (*ātman*), being all-pervasive, cannot be mutually enveloped by one another, their connection with a body is real. For this very reason, [there exists] the body of the Vidyeśvaras and others, which is established by scripture (*āgama*).
