Regarding the argument formulated here by someone for the purpose of refutation: "Even the Vidyās and the Lords of Vidyās (Vidyeśvaras) do not possess a real body, because that would entail the consequence of their being non-omniscient, just like Devadatta and others"—this [argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) on account of the Māyāgarbhas and those holding office, such as Śrīkaṇṭha and the rest. This is because they...

For it has already been stated that omniscience exists even while possessing a body. As was said previously: "The Mantreśvaras, who reside above and below and possess incomparable splendor... Furthermore, [the reason] is inconclusive with respect to yogis; for it is heard in scripture that even yogis possess omniscience while still embodied.
For this reason, the reason "because of possessing a body" is unestablished (*asiddha*), since such a body is impossible in that case. As it is said in the *Kiraṇa*:
"His body is said to consist of pure *yoni* and is not born of karma."
"Endowed with the nine powers beginning with Vāmā" means that,
through the conjunction with the powers beginning with Vāmā, [the Lord] is capable of performing the fivefold cosmic function (*pañcavidhakṛtya*). For this very reason,
while the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*s) perform the fivefold cosmic function, the mantras (*mantra*s) possess the capacity for bestowing grace (*anugraha*).
Distinction. || 2 ||
Commentary: Now, he begins to state that for these mantras, numbering seventy million, Ananteśa and the others are indeed the eight presiding lords (īśitāraḥ).
Among them are Ananta and Sūkṣma,
as well as Śivottama,
Ekanetra, and Ekarudra.
And the Trimūrti of immeasurable splendor. || 3 ||

1. Here, the formulation of the inference is as follows: The Lords of Knowledge and Ignorance (Vidyāvidyeśvaras) are devoid of connection with a real body, because they are omniscient. Since the absence of omniscience exists in Devadatta, who possesses a body, this Devadatta serves as the negative instance (*vyatirekadṛṣṭānta*).
2. There is a variant reading: *bhirnānaikāntikaḥ*.
Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin are the lords of the lords of the kings of kings.
Because they have not yet fully attained union, the Supreme Lords (Parameṣṭhins) are those who are to be enjoined. || 4 ||
The "kings" are the lords of the world, Indra and the others; their kings are the hundred Rudras;

and these [five] are the lords and sources even of those who rule over them, such as the Maṇḍalins and so forth—in other words, they are the Vidyāmaheśvaras. And these [are so called] because they have not yet fully attained the state of a yogin.
Because a portion of the impurity of their office remains, they have not attained complete equality with the Supreme Lord; thus, these [souls] are those who are to be impelled. 3–4.

*Dīpikā*: To clarify this very point, he introduces the resolution of a potential doubt by way of a preamble, stating "Now, even for these... and so forth; [the doubt being] that the word "of them" (*teṣām*) in the subsequent sūtra should be explained by supplying the word "Lord" (*īśvara*). He says: "Now, even for these... and so on, up to "not."
These are the great lords of the lords of mantras, extending even to those such as the Maṇḍalīs;
thus he says "the kings," and so forth. Now, since they perform the fivefold activity, are these equal to Śiva? No; thus he says, "And these," etc. (3–4).
Commentary: Now, since omniscience and omnipotence are possible for all eight of these [deities],
he states whether they are of an identical nature or if there is some distinction between them.
Even though they possess omniscience and other such qualities, they remain subject to instruction due to a trace of impurity;
[the reading is] "the Vidyeśvaras and Maheśvara."
And thus, the mantras situated below are distinguished from one another.
Although all possess the capacity for perception and action regarding all objects, nevertheless, each one is to be directed by those situated immediately above them; thus,
because they remain below due to the persistence of a trace of impurity characterized by being subject to instigation,
there is a deficiency in their agency relative to those above, which constitutes their mutual distinction.
As it has been said:
"For whoever is superior in qualities over another, he is considered to be above him.
Not only these [deities] are thus distinguished, but even the mantras situated below them are likewise so.
They possess mutual distinctions. || 5 ||

*Dīpikā*: "A deficiency in agency by way of a *kalā*"—the sense is that their omniscience, however, is equal. "Those situated below that"—the sense is that the creation of the *mantras* follows after the creation of the *vidyeśvaras*. || 5 ||
The commentary: He specifies those very mantras; and they are the manifest lords of mantras (mantreśvara-vyakta).
Impelled by the power of Śiva,
they bestow grace upon those men with whom He becomes united.

And those mantras, impelled by the power of Śiva (śiva-śakti) through the manifestation of the supreme and non-supreme lords of mantras, bestow grace upon certain individuals at certain times in accordance with their fitness; however, they do not act independently of fitness, for that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). || 6 ||
Dīpikā:
"Of some," and so forth; the meaning is that they become the instruments for [bestowing] grace. || 6 ||
Commentary: That half [of the path] depends upon the body of the practitioner throughout the entire course.
Having performed his office until the end of the cosmic duration,
he enters Śiva along with the Lord.
Without a locus, there is nothing else; the primary [cause] is not inferior to the transformation.
Having established authority over the Lord, he is desired.
It departs when its own path is withdrawn. || 8 ||
Of those mantras numbering seventy million, half depend upon the Lord as their support, requiring His body— the physical form— as a basis for those who employ them and bestow grace.

"Dependent on that" means dependent on the Īśvara who is the subject of the *Ācāryādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the Teacher). Having fulfilled his own office— characterized by the grace bestowed upon those to be graced— within the entire path consisting of Māyā, at the end of the period of maintenance (*sthitikāla*), that is, at the time when even the path of Māyā ceases, he is "together with the Īśvaras," meaning accompanied by the Mantreśvaras.

He attains union with Śiva. Now, as to what the meaning of the first half [of the verse] is, he says: "without a substratum" (vinādhikaraṇena). The other, that is, the second half, states: "by the will of the Lord" (īśeṣṭam). Wherever there is the desire for grace on the part of the Supreme Lord, there, by His will alone, it occurs "without a substratum."

This is independent of the section concerning the characteristics of the teacher (*ācāryalakṣaṇa*). This *śuddhavidyā* is the primary transformation (*pradhānavikṛti*). Having exercised its authority everywhere below it throughout the path of *māyā*, it withdraws when the dissolution of its own respective path—the path of grace—is completed.

It is liberated. This has been stated by the venerable Sadyojyotiḥpāda: "In this world, half of the mantras gathered by Śiva for men depart after bestowing grace upon them, even without the form of a teacher, when they are employed by the Lord. (8)
The *Dīpikā*: He explains the two subsequent sūtras in order to elaborate upon this very point. Regarding the passage beginning with "of them" (*teṣām*), the meaning is as follows:
among those mantras numbered at seventy million, those which...

Those whose impurities have been fully ripened, numbering three and a half crores, become liberated at the conclusion of the period of creation solely by the permission of Ananta, their own cause; others, however, [remain] until the great dissolution (mahāpralaya). As it is stated in the Mataṅga:

Then those women, abiding in their own proper conduct and obeying the command of their husband, remained with half of the army while the rest departed; having thus deliberated among themselves, they [remained]. (8)
Commentary: Having thus stated the mantras, he speaks in order to describe the Mantreśvaras. 1.
The thirty-third verse from the *Tattvasaṃgraha* contained within the *Aṣṭaprakaraṇa*.
2. Chapter on the Reality of Knowledge (Vidyātattvapaṭala), Verse 14:
Then, [the Lord] is manifested as Ananta and the others, due to the state of being the knotted thread of the Lords (patīnām).
It produces one hundred and eighteen [types] of bodies commenced from the *kalā* and other [tattvas].
And having pervaded that [universe] which possesses a self (sātmaka), it remains for the sake of rest;
thus, the Māyā-tattva—which will be described later—has within it a collection of atoms resting therein.
Therefore, by virtue of being the "knot" (granthi), for those presiding over its interior who have bodies composed of *kalā* and the other categories, [it serves as their foundation].

The meaning is that the Supreme Lord, manifested as Ananta and others, creates one hundred and eighteen lords of the maṇḍalas and so forth; that is to say, He brings about for them the state of having a body composed of the *kalās* and other principles. Now, [one might ask]:
"But there are another one hundred and eighteen who hold authority over Māyā."

By the passage beginning with "of the Vidyeśvaras," it is stated that these [Vidyeśvaras] are directly favored by the Supreme Lord. However, here it is stated that the Blessed One, manifested through Ananta and the others, is their cause; thus, there appears to be a contradiction. It is not so, because agency in the act of bestowing the connection with the *kalās* and other categories belongs only to Ananta and the others, and not to the Supreme Lord.
"Śiva is said to be the agent in the pure path, while Ananta is the Lord in the impure," according to scripture.
Since he directly bestows grace upon those who possess *kalā* and other factors and enjoy worldly experience, there is no fault whatsoever. || 9 ||
The *Dīpikā*:

Having thus described the direct creation of Śiva concerning the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), [the author now] describes his creation concerning the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*) by means of Ananta and the others.

He introduces the sūtra beginning with "tataḥ" (therefore) in order to explain this. Regarding the passage beginning with "ittham" (thus) and "tasmād granthitatvataḥ" (therefore, because of being bound by knots), according to the method that will be explained, there are those among the *pralayākalas* who, by virtue of the varying degrees of the ripening of their impurities (*mala*), possess the authority for the station of the supreme Mantreśvara; preceded by their creation, [the Lord acts] through the superintendence of Ananta.

"He brings about the conjunction with the body of *kalā* and the other [categories]. This means that while the manifestation of omniscience and other qualities for Ananta and the others occurs directly from the Supreme Lord, their possession of a body composed of *kalā* and the rest occurs through the presiding authority of Ananta.
As for the phrase "he [the Lord], however, [bestows grace] upon those joined with *kalā* and the rest," etc., [one might object]: "But..."

Because they possess completeness and the status of being enjoyers, there would follow the undesirable consequence of their being similar to ourselves and others; this is not so, because the body and its experiences are necessarily bound to their specific office (*adhikāra*), and because their power of vision and action (*dṛkkriyā*) has been manifested by the Supreme Lord. As it has been said: "Even when conjoined with *kalā*, they are not subject to the *kalās*."
"Like a herd of cattle," [so it is said]. || 9 ||

1. There are eight Maṇḍalins at the summit of Kalāmasta; Śrīkaṇṭha alone resides in Guṇatattva; there are one hundred Rudras who support the Brahmāṇḍa and reside at the summit of Guṇa, including Krodha and the others; and Vīrabhadra alone is the presiding lord over the hundred Rudras. In total, the number becomes one hundred and eighteen.
Commentary: He says that they, too, are the appointers of others:
"The Blessed One, having entered into them as well..."
[He saw] the lords of the worlds together with their consorts—
those from whom all this [universe] proceeds, whose power is bound by karma. (10)

The Supreme Lord, having presided over those eight [deities] beginning with Maṇḍalin, likewise makes other impure lords of the worlds (bhuvaneśas), such as Brahmā and others, possess their powers of vision and action (dṛkkriyā-śakti) fully stimulated;
this is to be connected with what precedes. He describes what kind they are by saying: "from whom all this [proceeds]."
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "from whom this entire world, characterized by the mobile and the immobile, manifests.
Their power is bound by karma; because the karmic fetter—which acts as a restraint—has not ceased for these *sakala* souls, they receive grace from the Supreme Lord. || 10 ||
1. In the *Mokṣakārikā* of the *Aṣṭaprakaraṇa*, verse 83. *Dīpikā*:
Regarding what was stated [in verse 82], "those beginning with Brahmā are possessed of impurity," others [hold that] the mantras originate from *pradhāna*.
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others are supreme; they are possessed of *añjana* (impurity) and reside within the cosmic egg," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "those whose powers of vision (*dṛk*) and action (*kriyā*) have been stimulated," this refers only to the extent of their respective paths (*adhvan*). He explains the passage beginning with "of what kind? and so on, raising the doubt that this very point is what is expressed by the second half of the verse.
The phrase "characterized by the stationary and the moving" means consisting of the fourteenfold creation of beings.

As the Sāṃkhyas say: "The divine creation is of eight varieties, the animal womb is fivefold, and the human is of one kind; thus, in brief, is the elemental creation. And because of dependence on karma...
He states that their sovereignty extends only as far as their own respective domains in the verse beginning with "The karmic bond" (kārmaḥ pāśaḥ), etc. (10).
The commentary does not establish these alone; rather, it establishes the authors of the beastly scriptures.
The sacrificial animals, which follow after him, are endowed with the instruments for accomplishing their own purposes and remain situated within the limits of time and place. || 11 ||
The authors of the *paśu* scriptures— such as the Arhatas, Sāṃkhyas, Pāñcarātras, and others— namely Arhat, Kapila, and so forth, as well as their presiding deities,
are bound by their own ignorance to the fruits taught in those respective scriptures and to the causal instruments that serve as the means to attain them.
The phrase "it effects [everything] as far as the world of Kālāgni" is to be connected with the preceding [verse]. || 11 ||
1. "Those who are presiding over" means those [presiding deities] over whom [the Lord acts].
By acting as far as the world of Kālāgni, it is through this succession that the Lord alone creates the universe; such is the commentary (vṛtti).
Now, having created these, the Lord acts; he says:
"Having pervaded these, along with their instruments, by means of his own splendor for the sake of their maintenance..."
He unites with beings for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose, remaining unobserved by them.

Having thoroughly presided over these [entities]— which are joined with the instruments of action (*kāraka*), the means of enjoyment (*bhoga-sādhana*), the principles (*tattva*), the states of being (*bhāva*), the worlds (*bhuvana*), and so forth— by means of His own splendor, that is, by His power of will (*sva-icchā-śakti*), for the sake of accomplishing His own purpose;
that is, for the fulfillment of His own activity, or alternatively, for that which is sought after by His own selves.

The purpose of the *puruṣa* consists of experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*). It impels [the *prakṛti*] for the sake of accomplishing that purpose, but not like a madman, nor without a purpose, since even a dull-witted person does not act without aiming at a purpose.
Nor is it for the sake of sport, because that is impossible for one who is devoid of passion and the like. Nor is it for its own sake.
Because it is complete; [he] is one whose actions regarding that [body] are unknown by living beings due to the power of ignorance. || 12 ||

Having thus described creation (*sṛṣṭi*), he introduces the sūtra beginning with "sthitau sakārakāni" in order to describe persistence (*sthiti*). Regarding the passage beginning with "atha," the word "etān" refers to the experiencing selves (*bhoktṛn ātmanaḥ*).

He explains the phrase "for the sake of accomplishing their own purpose" (*svārthasiddhyartham*) as referring to the categories (*tattva*) and so forth; [he explains] "of one's own" (*svasya*) as referring to insentient things (*acetanānām*).

It has been stated that there is no activity for those things not presided over by volition (*cetanā*). Furthermore, he explains it otherwise with the words "or else" (*yadvā*) and so forth: even experience (*bhoga*) does not proceed of its own accord for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), because it is formless (*amūrta*), like a substance (*dravya*); and the person, being non-autonomous (*asvatantra*), does not himself proceed toward the purpose of experience.

Thus it has been stated. However, one must not explain this as being for the sake of fulfilling his own creative activity or purpose; to this he says: "That [activity] also has itself as its motive," and so forth. || 12 ||
Commentary: Having thus far described emanation and maintenance, he speaks in order to describe dissolution:
"having withdrawn the means of experience."
Having taken recourse to its cause,
it occupies that which possesses a self and remains there for the sake of rest. || 13 ||
For those who are destined for existence and weary of cyclic existence, he is the benefactor of all beings, because he is devoted to their welfare. || 13½ ||
At the end of the period of persistence, having withdrawn the means of enjoyment— the body, the organs, the worlds, and so forth—

and having caused them to merge into the causal principle called *māyā*, [the Lord] presides over that causal *māyā* which contains within it the multitude of individual selves (*ātman*) of those subject to transmigration.
He remains for the sake of providing rest to those exhausted by wandering through the paths of existence;

the meaning is that He brings their activities to a cessation. Why? It is said: "Because He is intent on the welfare of all beings," since the Supreme Lord is engaged in promoting the well-being of all creatures and removing their weariness.
It brings about for them a state of rest characterized by sleep. || 13½ ||
The *Dīpikā* states: "By the words 'the means of enjoyment' (*bhogasādhana*) and so forth, the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is proclaimed"; thus he says, "that much," and so on. || 13½ ||
Commentary: Then, having reached the end of sleep...
Again, it proceeds as before. || 14 ||
At the end of the sleep whose duration will be described, the Supreme Lord acts once again at the dawn of day as before. (14)
The commentary.

He says that even during its state of sleep, the powers of action and so forth remain intent upon the accomplishment of their respective effects: The powers of action and so forth, even during its [the Lord's] sleep, remain engaged in the production of their respective effects; thus he says:
Even while in sleep, he remains awakening those capable of being awakened,
restraining those who are to be restrained, ripening the karma of those under the influence of karma, and manifesting the powers of *māyā* that are ready for manifestation.
Seeing every category of thing exactly as it is. || 15 ||

Just as in the waking state, even in the state of deep sleep, He awakens those fit for awakening according to the degree of ripening of their impurities, restrains those fit for restraint by His power of obstruction, brings the karma of ritualists to fruition and transformation, and makes the powers of Māyā ready for manifestation.
He remains beholding everything—consisting of the conscious and the unconscious, as well as all states of being, beings, and worlds—exactly as it is.

We shall explain that "in whatever manner" means that his perception of the nature of things does not, like that of people such as ourselves, correspond to an unreal state of affairs. Thus, by this much, the threefold task characterized by the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world has been described here.
The conclusion of the section.
Thus ends the fourth section in the *Mṛgendravṛtti* composed by Śrī Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, son of Bhaṭṭa Vidyākaṇṭha.
The *Dīpikā* says: "Now, just like the multitude of individual selves (*ātmavrāta*), the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is also indeed devoid of activity during the time of sleep;
in order to refute this, the Sūtra beginning with 'Even in sleep He exists' (*svāpepy āste*) was stated. Thus he says: "In that [state of] sleep, etc. (*tatsvāpepi*, etc.).

But how, then, can there be a distinction between the Lord’s functions of dissolution (*laya*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and authority (*adhikāra*)? We reply: it is through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) based on His presiding over specific states of the *bindu*. As it has been said: "By way of metaphorical designation, He is the one who possesses authority, the enjoyer, and the one who effects dissolution. For this very reason, [He is so designated] because of His presiding over the worlds (*bhuvana*) beginning with Nivṛtti.

He will state that the designation of the Lord as "possessing cessation" (*nivṛttimat*) and so forth is merely figurative (*upacāreṇa*). There is no contradiction, for "cessation" refers to His station, and thus the Lord is also said to "possess cessation" and so on. However, it has been stated in the *Svāyambhuva* that for those souls who have attained their respective levels through initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other means, their distinction is indeed real: "Whoever should desire enjoyments in a particular place... and so forth.

He is appointed to that very task; he becomes a possessor of *siddhi* through the power of mantra. Regarding the phrase "obstructing those who deserve obstruction by means of the power of obstruction":
now, is it not said that "obstruction" (*rodha*) is concealment (*tirobhāva*), defined as non-deviation from appropriate experience?
And in the state of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), there is indeed an absence of obstruction. Therefore, how can it be said that he is "obstructing those who are to be obstructed"? This is not so.
This is the fault. The meaning here is that by means of resting [them], he renders those who ought to be restrained fit for restraint.

"And the powers of *māyā*" means the causal powers residing within *māyā*. Regarding this very point, at the conclusion of the section, he states the reason with the words beginning "tadiyatā" (by this much), which is well known in the world.

Thus, the triad of functions beginning with creation has been described here; however, the intention is that the other two functions established by the scripture will be demonstrated in another section. Thus ends [the section] in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā* composed by Aghoraśivācārya.
The fourth chapter, the Determination of the Three Acts of Counteraction (*patikṛtyatrayanirṇaya*), is completed.
The fifth chapter is the Section on the Five Acts (*pañcakṛtyaprakaraṇa*).
Now, regarding the meaning of each term as projected by all the words for acts contained in the Root Sūtra:
A new section is commenced to explain the two remaining types of action, known as *anugraha* (grace) and *tirobhāva* (concealment).

Here, the connection between the words of the sūtra and their meanings is clear. The contextual connection, however, should be understood through the section called the *vidyāpāda*. This [connection] is also of the nature of the sentence.
By such statements as "The creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and liberation of the world constitute His activity," the *pāṭalika*—
who, as was introduced in the previous chapter, awakens those capable of awakening— is further addressed regarding the section on the power of darkness (*tamaś-śakti-adhikāra*).
Upon the cessation [of that state] and its subsequent withdrawal,
Śiva, the kinsman of the world, manifests through his power of vision and action the infinity of the individual soul (aṇu). || 1 ||
1. Regarding the variant reading *aprasiddhaṃ tu*:

[it refers to] "by the power of darkness" (*tamaśśaktyā*) and so forth; that is, by the power belonging to the Lord which is called *vāmā*, or by its authority (*adhikāra*), which consists in its subordination (*nyagbhāvana*) and its nature as a veil (*āvṛtitva*).

This "fall" (paricyuti), which consists of the cessation of [worldly] activity, is the state of being oriented toward liberation (*kaivalya*). As it has been stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "When that [bondage] has perished, by means of this [state], one attains the supreme beatitude.
When this fall has occurred, the Supreme Lord, intent upon the upliftment of the world, [acts].

This [text] reveals the infinity of vision and action belonging to the soul, which is as minute as an atom. It has been stated that since vision and action are indeed eternal, their infinity—which was previously obscured because they were delimited by impurity—is manifested through the removal of that obscuration via the transformation of the soul;

it is not, however, a production of something previously non-existent. We shall explain this further in the discussion on *satkāryavāda* (the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause). || 1 ||
The Lamp (Dīpikā).
Now begins the section on the Five Acts (*pañcakṛtyaprakaraṇa*).
He introduces the section beginning with "Of the authority of the power of darkness" (*tamaśśaktyadhikārasya*) and so forth with the words "Now," etc. [Objection: But surely...

By the passage beginning with "He is omniscient because He is the creator of all," the omniscience of the Lord will also be stated in this very section. Therefore, how can it be said that two functions are being stated?
There is no fault, for it was mentioned as an incidental indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) because it occurs first. For this very reason:

It should be understood that even the fivefold relationship mentioned here is stated as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). Likewise, because the acts of maturation and so forth— such as "causing one to cook" (*pācayan*) and "the object of the object" (*karmikarma*), which were previously indicated at the end of the preceding chapter—
are for the purpose of grace (*anugraha*) and concealment (*tirobhāva*), the sūtras that expound them are [treated] separately.

The application of the connection: Now the connection of the aphorisms (sūtras) that establish omniscience is being stated. In this regard, the topical and the contextual connections are as previously described. The connection pertaining to the aphorism, however, is expressed by the term "the all-knowing one" (*sarvavit*). Furthermore, the connection consisting of the sentence is of various kinds, such as through [aphorisms] beginning with, "For that very [omniscience] is to be known by him."

By the phrase "seeing everything of the *pāṭalika*," this is indicated. Therein, because the concealment (*tirobhāva*) of the shore is described as having the nature of the enjoyment of experience (*bhoga-bhojana*), and because that [concealment] is established by implication through the performance of creation and so forth, it was not explained separately by the author of the Sūtras. However, grace (*anugraha*) is [explained] by the passage beginning with "of the authority of the power of darkness" (*tamaś-śakty-adhikārasya*).

He says "it is declared," etc. Regarding the phrase "upon the falling away from that [state] consisting of the power of darkness (tamaś-śakti) and so forth," he states that this term is to be explained as being related to the individual soul (aṇu), beginning with "that which... and so on; the ellipsis is "from that [state] characterized by impurity" (malādhikāra). Furthermore, he states that the "falling away" here occurs precisely through the desire to abandon that [impurity], namely, "the state of being oriented toward isolation" (kaivalya-abhimukhībhāva). He begins with "in this [state]," and so forth.

For this very reason, immediately after the descent of power (śaktipāta) has been ascertained through signs such as devotion and faith, the initiation (dīkṣā) of this [soul] must be performed by the teachers. The word "aṇoḥ" (of the atom/soul) is used in the singular to denote a class. || 1 ||
Commentary: Those whom he liberates during his sleep immediately become auspicious (śiva).
Whether withdrawn or arisen,
they are either individual phonemes or complete words.

The Supreme Lord bestows grace upon others who remain in the state of deep sleep; they indeed become Śivas at that very moment, yet they do not become qualified [for office]. This is because, due to the persistence of a portion of their impurity (mala), they lack the fitness for Śiva-hood by virtue of being subject to impulse, and because there is no utility for them as qualified agents at that time. Furthermore:

Whether during dissolution or creation, those whom he liberates also attain the state of Śiva immediately; there is no exception. Alternatively, due to the difference in the ripening of the collyrium (añjana) at these two times—creation and dissolution—they become recipients of liberation without further office (niradhikāra-mukti) through the manifestation of their Śiva-nature at that very moment, while those who are yogins with office (sādhikāra) attain the status of Lords (pati).

The meaning is that they become *ātman*s. In that regard, during the dissolution (*saṃhāra*), those who possess the authority of grace (*anugraha*) are then the *rudrāṇava*s; however, in the creation (*sṛṣṭi*), they are to become those possessing authority. At the commencement of the creation, those who are favored by grace along with their authority are the *patayaḥ* (lords), who hold offices such as the *parāpara-vidyeśvara*s.
[The opponent asks: "How is it that those to be graced attain the state of Śiva, even though [the scriptures] speak of the times of creation and dissolution?
[The author replies: It is indeed attained, because the ripening of impurity (*mala*) and the grace (*anugraha*) of the Supreme Lord are not restricted to specific times. || 2 ||
*Dīpikā*: "Of them" means "of those who are qualified. "Not by way of separation" means "without obstacle.
And this grace is performed by the Blessed One without reference to any external locus (niradhikaraṇa). || 2 ||

Commentary: Having thus described the specific nature of liberation for those favored during the periods of creation, dissolution, and sleep, he now states the specific nature of it for those favored during the period of maintenance.
Those whom [the Lord] favors during his abiding state become partakers of the station of Īśāna, the lord of the Rudra-mantras.
Having taken refuge in the Guru, who possesses consciousness. || 3 ||
1. There is a variant reading: *adhikārapadānugrahaḥ*.
During the period of maintenance (*sthitikāla*), the Supreme Lord resides within the Guru as consciousness;
by virtue of meditating upon Him, [the disciples] become endowed with a praiseworthy consciousness directed toward the higher and lower forms of supreme bliss (*niḥśreyasa*).
He favors those who are not deficient in their vehicles, because they differ from those whose powers are impaired by dullness and the like;
[he favors] the Rudras of the five and eight classes, the mantras numbered in the seventy million,
their lords, the Vidyeśvaras, and Īśāna, who is characterized as Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śānta.
The phrase "those who partake of that state" (tatpadabhājaḥ) means those who possess the state of *sālokya* and so forth; that is, they become associated with that very state. || 3 ||
The *Dīpikā* states:

"Even at the time of persistence (*sthitikāla*), [the Lord acts] by means of a substratum (*sādhikaraṇena*"; thus he says "in the substratum of the Guru," and so forth. And "of those lords" refers to the *Vidyeśvaras*, meaning the other Lords of Mantras (*mantreśvaras*), but not to Ananta and the others; for there is no such intermixture (*vyatikara*) between those two groups."
Because, by such statements as these, the possibility of falling away for those who have attained these [lower] levels will be explained;

whereas for those who have attained levels such as Ananta, falling away is not possible, because karma and the like cannot exist due to their having transcended *māyā*. And it is said in the *Raurava*: "Having enjoyed the enjoyments..."
"Having been endowed for a very long time with the hosts of celestial beauties, they become free from longing and attain the sovereignty devoted to the state of Śiva.

For this very reason, regarding the phrase "characterized by Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śānta," the word *īśvara*—which denotes Ananta—serves as an indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) for the status of the Vidyeśvaras. Therefore, of those...
The meaning is: of the Supreme Lord who, while in the state of dissolution, presides over the worlds beginning with Sadāśiva. || 3 ||
Commentary: Now, if those who attain that state do so due to a particular descent of power (*śaktipāta*), then how is that particularity to be known? To this, he says:
1. There is a variant reading: *dhiṣṭhāturlayāvasthāstha*.
For those embodied beings whose power falls so as not to return...
Their characteristic signs are yearning for liberation and aversion toward worldly existence.
Devotion toward the devotees of Śiva and faith in the ritual prescribed by his teaching— by this, inference from the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭa)—
[This is] for the sake of those whose intellects are coarse, even though [the reason] exists. || 5 ||
Since the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is difficult to discern for those who are bodiless, it concerns those with bodies:

those upon whom the power of the Supreme Lord falls so as never to manifest again; in them, upon that descent, there arises a longing for liberation, an aversion toward saṃsāra, devotion toward those intent on devotion to the Supreme Lord, and [devotion] toward His teacher.

And faith in the scripture (*śāstra*) is the mark or sign; by this very preeminent sign, even those of subtle intellect can infer the remaining web of fetters (*pāśajāla*) that is the cause for the continued existence in saṃsāra. Furthermore, when the aforementioned signs are merely weak, there is a loosening and weakening of the fetters for the bound soul (*paśu*).
The meaning is that even those of dull intellect can infer [this]. || 4-5 ||

The Dīpikā introduces the sūtra beginning with "yeṣām" (of whom) with the words "nanu" and so forth; the meaning is that, as an incidental consequence, the remaining Śākta liṅgas of grace are now being displayed. (4–5)

Commentary: Now, what is the use of this determination of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), which is so utterly unprecedented? Why is this—which is well-established in all philosophical systems as the cause for attaining isolation (*kaivalya*)—not determined by way of its inferential mark (*liṅga*)? As it has been said: "Not..."
"He who rejoices at a benefit and does not become angry at an injury—one who is equanimous toward all beings—is considered liberated while living. Thus it is said therein;
[this applies] to those who have attained yoga but still possess the vision of a beast.
The two manifestations of karma are equal for those who are fit for the fruits of seniority and so forth, in liberations that possess authority.
Furthermore, due to the distinction of the importance of skillful means (upāya),
those three are sought again;
there is a certain intermingling of the two.
Characterized by the accomplishment of passing away. || 7 ||

Those who have attained perfection through animal-like perceptions and animalistic forms of knowledge, as well as through the yoga taught by them— such as that composed by Kapila, Patañjali, and others—
and who have reached a state of equanimity through the clarity of the quality of *sattva*— for them...

Since the two individuals characterized by serenity and anger are equal with respect to the two types of actions consisting of benefit and harm, there should be no manifestation of anger toward the one who harms,
nor any manifestation of affection toward the one who benefits. Let this be so simply because it is logically consistent.

We do not deny this; however, there is this distinction here: regarding the liberations that possess specific qualifications (*adhikāravatī-mukti*), there is the superiority of the means—such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth—as will be described by the words "worldly-dharma-based initiation" and "Śiva-dharma-based initiation," and because of the devotion consisting of the love and faith directed toward attaining those respective levels.

Because of their distinctness. As it is stated in the venerable *Sūkṣmasvāyambhuva*: "Whoever should desire enjoyments in a particular place, he is directed to that very place; he becomes a possessor of accomplishment through the power of the mantra.
Therefore, because of the distinctness of the means [from the goal], the mantra—

In order to ascertain the fitness for the highest fruit characterized by the attainment of the status of Maheśvara and others, the eligibility for the intermediate fruit consisting of the attainment of the status of Mantreśvara, and the fitness for appointment to the subordinate offices such as those of the Pañcāṣṭaka and other higher authorities, three specific instances of karma are sought and investigated.

The intention is that, according to the degree of manifestation of devotion and faith—whether superior, middling, or inferior—those who possess the respective qualifications become recipients of grace by attaining the state of liberation (apavarga). And as for these three types of liberation with their corresponding qualifications that have been shown, from among them: "there is an intermingling of two."

Between the two types of liberation—the middling and the inferior—there exists an obstacle consisting of a certain fluctuation, due to the possibility of falling from one's own state or the possibility of attaining a superior accomplishment, as these states are situated respectively above and below [the highest goal]. However, there is no attainment of *apavarga* immediately thereafter; but in the third [case],...
The attainment of that [state] occurs immediately upon the completion of the qualification for the office of that rank. || 6-7 ||
1. "This" (idam): the meaning is the absence of joy and dejection toward benefit and harm.
[The *Dīpikā*: He raises an objection based on another school's view in order to introduce the aphorism beginning with "the gaze of a beast" (*paśudṛk*).

Regarding the phrase "nanu" and so forth, he explains that by the word "tat" (that) in the expression "tat-trayam" (the triad of that), a specific instance of action (*karma-vyakti*) is being referred to;

thus he says "the triad of action-instances" and so on. Furthermore, he states that the actions intended here are those previously mentioned, such as devotion (*bhakti*) and the rest; thus he says "devotion, faith," and so forth. [The opponent asks: "If this is so, then [is there no fault] here?"

The two specific actions mentioned, such as "rejoicing" (*hṛṣyati*), are not to be disregarded at all. No; the sense is that when these are joined, other factors such as devotion (*bhakti*) and faith (*śraddhā*) must also be required.
He introduces the sūtra beginning with "of the two" (*dvayoḥ*) with the words "And this... (*yaccaitat*) and so forth. [The phrase] "by the possibility of falling away" (*cyutisambhavena*).

Since the various forms of liberation consisting of the attainment of specific worlds endure only until the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), it is indeed possible for one to descend again at the commencement of a new creation due to the residue of karma (*karmaśeṣa*). [Objection: If this is so, then the very status of these two as "liberation" is lost. [Reply: True; however, the status of these two as liberation— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical flow of the argument.]

There is no contradiction, for it is indeed a semblance of liberation (*muktyābhāsa*). The phrase "by the possibility of an excellence of accomplishment" is an elliptical expression meaning "and by the possibility of liberation.

This is because, due to the ripening of impurity (*malaparipāka*), liberation is indeed possible even there through initiation (*dīkṣā*); for in every world (*bhuvana*), teachers (*guru*) reside. (6–7)
Commentary: Now, what is the cause of this variety of signs, by virtue of which liberation possesses threefold authority? To this he says:
But when the obstructive power of the Lord of Darkness has ceased by even a small amount or half,
these signs appear.
And when [the lifespan] of embodied beings has only a little remaining... || 8 ||
When that state of being an obstructer— which belongs to Lord Vāmadeva, the master of darkness who restrains both perception and action—
is partially ceased, half-removed, or slightly remaining, this gradation of signs arises for embodied beings. || 8 ||
1. Since gurus reside in every world (bhuvana), the meaning is that liberation is possible even there through initiation (dīkṣā) performed by those gurus.
— *Dīpikā*.

He states "Now," and so forth, explaining that the cessation of the Lord's authority regarding the power of concealment is itself the cause for the descent of grace and the arising of the signs [of spiritual attainment]. || 8 ||
Commentary: For this very reason, these three types of fitness are also [to be understood].
Having transcended [all], Maheśvara bestows grace upon the individual soul (aṇu) during his sleep,
because this [state] is characterized by authority.

Without regard for these three types of fitness (*yogyatā*), [the Lord] favors the individual soul (*aṇu*) during sleep. The term "individual soul" (*aṇu*) is used in the singular to denote the class. The sense is that He does not effect the favoring of souls at that time due to the diversity of their fitness.
He states the reason for this very point: "Because this [body] possesses an office (*adhikāra*)."
Since the three types of fitness depend upon qualification, and since qualification has no utility at that time, it is therefore not required. || 9 ||
The *Dīpikā* states:
"And it has been said that the cause of the impurity of the *adhikāra* is indeed the ripening of that impurity; thus [it is said], 'these three types of fitness,' and so forth.
Furthermore, this is produced by each preceding stage. However, fitness is not something whose nature consists solely in the ultimate ripening of impurity."

Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument]. Furthermore, "sleep" is merely an illustration; for even during the state of [waking] stability, there is the complete purification of impurities, the possibility of grace without a formal locus [of ritual action], and because it has already been stated that this possesses the characteristic of tranquility. || 9 ||
1. "Of the duration of its persistence" is the ellipsis. 2. "Of the cessation of the governing authority" is a variant reading. [End of] the commentary (*vṛtti*).
At the root of creation, in the third [state];
like sleep, during the withdrawal of the elements. 9½.
At the beginning of creation, at the end of the dissolution, and during the third withdrawal of beings whose characteristics will be described hereafter, those whom [the Lord] favors become Śivas,
like individual souls (aṇu) favored during the state of deep sleep. 9½.

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: "And in the third, at the withdrawal of the elements" refers to that which consists of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), because the dissolution of the three worlds and the intermediate dissolution will be described later. || 9½ ||
Commentary: Regarding what was previously stated—that [the Lord] bestows grace upon the individual soul (*aṇu*)—he speaks in order to define the term *aṇu*:
"That which is produced by setting aside [the gross body]."
That which is of such a kind is called subtle. || 10 ||

The word "he" (saḥ) refers to that soul who is the recipient of grace at the beginning of creation as just mentioned, or during the third [state], namely the dissolution of the elements or the state of deep sleep;

having cast off—that is, removed—[the impurity] by which he is made such, and by which he becomes one whose nature as Śiva is manifested, he is to be known as the one denoted by the term *aṇu*. Thus, the *aṇu* is purified.
Thus, up to this point. || 10 ||
The *Dīpikā* connects the sūtra "sa yad vyapāsya... with the phrase "svāpeṇum" and so forth;

the word "sa" [in the sūtra] refers to the impurity (*mala*) and so on, as is understood from the context. The word "yat" has the sense of "yasmāt" (because), and by the pronoun "tat" in the phrase "tadvidhaḥ," that which is to be favored is indicated.
He says that [the soul] is "perceived" as one whose nature as Śiva has been manifested; the sense is that because it is free from bonds (pāśa), it is subtle and therefore not called "heavy. || 10 ||

Commentary: Thus, that which was previously stated—that [the Lord] awakens those capable of being awakened—has been demonstrated through the infinite manifestation of the act of awakening. Furthermore, that which was indicated by the phrase "restraining those to be restrained" and so forth, refers to those whom He liberates from sleep (svāpa).

By this [previous statement], it was elaborated on the grounds that while some indeed receive such grace, for others there is an implied exclusion by implication. Now, however, in order to examine what was stated—that "the agent causes the karma to ripen"—he says: "In the same way, the seed of the body and so forth..."
He causes it to be cooked until it is served. || 10½ ||
The powers of the Blessed One are extended toward all effects.

By means of them, He brings to fruition—that is, renders ready for the granting of its fruit—the karma of embodied beings which is the cause of their body, senses, caste, lifespan, and experiences, even while that [karma] remains dormant. || 10½ ||

The *Dīpikā* connects the sūtra beginning with "tathā" [to the preceding context] with the words "tadevam" and so forth. It states that for this very reason, since the obstruction is already implied by the sense of the matter, the remaining elements such as the ripening of karma (*karmapāka*) and so on are expressed by the words "tathā" and so forth; thus he says.
"Idānīm" (now), and so forth. He explains [the phrase] "until the time of entry. "At its sleep" is an elliptical expression;
the meaning is that even during the period of maintenance, it continues to ripen that karma until the time of the creation of the body and other factors that are to be commenced by it. || 10½ ||
Commentary: Because it did not attain the status of a factor for [spiritual] fitness.
It would have to be immediate, like [the effect of] medicine and the like. || 11 ||

The limb that brings about fitness (*yogyatā*) or worthiness (*arhattva*), namely the refinement known as *pāka*, must be cultivated; otherwise, that karma—like a medicinal drug such as *harītakī* taken at the very moment [of administration]—would not be "fruit-bearing," meaning it would not yield its result. This is the sense.

As they say: "A substance such as the *hārītaka* fruit, though existent, is incapable of accomplishing its own effect when its ripening (*pāka*) has not been attained, because it has not reached the ripening that constitutes a factor of its functional capacity (*yogyatā*). In the same way, karma, though existent, is incapable of yielding its fruit when unripened; therefore, it depends upon ripening. (11)
Commentary: He states that its cooking does not occur by itself:
"Even though it is fit for cooking, it cannot be cooked [by itself]."
One does not destroy oneself by means of oneself;
this is the common nature of everything that undergoes transformation.

Even though it is fit for cooking, it is not capable of cooking itself by itself. For this is the common characteristic of every transforming entity, such as milk and the like: that its state of transformation occurs only by depending on something else, and not otherwise. And because of this state of transformation...

The ripening of karma also depends upon other factors. By this, it is also revealed that [the Lord] brings forth the powers of *māyā* into a state ready for manifestation; for even those [powers] are subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*). And it has been stated that it is not possible for these—impurity (*mala*), *māyā*, and karma—to undergo transformation by one who is not the Supreme Lord.

"It rules" (īśati) is not faulty; for there is a traditional rule (smaraṇa) stating that the suffix *kvip* may optionally be applied after all nominal stems (*sarvaprātipadika*) in the sense of "he acts like [that thing]" (*īśa ivācarati*). || 12 ||
The *Dīpikā* states: "Even that which is fit for cooking," and so forth; the intended meaning is that because [the fire] is insentient, there is a contradiction in action directed toward itself.
Furthermore, he says "by this" and so forth, and "not of these" and so forth, to show that this same logic applies equally to Māyā and the others as well.
The meaning is that because the Puruṣa lacks independence, it does not possess the capacity for transformation. || 12 ||
Commentary: Thus far, the supreme Lord’s status as the creator of all has been established. For this very reason, his omniscience is also proven; thus he says:
He who is omniscient, by virtue of being the creator of all things, knows and performs everything along with the means, the constituent parts, and the fruits.
Thus, it is well established that "it is indeed that. || 13 ||

The Lord’s omniscience follows from His being the creator of all; for without knowledge of all objects, His status as the creator of all would be untenable. For indeed, only one who knows the accomplishment of a particular action, its constituent parts, and its fruits—and who possesses the intention to employ various diverse causal factors for that purpose—is capable of being the agent of those respective actions.

Just as a weaver and others are capable of producing cloth and so forth, so too [the Lord is capable of all effects]. Therefore, one who is ignorant in that regard is not competent to perform such work, just as a fool is incompetent in the presentation of logic and sacred knowledge. This being well-established means that it is non-deviant (avyabhicārī). || 13 ||

The *Dīpikā* introduces the sūtra beginning with "the omniscient one" (*sarvajña*) with the words "tadiyatā," and explains that very point with "sarvakartṛtvādeva" and so forth. In the phrase "yatkriyāsiddhim," the term "kriyāsiddhi" refers to the material cause (*upādāna*) which is the basis for the accomplishment of an action.

This is the meaning: for a maker of cloth and the like understands his work—the cloth and so forth—along with its means, such as the threads; its auxiliary factors that provide assistance through cooperation, such as the shuttle and loom; and its purpose, such as clothing. And the Blessed Lord is the maker of all this indeed.
Together with the world of pure and impure selves, its material cause which consists of *māyā* and *mahāmāyā*, its auxiliary cause here which consists of action and service to the Lord,
and its fruit which is the enjoyment of objects within the paths of purity and impurity as well as liberation.

Because he knows the effect by having performed it well, this [being] is established as omniscient. For all of this is such that, when performing an effect with a substratum, he is not perceived; therefore, he performs it without a substratum, just like the light of a lamp and so forth. [Objection: But is it not the case that all cognition is necessarily associated with a substratum characterized by a body?

It is perceived as performing its own function; nevertheless, since the existence of a body has already been refuted in the case of the Lord, if that [function] were admitted to be without a substrate, then the Lord—
being characterized by his own function consisting of the cognition of non-universal objects— would result in being nothing but ignorant.

That is not so; because [the reason] is inconclusive due to the case of air (*vāyu*). For although air is observed in this world to perform the act of breathing by means of a substratum characterized as a body, it nonetheless causes the shaking of trees and so forth without a substratum.
In the same way, knowledge will likewise act [without a substratum]; thus, its lack of a substratum establishes omniscience in this context.
1. There is a variant reading, *kāryeṇa sarve*.
And because this [consciousness] is devoid of obscuration (*āvṛti*), it does not depend upon a manifestor (*vyañjaka*).
Therefore, that is not subject to doubt, nor is it ever contrary [to reality]. (14)
Commentary: Śiva’s omniscience does not depend on a manifesting agent because it is devoid of beginningless veils;
nor is it characterized by doubt, error, or indecision, as is the case with transmigrating beings, for that very reason. || 14 ||
Dīpikā:

For this very reason, the knowledge of the Lord is not similar to the knowledge of those such as ourselves, because it is unobscured; thus he says "of Śiva," and so forth. This is also an elliptical indication [that includes] action as well. || 14 ||
Commentary: For instance, those which perceive the manifestor.
Because it is enveloped by the powers of impurity (mala-śakti), those [powers] may appear obstructed in accordance with the nature of the manifesting agent. 15.

Indeed, those cognitions which, being veiled by the power of impurity (*mala-śakti*), require the manifesting agent (*vyañjaka*) such as *kalā* for the production of experience, become obstructed even with respect to their objects of knowledge (*jñeya-viṣaya*) when they encounter such a manifesting state, because that manifesting agent, such as *kalā*, possesses only limited illumination. But this is not the case for the cognition of the Lord (*aiśvara*).
Such knowledge [is established] from the very reason previously stated, namely, its being devoid of obscuration (*āvṛti*). Thus it has been said in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
"Because he is free from beginningless impurity, he is omniscient; therefore, he is Śiva. (15)
And since its occurrence is from this [cause],
it is neither perceptual nor inferential.
Even the stainless knowledge of Śiva, though derived from scripture, does not manifest clearly at all times regarding all things. 16.

For perception is knowledge that depends upon the senses (*akṣa*), because it conforms to the activity—both its proficiency and lack thereof—of the senses, and because it conforms to their presence or absence; thus, [knowledge] that contradicts this would not be perception. And since such is the case with the cognition of Śambhu, it is therefore not perception.

Nor is it inferential, because that operates in dependence upon perception. Verbal knowledge, however, is cast far aside, since its object is something entirely beyond the senses. And nothing is beyond the perception of the Blessed One;
therefore, his knowledge shines forth with respect to all objects. But not...

Indeed, even in the *Āgamas*, the connection of the Lord with a body and sense organs is heard of in such passages as "five-faced, fifteen-eyed," and so forth. Even though that [connection] exists, why are the Lord’s knowledge and action not dependent upon it?
His connection with a body and sense organs is not for the sake of employing them in knowledge and action; rather, [He possesses them] by His very nature.

Because He possesses the power of perception and action regarding all objects, and because He is capable of performing creation, maintenance, and so forth by mere will; furthermore, He assumes a form for the sake of bestowing grace upon His devotees. Otherwise, meditation, worship, and the like would be impossible in a formless being. As it is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*: "For the sake of the practitioner's objective..."
Its form has been described: "It has hands and feet everywhere; it has eyes, heads, and faces everywhere. (16)

Dīpikā: For this very reason, he raises an objection with "nanu" and so forth, and provides a rebuttal with "nāsya" and so forth; the remainder is that the conjunction of the body and the senses is stated in the Āgamas. || 16 ||
That single [consciousness], due to the infinity of objects,
undergoes an infinity of divisions; its agency likewise follows from its non-difference from that [consciousness].
In that very same way, it is so by way of metaphorical designation. || 17 ||

Commentary: First, regarding that single cognition whose nature is the manifestation of an object as it actually exists, its infinity—which is merely figurative and produced by the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—is established because of the infinity of objects of knowledge; this applies even to the scripture itself.

The infinity [of scriptures] is merely figurative, due to the division of streams, the division of students, the division of propagators, and their respective higher and lower status. From this perspective— that "the power of the Wielder of the Trident is one alone, consisting of all knowledge and action"— agency as well is non-different from that knowledge.
In the same way, infinity is established through figurative designation. || 17 ||

Dīpikā: This has already been stated previously; now, that aforementioned figurative multiplicity of those two is elaborated upon by the words "that is one," etc., as he says "as it truly exists," and so forth. 17.
Commentary: Now, this verse is intended both to summarize the meaning already described and to introduce what remains to be explained:
"By means of [the perspectives of] existence, essential nature, instrument, purpose, and the object of injunction..."
Those who know the true nature of the Lord as it has been declared by me liberate living beings sunk in the mire of worldly existence;
O men, do not [seek this] from others at great length, for it is of the nature of the fetters binding the individual soul (paśu). 18.

Then, having apprehended the body and other objects as possessing the property of being effects, [the author] first establishes the existence of God with the words, "We know its creator," and so forth: "He is eternal because He is not limited by time; He is all-pervading because He has no spatial location; and He possesses the power to produce things both successively and simultaneously, because of the successive and non-successive production [of effects]."

Its essential nature has been stated. Furthermore, by the statement "the instrument is not other than power; power is not insentient, for it is consciousness," the instrument has been described. By the statement "liberation is the fruit of its application, while worldly enjoyment follows as a consequence," the purpose is thus explained. [The powers are: the creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and liberation of the universe.

By the word *kṛtyam* (that which is to be done), the fivefold object of injunction is stated. Furthermore, that his vision is knowledge—and that it is neither perceptual nor inferential, as established by the passage beginning with "nāpy adhyakṣaṃ nāpi tallaiṅgam"—is determined by these [verses].
Thus, by means of these factors—existence, essential nature, instrument, purpose, injunction, and vision—which have been briefly stated, [the Lord is described].
Those persons who know—that is, understand—the true reality (satattva) liberate those transmigrating beings who are submerged in the mire of saṃsāra.

They do not, however, liberate those who know the Lord merely as having the form of a beast or the form of a fetter. This refers to those proponents of the doctrine of the Lord whose nature is the Person (puruṣa), according to whom "all this is indeed the Self" and "all this is indeed the Person."

Or [the view] of those who maintain that Īśvara consists of karma, time, the unmanifest (avyakta), and other such bonds (pāśa): since the purpose of the bound souls (paśu) is fulfilled merely by being bound by those [factors], they would lack sovereignty (anīśvaratva) because they depend on something else— just as one depends on shackles and the like for their conjunction with or separation from various objects— and thus, liberation from the bonds through the realization of such an Īśvara would be a source of ridicule for all the world.
For this reason, the word "beast" (*paśu*) has been employed here to introduce the true nature of the self (*ātmatattva*), which is about to be commenced in the immediately following section. 18.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, on the Fivefold Acts, in the *Mṛgendravṛtti* composed by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, son of Bhaṭṭa Vidyākaṇṭha.
[The] *Dīpikā*.

And for Maheśvara who stands thus, thorough knowledge would be purposeless; therefore, he says "by these [means]," and so forth. For this very reason, it has been stated by the Teacher that one must be a possessor of knowledge (*jñānin*);
as it was said by the Teachers regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*) and exposition (*vyākhyā*): "For the teacher who performs [these acts], knowledge is primary."
And he states that this purpose is not possible for those who know the Lord according to other philosophical systems, beginning with the words "But not in detail," and so forth; because, for them,
[the world] is preceded by an intermediate cause in the form of *paśu* (bound souls) and *pāśa* (fetters), this purpose does not arise from their knowledge.

This is indeed possible. For instance, Nature (prakṛti) itself is accepted by certain knowers of the supreme self and by the followers of the Pañcarātra as being denoted by the term "Nārāyaṇa," the Supreme Brahman. Since that [Nature] is the material cause, it must necessarily have another sustainer (dhātṛ), just as the threads and other materials which are the prakṛti of a cloth must have one. For whoever...

"Golden-wombed (Hiraṇyagarbha) arose in the beginning; once born, he was the sole Lord of all that exists"—based on the meaning of such scriptural passages, those who know the inner self (adhyātmavid) declare that the one called Hiraṇyagarbha is a modification of that primordial nature (prakṛti) and is the Lord (Īśvara).
Alternatively, according to the various Pāñcarātrikas, he is characterized as the fourfold Self (Cāturātmya), as it has been said: "The Lords are indeed those [four] abodes."

Since Kṛṣṇa, Aniruddha, Makaradhvaja, and Rauhineya are beyond Prakṛti, they too— because they possess birth and cessation— must have another creator, just like Brahmā, Indra, and the rest. Furthermore,
as for the Lord (Īśvara) described by the Pātañjalas as being [distinct] due to the conjunction with *buddhi*, and [the self] due to the conjunction with the mind (*manas*)...
This conjunction, which is accepted by the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas as the means for attaining the state of Īśvara,

is itself non-eternal and non-pervasive precisely because it is a conjunction— just like the conjunction between a jar and a cloth— and therefore the status of Īśvara is not universal or eternal. Consequently, even for the lords of the worlds (bhuvaneśvaras), [the attainment of sovereignty] depends upon another creator...
It must be so; for he who is the creator (*dhātṛ*) of all things is precisely the one we accept as Maheśvara. This is because it is not established that any other creator could have preceded him.
[Objection: But since the Lords (*īśvara*) established by other philosophical systems are themselves established by both worldly experience and the Vedas, how [can this be]?

If it is argued that the status of Maheśvara is being rejected, that is not so; for his very status as Maheśvara is demonstrated by the Vedas and other scriptures, as well as by worldly consensus. Thus says the Śruti: "Rudra is indeed one; there is no second who stands alongside him.
Here, by the restriction and the negation of a second, it is made known that Rudra alone possesses the status of Maheśvara.
"Even among the Rudras, [the name] 'Obeisance to Maheśvara, the blue-throated one, accompanied by Ambā' [is supreme]. Even in the Purāṇas it is said:

'Neither through medicinal herbs, nor through mantras, nor through human means of accomplishment is such auspiciousness attained as that which comes from the chanting of Your Name. And in the Mahābhārata and other texts, regarding those who perform the worship of Vāsudeva..."

In hymns such as the *Svapna-śatarudrīya*, he alone is renowned as Maheśvara; for this very reason, in the tenth chapter of the *Bhagavadgītā*, the venerable Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭāraka [states]: "He who knows me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds (*lokamaheśvara*)," thus referring only to the limited domain of the seven worlds beginning with Bhūḥ.

He states that [the Lord's] status as Maheśvara refers to this, and not to the domain of all *tattvas*, worlds (*bhuvana*), and so forth. How then is it stated in the *Bhārata* that "there is no deity higher than Keśava"? For this very reason, he is declared to be superior to the eightfold class of divine origins (*devayoni*)—ranging from the *viśāca* up to the Grandfather (*pitāmaha*)—which pertains to the material creation (*bhautikasarga*). But not...

What contradiction is there in [the statement] "from Maheśvara"? As it has been said: "The divine creation is of eight kinds, the animal birth is fivefold, and the human is of one kind; thus, in brief, is the elemental creation. In this very same way, it should be understood in cases such as "Brahmā and the Brāhmaṇa," and so forth. As it has been said: "Agni is indeed the lowest of the gods, Viṣṇu..."

The term "supreme" (parama) is well-known even in the world through such titles as "Lord of Cakrapura" and "Lord of Madhurā" applied to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others. It is the Blessed One alone who is renowned by such names as Bhīmeśvara and Bhūteśvara at the self-manifested sacred sites (svayaṃbhūkṣetra) of Prayāga and other Maheśvara locations.

Even in the locations of consecration (pratiṣṭhā), [the rites are performed] by means of Brahmeśvara, Someśvara, Rāmeśvara, and so forth. And therefore, although it is recited that "sovereignty belongs to the mistress" (svāminyaiśvarya), nevertheless, its lordship over the subordinate deities is seen in the naming and other functions regarding the children and others who have attained their respective positions. Furthermore, there is another form of lordship.

Since the form of the Lord is established even among extremely fierce kings and others, by worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhi*) alone, that very Maheśvara is established. And it is said in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*: "The Lord is to be understood through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).
Nor is what is well-known devoid of authority. As they say: "Words [denote] substance, genus, and action..."

"Furthermore, there is another [type] based on quality (*guṇajāti*); then there is the etymological (*yaugika*), the conventional-eti-mological (*yogarūḍha*), and those established by common usage (*prasiddhi*) alone—just as in the cases of *sūryaugha*, *calana*, *śukla*, *paṅkaja*, and *paṅkaja*.
A word is said to be of such a kind because it denotes its respective meaning. Now, it has been asked: [The opponent objects: "But was it not stated..."
The followers of Jaimini’s school maintain that common consensus (*prasiddhi*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), like the case of the yakṣa in the banyan tree. That too is incorrect;
for it has been stated that every relationship between a word and its meaning is based upon common consensus.
If that consensus were not a valid means of knowledge, the meaning of the Veda itself would be unestablished, and thus everything would be inconsistent. This is established by scripture (*śāstra*).
Thus, Maheśvara alone is established as the Lord of the world. And we have stated in the *Pāṣaṇḍāpajaya*:

"Having brought down the sovereignty of the Moon-crested Lord—which is proclaimed by the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇic passages, the foremost of sages, and others—how can human beings be so utterly deluded once again?"
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the "Examination of Grace and Other [Means]," in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā* composed by Aghoraśivācārya.
1. The meaning is that renown as the Lord is attained through these words.
Now begins the sixth chapter, concerning the characteristics of the bound soul (*paśu*).
Now, regarding that which is the cause of the universe...
The definition of the self has been attained;
it is almost entirely contained within the Lord’s own statement.
Nevertheless, a formal enunciation is now stated. (1)

Commentary: Now, the definition of the Self (ātman), whose name was indicated at the end of the final chapter, is being stated; thus, the connection between the chapters and the connection within the section should be understood. As for the Sūtras and so forth:

These [points] are to be inferred as before; stating them again for each chapter would result in excessive redundancy. The Self (Ātman) is the cause and the motive for the activity of the entire universe, because it brings about the production of bodies, organs, and worlds as the means for its own experience. Of that Self...

The definition [of the Self] is now stated, as its opportunity has arrived immediately following the discussion of Īśvara. Although this [definition] follows as a consequence of the proof of Īśvara in the statement, "The creator of the world must be one whose nature is established by itself," it is as follows: "Consciousness, consisting of the powers of knowledge and action, exists in the Self at all times; and because it is heard [in scripture] that in liberation it is present everywhere."
The method of exposition has been stated almost entirely in the passage beginning with "the face" (*mukham*) and so forth;
nevertheless, a brief summary of its nature, along with its underlying rationale, is now being set forth. (1)
The Lamp (Dīpikā):
Now begins the sixth section, concerning the characteristics of the bound soul (paśu).
Regarding the phrase "of that which has the universe as its cause," he states that the word "atha" (now) signifies immediate succession.
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "athedānīm" (now then), etc.: the connection to the *sūtra* (aphorism) is through the word "aṇoḥ" (of the atom/individual soul);

the connection to the meaning of the word (*padārtha*) is by way of being the referent of the word "paśu" (the bound soul). As for the connection consisting of the sentence (*vākya*), it is through such sentences as "Consciousness, whose nature is vision and action, exists eternally in the self," and so forth. But [one might ask], how is this [to be understood]? It is according to the aforementioned method.

If one asks, "What is the purpose of this section regarding the definition of the self? he says, "It is with supporting arguments," and so forth. Only the sentience of this self has been established; here, however, its distinctness from the body and other such qualities are demonstrated through reasoning. || 1 ||
The earth and other elements are the effects; God is their creator.
That creator does not require those effects for his own purpose, because he is not insentient by nature.
There is no lack of purpose, because of the importance of the agent. || 2 ||

Commentary: First, it was previously stated that earth and other elements possess the nature of being effects due to their having a specific arrangement and so forth. Furthermore, the Lord has been established as their creator by the arguments mentioned earlier. That effect is useful for him.

There are four positions: [the earth and so forth] being useful to itself, not useful to itself, useful to another, or [useful to neither]. Among these, it is first of all not useful to God (īśvara), for no purposeful activity whatsoever is performed by the earth and so forth within His own self, because His nature is eternally perfect. Nor is that effect—the earth and so forth—produced solely for the sake of the earth and so forth.

Because they lack consciousness, there is nothing for them to accomplish; for it is only for one who possesses consciousness and desires the fourfold aims beginning with dharma that there can be something to be accomplished, not for an object such as a jar. Nor is this effect purposeless, because of the gravity of the agent;
even when an effect is produced by an agent in a general sense, it does not become purposeless—how much more so in this case?
By Brahmā and others, the creators of the world impelled by the Supreme Lord, the purpose for performing that work has already been demonstrated. (2)

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: Here, first of all, the existence of the self (*ātman*) has been established by means of a *pariśeṣa* (residual) inference starting with the words "the state of being an effect" (*kāryatva*). To this he says: "First of all, the state of being an effect," and so forth. Now, one might object: "But that [self] is non-existent, because there is experience [of results] from karma," and so on.

The doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmyavāda*), which indeed rejects ultimate liberation, has been refuted. True. For this very reason, in this context, the fact that [the self] is distinct from the body and so forth is established in order to refute the Cārvākas and others; thus there is no redundancy. Regarding the passage beginning with "In that regard, not first," etc.: [one might object], "But since the Supreme Self is one, according to the maxim 'I do not delight being alone'..."

The proponents of the doctrine of sport (*krīḍā-brahmavādins*) maintain that the Lord, characterized as the Supreme Self, produces effects such as the earth and so forth for the sake of His own sport. That is not so; for the plurality of selves will be stated [later] and has already been established previously. Furthermore, according to the theory of sport, [the Lord would be like] a king with his animals, and thus of that Brahman—

Since nothing can obstruct the will of the All-Powerful One, even such means to liberation as "the Self must be known" would be fruitless due to the lack of boldness on the part of all persons; thus, liberation is impossible. This remains true even under the doctrine of a variegated Brahman (*citrabrahmavāda*), because of [the obstruction by] inherent nature (*svabhāva*).

Because it would not terminate [the cycle], just as heat does not cease from fire, liberation itself would be impossible. Furthermore, the faults already mentioned—such as the loss of non-duality (advaita-hāni) under the view that Brahman is quiescent—are indeed applicable. As for what was stated regarding "this being an effect" and so forth, namely that "even a dull-witted person does not act without a purpose," the purpose has been explained at length previously.
The meaning here is that for one who is liberated, he is indeed Śiva. || 2 ||
By process of elimination, that [body] exists for the sake of another;
he is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who is distinct from those two. || 2½ ||

1. Regarding the Supreme Lord’s performance of actions, there is a variant reading: *tattadvyāpāritaiḥ*. 2. In the manuscripts, the reading *namāmyaham* is found. 3. This is verse 5½ in the section on the examination of the characteristics of a husband (*patilakṣaṇaparīkṣāprakaraṇa*).

Commentary: That refers to the effects such as earth and so forth. To the question "Who is the 'other' (para) here?", he says: "the Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajña). The meaning is that the Knower of the Field—the subject under discussion who is distinct from both the agent and the effect—is the bound soul (paśu), the Self (ātman). || 2½ ||
Commentary: Here, for the sake of refuting the self according to the views of the Cārvākas, this objection is raised: "The other [body] is the self, because it serves that purpose."
Are not the earth and other elements indeed for the sake of others? || 3 ||
Now, it may be argued that since the earth and other elements have observed purposes, they must exist for the sake of another;
and that "other" here is simply the body, for it is the body whose constituent parts and utilizers are earth, water, fire, and air.
Therefore, the self cannot be inferred from the fact that the earth and other elements exist for the sake of another. (3)
Commentary:
Here is the reply:
The body also exists for the sake of another, because it is insentient.
One practices even more easily. || 3½ ||

The body, too, exists solely for the sake of another because it is insentient, like the earth and other elements; thus, its being for the sake of another is all the more established as being for the sake of something else. Consequently, since both the body and the earth and so forth exist for the sake of another, it is logical that the "other" here is the Self alone. (3½)
Commentary: Now, it might be argued that this would indeed be the case if consciousness were something other than the body;
however, consciousness arises within the embryo and so forth, which are modifications of the four elements—earth and the rest—and which serve as the cause for the vital breaths and other functions.

Just as the capacity for intoxication arises from the transformation of substances such as fermenting agents (*kiṇva*), so too is the notion of "I" observed only with respect to the body, as in "I am thin" or "I am fat. Furthermore, no self (*ātman*) is perceived apart from that [body], because the claim that "the self exists in the body" is refuted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), much like the statement that "there is a horse-horn. Now, if...

The self is established through inference—such as "the eyes and other organs exist for the sake of another because they are composite entities, like the parts of a bed," or by means of the fact that instruments must be employed by an agent.
This is not correct, because it is unestablished against the Cārvākas who deny the self; for these [Cārvākas] do not accept such [premises].

There is no means of valid cognition other than direct perception. Furthermore, even if the self were established through inference, it would follow that the self, like Devadatta and others, is an "other. For that which shines forth by itself is the self, whereas that which is illuminated by it is "other"; thus, the distinction between self and other exists only for that which is manifesting.
There would be confusion and a lack of stability. As it has been said: "If the self were an object of cognition, there would be another who is its cognizer.
In that case, the self would become 'other,' for it is that which is measured [as an object] which is other.
