Likewise, consciousness alone shines forth, while everything else is illuminated; and that which is illuminated must be an object (*karman*).
"How can there be [action] without an agent? Therefore, it might be suspected that the self (ātman) distinct from the body is not apprehended through inference;
rather, it is the body itself, characterized by consciousness, that exists as a real entity. Anticipating this, he says:
"1. Of that"—meaning, of that inference.
If it were conscious, it could never be an object of experience,
because that which is an object of experience is observed to be subject to modification.
Pots and other such objects are devoid of consciousness; and if that were the case, then consciousness would not exist even when the corpse is present, because [the corpse] is a living being.

Now, you might think that the body itself consists of volition; for it is observed that when something increases or decreases, that which undergoes increase or decrease is of the same nature as that thing— just as heat follows the increase and decrease of fire.

Furthermore, since consciousness imitates the growth and decay related to the body—which are caused by factors such as youth, old age, eating, and fasting—consciousness must have the body as its very self. Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that the body alone is the conscious entity. Now follows the refutation of this: "No, because [the body] is an object of enjoyment and because it is subject to modification."

That [body] is also thus: the body is never conscious, because it is an object of experience and because it is subject to modification. Whatever is subject to modification, subject to transformation, and an object of experience is observed to be insentient, such as jars and the like. The body is of this same nature; therefore, it is not conscious.

[Objection: But surely, being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of [the case of] women and so forth, since even though they are objects of enjoyment, there is an absence of sentience (*caitanya*) therein. [Reply:

It is not inconclusive, because it is that very body belonging to her which is the object of enjoyment. [Objection: If this is so, why is there no experience (*upabhoga*) by a lifeless body? [Reply: There certainly is, in accordance with its particular state.

The enjoyment [of the object] belongs to carnivorous beasts and the like, and not to lovers and the like; for since the beloved undergoes a change of state, she becomes a cause for the sentiment of disgust (*bībhatsa-rasa*) due to her transformation. As it has been said: "This is no longer her face; where is that nectar of her lower lip? Where are the sidelong glances of the long-eyed one?"

By means of the words "in which," etc., it should be understood that the same applies to elephants, horses, and so forth. Therefore, it is established that because the body is subject to modification and is an object of enjoyment, it is insentient; and because it is insentient, it exists for the sake of another. Again, he raises the objection of another's view: "because [the effect] exists when [the cause] exists," meaning that when something exists, another thing comes to be, and when that [cause] is absent...
Furthermore, its absence [is observed] when that [body] is absent; it is its effect, just as coldness is the effect of snow.

Moreover, since consciousness exists when there is a transformation of the specific elements that constitute the body made of semen and blood, and does not exist when that [transformation] has been destroyed, consciousness is produced by the transformation of specific elements. Or rather: [the same conclusion follows].

If you say this, it is untenable. For [the following reason]: consciousness does not arise even when a corpse is present. Here, one must necessarily accept the rule that "that whose existence occurs only when another exists is the effect of that.
Otherwise, it would be impossible for something to be its effect if it were to exist even in the absence of that [cause]. Just as [consciousness arises] only when fire is present...

Smoke that arises is indeed the effect of fire; likewise, if consciousness were to exist only when the elements that initiate the body are present, and its non-existence would necessarily follow from their absence—such that it were perceived as being connected to that body—then [the argument would hold]. However, even while the body exists, there is a departure of consciousness during states such as embryonic development and at subsequent times.

It has been observed [that consciousness exists when the body exists]. Therefore, that [observation] does not establish the existence of a sentient being as non-different from the body. Now, one might object: even in a dead body, because the air consisting of breath and so forth has departed, as has the heat consisting of fire, there is no presence of the elements that constitute the body as there is in the state of life; therefore, in this case [of death], there is insentience.

And as for that existence which, being present, cannot be rendered inconclusive [by the absence of consciousness], do not say so; for even some who have lost their vital breath (gatāsavaḥ) are observed for some time with moving joints and warmth. And in their case, just as in the state of being alive, although there is the presence of the elements that constitute the body, consciousness does not arise.
Furthermore, even when the entire collection of causal conditions is present during the embryonic stage, consciousness is sometimes absent.
Therefore, "existence" (sattva) is indeed inconclusive (anaikāntika) as a reason for proving [the existence of a soul]. || 5 ||
1. "At a later time" means at the time of death.
2. Regarding the variant reading: "Therefore, consciousness is not the initiator of the body because [it] exists [only] when there is a sentient being. — *Dīpikā*.

He constructs an introductory framework (*pīṭhikā*) in order to explain the fragment of the aphorism beginning with *cetanaśced* (if [the self] were conscious), starting with the objection: "But [if it were so], it would not be other than the body. He states that this applies even in the womb and so forth—that is, even while situated in the embryonic body composed of semen and blood; by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it also includes those born from sweat and the like. Furthermore, he says that if the self were other than the body, there would also be a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

[Objection: "I am the seer," and so forth; indeed, the conventional usage "I am the body" is also observed. [Reply: True. Like the expression "the head of Rāhu," it is figurative (*aupacārika*) and not primary (*mukhya*). [The author] raises the doubt regarding the distinctness of the self from the body by means of inference, starting with "Now," and so forth. [In the phrase] "of the instruments," and so forth: because the eyes and other senses are instruments like weapons and the like, they must have a prompter (*prayojaka*), namely, an agent (*kartṛ*).

He refutes [the objection] with the words "it must be so" by stating "that is not tenable," and so forth. The meaning is that since beds, seats, and mountains are observed to exist for the sake of an aggregate body, the sense organs must also exist for the sake of a body; however, in reality, they do not exist for the sake of another. This is the intended sense.
He explains this very point with the words "Now, if you think," and so forth. He explains the subsequent sūtra, "If the body were conscious," and so forth.

Regarding that which was stated—that the notion of "I" is observed only in the body—that is not so; because the body is also perceived internally through sensations such as pain, and externally through distinctions such as softness and hardness.

The self, whose nature is that of a synthesizing subject determined precisely through its own self-awareness, is established by self-consciousness as distinct from the body. Therefore, the objection that the self would consequently be "other" (external) because it is an object of inference is also refuted. Furthermore, if the body itself were the self, then upon seeing another's body, [one would perceive] another's consciousness...
Since one perceives a body that is devoid of passion, hatred, and so forth when it has passed away,

it is understood that there exists a person distinct from the body. Now, seeking to demonstrate that even the Cārvāka cannot avoid inference, the author establishes the insentience of the body by means of inference.

"Because it is an object of enjoyment," and so forth; furthermore, the body itself is not the self, because it is perceptible by the external senses, like a jar or other such objects. As for what was stated—that consciousness, being produced from a modification of the elements, is established as being like the power of intoxication in liquor—this is explained by raising the objection of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "it exists when [the cause] exists. Thus he says: "When that exists," and so forth.
He explains the section on the aphorism of refutation beginning with "yatsadbhāva eva" (only when that exists), etc. || 5 ||
1. There is a variant reading: *prayojakena*. 2. The meaning is that the subsequent sūtra is a sūtra of resolution (*samādhāna*). [End of] the commentary (*vṛtti*).
"Is it not the case that consciousness is possible in the state of being alive due to a specific modification [of the elements],
whereas in a body whose life has departed it is absent because such a modification is lacking?"— thus he raises the objection once more from the very standpoint of the Cārvāka.
If it is argued that [the object] exists because of the distinctness of the transformation, then there would be no memory. || 5½ ||

Due to the distinctions between stages such as childhood and youth, and due to the specific differences between each intermediate stage caused by the repeated transformations of the elements that constitute the body, the consciousness that exists during the state of the living being (*jīva*) is produced by such transformations of the elements.

The various cognitions that manifest numerous objects such as this or that jar, cloth, or cart arise—only due to the specific transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*)—as each subsequent one follows upon the cessation of each preceding one, and not from anything else. Therefore, the objection that consciousness is something other than the body is [answered as follows]: the rebuttal here is that memory does not [arise] with respect to each object... [as stated in the verse].
If it is admitted that the specific cognition of transition is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), then memory cannot be accounted for;

this is because the specific transformations occurring in succession are distinct from one another, and what is not cognized by oneself, or is cognized by one person, is not remembered by another. For indeed, what has not been experienced, or what was experienced by Devadatta, is not remembered by Caitra or anyone else.
It is possible to remember. || 5½ ||
1. There is a variant reading, *sakragaṇābhi*.
[The author of] the *Dīpikā* explains "not memory, that... with the words "that... and so forth; this is the intended meaning.

This cognition consisting of jars, cloths, carts, and so forth, which has been described as sequential, is not the nature of the self; rather, it is purely mental and consists of determinate conceptualization (*adhyavasāya*). That which synthesizes those cognitions is the agent-form, which is called the "self" established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

Thus, for this very reason, that which was stated—that [the self] consists of those [qualities] because of the body's growth—is also refuted; for it is only cognition (*jñāna*) that possesses such a nature. Furthermore, [the argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since we observe that some possess large bodies yet have small intellects, while others possess small bodies yet have great intellects. Thus [ends the commentary on verse 1½].

Commentary: [The opponent might argue: "Let there be no such memory; what is lost by this? To this he replies that even that is incorrect, because [the object] is clearly perceived (*supratītatvāt*). Thus:
"Nor is it so, because it is clearly perceived."
Therefore, there exists a body other than the intelligent one.
1. There is a variant reading: *sakramasaṃvedanā*. 2. There is a variant reading: *sakramaṃ jñānam*.
First of all, it is impossible to deny memory, which is well-established among all people.
And memory is thus accounted for: even though the body undergoes repeated transformation (*pariṇāma*), [memory persists].

Since that which possesses a single nature is the experiencer of various cognitions when their respective objects are present, it must also be the synthesizer; therefore, for this reason—as well as from the logical ground characterized by the impossibility of memory otherwise—it follows that there exists a rememberer distinct from the body. Nor should it be asked: "What is the use of these [arguments]?"

"By means of useless reasons and so forth for one who cannot endure the inference of others. For even though the Cārvāka does not desire it, just as poverty follows a poor man against his will, inference forcibly attaches itself to him; for instance, even by that proponent of perception as the sole means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), when no reality distinct from the four great elements is admitted...

Earth, characterized by stationary objects such as clay and stone, as well as water, rivers, oceans, and so forth— because of the diversity of their qualities, it is not possible to comprehend all of this through perception. This is because perception has specific individual instances as its cause, and thus lacks the capacity to grasp the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) regarding all objects contained within the entire universe.
Because of its capacity for endurance (*kṣamatva*). Furthermore, that which possesses solidity is earth, as in the case of ground, stones, mountains, and so forth;

in the absence of earth, there is an absence of solidity, as in the case of wind and other elements. That which has the nature of fluidity is water, since even oil, ghee, milk, and the like are water—such apprehension of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is a constituent factor of inference.

It must be postulated that when the body is made the subject (*pakṣa*) of the argument, the hardness and other qualities residing therein cannot be ascertained to be properties of earth and the other elements. Furthermore, even the fact that [the body] is composed of the four elements beginning with earth cannot be understood without inference. Moreover, perception alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The investigation into whether [this] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or not is not determined by perception (*pratyakṣa*), as it is not [itself] inference and so forth.

As Dharmakīrti said: "Because the commonality of being a means of valid cognition or its opposite is established through the exclusion of others, there exists another means of valid cognition. It is not only that inference is established by perception.
To provide conviction regarding this, the inference by elimination (*pariśeṣānumāna*) has been demonstrated here at the commencement of the treatise;

however, it is not for the purpose of establishing the Self, which is directly perceived through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), because no other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is required for that. As they have said: "The finality of all means of knowledge lies in the experience itself."
It is concluded: "What need is there for other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in that case where there is cognition by itself through that very [nature]? This has been explained.

As for the argument that memory exists because of a specific modification (*pariṇāma-vaiśiṣṭya*), the meaning of the entire verse—"if not, then there is no memory"—is as follows: even though a subtler consciousness is possible during the state of a corpse (*śavāvasthā*), [memory does not arise].

The phrase "due to the particularity of transformation" (*pariṇāmavaiśiṣṭyāt*) is explained as being intended to establish the absence of memory, based on the suspicion that it represents the view of another school; this is then resolved [as follows]: "Nor is it so, because it is well-known [otherwise]. For it is not established anywhere that for one who has departed [from the body], there is a more subtle consciousness but no memory. On the contrary—
This is well-known: that in a body devoid of a living soul, such as a piece of wood or a clod of earth, consciousness simply does not exist.
Therefore, even when it is explained in this way—that there exists a rememberer distinct from the body—there is no fault whatsoever.
1. There is a variant reading: *vyaktigatatvena*. 2. There is a variant reading: *grāmānyāsthiter anyādhiyogataḥ*. — Dīpikā.

He explains [the passage] beginning with "nor even thus" by means of the verse beginning with "all the world," and so forth. And because memory is thus [dependent], for this very reason the logical reason—"because it exists when that exists"—is unestablished (*asiddha*). For indeed, when the absence of something in a certain place is established, if that thing arises there upon the presence of a specific object, it would be considered its effect even in the absence of similarity to it.
It is established [that the self exists] like fire from a sun-crystal and so forth; however, this is not because of the possibility of its existence there [in the crystal].

For at that time, in the presence of light and so on, it is established as being merely manifested, just like a jar. Furthermore, the existence of the self is even more likely here [in the case of the body], since it is the pervader of those respective effects.

Because the self is established as distinct from the body—which is grasped through self-awareness—for the sake of proving its existence, just as a jar or other objects are [established] through perception. [Objection:
But how could it have existence prior to the union of semen and blood?
[Response: In that case, doubt alone would be appropriate; but that is not so, because there is certainty through inference based on the impossibility of otherwise accounting for memory.
In the context of everyday practice, it is established that the actions of living beings— such as contraction and expansion resulting from the employment of places and articulations—

are invariably concomitant with the recollection of what is beneficial and what is harmful; thus, even for children, such observed actions lead one to infer their own causes, namely experience and memory.
The existence of the sentient being (*sattva*) is established even prior to the union of semen and blood;

otherwise, due to the absence of a cause, contraction and other such movements would not occur in those infants. Nor should it be suspected that these [movements] arise solely from the inherent power of the object (*vastu-śakti*), like hunger or yawning, and thus lack a [specific] cause.

Because perception occurs as preceded by effort. As they say: "How could there be pushing or pulling of the wind without effort? Nor is effort possible prior to cognition; for even in infants, the capacity to experience hunger and so forth is inferred from their most intense crying.
For infants born only a day prior, even as they draw [the breath] from one moment to the next with a special effort—
preceded by the protection of the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa) and avoiding vomiting and so forth—
they attain the fruit characterized by satisfaction; this is observed until the point where they swallow [the breath].

Since it is understood that effort and the like are preceded by the recollection and comprehension of what is beneficial and harmful, how could this [arising of such actions] occur solely through the power of the object? However, in the case of hunger, yawning, and so forth— just as with hair and nails—
it is indeed appropriate that they are not seen to be prompted by a prior recollection of benefit or harm.

Arising occurs through the power of the object itself, and not from contraction and so forth; therefore, by the very fact that such [contraction] would otherwise be impossible, the seer is established as existing prior to birth. As it has been said: "The initial arrangement of the organs, the upward movement of the vital breath, and the striking against the various locations do not occur without prior experience."

Thus: he refutes the claim that "inference is unestablished for us" with the words "nor should it be said," and so forth; and he states "moreover," and so forth, to show that even the authority of scripture (*āgama*) cannot be denied by them. The phrase "not only is [the existence of] earth and so forth established by perception" is the ellipsis to be supplied. For this very reason, [he speaks of] inference.

"And for the purpose of making that known" means for the purpose of making its validity known. For this very reason, that which was stated by the proponents of the sentience of the senses— that although the body is the object of experience, since it is the senses themselves (distinct from the body) that are the perceivers, there is no establishment of a self distinct from them— that too has been refuted by inference.

It should be understood as follows: if those very things which are established in the world as the sense organs, such as the eye, because the existence of form and so forth would otherwise be impossible, are designated by you as sentient, that is incorrect.
For they are established only as instruments, like a mirror, due to the impossibility of sentience [in them]. As it has been said even by the Buddhists:

"Because of the desire for what is superior and inferior, and because of the cognition of destruction and arising, this person perceives the self as distinct from the sense faculties and so forth. Now, if [it is argued that] those [faculties] are other than that [self], then there is a dispute merely over the name, [claiming] "that very thing is the self. Therefore, since in your view the collection of sense faculties is material (*bhautika*), while in our view...

Because of its association with the three *guṇas*, an enjoyer distinct from the body and so forth must be admitted, just as in the case of a bed and such. As for their claim that the body exists for the sake of [the self], that has already been refuted on the grounds that the body itself is an object of enjoyment. Regarding what was said—that the self is "other" because it is inferable—he refutes that with the words beginning "but not," and this...
"This has already been shown" means he summarizes the stated point with the words "this is concluded. He states another interpretation beginning with "as for transformation," and so forth. || 6 ||
Commentary: Having thus established the category of the individual soul (*paśu*), he says the following in order to describe its specific characteristics:
"It is neither non-pervasive nor momentary."
He is neither solitary nor insentient;
he is not a non-agent, for through union with undivided consciousness, he attains the state of Śiva at the end of the bonds.

And that self is neither non-pervasive nor momentary, because it is unconditioned by space and time. As it has been said: "That entity whose existence is unconditioned by space and time is held to be eternal and all-pervading; thus, the self possesses pervasiveness and eternity. It is not [otherwise].

And yet, he is one; for it is impossible to deny the observation of the specific determination of birth, death, and the sense organs among those who have realized that "He is the one Controller, the inner Self of all beings"—an observation which, like that of the knowers of Brahman, serves as a proof for the plurality of persons. Nor is it the case that...

He is not insentient like the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas, nor is he a non-agent like the Sāṃkhyas, nor is he joined with adventitious consciousness as some [others] maintain. Why? He says: "Because Śiva-nature is heard [to be attained] at the end of the bonds.
This means: at the end of the bonds—namely ignorance (avidyā) and so forth—when those obstacles have been removed.
For it is heard in scripture that the manifestation of the Śiva-nature of this self occurs; and thus it has been said:

"Now, for the sake of liberation from the bonds of karma known as the impurity of the self and Māyā, and for the manifestation of the Śiva-nature, knowledge proceeds from Śiva. Nor is that Śiva-nature endowed with attributes such as non-pervasiveness.

Or rather, [the Self] is devoid of knowerhood, agency, and so forth; for it has been established previously that it is distinct from those various [attributes] through such statements as: "It is eternal because it is not limited by time; because it is all-pervading, it does not occupy a specific location," and so on. Nor is it the case that its pervasiveness and other qualities arise only in liberation and are absent during the state of transmigratory existence.
This must be considered; for it will be demonstrated that the arising of what is non-existent is impossible. Thus [ends section] 7.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Mṛgendravṛtti composed by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Vidyākaṇṭha. [The Dīpikā:]

He explains the sūtra beginning with "not non-pervasive" (nāvyāpaka) and so forth with the words "and that self" (sacātmā) and so on. Furthermore, the pervasiveness and other attributes of the self have been established incidentally in the section refuting the supreme liberation (paramokṣa-nirāsa-prakaraṇa), and thus they are not elaborated upon here. Now, an objection is raised: "But even this [self] is insentient (jaḍa) and is manifested by the cognition of external objects; such is the distinction of the Naiyāyikas. That is not so.
It has been stated that [the self] always appears precisely as non-objective (*akamatayā*).
Furthermore, even the manifestation of objects is not possible within this insentient nature, because it would be like another self, due to the lack of manifestation therein. To explain:
this manifestation of the object is not the intrinsic nature of the object, because the latter remains undifferentiated.

Because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence that everything would be manifest; rather, [consciousness] has the very nature of the self (*ātman*). And if that were not manifest, it would follow that nothing at all is manifest, resulting in the blindness of this world. As it has been said: "For one who does not perceive the apprehension itself, the perception of objects is not established. Thus, the self is established as being eternal. As for those who [hold that consciousness exists] in the absence of a body...

Due to the absence of consciousness [in the self], the followers of the Vaiśeṣika tradition, conditioned by their habitual tendencies, claim that consciousness is not the essential nature of the self.

In response to them, he says: "And it is not as some [maintain]," and so forth. Even by them, knowledge—just like the fruit of karma—must be admitted to reside therein in the form of a potentiality (śakti), because in the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda), there is no production of what is non-existent.

Because it will be refuted [later]. [Objection: But surely you yourselves admit that the fruit of karma exists only as a mental construct (*buddhistha*). [Reply: True. However, there is no contradiction because its status as an example applies to its existence in the form of a latent capacity (*śakti*). For this very reason, the doctrine of transmigration (*saṃkrāntivāda*) is also refuted.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Investigation of the Category of the Bound Soul (paśu), in the Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā composed by Aghoraśivācārya.
1. Verse 21.
2. The sense is that, because it is of the nature of self-luminosity (*prakāśa*), the state of being the object of luminosity (*prakāśamarmatva*) is impossible within itself;
for there is a contradiction between a single entity being both agent and object.

Now begins the seventh chapter, on the characteristics of the bonds (*pāśa*). Commentary: [The Lord] removes the net of bonds from the individual soul (*aṇu*) who was previously bound; this is derived from what is set forth in the root aphorism.

There are three sections intended to define the category of *pāśa* (the bond), which remains after the three categories characterized as *paśu*, *pāśa*, and *īśvara* have been established, and which was introduced in the immediately preceding chapter. In this context, the connections— namely, those between the sūtras, the chapters (*prakaraṇa*), the sections (*pāṭala*), and the individual topics (*pādārtha*)— are very clear.

The nature of the fetters (*pāśa*) should be understood through such statements as: "But that which consists of speech is *prāvṛti*; in the *śabala* [state] there is *karman*; *māyā* has a fourfold effect;
the qualities (*dharma*) born of the fetters have been proclaimed in brief as being manifold. Now, the fetters are ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest.
Now they are described briefly—
those at whose destruction the atoms of the world become lords.

The word "atha" (now) means immediately after the category of *paśu* (the bound soul). Ignorance (*avidyā*), lack of knowledge (*ajñāna*), the ointment (*añjana*), and the individual soul (*māṇava*) are the bonds (*pāśa*). Those which have these at their beginning are the bonds known as *karman*, *māyā*, and *rodha-śakti*.
Now, at this time, they are being described briefly and in summary. Upon the removal of these, one is liberated from the state of being a bound soul (*paśyatva*).

The individual souls (aṇavaḥ) become lords of the universe. In that regard, the manifestation of sovereignty independent of others, like that of Śiva, constitutes the equality of the liberated souls (muktātman) with the Lord (pati). However, for those who hold offices such as Vidyeśvara and the rest, there is the performance of the fivefold cosmic functions (pañcavidhakṛtya). Now, concerning liberation...
If it is asked, "From what is it previously determined that the atom (aṇu) is bound? [the answer is: because its omniscience and omnipotence regarding all objects would otherwise be contradicted.

Now, the statement "Śiva is free from beginningless impurity, omniscient, and the doer of all" is a restatement of the latter half [of the verse] in conjunction with the word "Śiva" established in the former half.
2. The meaning is that what was introduced [in the previous verse]—namely, "because of the scriptural statement regarding Śiva-nature at the end of the bonds"—[is being explained here].
3. This is the sixth verse in the section refuting the supreme liberation (*paramokṣanirāsa*). *Dīpikā*.
The seventh chapter, on the characteristics of the bonds (*pāśa*).

Now, regarding the phrase "ignorance and the rest" (*avidyādayaḥ*), he says "Śiva," etc., in order to explain the connection [of this chapter] with that [previous section]. Therein, the connection of the aphorism is with the words "the net of bonds" (*pāśajāla*); it is topical by virtue of belonging to the *Vidyāpāda*, and it is sequential [within the chapter].

This is indicated by the phrase "ending with *pāśa*. That which pertains to the meaning of the word (*pādārthika*) is so called because it consists of the meaning of the word *pāśa*; that which consists of the sentence (*vākyātmaka*), however, has already been explained.

In that regard, he says "ignorance" (*avidyā*) and so forth, because the unique nature of each of the fourfold [impurities] is first proposed as something to be stated by the aphorism beginning with "ignorance" (*avidyā*). [The impurity] is *āṇava*.

"Paśu" (the bound soul) means the *mala* (impurity), which is the beginningless obscuration of the individual souls (*aṇu*). He explains the meaning of the word "pati" (the Lord) with the words "therein," etc.
By the inclusion of the term "etc. in "Vidyeśvara and so forth," the *mantras* and others are included. The self (*ātman*) is not possessed of *mala* because of its purity.
Nor should it be thought that the reason [purity] is unestablished or equivalent to the point to be proven (*sādhyasama*), since by its very nature...

The person (*puruṣa*) is indeed possessed of impurity. Because that impurity is his very nature (*tatsvabhāvatva*), it cannot be removed—just as [one cannot remove] his eternality or omnipresence—and thus there would follow the undesirable consequence of no liberation (*anirmokṣaprasaṅga*). Therefore, he offers a rebuttal by stating "of knowledge and action," etc., implying that because liberation is otherwise inexplicable, the person must be admitted to be pure. This is the meaning: the Self...
Bound by some beginningless bondage, he is like a dependent animal bound by a rope; that which is his bondage is *mala*. Thus is the proof of *mala*. || 1 ||
1. "Are to be grasped" is the ellipsis; for otherwise, in the absence of bonds, there would be no dependence on another.
It must be stated what its basis is.
If it were intrinsic, then the term "liberated" would cease to apply to those who are liberated. (2)

For a person who is free from bonds, there is no state of being bound; and for one who is unbound, what could cause dependence on another? It is this dependence that results in the attainment of the undesirable and the obstruction of the desirable, even against his will. Now, if you think that this dependence is not caused by bonds but is rather innate, then—
The word "liberated" ceases to apply to liberated atoms; for in common worldly usage, the word "liberated" is well-known to refer to one from whom the bonds have departed. || 2 ||

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: "If there were an absence of dependence [on another], it would follow that there is no distinction between bondage and liberation"; thus he says, "For otherwise," and so forth. Now, it was indeed argued that even if the soul possesses impurity, if that impurity were inherent (*svābhāvika*), it would follow that liberation is impossible.

That is not so; for, by means of the passage beginning with "Now, if you think," etc., the intrinsic nature [of the self] is refuted after raising an objection, and thus the self must be admitted to be impure due to its dependence on another. But surely, even in that person who is pure, there exists a connection with *prakṛti* consisting of the *tamas* and *rajas* qualities?

Attachment indeed arises in the self as a result of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just as it does in a crystal gem. Therefore, there is no absence of distinction between bondage and liberation. To this, it is replied: Thus, that attachment produced by passion which has been shown to belong to the transmigrating self is caused solely by impurity; it is not without a cause. If it were without a cause, [it would never cease].

Passion would exist not only during the state of saṃsāra, but also during the state of liberation, because there is no distinction [between the two states]. But surely, Nature (prakṛti) produces passion only toward that person for whom its mandate (adhikāra) has not ceased; it does not produce it toward one for whom this mandate has ceased—thus, there is indeed a distinction.

"What is the use of this stain that is without a cause? To that we say: no. If a stain were not admitted, there would be no attachment for that person who is pure by nature even toward impure objects, just as there is no attachment for a Brahmin toward impure substances. As it has been said:
If impurity does not belong to the person, then by what is attachment to enjoyments produced, since such attachment is observed toward them?

From this it is concluded that he is not pure by nature, but rather is indeed possessed of impurity. If it is argued that this attachment has its fuel in the principle of passion (*rāga-tattva*), that is not so; for even that [passion] does not arise without a cause.
Because there is no distinction [between states], there would be no liberation at all. Nor should it be said that dependence is caused by karma;
for you accept that karma is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*), and not, as the Naiyāyikas and others do, a property of the self (*ātman*). And therefore, only while the intellect exists—
The following thought occurs to him: "But that cannot be so in the state of isolation after dissolution (*pralayakevalāvasthā*), because at that time the intellect (*buddhi*) is non-existent.
As it has been stated even by you yourselves: 'From primordial nature (*prakṛti*) comes the Great One (*mahat*); from the Great One, the I-principle (*ahaṅkāra*).
Therefore, in that state, there could be no karma to distinguish between bondage and liberation. This is the prima facie argument (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
This leads to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). For it has been stated even in the *Parākhyatantra*: "That which is pure cannot be a coloring agent.

Now, the proponents of the theory of the impurity of *māyā* (*māyāmalavādinaḥ*) might argue: "Let *māyā* itself be the impurity, since its nature is that of a deluder. Or else, [they might say] it is *pradhāna* itself, conjoined with the fivefold *viparyaya* (misapprehension) characterized by *tamas*, *moha*, and so forth.

"Then what is the use of anything else?"—thus say those who maintain that impurity (*mala*) is innate. To this we reply: Impurity would have to be *māyā* either by its very nature or by way of its effects. It cannot be by way of its effects; for since those [principles] such as *kalā* and the rest are established through their own respective effects, there is no evidence for them being the cause of any further effect.

Furthermore, it would follow that there is no distinction between the various principles (*tattva*). Moreover, since those [impurities] arise only at the time of creation, the aforementioned consequence applies even in the state of dissolution alone.

Even if impurity exists by its own nature, because there is no difference in it, the consequence follows that upon the liberation of one, all would be liberated. [This must be denied] for each individual soul (*puruṣa*).

If that [māyā] were distinct [from the soul], it would be insentient; and because it is manifold, it would necessarily be an effect—just like cognition and so forth—and thus something other than that [soul], namely *māyā*, would have to be postulated. Furthermore, if that [māyā] were itself a "taint" (*mala*), the same logical consequence would apply; therefore, yet another [entity] would have to be postulated, leading to an infinite regress. Nor can it be argued that, as in the case of the "taint," there will be distinct powers (*śakti*) for that [māyā] corresponding to each individual soul.

Because one power cannot be joined with another power; we shall explain that the cause exists only in the state of power (*śakti-avasthā*), while the effect exists only in the state of manifestation (*vyakti-avasthā*). [Objection: But how was the connection of Māyā with power mentioned in the passage beginning, "producing the powers of Māyā which are fit for manifestation"? [Response: Precisely for that reason, in that context, it refers to the effects themselves within the cause.
It has been stated that these exist in the form of potencies (*śakti*), but they are not the potencies of a cause that produce an effect;

we shall explain this further under the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). Now, if it is argued that these impurity-potencies (*mala-śakti*) are distinct from the potencies of the cause of the universe, then the existence of a separate impurity (*mala*) is established, and the dispute is merely over its name. Thus...

This must also be stated regarding the view that impurity (*mala*) is innate; thus, the existence of an impurity distinct [from the self] is established. And that [impurity] of the selves is beginningless, like the redness of copper or the blackness of iron. For this very reason, although impurity is a separate entity, it is included within the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*), because without it, the state of being a bound soul would be impossible. || 2 ||
1. "Of the person" (*puruṣasya*) is the ellipsis.
2. "Of the perfected one" (*siddhasya*) is a variant reading.
3. "Only attached" (*sakta eva*) is a variant reading.

4. This means "of the self. 5. This means the consequence that there would be no distinction between bondage and liberation. 6. By the word "etcetera," great delusion (*mahāmoha*), darkness (*tāmisra*), and blinding darkness (*andhatāmisra*) are to be understood.

7. The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of no distinction between bondage and liberation. 8. This is the final verse of the section defining the nature of the Lord (pati). Commentary (vṛtti).
Explaining this very point, he says:
"Mastery is seen for one who is free from bondage; for one who is bound, there is subservience."
Such is the extent of bondage and liberation for those who are bound and those who are liberated. || 3 ||
This alone is the state of bondage for one who is bound: that while being fettered, there is a state of subjection to those fetters;
the meaning is that it is dependence upon the independent Supreme Lord. And this alone is the state of liberation for one who is liberated:
that through the departure of bondage, there is mastery over them, which is the manifestation of autonomy. For it is thus observed in the world.
One who is free from bondage is called "master" (vaśī), and one who is bound is called "subordinate" (vaśya). || 3 ||
Commentary: To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "That dependence is bondage."
If that [Self] were eternal like consciousness and so forth,
then the collection of means for liberation would be useless, since it would be attained by this very [eternal] intellect.

Therefore, for that reason, this dependence of the self upon others in the attainment of desired objects and so forth implies its state of being bound; for there can be no contradiction of independence for one who is not bound. Nor is this [dependence] beginningless for the self.
It must be accepted as eternal, like the powers of knowledge and action; for otherwise, an undesirable consequence would follow. To explain:

if that dependence of the self were accepted as eternal—just as consciousness and so forth are eternal—then because it would never be abolished, the collection of means for liberation, such as the yoga of knowledge and the like, which are desired even by our opponents, would be rendered useless.

Because there is no manifestation of freedom, the Self remains eternally bound; therefore, enough with this notion—that such a way of thinking is the cause for the non-cessation of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). Thus, it is established that [bondage] is produced by the fetters (pāśa).
Dependence upon others; and the snares are añjana and the rest. || 4 ||
The *Dīpikā* states:
Even though [the self] is beginningless, its dependence on that [body] is not eternal; thus he says, "Nor does this belong to the Self," and so forth. (4)
The commentary: That indeed is the Self;
it is the eternal, all-pervading power of consciousness—
Even a treasure [is used] for the accomplishment of one's purpose;
otherwise, one does not seek strength from either the Pāśava or the Śāmbhava [powers].

For if the individual soul (*aṇu*) were not its conscious power (*cicchakti*) obstructed by beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), then— even though it remains the locus of the eternal and all-pervading conscious power— how could there be this "belonging to the bound" (*pāśava*), which is appropriate for the bound soul (*paśūcita*), for the sake of accomplishing the object characterized as experience during the state of bondage?

It seeks and requires the stimulation of the *kalās* and other factors through its own power; and for the sake of liberation, how could it seek the power of Śambhu? It does not wait for such power otherwise, because if fetters (*pāśas*) were not admitted, then—since [the self] is by its very nature the stainless essence of consciousness—the search for that [power] would be purposeless.

Since, in both states, this [individual soul] requires the arousal of power— whether it be of the bound soul (pāśava) or of the Supreme Lord (pārameśvara)— therefore, there exists in him something that obstructs knowledge and action, by which the impairment of his sovereignty is brought about. || 5 ||
The *Dīpikā*:
He establishes this very point—that [the self] is bound due to dependence—by means of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), starting with the words "He indeed is the Self," and so forth. 5.
Commentary: That obscuration of this individual soul (aṇu) exists within the fivefold stream of Śiva.
It has been proclaimed through many synonyms,
yet it is always unseen by the ignorant.

The veil over this Self, which is its impurity (*añjana*), is designated by the names that will be mentioned in the Śaiva scripture *Pañcasrotas*; however, it has never been understood by the *paśus* (bound souls), who are the authors of the scriptures for the *paśus*. || 6 ||
The commentary: Now, he states by which names that [reality] is described in those scriptures:
"the state of being a bound soul (paśutva), the mist of the bound soul (paśunīhāra)..."
By means of the collyrium that removes the impurity of death and fainting, and through the destruction of the root of sin, such as the veil of ignorance, disease, and exhaustion; (7)
And that [ignorance] is not distinct in each individual self; rather, it is one, though possessed of manifold powers that veil consciousness. Thus he says:
"That one [is] for all beings..."
It is great, dense with consciousness and other [qualities],
and possesses a multitude of powers that abide within each individual and persist until the end of their own time. || 8 ||
Commentary: The obscuration of even this fourteen-fold creation of elements is but one.
To provide the reason for this, he states "beginningless" (*anādi*) by way of a qualification.

Because, according to the reasoning that will be stated, it is beginningless for all beings; it is not adventitious like the bondage of *māyā*. For this very reason, it is one. If it were manifold, then because it would be insentient, its beginninglessness would be untenable due to its being preceded by other causes. Nor, even if it were preceded by other causes, [would it be beginningless].

It should not be argued that its beginninglessness will be established because it acts as a binder through a succession [of causes] like *kalā* and the rest; for as it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*:

"Just as his impurity (*mala*) is beginningless, so too is his karma beginningless. If that which is beginningless were not established, by what cause would there be such diversity? Therefore, karma is beginningless, and *māyā* is likewise."

"It is so," [he said]. For just as with Śiva, there is no possibility of re-bondage for one who has realized that [truth]. Or, if such [bondage] were to exist, we shall explain later that there would be no freedom from impurity (*mala*). "Dense" (*nibiḍam*) means thick, impenetrable;
because it obscures the all-pervading selves (*ātman*). "Great" (*mahat*): because it resides within each individual self.

It is endowed with a multitude of powers that expand according to the specific time of each individual's transformation. Thus it has been stated in the *Tattvatrayanirṇaya*: "The powers of impurity are distinct for every self, and they conceal its qualities."
1.11 – The eleventh verse. *Dīpikā*:
Now, since impurity (*mala*) is unitary, one might object that if someone were liberated from that single [impurity], the consequence would be the liberation of everyone; to this, he says:

And [the phrase] "not that which is one by one distinct" and so forth; [the phrase] "of the fourteenth kind" and so forth—since this is well-known, it is stated as an illustration for bound souls (*baddhātman*), and thus there is no contradiction. Regarding [the phrase] "residing in each individual self" and so forth: that obscuration does not transform of its own accord because it is insentient (*acetanatva*).
Nor can it be removed by the knowledge of the Self, because it is a substance, like a cataract. For just as a cataract, even when recognized, cannot be removed without the operation of the eye,
so too this [impurity], being a substance, cannot be removed without the operation of the Lord known as initiation (*dīkṣā*).
It has been stated that [this] cannot be turned back, and we shall explain it further. || 8 ||
Commentary:
And that collyrium is either situated at the beginningless [limit] or it is proximate.
If that [bondage] is the cause of that [suffering], it is otherwise than that;
if it were not so, it would obstruct only those who are already liberated, and thus effort toward liberation would be in vain.
Therefore, that [bondage] resides in those selves from beginningless time as something beginningless; it does not exist as having a beginning.

Regarding this very point, he states the reasoning: "Or else, later... (*arvāgvā*). For if it were admitted that [bondage] exists in the selves as something having a beginning, then one must state the cause for its conjunction with them—this is the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) to be supplied. "Therefore, otherwise... (*tadato'nyathā*): if...

But then that *añjana* (impurity) would embrace the Self even without depending on any other cause. In that case, it follows that it would obstruct even those who are liberated, rendering their vision and action blocked. If you ask, "Let it be so; what is the fault?"—then the effort for liberation would be in vain, because liberated selves would again and again become joined with impurity.

In this liberation, which is like the bathing of an elephant, effort is indeed in vain; for due to the recurrence of impurity, the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāritā) may arise once again. Therefore, the impurity of the selves is not adventitious; rather, it is beginningless (anādi). Thus it has been stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva* and other scriptures: "Now, the impurity of persons is beginningless."
Thus, the state of being a bound soul (paśutva) has been fully described. || 9 ||
The *Dīpikā* [comments]: It establishes its very beginninglessness with the words "And that collyrium," and so forth. || 9 ||
Commentary: Now he states another argument for this very point:
"That one [entity] indeed possesses many numbers."
Because it possesses such an origination;
however, its powers are not unitary, since simultaneous liberation is not observed.
That [consciousness] is one, because there is no evidence for its multiplicity.

For that which is such—possessing qualities such as being transformed into multiplicity—is seen to be produced like a jar or other objects when it is multiple. But this [consciousness] is not subject to production, because it is the beginningless veiler of the Self.
For this very reason, it is one; for if it were manifold, it would have a beginning, since it would be preceded by causes.
To demonstrate what was stated—that it is like a collection of powers residing within each individual soul that perish at the end of their respective times—he says:
"But those powers... Even though it is one, its powers are many, residing within each individual soul and obstructing the activity of consciousness.

The powers must be admitted to be impermanent; otherwise, if they were one, then upon that [power] departing from a single person, liberation would occur for everyone simultaneously. Since liberation is not observed to occur at once, it is therefore logical to accept the multiplicity of those powers. || 10 ||
Dīpikā: Now, he states another argument for this very point; the words "in oneness" are to be supplied as the remainder. || 10 ||
Commentary: Nor do those powers obstruct or depart independently. What then?
[They act] as that which has been indicated as an inseparable concomitant by the statement beginning with "Action is powerful in its activity," and so forth.
One characterizes the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*) of the Supreme Lord through its function:

that which does not arise within [the soul] is inseparable from it. It should be understood that because it follows upon impurity (*mala*), the power of concealment makes itself internal to the soul by means of that impurity, thereby acting as a fetter (*pāśa*).
Among them, the power of Maheśvara is Śivā,
who bestows grace upon all simply by following the path of dharma.
It is metaphorically designated as a "noose. || 11 ||

Because they conform to the attribute characterized by obstructing the activity of consciousness (*cit*), those powers of impurity (*mala-śakti*) are metaphorically designated as "fetters" (*pāśa*) by the power of Śiva (*śaivī śakti*). However, their status as fetters is not primary in that sense. Why? The reason for this is stated right here by means of a qualification: [the power of Śiva] is "gracious toward all."
"Śveti. For she, by virtue of having the nature of bestowing favor upon the entire world, is the accomplisher of that [world's] ultimate welfare. || 11 ||

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: Having thus established the bond known as *mala*, he introduces the sūtra beginning with "tādātmya" in order to establish that which consists of the power of obstruction (*rodhaśakti*). He says: "And those are not its powers," and so forth.
But why is it that immediately after the impurities (*mala*), only the power of obstruction (*rodha-śakti*) is established, and not *māyā* and the others?
To this he says, "The covering" (*prāvṛti*), etc. The meaning is that the fetters (*pāśas*) are being explained according to the order of their enumeration.
He explains that very aphorism with the words "of these," etc.; it has been stated that the division of even this single power is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*).

Furthermore, the phrase "because the powers of impurity (*mala-śakti*) are insentient" is an elliptical expression for the fetters (*pāśa*) such as impurity and the rest. Since it is impossible for there to be a well-established presiding over by a sentient being, it was already stated previously that the power of Śiva—which follows those properties—is metaphorically called a "fetter. As he will say:
That [destruction] has indeed been stated for Māyā while it still possesses its functional authority (adhikāra), as well as for karma. || 11 ||
1. This is the final verse of this section. Commentary:
And thus.
And when it attains its full unfolding, it transforms those [waters] into the very limit of the ocean through its variegated luster.
That is then called "favorable. || 12 ||

From the nominal stem *pariṇāma*, by adding the causal suffix *ṇic* in the sense of "the meaning of a verbal root," the form *pariṇāmayati* ("he causes to transform") is derived. These powers residing in all beings are his [the Lord's] own; the power of the Lord (*pati-śakti*) joins them with transformation until the end of their obstruction—that is, for as long as their period of authority lasts—by means of her variegated splendor.

When it performs the act of looking upon the womb as its cause, it is then called "gracious" (*anugrāhikā*). By the word *ka*, the head is meant—the Lord (*īśāna*) whose sole activity is constant grace. This is indicated by the mantra-linga "the head of Īśāna. He alone is compared to the sun because he is eternally engaged in bestowing grace upon the entire world. From that [sun], [it] proceeds...

When she brings about the unfolding— the expansion of the inner disposition— of the multitude of individual souls, whose own essential natures have been made manifest by the light of knowledge that illuminates supreme bliss, she is then called the "Bestower of Grace" (anugrāhikā). || 12 ||
The *Dīpikā* [comments]:
"And thus," etc., establishes that power is indeed one. || 12 ||
1. "Of that" means "of the impurity. Here the Sage asks:
"That which is to be graced by Śambhu through consciousness and so forth..."
Because they are mutually contradictory,
how could a power that is all-encompassing and benevolent toward all be capable of [exerting them] simultaneously? (13)
And for the Lord of the World, who acts for the sake of benefiting living beings,
no harm can enter his person.
Furthermore, it is logical that there is piercing. || 14 ||

The conscious [entities] consist of the individual selves (*sakalātman*), and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," the unconscious [entities] consist of impurity (*mala*), karma, *māyā*, and their effects.
All of this is indeed to be graced by the Supreme Lord precisely because of His sovereignty over all.
Furthermore, such a state of being graced for these conscious and unconscious entities—the bound souls and their fetters—is not possible at the same time.

For instance, if the fetters (*pāśas*) were to favor the bound soul (*pāśya*), there would instead be its subjugation rather than its favoring; and if they were to favor the conscious beings (*cits*), those who are bound by them would become subordinate.
Thus, because of this mutual contradiction, their simultaneous favoring is impossible. How then [is it possible]?

The power that bestows grace upon all has been described. For the Lord, who is engaged in favoring all beings out of compassion and who acts for their benefit, the web of bonds such as *māyā* and others—which cause harm and bestow suffering—is [nevertheless] an object of grace; for [the bound soul], whose powers of perception and action are veiled, [is favored by this very bondage].

The prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that even though sentient beings are afflicted by the pain of suffering such as lack of autonomy, it is not appropriate for the Bond (*bandha*) to cause them further distress through its own affliction, out of a desire to favor them. || 14 ||

The *Dīpikā* explains the two introductory sūtras beginning with "of Śambhu" as follows: "Of consciousness," etc.; "all who possess the *sakala* [aspect]" means all individual souls (*paśvātman*), and not merely those who are already established as *sakalas*. Thus, they attain perfection.

Accepting this very point, it should be explained here as well that, as before, a specific cause is established solely from a specific effect; for even the Vijñānākala and the Pralayākala are subjects to be graced. || 14 ||
1. "Endowed with the three impurities" (malatrayayutāḥ) means they are well-known as *rasakas*.
2. There is a variant reading: "grāhakasyāt". [This is] the commentary (*vṛtti*).
The established conclusion, however, is:
"He does not grant grace to the atom of impurity for the sake of its torment."
But whatever is done must be done by means; it cannot be otherwise.

It is true that consciousness is the power that favors both the sentient and the insentient; yet, it is not illogical for its favoring of them to occur even at the same time, as there is no mutual contradiction between them. However, it does not effect a favor toward the impurity in the form of a transformation for the sake of the atom's suffering.

Rather, it is solely for the sake of favoring [him]. For in that matter, whatever is appropriate must be done by means of a proper method (*upāya*), and not without a method; and this is a truly excellent method. || 15 ||
The *Dīpikā*:

He composes an introductory framework (*pīṭhikā*) in order to explain the aphorism of the established doctrine (*siddhāntasūtra*). With the words "It is true," etc., he asserts the absence of the first objection; and with the words "Nor of this," etc., he likewise asserts the absence of the second objection.
He makes a formal declaration: "Not [the case] for the atom," and so forth. Therein, he establishes the first declaration with the words "For in that case," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: the conformity to the attributes of consciousness (*cid-dharma*) is solely for the sake of favoring consciousness (*cid-anugraha*). And because that [conformity] occurs at a time preceded by the favoring of non-consciousness (*acid-anugraha*) in order to manifest its state of Śiva-hood, there is no contradiction with what was previously stated. || 15 ||
Commentary:
That is to say,
it does not exist in darkness that possesses functional capacity.
Liberation occurs for someone;
even their qualification ceases through the transformation of that capacity.
Even that [cognition] would not arise from itself alone,
because even for a suitable object,
it does not occur in every way or at all times.
That which is insentient is employed by consciousness. || 17 ||

It is said that as long as the *adhikāra* (dominant influence) of impurity (*mala*) persists, liberation does not occur for anyone; for it is precisely the cessation of that [influence] which is denoted by the term "liberation. And this *adhikāra* is brought to an end through the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of its power.
Furthermore, even for a substance capable of such transformation, that transformation cannot occur spontaneously in every respect.
Furthermore, since at all times an insentient entity, when impelled by a sentient being, is observed to produce various effects;

therefore, there is no mutual contradiction between the act of favoring [the soul] for that purpose and the transformation into collyrium and so forth. This constitutes the refutation of the first objection. || 17 ||
Commentary: Now follows the refutation of the second [objection]. Just as by means of alkaline substances and so forth, a physician—
Even though it provides food, it does not satisfy the sick;
because it yields only a limited object, it is perceived as a cause of suffering. || 18 ||

Although the Supreme Lord is "Vāma" (the Left-hand path), because he bestows sufferings such as birth and dissolution upon individual souls (*aṇu*) whose faculties of perception and action are enveloped by bonds— acting through the influence of the respective powers of those bonds— he is not understood to be the cause of suffering, since his activity is solely directed toward their ultimate liberation. Just as a physician [acts] with caustic substances, surgical instruments, and so forth...

Even though it causes pain to the patient, because it accomplishes the desired goal characterized by health at the end, the cause of that pain is not perceived as something that bestows suffering. || 18 ||
1. From the verbal root *dṛg* (to see) with the suffix *lyuṭ* and the substitution of *an*, the form *drāvaṇam* is derived; its meaning is "death. [This is] the *Dīpikā*.
For this very reason, the absence of even the second objection is shown by means of an illustration, beginning with the words "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth.
He says "as follows," beginning with "yathā" (for example), in order to demonstrate this. || 18 ||
Commentary: Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of the Supreme Lord, the Blessed One, whose essential nature is absolutely pure, in following after the bondage of fetters? To this, he says:
Because the Great Lord is omnipresent, his presiding power is never obstructed;
nor is there anything further to be accomplished for him.
He attains indifference toward that. || 19 ||
The Lord’s presiding presence is never obstructed; because He is omnipresent, possesses great lordship,
and is the creator of all, wherever there is anything to be done, He reaches that very place and, by presiding over each respective agent, He Himself accomplishes everything.

"It acts" has been stated in the *Īśvarasiddhi*. "Indifferent" (*udāsa*) means one who remains aloof; the state of being so is "indifference" (*audāsya*), which signifies non-agency (*akartṛtva*). || 19 ||
Commentary: Having thus established that [the sun] simultaneously benefits all, and while demonstrating that very point, he explains the meaning of the word "benefit" (anugraha).
1. There is a variant reading, *tādātmyam*.
What is called the "favoring" (*anugraha*) of the locus (*dharmin*) is its conformity to that [locus's] properties (*dharmas*).
There is no woman at all who is never compliant with her husband.

The conformity of the properties (*dharma*) of the subject (*dharmin*) that is to be assisted is the assistance rendered by the assister (*anugrāhaka*), just as the sun assists lotuses whose nature is to expand sequentially. No such property belongs to any subject whatsoever, which—
It is not followed nor presided over by the Supreme Lord, because He is all-pervading. || 20 ||
1. *Anugrāhyasya* is an alternative reading.
The *Dīpikā* explains the meaning of the word "anugraha" (favor/grace) with the latter half [of the verse], beginning with "dharmiṇaḥ," regarding the Lord (*īśa*).
It is said that "the empowerment of all is taught"; thus he says, "of what [is it]? and so forth. // 20 //
Commentary: And thus,
the mist of the preceding section has passed—
For one who possesses vigor, prosperity increases;
for another, there is the favoring of cattle, because that action is for their sake. || 21 ||

The grace toward that bound soul— the beast— increases and flourishes, even while he remains in such a state where the power and capacity of the mist of darkness and impurity, which consists in its function of obstructing the vision of the highest good, has reached its consummation.

It becomes abundant; that is to say, when the power of impurity (*mala-śakti*) has ceased its authority. But for others, regarding the net of bonds (*pāśajāla*) such as impurity and so forth, their "being for that purpose" (*tādarthya*) consists in their being the motivators (*prayojakatva*) of the transformation of karma and the like;
from that, grace (*anugraha*) arises. That very [grace] which is the motivation for the transformation [of the soul] for the sake of the liberation of bound souls— [End of excerpt]
The meaning is the favoring of the nooses. || 21 ||
The *Dīpikā* states: "By the words beginning with 'gone' (*gatā*), the very meaning already expressed is being restated"; thus he says, "And in this way," and so forth. // 21 //
Commentary: And so, he states what is established regarding the subject at hand: "the state of being a cognizer and the state of being subject to transformation..."
It is the following of the two dharmas; it occurs upon the cessation of the impurity that possesses authority and its subsequent falling away. || 22 ||
Regarding "of the impurity that possesses authority":

when there is a falling away— that is, a slight loosening— due to the cessation of the authority of the "eye-salve" of the *āṇava* [impurity], which results in the departure of the downward-facing power of the Supreme Lord that has existed since beginningless time and which brings about the state of that [impurity].

The soul's favor consists in its conforming to the attribute of being a cognizer, while the favor of the bonds consists in their conforming to the attribute of being subject to transformation. || 22 ||

The *Dīpikā* states that the conclusion of the second half [of the verse] is reached with the words "by being the cognizer," and so forth. Furthermore, it explains the passage beginning with "and thus in the present case" up to "in the event of a lapse" with the words "occurring through the existence of that," and so forth. || 22 ||
The commentary: Concluding, he says:
"Thus, simultaneously."
For that [liberation] is indeed easily accomplished through the gradual stages;
it has already been explained as resulting from Māyā while it still possesses its functional authority and from Karma. || 23 ||

By the reasoning thus stated, the simultaneous grace of both the conscious (cit) and the unconscious (acit) is not contradictory; rather, [their] sequential [grace] is easily established and not difficult to justify. This applies equally to the impurity (mala) and to Māyā, along with its own jurisdiction extending from *kalā* down to the earth (*kṣiti*).

The grace (anugraha) characterized by the manifestation of the *kalās* and so forth, as well as their withdrawal, consists in bringing about the readiness of *karman* to yield its fruit; this very grace, although not explicitly mentioned in relation to *māyā* and *karman*, should be understood as having been already described. In every way and at all times.
"Because that which is insentient is to be employed by consciousness," since this has been stated as a general rule for everything.
Thus ends the section on the examination of bonds (*pāśaparīkṣāprakaraṇa*) in the *Mṛgendravṛtti* composed by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Vidyākaṇṭha.
1. In this very section, the seventeenth verse. *Dīpikā*:
Now, by way of a bold assertion (*prauḍhavāditā*), [the author] [states that] like the sun and so forth, [the Lord...]

Because [the Lord] bestows grace through mere proximity, the simultaneous grace of both the conscious (cit) and the unconscious (acit) is not illogical; rather, it is stated by way of a conclusion that it occurs "even more so" sequentially. Thus he says: "Concluding," and so forth.
This concludes the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā* composed by the teacher Aghoraśiva.
The seventh chapter, the Investigation of Impurities and the Like, is completed.
Now begins the eighth chapter, the Investigation of Karma.
This follows from the section concerning the examination of the category of *pāśa* (fetters).
1. Immediately following this, there is the introduction to the examination of the noose of karma (*karmapāśa*), as indicated at the end of the preceding chapter.
The categories of meaning (*padārtha*) and other relations pertaining to it have already been stated at the very commencement of the previous section.
Now, [regarding] the senses, the body, and their objects...
The connection with consciousness is inferred from the fact that there is a future existence, since that which is not yet to come cannot be without a cause.

The word "atha" (now) refers to the period following the investigation into the two bonds known as *āṇava* (atomic) and *rodha-śakti* (the power of obstruction). It denotes the conjunction (*yoga*) of the conscious self (*cidātman*) with the sense organs— both internal and external— the body in its gross and subtle forms, and with objects, which are the domains of the senses.

Because it possesses the quality of arising from a future state, its cause is inferred as the instrumental condition (nimitta). For nothing that possesses the quality of arising can ever be without a cause. || 1 ||
1. "And that [result] has indeed been stated regarding action" means that it was indicated at the end of the immediately preceding chapter.
*Dīpikā*: Now begins the section on the investigation of action (*karma*).
Now, with the words "atha indriya" and so forth, he introduces the topic of the section.

Regarding the phrase "the relations of the categories and so forth," the connection pertaining to that specific chapter has already been indicated at the end of the preceding chapter, as it was stated that the relation of the ritual action (*karman*) has been explained. Likewise, the verbal form [of the connection] is the seed.

By such statements as "of the body, etc."; however, other relations have already been mentioned in the preceding section. Therein, the cause of the soul's connection with the body and so forth—which was established in the section on the category of the *paśu* (bound soul) by way of its being distinct from the body, and in the immediately following section by way of its being possessed of impurity—is now established by this present section.

Thus he says, "by the senses," and so forth; here, the term *nimitta* (cause) refers specifically to a cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*), because God is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). As it is stated in the *Mataṅga*: "But the Lord is the instrumental cause," and as he will say here:

"Because it depends on Īśvara, avidyā, and so forth, that [cause] is called 'cooperative'. Therefore, this is the meaning: [The rest of the passage follows: ...and thus the sense is this: [the text continues with the explanation of how the Lord acts through the cooperation of other factors].

Whatever conjunction of the self with the body and so forth—which serve as the means for experience—is produced, like the conjunction of threads and the like, it must have some auxiliary cause; that which serves as this auxiliary cause is karma. As it is stated in the *Svāyambhuva*: "And from karma arise bodies, objects, and organs."
Now, it might be argued that bodies existing at the beginning of creation do not have karma as their cause;

rather, it is only those occurring at subsequent times that do so. As they say: "The first body has its root in the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*); others than that are understood to have their root in karma. This is not so, for persons always possess bodies and the like.

The existence of karma is established by the fact that the diversity of enjoyments cannot otherwise be accounted for; this is because even at the time of creation, the scriptures record the diversity of births among beasts, birds, wild animals, reptiles, stationary beings, humans, and so forth.
Furthermore, since karma must be established even during the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), it follows that the bondage of the body through beginningless karma is proven. || 1 ||
Commentary: Having thus established the cause in its general sense, he speaks in order to explain its specific nature.
1. This means "in the immediately preceding section."
2. In the Mataṅga-vidyāpāda, in the chapter on Puṃpradhāneśvara, verse 19:
Because it exists in specific locations, because of its diversity, and because of its momentariness...
And because it is restricted to each individual and because it is continuous, it possesses that quality. || 2 ||

Regarding that consciousness (*cit*) which is conjoined with the faculties, the body, and their objects, there is its existence within fixed states such as gods, humans, and animals; and there is its diversity, for the bodies, faculties, and objects of living beings are indeed seen to be manifold. In this regard:
The diversity of birth, place, time, and so forth is well known; so too is the diversity of the sense organs. For example:
elephants have tongues that can be turned back; serpents have eyes on their ears;
owls and others do not see in the light; and among humans, some possess wide vision even though they are men.

The failure to perceive even subtle objects, which is common even among vultures, is here surpassed by the capacity for perceiving subtle meanings. Furthermore, there is a diversity of sensory objects:
just as the cātaka birds subsist on drops of water falling from clouds, while peacocks and chickens feed on refuse, [the yogin] instead tastes the nectar of the filaments of the lotus.

"Of the honey-bees, the essence," and so forth. For the body and the rest are momentary and impermanent; and because they are restricted to each individual person, for there is no commonality among bodies, senses, and objects, as that would entail an equality of experience. And because they constitute a continuum, by virtue of being a continuum of living beings who are their respective causes.

Even in another birth, the body, senses, and so forth remain. For example, from the karmas that bestow caste, lifespan, and experience, once the karma bestowing lifespan has been exhausted, even for one who has died, those very same karmas that bestow caste and experience continue to exist through a causal series (*saṃtati*). They do not, however, migrate toward another [body]. And by means of those two...
The conjunction with various species, bodies, and sense organs is brought about. For this very reason,

it is inferred that each such action is capable of bestowing those corresponding qualities— namely, the diverse, perishable, and individually determined bodies, sense organs, and objects existing in various places, as well as those occurring in other future births.
Because qualities that do not exist in the cause are not perceived in the effects. || 2 ||
1. There is a variant reading: *andhaprāyāṇām api*. 2. Here, the particle *api* has the sense of *ca* (and). — *Dīpikā*.

He states that the sūtra "tasya" (of that) expresses that [the self] is an effect—due to its multiplicity resulting from the difference in its own nature for each individual, given its lack of consciousness—just like the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. He says "in this way," and so on. Furthermore, he states that "momentariness" does not mean perishability at every moment as held by the Buddhists; thus he says "impermanence," and so on, [referring to the case] of perishability at every moment.
The sense is that it is not logically tenable for actions to yield results at a later time.
Regarding the phrase "by way of the continuity of the series of living beings who are the respective causes," and so forth:
therein, the "continuity" (santatatva) arises because the subtle body persists until the end of the kalpa or until liberation.

However, because the actions that serve as the respective causes for the gross body and so forth persist in a continuous stream (*santati*), those bodies and so forth are also said to exist in a continuous stream. For this very reason, he says "just as," etc.;
and precisely for this reason, according to the principle that "there is no sequence in a single [moment]," [the results are produced] by those [karmas] which bestow birth, lifespan, and experience.

It is well known that the body is originated by actions (*karma*). [The phrase] "determined for each individual" implies that, for this very reason, the agency belongs to the selves alone, as they are distinct from one another. Now, an objection might be raised: since the person lacks independence due to dependence on karma, it follows that he cannot be an agent. That is not so; for the actions...
They are incapable of making the person independent, but rather of producing results. For instance, the person is of two kinds:

one whose activity is occupied by another action, and one whose activity is not occupied by another action. Among these, that person who is impelled to accomplish a certain result according to the power of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) [yet] accomplishes something else...

One attains the fruit. Just as one engaged in digging a field might discover a hidden treasure, that very person is said to be impelled by another karma. As it has been stated: "From whatever [cause] the fruit of previously performed karma remains, like a hidden treasure, from that very cause it becomes intent upon manifesting itself, like one with a lamp in hand."

Thus, the intellect functions. And it is not on this account that its agency in that [action] is absent, because even the one who is impelled possesses agency. For there is the agent of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites out of desire;
the agent of the Agnihotra, Aṣṭakā, and other obligatory or occasional rites through the notion of being an agent; and he who...
