Indeed, because their purpose is directly perceived, the agency of those who commit acts such as killing a Brahmin or stealing another’s property—driven by fear, passion, and so forth—is clearly observed. As it is said in the *Mataṅga*: "Whosoever, having been brought under control by a particular disposition through the will of Śiva, is employed in actions for the sake of experience, he then becomes of that very nature."
Having begun thus, even when impelled by someone else, he is perceived as being exactly the same—whether filled with respect or disrespect, or acting out of fear or the power of passion. (2)
Commentary:
Furthermore,
because it depends upon the ignorance of the Lord (Īśvara) and so forth.
That is called the auxiliary cause;
because it is produced by the operation of karma, the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) is [so named] due to its subtle nature.

Since He necessarily requires the divine obstructive power (*rodha-śakti*) denoted by the word "Lord" through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as well as ignorance (*avidyā*) characterized as impurity (*mala*), and— by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*)— also *māyā*, for the purpose of bestowing the fruit [of action], therefore this karma possesses the status of a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*), but not independence (*svātantrya*).

It has been stated that [the Self] is devoid of consciousness; for this very reason, its dependence [on auxiliaries] is merely figurative. It is not, however, like the potter’s dependence on the thread, staff, wheel, and so forth;

otherwise, because the potter also depends on the thread, staff, and other tools, he too would possess the status of an auxiliary (sahakārin). Furthermore, since [an effect] is produced by activity...
It is called *karman* because it is performed (*kriyate*); and because of its subtlety, it is said to be "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*). || 3 ||
1. Chapter on the Determination of Dharma and Adharma, Verse 37. *Dīpikā*:
He explains the phrase "is able to establish its very state of being a concomitant cause" (*sahakāritvam evāsya sādhayitum īśa*) and so forth, beginning with the word "Īśa" (*īśa-śabdena*).

The meaning is this: as the agent, he requires the Lord (Īśa) who is denoted by his own term; as the instrument, he requires the previously mentioned power of obstruction (rodha-śakti), which is indicated by the word "Lord" and is inseparable from Him; as another auxiliary cause, he requires impurity (mala);
and as the material cause, he requires Māyā. For it is thus in the case of all effects, such as the body and so forth.

The three causes—consisting of the agent (*kartṛ*), the auxiliary (*sahāya*), and the material cause (*upādāna*)—are inferred in the case of a jar and so forth, but there is not just a single producer. Rather, based on the existence of examples such as the jar, it is the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*) beginning with the agent that produces the effect.
As it is stated in the *Parākhyam*: "That which is called the Lord is the efficient cause (*nimitta*); the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is the auxiliary; the material cause..."

And that which is subtle and connected to all effects—that triad of causes—by means of it, every effect is inferred. For there is no single producer; rather, a collection [of causes] must be the producer. Thus, he says "but not its status as a *nimitta-kāraṇa* (efficient cause)," beginning with "not independence," etc. Now, regarding action (*karman*)...

Since dharma and adharma—such as the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) or the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*)—are perishable by virtue of being of the nature of performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), how can they be the cause of a result that occurs at a later time? To this, he says: "Furthermore," and so forth. The meaning is this: action (*karman*) is not merely the performance itself, but rather the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by it.
Thus it is. Now, he says that because of its subtlety, it is denoted by the word "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*), beginning with the words "And because of its subtlety," etc. (Verse 3).
1. When [it is said], "the producer and the single causal complex," this is a variant reading. [This is] the commentary.
And that.
It is the progenitor, the sustainer, and the object of enjoyment—
the triad of means beginning with the inner self (adhyātma)—
because it is the source of both truth and untruth.
[It is] that which has the nature of dharma and adharma. || 4 ||

Since the body, the senses, the worlds, and so forth, arise through their connection with various bodies and instruments solely for the sake of experiencing the fruits of karma, [Kāla] is their cause by way of being the efficient cause (*nimitta*). Furthermore, it is that very same [Kāla] which, as the giver, possesses the quality of sustaining them for a specific duration of time. Moreover, they possess the quality of being objects of experience (*bhogyatva*) by means of those fruits. Furthermore, there is the triad of means consisting of the internal (*adhyātma*), and so on.
That which has the triad beginning with *adhyātma* as its means (*sādhana*) is described as such.

In this context, by the word *adhyātma*, that which functions with respect to the self (*ātman*) through proximity as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is called the mind (*manas*). By the inclusion of "etcetera" (*ādi*), speech and body are understood. And thus:

The accomplishment of mind, speech, and body consists respectively of activities of a virtuous nature— such as meditating upon, paying homage to, praising, reciting hymns for, and making offerings to one’s chosen deity— and [the corresponding misdeeds] such as the desire to harm others' property, slandering them, and injuring them.
That whose accomplishment is performed through mind, speech, and body is of the nature of unrighteousness (adharma);
or else, that which pertains to the internal self, the elements, and the divine, having these as its causes, is categorized as adhyātma, adhidaiva, and adhibhūta.

Whatever pleasure or pain arises, the means for all three kinds of it is as follows: indeed, internal pleasure and pain arise through the power of karma, manifesting as mental serenity or agitation and so forth; external [pleasure and pain] consist of the enjoyment of women or being overcome by elephants, lions, and the like; and supramundane [pleasure and pain]— [The text continues: ...arise from the influence of celestial beings. Thus, all three types of experience are produced by the force of past actions. Therefore, one should strive to cultivate wholesome karma. This concludes the section on the causes of pleasure and pain.
And it is produced by desirable and undesirable wind, rain, heat, and so forth. That [action] consists of truth and falsehood;
that action has the nature of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), because its material cause is truth and falsehood. Action whose material cause is truth is of the nature of merit;
action whose material cause is falsehood is of the nature of demerit. || 4 ||

1. Regarding the variant reading *viśvotpāda* (the arising of the universe), the *Dīpikā* explains: "by way of being a cause" means by way of being a cooperative condition (*sahakāritva*). The phrase "of that very [cause]" and so forth refers to experience (*bhoga*) and the like. The phrase "and the object of experience" and so forth [refers to the same].

The phrase "of fruits consisting of pleasure and pain" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. By the words beginning with "adhyātmādi," he states the distinction between actions (*karman*) based on the distinction between their causes; by the words beginning with "yadvā," he offers another interpretation in order to establish those respective distinctions based on the distinction between the fruits.
He explains the sūtra beginning with "tatsatya" with the words beginning with "tacca karma."

The phrase "because of having truth and falsehood as their nature" is an illustration [of a broader principle], including [the factors of] favor and injury, giving and taking away, and the specific nature of the recipient (*pātra*) and so forth. As it has been said in the *Aṭaṅga*: "Furthermore, [the merit] is distinguished by the specific time, again by the specific recipient, further by the specific field (*kṣetra*), and yet more by the extent of the wealth," and so on. (4)
1. The fifth verse in the chapter on the determination of dharma and adharma:
"In sleep it undergoes fruition;
it is employed in its creation."
And at the end, it abides in illusion; moreover, that which has not been experienced does not go to dissolution.

And at the time of dissolution, during the sleep of all beings, it undergoes ripening and transformation on all sides; immediately after creation, it proceeds toward its respective experiences; and finally, at the time of withdrawal, it exists within Māyā in the form of latent impressions (saṃskāra). It does not [cease to exist].
And that which has not been enjoyed perishes. || 5 ||

*Dīpikā*: Regarding the phrase "and at the end," etc., since actions such as agriculture are observed to be *saṃskāras* (refinements) of the material elements (*prakṛti*), it is illogical for them to be *saṃskāras* of the self (*ātman*) as postulated by the Naiyāyikas and others. And as for the self...

Because of the undesirable consequence [of karma] being transformed and so forth, we shall explain that Māyā—established as the substratum of action through the medium of the intellect (buddhi) and other faculties—is itself the material cause. Nor is it the case that [karma] remains unexperienced; for it has been said: "Karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of kalpas if it has not been experienced. (5)
The commentary says: To provide a conclusion, he states:
"Thus, [the sequence] beginning with Māyā and ending with Kāla—"
This [karma] is the initiator, beginningless,
and though it is a manifestor,
it is obstructive and does not lead to liberation.
Thus, this karma, whose nature has been established, is the impeller of the body, the senses, and their objects situated within the path (*adhvan*) beginning from Māyā and ending with Kālāgni;
its sovereign power extends only this far, because there is no praise [of its activity] above Māyā. And although this [karma] is produced by [its own] operation, it is...

Nevertheless, because it is eternal by way of its continuous flow (*pravāha*), it is hardly necessary to state that its having a beginning is untenable. Furthermore, although this karma, being of a pure nature, manifests merit (*puṇya*), it is nonetheless an "obstructer" (*rodhin*), meaning it is an impediment and a cause of saṃsāra. Why is this so? He says: "because it does not lead to immediate liberation."

Because even meritorious action (*puṇya-ātmaka-karma*), while existing, does not lead to liberation (*mukti*) or final release (*apavarga*); rather, it serves only as an obstacle to them. For it is only through the destruction of such action, or its neutralization (*sāmya*), that those who have attained grace (*anugraha*) in accordance with the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) achieve isolation (*kaivalya*). Now, [it may be argued: "But surely that which is not for liberation..."
Thus, what was said is incorrect; for even when karma exists, liberation is traditionally taught on account of its equilibrium. As it is stated in the *Kiraṇa*:

"When karma has become equalized, then, by the force of time, one is initiated by the Guru through the descent of the intense power (tīvra-śakti), just like Śiva who is omniscient. This is not a fault, for such a person...

Even though action exists, it is non-existent because it is fruitless due to its power being mutually obstructed, like an action performed after initiation (*dīkṣā*). As stated by Kheṭakanandana: "Even if performed, it would not lead to fruit, like a seed sown in saline soil; one must set aside that which arises from the conflict with a more powerful specific scripture."
Karma alone [is the cause]. || 6 ||
1. In the *Tattvasaṃgraha* of the Eightfold Treatise, verse 37.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the *Karmavicāra-prakaraṇa*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Vidyākaṇṭha.
*Dīpikā*: "Because of the lack of praise for that which is above *māyā*, etc. This means because of incapacity.
For there is an absence of such action therein, and because it has been stated [only] as existing within the intellect (*buddhi*). What, then, is there in that case?
We state that the auxiliary cause consists of action (karma) characterized by the service of Īśvara and the impurity of eligibility (adhikāramala). For this very reason,

because things are of such a nature at every dissolution, he says that the beginningless stream of the succession of bodies and karma has already been explained previously, according to the analogy of the seed and the sprout.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "What is this? and so forth, and "From the exhaustion of karma" and so forth, the meaning here is as follows:

for those who have received initiation through the ripening of impurities (*malaparipāka*) and the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), by means of that very [initiation], there occurs an equilibrium between the two previously mentioned types of karma—those caused by desired and undesired objects.

"Liberation results from the exhaustion of karma. As they say: "He who does not rejoice at a benefit received nor become angry at an injury, being equanimous toward all beings—he is called one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). This should not be explained as referring to the cessation of two contradictory actions, for such [equanimity] exists even during the state of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).

And because it is impossible for there to be a cause for the discharge of [karmic] power; likewise, when here [in this world], in that which consists of merit and demerit (dharma-adharma) as the cause of results characterized by the ripening of merit and demerit— such as heaven, hell, and so forth— or in that which consists of merit as the cause for attaining the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka) in heaven.

The two extremely harsh karmas, characterized by unrighteousness and serving as the cause for the Raurava and Avīci hells, reach their fruition through intense momentum; they manifest as the unseen results of longevity and non-longevity for a person who is utterly defiled, whether his body has already fallen [at death] or has not yet fallen.
If they were to arise simultaneously,
then because it is impossible for those two opposing actions to simultaneously bestow the characteristics of pleasure and pain such as heaven, hell, and so forth,
and because they are equal in strength, it would also be untenable for them to produce results sequentially.
Furthermore, since no other mode besides succession and simultaneity is possible, and having considered that for someone at some time even contradictory actions may result in an unexhausted state,
the Lord, due to the contradiction of those actions, uplifts the person by means of *niyati* (the principle of necessity) presided over by His power. (From the Mataṅga Tantra).

In this ripening of dharma and adharma, which is indicated by the movement of the scale’s tip, when one perceives that destiny arises from the removal of that [karma] within the action, then, because it is impossible for the experiencer to exist simultaneously in both [states],
it remains as if empty. However, when all the karmas of someone have at some time emerged in their entirety...

And when [the impurities] have reached full maturity, the supreme power of the Lord (pārameśvarī śaktiḥ), having destroyed all those opposing factors, bestows the state of the "isolated one through consciousness" (vijñānakevalitva); however, it does not grant liberation (mokṣa), because that is invariably preceded by the maturation of the impurity (mala).
As it is said in the *Kiraṇatantra*: "At that time, there is no [further] experience of worldly enjoyment. And this very [state] exists even during the stage of worldly existence (bhava).

The "equality of karma" (karmasāmya) is being described; it does not, however, mean the equality of two masses of merit and demerit. Consequently, when for a certain person at a certain time there occurs such an equality of the two types of karma—desirable and undesirable—motivated by [external] causes, and which is joined with the descent of power (śaktipāta) resulting from the ripening of impurities, then for that person, through initiation (dīkṣā)...

He will state that liberation will occur through the exhaustion of karma. For this very reason, the objections and refutations beginning with "nanu" (but surely) have been rejected by those learned in the scriptures and should therefore be disregarded. This is because, even in such sūtras as "When the two actions... and so forth, the term "another time" (*kālāntara*) denotes the ripening of impurity (*mala*).
Furthermore, the term *karmasāmya* was explained by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha in his commentary on the *Kiraṇatantra* as denoting the equilibrium of the two types of karma caused by benefit and harm.
Thus [ends the section] in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā* composed by Aghoraśivācārya.
The eighth chapter, "An Examination of Karma," is completed.
1. *Avīci* is the name of a certain hell.
2. Verse 15 of the "Chapter on Necessity" (*niyati-paṭala*).
3. There is a variant reading: *śarīradvaye*.
Now begins the ninth chapter, on Māyā.
Now, by the word of the Omniscient One:
The characteristic of one who has entered the path is now being described, even slightly and by way of reasoning, regarding the knot and the snare. (1)
Now, the word "atha" (then) signifies immediate succession;

in this section examining the nature of the fetter (*pāśa*), immediately following the investigation into the fetter of karma, a brief definition of the fetter known as *māyā*, which consists of the knot (*granthi*), is stated. Furthermore, at the conclusion of the preceding chapter:
The connection [of this section] should be understood as being topical (*pāṭalika*), due to the introduction of the word "illusion" (*māyā*).

The fourfold connection, beginning with that of the word-meaning (*padārtha*), has already been explained previously. The phrase "of that which is established by the words of the Omniscient One" refers to that which was accepted to be spoken by the introductory sūtra beginning with "the power of the veil, the ministers of karma," and so forth.
"A little" [is said] because it is not possible to state even in brief the entire definition of *māyā*.

Thus it was stated by the venerable Vṛhaspati: "Even the speech of all the perfected ones (*siddhas*) would be exhausted if uttered for a long time; because of the infinity of *māyā*, the number of its currents cannot be told."
"Even by means of a mere trace of reasoning" means not solely by means of scripture (*āgama*), but rather that its definition is stated as being established even by a small portion of reasoning—
that is, by a slight inference.
— *Dīpikā*.
Now begins the ninth chapter, on the characteristics of *māyā*.
He states that by the aphorism beginning with "atha" (now), the declaration of the characteristics of *māyā* is being promised, saying: "regarding the category of *pāśa*.
Furthermore, he says that the topical connection (*pāṭalika-sambandha*) is indicated by the phrase "māyā and so forth," saying: "of this [category]," and so on.

"Padārthādi" and so forth. The connection with that word-meaning (*padārtha*) is by way of the word-meaning "bond" (*pāśa*). The contextual connection is likewise solely by way of the "Knowledge" (*vidyā*) section. The connection with the Sūtra is by means of the phrase "the net of bonds. The connection consisting of sentences is also manifold, through various statements such as "of Māyā, which possesses authority," and so on. And for this reason, there is a connection with the sentence.
He says that this has been indicated by the words of the Omniscient One: "By the power of the Lord of Veils," and so forth; as well as "Not indeed," and so forth.

The meaning is that because the streams of effects, consisting of both common and uncommon forms, are infinite, their specific distinctions cannot be stated; rather, here only the essential nature of their cause is established. || 1 ||
The Commentary:
That single, inauspicious seed of the world possesses manifold powers.
It is co-existent with its auxiliaries, non-obstructive, pervasive, and imperishable. (2)
That [Pradhāna] is one, because it is the supreme cause and because there is no evidence for its multiplicity.
It is "inauspicious" (aśiva) because it causes delusion. It is the "seed" (bīja), the material cause of the world, and it is endowed with diverse powers.
It binds the individual souls (aṇu) by obstructing the auxiliary karmas until the end of their respective terms of authority.

That is its nature (*tacchīla*), which obstructs the end of the section on auxiliary causes (*sahakāryadhikāra*). This is because, in the absence of karma, the state of being bound (*granthitatva*) does not occur.
It is all-pervasive (*vyāpin*), meaning it is omnipresent; it pervades its own effects. It is imperishable (*anaśvara*) because of its eternity.

Because it persists even during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), like the *ātman* and the Lord (*īśvara*). As it is stated in the *Tattvatrayanirṇaya*: "Śambhu, Puruṣa, and Māyā—this triad of principles is eternal, all-pervading, and endowed with the power of agency; it remains awake even while the products [of nature] are asleep. (1)
1. Third Verse. *Dīpikā*:
He states that by the words "That one," etc., he proposes the definition of *māyā*.
Regarding the phrase "that state of being knotted," and so forth: he will demonstrate oneness and the other qualities immediately thereafter.

Regarding the statement "it is inauspicious because it causes delusion," and so forth: although it manifests consciousness by means of its effects, it is called "inauspicious" and "delusive" because it generates the cognition of a self and so forth in relation to what is not the self and so forth, thereby acting as a cause of delusion.
"The seed of the world," and so forth. That which is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the body, the senses, the worlds, and so on, is Māyā.

"Endowed with diverse powers" means that its effects consist of various forms of power. As he will state later: "In dissolution, the effects exist in the form of powers resting upon that [Māyā]; in manifestation, they exist in the form of manifest entities."

"They operate for the sake of accomplishing an effect"—this is what is meant. However, it should not be explained that Māyā possesses multiple powers (*śakti*) that produce various effects; for a power cannot possess another power, and because the production of something from non-existence (*asadutpatti*) will be refuted later. Furthermore, this has already been explained previously: since [Māyā] is the material cause (*upādāna*), like clay and so forth, it does not require auxiliary causes.

"It does not produce effects such as the body by means of that [permanent] nature," and so forth; "of the auxiliary conditions," and so forth; and its "pervasiveness" is due to its pervading all its own effects—thus he says, "and pervasive," etc., and "and imperishable," etc., regarding the continuum of the body and karma.
Like the series of seeds, sprouts, and stalks, this too is without beginning, middle, or end.

As they say: "It is impossible to state that 'this is before' and 'that is after. For this very reason, this [universe] does not undergo transformation in its entirety, like milk turning into curd; rather, it should be understood that it transforms only in part, like a drop [of oil] on a surface, according to the analogy of the ghee-insect. || 2 ||
Commentary: It has been stated that [the agent] is also [known] by means of reasoning (yukti) even in a slight degree. Therefore, he demonstrates that reasoning:
"By which the agent is inferred."
By the reason of the nature of the world,
there is also no grasping [of a cause] without threads for a cloth. (3)
It is said that because the world possesses arrangement (*sanniveśa*) and so forth, it possesses the property of being produced (*utpattimattva*), which thereby leads one to infer a creator.
By that very same property of being produced, let the material cause (*upādāna*) also be inferred;
for the production of things that possess the quality of being produced is never observed to occur without a material cause. Just as...
In the absence of threads and so forth, there is no cloth and the like. || 3 ||
The *Dīpikā* connects the sūtra beginning with "kartṛ" (the agent) with the phrase "also by means of reasoning," and so forth.
In that regard, he states that the reasoning for the existence of Māyā is expressed by this [sūtra], beginning with "because of possessing configuration," and so on. (3)
Commentary:
Furthermore,
it would have to be insentient.
Because the effect is observed to be insentient;
otherwise, the fault of the cause being unrestricted would entail that everything could arise from anything.

And that state of being knotted is insentient, because its effects, such as *kalā* and the rest, are observed to be exclusively insentient. Otherwise— that is, if one were to admit its sentience despite the observation of its insentient effects—
there would be a violation of the principle of causal regularity, which is termed "the destroyer of all."
The fault of destroying all inference and abolishing every conventional practice would thus result. || 4 ||

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: It states that it is precisely because of being a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) that it is insentient, beginning with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). As it has been said:
"Whatever entities possess a certain form, they are produced from causes of that same form. (Verse 4)
Commentary: He states the reasoning to establish the non-perishability and omnipresence previously mentioned:
"If this effect were impermanent..."
Furthermore, from what does it arise? And if it were non-pervasive, how could it belong to all [beings] in every respect? (5)

If, at the time of the world's dissolution, even the material cause called *māyā* were to perish, then from what material cause would the world arise again at the beginning of creation? Therefore, it is not subject to impermanence. Now, if it is argued that the Lord will create the material cause at the beginning of creation, this is not tenable; for if that were so—

Just as its effect [cannot arise], this [power] also cannot arise without a material cause (*upādāna*); thus, another material cause would have to be postulated for that, and yet another for that, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). However, there is no such fault if it remains in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*) through the withdrawal of individual manifestations. Thus, even if it were non-pervasive (*avyāpin*), there would be no problem for that which faces in all directions.
The effect would not arise; therefore, pervasiveness must necessarily be admitted. || 5 ||

The *Dīpikā* states: "Pervasiveness must necessarily be accepted; therefore, it is precisely within its own effects that [this occurs], such as in the case of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) consisting of the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyātattva*), the scriptures, and so forth."

He will state that the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) is indeed something else, consisting of the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*), which is denoted by terms such as *kuṇḍalinī*—namely, "the womb of the universe. He will also say, "From Power (*śakti*) arises Sound (*nāda*), then the Point (*bindu*)," and so forth; and in the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*) as well, "of the supreme Māyā"; and in the venerable *Raurava*, "above Māyā is Mahāmāyā. (5)
1. This means [the scriptures] such as the Kāmika and others.
[This is] the commentary (vṛtti). Now follows the presentation of reasoning for [their] unity.
That which is seen to have multiple minds as its cause is not something that possesses origination; therefore—
Let one [of these] be accepted. || 6 ||

For this reason: whatever is manifold and insentient is observed to be produced, like a jar or a cloth; but this [Brahman] is not produced, nor is it born from a cause, because it is the supreme cause. Therefore, it is one, for there cannot be many supreme causes. || 6 ||

Commentary: Now, if in the production of the world there were a multiplicity of material causes (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), as in the atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth imagined by others, then what [fault would there be]?
The fault is as follows: a cloth is seen to arise from a collection of threads; thus, the one is produced from the many. (6½)
For it is observed that the production of a single cloth arises from many threads;
likewise, let the entire world arise from multiple causes.
Thus, enough with the postulation of a supreme cause in the form of a knot—this is the objection. (6½)
Commentary: Here is the refutation: that [cause] is also manifold, yet from a single [effect].
O King, it is born from a seed. || 7 ||
As for what was stated by you— that the cause of a cloth consists of multiple threads— even though that [cause] is manifold,
the production of various forms such as cloths arises from a single substance, such as silk or cotton. In the same way,
at the beginning of creation, the world arises from Māyā-tattva, which is the supreme cause known as the substratum of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
There is no fault whatsoever. || 7 ||
The commentary: He refutes those whose position is that the manifestation and disappearance of the conscious and the unconscious occur solely from the Supreme Self.
For those according to whom some effect arises from some cause that is a phenomenon,
for them [it is established] by means of the mark of smoke.
Why is water not inferred? || 8 ||
By those who accept the arising of even that which is uncreated from the cause that is the nature of consciousness (*cid-dharmaka*),

why is the inference of water from smoke not performed? For, since the specific restriction between cause and effect would be impossible, it would follow that something could arise from what does not possess its nature, just as [an effect] is not seen [to arise from such a source].

From the mark of smoke, there is sometimes the attainment of water. For thus, it is never observed that something of a non-conscious nature arises from a conscious nature which is its opposite. If that which possesses a certain nature were to arise from that which does not possess that nature, then everything could arise from everything. 8.

The *Dīpikā* introduces the sūtra beginning with "of whom" (*yeṣām*) with the words "of the Supreme Self alone," and so forth. This is also an elliptical indication [that includes] the supreme primordial nature (*paraprakṛti*) known as Nārāyaṇa, because the reasoning (*nyāya*) is the same. He states this very point:

"Because it does not have that as its intrinsic nature," and so forth. Precisely because it is the material cause (*upādāna*), the previously mentioned defects such as insentience (*acetanatva*) and the like necessarily follow. || 8 ||
The commentary: He speaks to those who maintain that the world has atoms as its cause:
"For those for whom the world has the primary elements as its limit..."
The atoms are the cause;
because of the reason stated previously,
the subtlety of cognition is indeed known.

For those for whom the atoms (*paramāṇu*)— extending from the element earth up to the primary elements (*bhūta*)— are the cause of the world, the subtlety of their knowledge, which is the cause for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), arises from the aforementioned cognition of the six categories beginning with substance (*dravya*), or from the comprehension of the sixteen categories.
The sharpness of their awakening has been understood. Those who assert that atoms are the cause, by means of an intellect capable of such subtle vision, do not deserve censure.

For some have denied the very status of being an atom to atoms, on the grounds that they would possess six parts due to simultaneous conjunction with six [other atoms]. As for the possession of six parts...

Because they must be excluded [from being the cause]. Furthermore, since they are insentient and manifold, like jars, cloths, and so forth, they too must necessarily have a prior cause; how then could they possess the status of the ultimate cause? Consequently, the world cannot have them as its material cause. || 9 ||
1. For those [who hold] that the world consists of atoms (*paramāṇu*), with its existence and end limited by the primary elements such as earth and so forth—this is a variant reading.
*Dīpikā*.

He explains the sūtra beginning with *bhūtāvadhī* and so forth with the passage beginning *yeṣām* and so forth. [Objection: But surely the atoms themselves, joining together in the sequence of dyads and so on, will be the ultimate cause.
What here is untenable, such that we should be reproached in this way? [Response: Regarding the phrase *paramāṇūnām* and so forth—it is for this very reason.

The intended meaning is that because it possesses a specific configuration (*sanniveśa*), it must be an effect. Furthermore, he states the refutation even if the status of being an atom (*paramāṇutā*) is accepted, beginning with the words "Moreover" (*kiñca*). Nor is there any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of this reason (*hetu*) by means of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, since those too have been made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣīkṛta*). Nor is the reason one whose application is superseded by the lapse of time (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because it is not contradicted by perception or scripture.
For even in our own scripture, if one were to take established atoms as the subject of inference, the acceptance of your scripture would necessarily follow for you. That is incorrect;
because in our scripture as well, atoms are [established] by means of scriptural citations regarding the measurement of time and space, and so forth.

Since your own scripture is accepted as established, how can it be subject to the fallacy of "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) by means of its own sublation? This is just as when those who seek to prove that [the universal] is present in every individual (*vyaktisarvagatatva*)—
in order to sublate the property of omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) asserted by the Naiyāyikas regarding the universal as the locus (*dharmin*)— [commit this fallacy].
The reason for the Vaiśeṣikas is that [the universal] is not perceived apart from its individual instances. And just as for the Naiyāyikas, regarding the substratum *samavāya*,
there is the sublation of two properties— namely, perceptibility and being inherent— which are accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas.

For those who seek to establish both the eternal inferability and the independence [of atoms], the reason is not declared by you to be "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), precisely because the subject (*dharmin*) is established for both parties; likewise, between my reason and your reason— both residing in their respective scriptures— for those who seek to establish impermanence and permanence respectively regarding atoms already established, [the same applies].

The reason is not "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa). However, if the subject (dharmin) is not established for one of the two parties, that is indeed a fault. For example, when one seeks to prove the impermanence of the subject called "inherence" (samavāya)—which is accepted by the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas—the reason "because it is a relation, like conjunction" is entirely [unestablished] for those belonging to other schools.
"Because of the absence of equality. For this very reason, the argument—"atoms are preceded by causes because they possess form, like jars and so forth"—is not *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed) for us;
rather, it should be understood as being [mistimed] only for those other schools who do not accept atoms.

"But surely this is a non-conclusive fallacy (aprayojaka-hetvābhāsa)," says a certain commentator on the Nyāyabhāṣya. That is not so; for there is no such thing as a non-conclusive fallacy. The author of the Nyāyasūtras [states] that inference is the cognition of an imperceptible object possessing a mark, derived from a mark characterized by five features.

Having inferred the definition of a logical mark (*liṅga*), [the author] stated that there are exactly five fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)—namely, the established (*siddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), the mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), and the counter-balanced (*prakaraṇasama*)—which serve to exclude it. The Commentator also [states] that this is its "determining name. For this very reason...

The claim that [the world] has the elements (*bhūta*) as its ultimate limit is also refuted; for since "being an effect" is established by such reasons as having parts, and since atoms are precluded from being causes, another cause must be sought.
Furthermore, this body, consisting of effects and causes, is produced by *māyā* and so forth in this world, even according to the Sāṃkhyas.
Mauna is held to consist of twenty-four principles (tattvas), because it exists as the state of fulfilling the qualities (guṇas).

Herein, the five gross elements and the five subtle elements (tanmātras) are denoted by the term "effect" (kārya) and serve as the substrata for the sense organs; the ten sense organs and the three internal organs constitute the instruments (karaṇa) according to their source.
They begin the transition into another womb. Thus it has been said by the Teachers:

"This effect is set in motion by the instruments (karaṇas) having entered into it; however, because they are not all-pervading, the instruments exert their activity by presiding over the effect. If this is so, then Nature (prakṛti), which consists of the qualities (guṇas), is itself the reality established as both cause and effect.
The Sāṃkhyas [claim]: "That is incorrect, because the principles (tattvas) beginning with *kalā* are established by reasoning.

For instance, since the powers of consciousness (*jñatva*) and agency (*kartṛtva*) are obscured for the impure person, he does not possess the status of an enjoyer of the worlds, as is the case with the *pralayakevalin*. Therefore, there must necessarily be two principles that manifest these two [powers]."
The *kalā* and *vidyā* [tattvas] are established. For one whose nature as consciousness is manifested, there is no activity, just as there is none for one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*);

therefore, passion (*rāga*) is necessarily established as being required for such activity. Since activity entails the necessity of both the power of limitation (*kala*) and the power of determination (*niyati*), these two are established. And *niyati*...

There is a dependence upon objects such as effects and instruments. Since the previously mentioned qualities (*guṇas*), which are its causes, are insentient and manifold, there must exist another cause for them, just as there is for the sense organs;
thus, that which is called the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) is established as distinct from the qualities. For this very reason, they desire that to be the reality of which they speak.

The followers of the Pañcarātra maintain that this Blessed Lord Vāsudeva is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) which transcends the qualities (*guṇas*). They declare that the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is eternal and that nothing exists beyond it; thus, *prakṛti* is established. Furthermore, since even the *pradhāna* (the primary cause) is determined for each individual soul (*puruṣa*) and is therefore manifold, it must follow that these principles (*tattvas*) are distinct for every individual soul.

Because it would follow that there would be an equality of enjoyment [for all]. In that case, since they are insentient and manifold, their status as a cause is established; and since the soul could not be an enjoyer if it were not joined with them, that supreme cause, Māyā, is thus established.
For this very reason, the Buddhists and others hold that things arise only as aggregates and cease only as aggregates.
They say that the causes of the body and so forth are simply the body and so forth themselves; their position is cast far aside. || 9 ||
1. The meaning is: from a logical mark (*liṅga*) ascertained through a statement consisting of the five members beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*).
2. This refers to verse 4 in the eighth chapter of the *Tattvasaṃgraha*.
3. The meaning is: regarding [the properties of] being a knower (*jñatva*) and being an agent (*kartṛtva*).

Commentary: Now, when it is observed that [the self] arises from the body, senses, and so forth— which are related to its mother and father— by producing a body and organs similar to their respective [parents], then...
Anticipating the objection, "What is the use of postulating an unseen cause such as *māyā* and the like? he says:
"If the body and so forth [of the Lord] were [identical to] the body and so forth [of the individual], then upon the cessation of all those [bodies, etc.],"
What need is there to speak of the destruction of all [suffering]?
One who is omniscient would not speak falsely. || 10 ||

If it is your position that the bodies and sense-faculties of living beings have as their cause the union of mother and father along with [the prior] body and sense-faculties—because they exist when those exist and do not exist when those do not exist—then let it be so. However, you must be questioned on this point: since there is the production of bodies, sense-faculties, and so forth at the time of the dissolution of all things and the total destruction of the universe; [how is this explained?]
What kind of state is this? Now, if it is argued that the destruction of all entities occurs only through succession and not through a simultaneous withdrawal of everything—that is incorrect;
for [this truth] is sung in the authoritative scriptures such as the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇa.
Since the dissolution [of the world] cannot be denied, and since even the initial creation would not be accepted if that were denied,
one who asserts that neither the creation nor the dissolution of the world is possible would thereby abandon omniscience itself.
The *Dīpikā* states: "Even if that position is accepted, the refutation [of the opponent's view] regarding the body and so forth is expressed by the sūtra beginning with 'śarīrādeḥ'. Thus he says:
"mātā" and so forth, referring specifically to the sequential destruction of the body and the rest.
The meaning is that the postulation of the unseen is logical because it is like what has been seen upon observation. He refutes this with the words "That is incorrect," and so forth;

for the non-existence of the dissolution of all things does not follow from mere non-observation, because the dissolution of all things is established by both reasoning and scripture—this is the sense. For this very reason, he says "Śruti, Smṛti," and so forth. 10.
1. The meaning is: "even if one accepts the Buddhist position.
2. This pratīka is not seen in the mātṛkās.
3. *bhāvo'stu* is a variant reading.
Commentary: Now, how can one who asserts the absence of destruction be considered a speaker of falsehood? To this he says:
"That property which [exists] even in a single part..."
When a subject is already established,
by what means can its arising from every [cause] be prevented? (11)
Having seen the death of millions of embodied beings gathered together,
that time [of destruction] is also perceived.
Wherein there is the destruction of all beings without exception. || 12 ||

For the Omniscient One has declared that his own words must be examined for their validity through logical proof. As he said: "O monks, my words should be accepted after examining them from all sides—like gold [tested] by heating, cutting, and rubbing—but not out of respect. And this [examination] is possible when there is the potential for destruction.

The logical justification is indeed unassailable: namely, when a property such as smoke, light, or burning is observed in one particular part of a given subject (*dharmin*) such as fire, what could possibly prevent that same property from arising in all parts of it?
Consequently, [if the property were restricted to one part], there would be famine, pestilence, and the collapse of structures in other parts.

Having observed the gradual downfall of millions of multitudes of living beings, the time for the destruction of the entire world—though proclaimed in the sacred scriptures—is also delineated by means of inference. || 12 ||

The *Dīpikā* states: In order to demonstrate that this [position] is also established by reason, he expresses the doubt regarding the sūtra beginning with "in one part" (*ekadeśe*) and so forth, starting with "Now," etc. His [the opponent's] status as a proponent of universal falsity (*sarvamithyāvāditva*)...

To demonstrate that, he first presents those words beginning with "by the omniscient one" (*sarvajñena*). With the intention of showing that this [statement] is contradictory because it asserts the absence of the destruction of all things—which is established by reasoning—he says "and this," and so forth.
He demonstrates that very reasoning with the words "of whom," and so forth. (12)
Commentary: And at that time, all effects had been withdrawn into Māyā; thus he says:
"The effects have that as their support."
In the process of withdrawal, they exist in the form of powers (śakti);
in the process of manifestation, they function in the form of manifest entities (vyakti) for the accomplishment of purposes.

Based on the arguments previously stated, that causal principle called *māyā*— which has been established as possessing qualities such as eternity and omnipresence— is the substratum for the body, the instruments, the worlds, and so forth;
these remain in the form of potential power (*śakti*) at the time of dissolution, but during creation they exist in a manifest form (*vyakti*).
Since they become active for the sake of accomplishing their respective purposes, everything is well-established. || 13 ||

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: "At that time," and so forth; because it is the subject under discussion, it possesses the quality of being the destroyer of all. For this very reason, he states that the *māyā-tattva*, which is the substratum of the power of the second effect, is established.
"By those previously mentioned," and so forth. || 13 ||
Commentary: Here, the Sage, unable to tolerate the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), asks: "The taking up of causal factors such as threads..."
If the cloth does not exist, there is no one seeking the cloth;
if it does exist, even the word "agent" (kāraka) disappears— thus the world is ruined.
The efficacy of the causal entity lies in the production of a non-existent effect. (14½)

As for the claim that the world exists within the supreme cause called *māyā* in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*), that is not tenable. For indeed, the postulation of the unperceived should be based on what is perceived. And it is observed that one who desires a cloth that is not yet present grasps the causal factors such as threads, the shuttle, and the loom; but this is not the case when the cloth already exists.

If [the effect] exists: for if the cloth already exists, even the term "agent" (kāraka) is not applicable to the threads and so forth, precisely because they already exist. For it is only in the case of the arising of what was non-existent that the causal entity is fruitful, and not otherwise. || 14½ ||
The *Dīpikā* explains the introductory question-sūtra beginning with "tantvādi" (thread, etc. by means of the passage beginning with "yadetad" (this which...).
Here, there are four positions among the proponents of the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavādins*). Some hold that the cause consists of a collection of potencies (*śakti*).
It must be accepted that it is the powers themselves that become manifest as the effect, as they say:

"Due to the transformation of an entity which is a mere collection of powers, at some time one power is manifested while another is dissolved. Others, however, maintain that the manifestation of entities is not a transition into a different form, but rather—

It is simply their state of being perceived. Therefore, because they are eternal, their dissolution occurs either within the nature of *pradhāna* or in some specific quality (*dharma*) of certain things. Consequently, it is understood that what is called "birth" is merely their gradual manifestation. As it has been said: "And [manifestation occurs] either through a sequence among the forms of objects of perception, or by the sovereignty of Śrī."

"Through the appearance [of things] within their own being, the notion of 'birth' is employed. Others, however, say that the effect is merely a particular arrangement of the cause, like bracelets, armlets, and so forth from gold. As it has been said: "The transformation of gold into a beautiful earring... [and] "...of tigers... [is merely a change in form].

"Or rather, it is the state of totality; or else, by what means are birth and destruction proclaimed therein? Others, however, have stated that because entities possess a nature characterized by a succession of diverse states, they undergo various specific conditions in sequence and thus receive designations such as "birth" and so forth. As they say: "The cause [appears] through the state of being the effect."
Or, when [the effect] remains [unmanifest], this [effect], having thus already attained the state of being an effect, would not be produced [anew].

Furthermore, in all four of these positions, the principle that "it exists even before its naming" is the very same logic used to establish the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryasiddhi*). He states that this is untenable with the words "that is not logical," and so forth, and he demonstrates that very point with the words "for instance," and so forth. || 14½ ||
Commentary: Here is the refutation:
Let [it] produce [cognition] from everything—
Everything desired shall be entirely attained. || 15 ||
Now, since that which is impossible [is not an object], what is your restrictive rule regarding that which is possible?
And I do not perceive any such thing.
If it is a power, then it is a case of proving what is already established. || 16 ||

Let alone the production of what already exists; regarding the production of what does not exist, if one accepts the efficacy of causal factors such as the shuttle, thread, and loom, why do they not produce everything desired from all things? Or, if it is argued that it is impossible [for them to produce everything], then their efficacy is not established.
Because we observe that any particular effect arises from some specific cause, rather than everything arising from everything;

if that is so, then whatever arises from a particular cause must arise from that very cause and not from another. In this regard, what is the determining factor for you? For we do not perceive any other determining factor within that cause.

By which specific capacity (*abhijñāna*) we might disregard everything else and grasp that very [cause] for one who desires its production? Now, if—out of fear that everything could arise from everything—one were to say that the power to produce that effect belongs only to that specific cause and to nothing else, then this very point has already been established; thus he says: "If it is a capacity (*śakti*), then it is proving what is already proven" (*siddhasādhyatā*). What is the use of anything else?

Regarding the cause of the specific determination of cause and effect: it is precisely the capacity (*śakti*) to produce each respective effect that will serve as the regulator; for that which lacks such a capacity is incapable of producing it, just as the procreation of a son is not possible for a eunuch. If this is so, then the possession of the capacity to produce that particular effect resides in that very cause.

By stating "not elsewhere," you are proving what is already established for us, as you have entered our own position by asserting that its effect exists there in the form of a potentiality (śakti). || 16 ||
The *Dīpikā* explains the aphorism of the rebuttal, beginning with "Let it be," and so forth.
It introduces the segment of the aphorism beginning with "If there were attachment," and so on, starting with "Now, from everything," and so forth.
The proponent raises an objection: "What is the use of another," and so forth. He explains the sūtra of the response:
"If it were thus," and so forth. || 16 ||
Commentary: He states the refutation of the [opponent's] accumulation [of arguments].
Otherwise, the collection of causal factors...
Because the occurrence [of cognition] is untenable, the scripture, the act of grasping, and the object also vanish; thus, that [position] is likewise refuted. (17)
Otherwise—that is, if one accepts the arising of what is non-existent—the very activity of the collection of causal factors would be untenable.
For what indeed could causal factors do for the production of an effect that is non-existent, such as the son of a barren woman?
And because the activity of causal factors would be impossible, there would be no such scriptural injunctions as "bring a lump of clay" for one who intends to make a jar.
Furthermore, the undertaking—that is, the grasping—and the purpose of those causal factors, which is the action characterized by their specific operation, would cease;
it would fall apart. And when that has ceased, there would be an obstruction of all activity. On the contrary, according to your position, the entire world would be paralyzed. || 17 ||
1. *upacayya* is a variant reading.
2. *pravṛttiḥ kim* is a variant reading. *Dīpikā*.
He explains the sūtra beginning with "otherwise" (*anyathā*) and so forth: "Otherwise," etc. (17).

Commentary: Now, it might be argued that the effect does not exist in the cause in the form of a potency (*śakti*); rather, it is simply the potency that produces it which exists there. However, since that which possesses the potency cannot produce something other than its own [effect], the specific determination of cause and effect is established.
Anticipating the objection that this might involve some deficiency, he refutes it:
"Now, there exists a causal power (upādāna-śakti), but the effect is not of the nature of that power."
A distinction between these two must be stated;
I do not perceive any such thing whatsoever.

Now, if it is thought that there exists in the cause a capacity (*śakti*) that produces specific effects, but the effect does not exist [in the cause] by way of its own nature as a capacity—this differs only in words, not in meaning. For you must state a qualification here: namely, that the capacity which produces each respective effect exists in the cause "by way of its nature as a capacity."
Or, regarding the statement that "each respective effect resides in its cause," we do not perceive any distinction whatsoever [between this view and our own].

*Dīpikā*: He states that the very same meaning expressed by the words "if there were power" (*śaktiśced*) and so forth is now being elaborated upon by the sūtra beginning with "but it exists" (*athāsti*).
"Is it not so? and so forth. He explains that very sūtra [with the words] "Now, if this is the opinion," and so forth. || 18 ||
Commentary: Since it is so,
therefore the producer is the regulator.
The capacity of a causal entity is determined either through positive and negative concomitance or by conventional usage. (19)

Therefore, it is established that the productive capacity (*janyaśakti*) of the causal entity is the regulator [of causality], such that "this arises from this alone. And that productive capacity is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and through traditional consensus (*prasiddhi*): for instance, a jar or similar object arises only when the lump of clay exists.
Non-existence is simply non-arising; such is the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Furthermore, this conventional usage is established even among children, fools, and women:
namely, that those desiring the production of a jar do not offer to the potter any material cause other than a lump of clay. Now, if the jar were already present in the lump of clay...

Then the pot would be perceived even without the activity of the potter; however, it is not so perceived. Therefore, the pot does not exist within the lump of clay; rather, it is produced from it by the potter, because the pot is perceived only after his activity has occurred. This is not so.

The non-perception of the jar there is due to the absence of the causes for its perception, not because of its non-existence. However, when it comes to possess the fitness for perception through the manifesting action of the potter's wheel and so forth, it is indeed perceived—just as a stake, subterranean water, and the like are [perceived] by digging and other such means. Now, if it is argued that the stake, subterranean water, and so forth exist prior [to their manifestation]:

There is indeed evidence for this; however, it is not the case that the jar exists within the lump of clay such that the jar arises from it. Rather, it is rightly stated that it is manifested. If this is so, then here too, evidence for existence—such as "because what is non-existent has no cause" and "because there is a selection of a material cause"—would be possible; therefore, the theory of manifestation (*abhivyaktivāda*) alone is logical.

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: "The power of the produced" (*janyaśakti*) means the power of the effect residing in the cause. Now, if it is argued that the notions of birth and destruction are untenable under the theory that the effect pre-exists (*satkāryavāda*), that is not so; for, in this view, "birth" is simply the possession of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Its absence, however, is destruction. For just as the self, although beginningless, is metaphorically said to have "birth" because it is endowed with purposeful activity through its connection with a body, so too its separation from that [body] is "destruction. It is for this very reason that he raises an objection, beginning with "But surely... and so forth; and he provides a rebuttal, beginning with "This is not so... and so forth. As the Sāṃkhyas say:

Because there is no production from a non-existent cause, because of the grasping of material causes, because of the absence of simultaneous occurrence, because an efficient cause does not produce what is impossible for it, and because of the existence of the cause, that which is to be accomplished must exist [prior to its manifestation]. Furthermore, even according to experience, birth and destruction are merely appearance and disappearance, since it is these two alone that are perceptible. For instance, in the case of direct perception:

And it is observed that milk itself becomes curd; nor can it be said that because things are momentary, curd is produced upon the destruction of the milk, for the doctrine of momentariness has already been refuted. || 19 ||

Commentary: If this is so, then the production of an existent entity is not tenable precisely because it already exists, as in the case of a pot or other objects that are currently perceived. Thus, he states that the same fault remains exactly as before.
Its manifestation, called "birth," arises from the dependence upon its causal factors;
by means of that, the form residing in the threads [is manifested].
It obstructs the form of the cloth. || 20 ||
Then, having been removed by means of a shuttle and so forth, the manifestation of the cloth is revealed. || 20½ ||
Thus, the production of an entity such as a cloth is understood in this way:

it is the manifestation of that [cloth], which exists in the form of a potentiality based upon the shuttle, the threads, the loom, and so forth; for [this manifestation occurs] by means of the form residing in the threads, which was obstructing the form of the cloth.
Immediately after the collection of causal factors such as the shuttle and so forth has departed, the manifestation of the cloth is revealed;

it is not the case that the cloth arises from the threads as something already existent, like another cloth currently being perceived. Furthermore, regarding manifestation itself—whether it is an effect previously non-existent or merely something to be made manifest—this constitutes the refutation of the conceptual constructions of the bad logicians.

It has not been written here for fear of excessive prolixity. Indeed, such speculations as whether manifestation—being of the nature of individualization—is itself manifested or not, are utterly remote from the case, just like light. For just as light, by virtue of its nature as light, is not to be illuminated by another light, so too [manifestation] is not [to be manifested] because its very nature is manifestation.
It does not depend on another manifestation. || 20½ ||
The *Dīpikā* states the objection regarding the sūtra beginning with "tadvyaktiḥ" (the manifestation of that): "If this is so, then... and so forth.
The intended meaning is as follows: if jars and other such objects already exist within clay and the like, just as they do within the interior of a house; [then what is the need for production?]

[Objects] are manifested by means of lamps and the like, through the activities of potters and others. What is this distinction: that "the lamp manifests the jar, whereas the potter produces it"? To resolve this, he explains the sūtra beginning with "That which... and so forth. This is what is meant: manifestation is indeed of two kinds; one...

The removal of that which obstructs the cognition of a real object—namely, the cause of non-cognition characterized by its connection to the object—is the means by which that obstruction is bound [and thus removed]. For example, the removal of darkness from a jar hidden by it is its manifestation (*abhivyakti*). But another [kind of manifestation]...

The removal of the obstruction to a form by means of an obstructing cause is, for example, like the removal of the previous form from clay and other materials when the form of a jar and so forth is obstructed;
this very term "origination" (utpatti) refers specifically to the manifestation of the nature of being a jar, just as [the term] refers to a specific type of Brahmin.

"By way of metaphorical designation (upacāra) such as 'ear' and so forth. [The author] says: "Manifestation (abhivyakti) also," and so on. Now, an objection: according to the theory that the effect pre-exists (satkāryavāda), since manifestation is also existent—just like any other entity—it follows that the operation of causal factors (kāraka-vyāpāra) is purposeless. True.

If manifestation were held to be existent in the same way as a jar or similar objects, then it would indeed be so; however, [in our view], that manifestation is made to appear by the operations of causal factors even though it was previously non-existent.

What is illogical here? Is it not the case that if manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is also non-existent and is produced by the potter, then what wrong has the jar done that it is not likewise produced? That is not so; for this [objection] is equal for both of us. Nevertheless, in the manifestation of a jar hidden in darkness, the manifestation is non-existent, whereas the jar itself is indeed existent.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: In this regard, it can be argued that just as manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is produced, so too is the jar (*ghaṭa*) produced. And just like that [manifestation], the same logical consequences (*prasaṅga*)—such as "manifestation exists" and so forth—apply equally; therefore, neither party may be held accountable for one [of these positions]. As it has been said:
"Where a fault applies to both sides, or where the rebuttal is equal, one [side] should not be singled out."

"One should question [the opponent] regarding the determination of such a meaning. However, the author of the *Vṛtti*, with the intention that there is no fault in either position, says: "In order to avoid false conceptualization (*kuvikalpa*). If this were so, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), starting from the point that manifestation (*abhivyakti*) itself must also be manifested because it is something to be manifested. Therefore, he says: "Because its nature is manifestation (*vyaktisvabhāvatvāt*)."

Furthermore, since it is admitted that manifestation occurs when the auxiliary conditions for that manifestation are present— due to its having the nature of being manifested— there is no fault whatsoever in its existence.
Therefore, within Māyā, which is of the nature of a cause, there exist [effects] in the form of potencies.
The conclusion of the tasks is established. || 20½ ||
Commentary: Thus, he states what is established regarding the subject at hand:
"Just as [the existence] of that which is hidden by a mat and so forth..."
Just as a cloth and the like are manifested through the removal of that [obscuration],
so too manifestation is not produced for what is non-existent, such as a thread from a knot. || 21½ ||

Just as when an object such as a cloth, which is delimited by a mat or similar covering, its manifestation is not produced by removing that particular covering— since it was not previously non-existent— but rather the cloth, already existing, is merely manifested; so too, at the time of dissolution, the effects beginning with *kalā*, which have merged into the nature of power (*śakti*), [manifest] at the break of day.
Because it is knotted, it is manifested through the operation of Ananteśa; thus, the supreme cause called Māyā is established.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Examination of the Characteristics of Māyā, in the *Mṛgendravṛtti* composed by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, son of Bhaṭṭa Vidyākaṇṭha.
The *Dīpikā*.
Thus he says, "It will be explained in this way," beginning with the words "tad evam" (in this manner).
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Examination of the Characteristics of Māyā, in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā* composed by Aghoraśivācārya.

Now begins the tenth chapter, concerning the effects such as the *kalās*. Commentary: Having established the composition [of this work] through both reasoning and scripture, [the author now discusses] that which constitutes its effect.

He states another section which is supplementary to that [previous one] in order to describe *kalā* and the rest. For this [section], the same fivefold relationship (*sambandhapañcaka*) as previously mentioned should be understood. [The topics are: *granthi*, *janya*, *kalā*, *kāla*...
Knowledge, passion, man, mother;
virtue, intellect, pride, mind, senses, elements—these are the sequence. (1)

From the principle of *māyā*, there first occurs the manifestation of the two principles designated as *kalā* and *niyati*; of *kāla*, which is expressed by the word "man" (*nṛ*); and of the specific principle that is the cause of the masculine suffix for the "person" (*puruṣa*).
From the principle of *kalā*, however, there is the manifestation of *vidyā*, *rāga*, and the unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is called *prakṛti* by the word "mother" (*mātṛ*).

From that [the Unmanifest] come the *guṇas*; from them, the intellect (*buddhi*); from that, the ego (*ahaṅkāra*). From the *taijasa* ego arise the organs of perception and the mind (*manas*). From the *vaikārika* ego arise the organs of action. From that known as *bhūtādi*, the subtle elements (*tanmātras*)—which were indicated by the word "mātrā" and so forth—arise; and from those subtle elements arise the gross elements (*bhūtas*).
Through this sequence, it manifests that which is to be manifested by virtue of being composed as this very text. || 1 ||

The *Dīpikā* connects the section beginning with "arising from the knot" (*granthijanyam*) with the following: "by means of reasoning and scripture" (*yuktyāgamābhyām*), etc., and "of this [knot]" (*asya ca*), etc. The connection of this chapter (*paṭala*) is stated at the end of the preceding chapter: "likewise, [the emergence] of the *kalās* and so forth from the knot."

It has been indicated. Even that which consists of sentences—such as the statements "the activity is the effect of the Māyā of karma" and so forth—is [included] precisely because it is an effect of Māyā. Other relationships, however, are those mentioned in the preceding chapter. In that context, by the statement beginning with "born from the knot," [it is shown] how Kalā and the others arise directly and indirectly from the principle of Māyā.
It is asserted that the emergence of the impurity of masculinity (*puṃstvamala*) occurs within the principle called *puruṣatattva*, which is one of the thirty principles;
thus he says, "from the *māyātattva*," and so forth. He states that by the word *kalā* here, according to the method of the *tantra*, both *kalā* and *niyati* are included:
"of those denoted by the term *kalā*," and so forth. And of the *puruṣa*...

He states that the form of the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), consisting of the arts (*kalā*) and so forth, is "form" (*rūpa*). With the words "by the word *nṛ*" and so on, he says—following the previous [explanation] and from the perspective of the doctrine of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*)—that "arising" (*janana*) is of the nature of manifestation (*abhivyakti*).
He then says: "Because this is woven together, it is to be manifested," and so forth. || 1 ||
The commentary: That which directly ordains [the means] for the sake of achieving the perfection of the body from another state;
How and for what reason it connects—such a thing is now being explained. || 2 ||

Lord Ananteśanātha, who presides over the impure path (aśuddhādhvan), manifests the effects beginning with *kalā* directly and without mediation for the sake of fashioning bodies and so forth for individual souls (*ātman*), because he is the one who binds them; and he likewise manifests *vidyā*, *rāga*, and the rest from other locations and positions beyond *kalā*.

Therefore, for what reason and in whatever manner one joins the manifested object—that is, how one applies it toward the accomplishment of the body and so forth—that very method is now being explained. (2)

The *Dīpikā* states that the word "agent" (*kartṛ*) must be supplied as an ellipsis by means of the sūtra beginning with "vidhatta. It further notes that what was stated in the *Kiraṇa*— namely, "in the impure path [Śiva is the agent]"— implies that Śiva is the agent in the pure path.
"Ananta is declared to be the Lord in the dark [aspect]. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the construction of the body and so forth," the meaning is:

for the purpose of establishing the subtle body (sūkṣmadeha), which consists of the thirty principles (tattvas) beginning with the effect and the cause; however, it should not be explained as being for the purpose of establishing bodies born of the worlds (bhuvana). For those [bodies] are treated in the section on the paths (adhvan-prakaraṇa).

Because it will be stated [later]. As he will say: "This body of this living being is *ātivāhika* (conducive to transport), due to a portion of the transformation within the womb of the dense forest of consciousness through contact with consciousness. This much alone is not sufficient;
therefore, for the sake of the prosperity of the objective world which is the foundational body, I shall describe the series of *bhuvana-tattvas*."

Regarding the phrase "for this reason" (*yasmāt*): the sense is that not only is scripture cited, but reasoning (*yukti*) is also stated for the manifestation of these principles (*tattva*). It should not, however, be explained as "from which material cause" (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), because that has already been expressed by the words "that which is directly [perceived]" and "from another term. || 2 ||
1. The final verse in the section on the faculties (indriya-prakaraṇa). Commentary:
The power of agency of the atom is eternal.
And it is all-pervasive like the power of the Lord;
yet, being shrouded by darkness, it does not shine upon objects when it is without favor.
Hara, having agitated Māyā, creates that principle called Kalā, which is luminous and its benefactor.
For that is indeed the supreme factor for engagement. || 4 ||

Although the agentive power (*kartṛśakti*) of the atomic self (*aṇu*), like that of Śiva and Śakti, is eternal and all-pervasive— since scripture declares it to be of such a nature even in liberation— nevertheless, because it is veiled by beginningless impurity (*anādimala*), it does not manifest without assistance regarding the objects to be accomplished. The principle called *kalā* removes [that veil], acting as its benefactor and enabler.

Hara, that is Ananteśa, [acts] "for the sake of the enjoyment of experiences" by those individual souls (*aṇu*) situated below; having agitated *māyā* and made it ready for procreation, he "creates," which means he manifests. For it is from that very principle called *kalā*, the supreme limb of activity, that the capacity for the soul's nature as an agent is established.

Because it is active; for it would not be possible for this [atom] to proceed without its status as an agent being stimulated by that [activity]. And its luminosity is due to its being the cause of illumination in one part of the atom by means of the removal of adventitious impurities. || 4 ||
The *Dīpikā*:

In that regard, first, in order to establish the principle (*tattva*) of *kalā*, he explains the two sūtras beginning with "the power of agency" (*kartṛśakti*). [He says] "of the atom" (*aṇoḥ*), etc. Now, one might object: even though the power of the person (*puṃśakti*) is obstructed by the impurity of karma (*karmamala*),...

At the conclusion of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), [the soul] will attain awakening through the power of Śiva (*śivaśakti*). Why, then, is there a principle called *kalā*? To this he says: "It is its animator," and so forth. For power (*śakti*) bestows experience only by presiding over another principle (*tattva*);

it does not do so directly. If it were direct, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other faculties would never arise. Therefore, this is the meaning:

Since the *mala* is established, the individual soul (*puruṣa*) does not experience pleasure or pain because it is veiled, as in the state of the *pralayakevalin*; therefore, there must necessarily be something that removes that veil.
Thus, the reality of *kalā* is established. [The phrase] "having agitated *māyā*" and so forth means "by its own heat."
Just as the swelling of a seed that has been manifested occurs, so too, through the conjunction of *māyā*, karma, and its fruition (*vipāka*), *kalā* arises.
And just as a sprout is produced from the conjunction of rice, husks, and other factors,
so too does the insentient *kalā* originate from the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, caused by *māyā*, the *puruṣa*, and karma.
The commentary says this very thing:
"by that [means] which is like a lamp."
Then,
for the atom whose consciousness has been awakened, it illuminates a single portion by tearing asunder the dense darkness. (5)

This very Maheśvara mentioned previously, at that time when Māyā is about to bring forth its products, [acts] upon the Self whose power of consciousness is extremely obscured by that principle called *kalā*, which is of the nature of light (*taijasa*) and,
because it provides a slight degree of illumination, is like a lamp.
Having pierced through the dense darkness, it reveals a single portion; that is to say, it strengthens the agency that was previously obscured by impurity. || 5 ||
1. At that time, there is a variant reading: *svacchaciter aṇoḥ*.
[The] *Dīpikā* [explains]: "the agency delimited by impurity (*mala*). Now, one might object: "By the destruction of impurity, does not knowledge (*jñatva*) also [arise]?"

It shines forth. True; however, even though that nature of consciousness (*jñatva*) has its own form manifested, it does not shine forth clearly without the instrument called *vidyā*, which will be described later. Thus, there is no contradiction. || 5 ||

Commentary: In the sūtra of enumeration, *niyati* (restriction) is also included by means of the word *kalā* for the sake of brevity. And in order to state that both *kalā* and *niyati* are designated by the term *kalā* according to their literal meaning (*anvartha*), he says:
The verbal root *kala* is that which [is used] in the senses of counting and impelling;
impelling is the act of driving forth.
Performing that function, she is a digit of darkness.

The root *kala* is one verbal root whose function is the sense of "reckoning" (*saṃkhyāna*); another root, *kala*, has the function of the sense of "casting away" (*protsāraṇa*). In this context, the primary form of the root *kala*—which performs the casting away, that is, the removal, of a portion of darkness or impurity—is the one whose function is "casting away. The second [root], however, is...

It functions for the purpose of enumeration through its limited extent of calculation and so forth; and because it is regulated by *niyati* (the principle of necessity), it is synonymous with the term *kalā*.
[The phrase] "is of the nature of *prakṛti*" is to be supplied as the remainder.
Commentary: Now, in order to declare that both the Self and the *kalā* possess the status of the agent (*kartṛ-kāraka*), he says:
"O Brahmin, these two..."
Existing as one and indistinguishable from [the self],
they have taken away the agency of the living being in the performance of the act of enjoyment.

The teachers have taught that this agent-factor called *kalā*—in the manner previously described by the phrase "when the procedure for the act of enjoyment is to be accomplished for that subtle individual (*aṇu*) who has not yet attained enjoyment"—is the very essence of the self.
Thus, the self is said to be the agent by virtue of being the enjoyer. Of that [self]...

Because it strengthens the power of the agent (*kartṛśakti*), the causal factor (*kāraka*) is the *kalā* which acts as the agent; for it will be stated by the words "the instigator" (*prayoktrī*) and so forth, down to "the earth," that she alone is the instigator. Anticipating the question of how these two [the *kalā* and the *niyati*] exist, he says:

"Having become one, as if not different" means having become unified such that their distinction is no longer perceived. And it has been said by the venerable Bṛhaspati: "Due to extreme intimacy, the consciousness of a living being appears as if it were non-dual.
By addressing him as "O Vipra," the speaker makes the listener, the sage, attentive. (7)

*Dīpikā*: Regarding the passage beginning with "kalā" and so forth—[the objection]: since *kalā* is insentient (*acetana*) and agency (*kartṛtva*) is a property of sentient beings (*cetana*), how can it function as the causal factor of the agent (*kartṛkārakatva*)?
