To this, he says "then" (*tarhi*) and so forth. [The term] *kāraka* means an instigator (*prayojaka*); [the state of being] an instigator is...
And because it occurs through the presiding power of its capacity for concealment, there is no contradiction. || 7 ||
Commentary: In order to state the function of the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*), he says:
"Thus, [it possesses] the manifest power of action..."
Desiring to see that which is within the range of vision,
yet unable to see it himself, he resorts to a request for favor.
For that purpose, the Lord, having agitated Kalā alone which is capable of producing [the world],
created the principle known as Vidyā.
The instrument of the Supreme Self is the body. || 9 ||

He whose power of action (*kriyāśakti*) has been manifested in the manner described is of such a nature that, desiring to see the object reflected within the sphere of the intellect (*buddhi*), he resorts to the requirement for the favor of vision— that is, of knowledge (*jñāna*). He depends upon the favor of the power of knowledge.
The intended meaning is as follows: the statement "being unable to see for himself" is presented as a reason by way of a qualification;

the sense is that because he is incapable of understanding by himself, Ananteśa, for that purpose, having agitated *kalā*—which is capable of manifesting the *tattvas*—and having turned it toward the generation of the born, [bestows it] upon himself.

He created the supreme, most excellent instrument known as *vidyā*. Its supremacy is due to its being a direct benefactor to that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Because it provides the application of the internal and external organs to the power of knowledge sharpened by it, they [the other organs] are subordinate. || 9 ||
The *Dīpikā* introduces the two sūtras beginning with "evam" (thus) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the *vidyā-tattva*" and so forth, it explains this as follows:
"by what has been stated," and so forth. "The power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is manifested" means that it has been established. Now, in this awakening...
The instruments (karaṇas) are indeed the intellect (buddhi) and so forth, as observed in the general and specific scriptures.
Therefore, from where is this "knowledge" (vidyā), distinct from them, established? To this he says: "Supreme," "excellent," and so on.
This is the intended meaning: [just as one travels] by means of a chariot, a path, and a lamp...
Just as in the case of [the verb] "he goes" (*yāti*) and so forth, here too, even though the fruit is accomplished by multiple instruments, knowledge alone is the supreme instrument;
for it is by that alone that one knows the object of enjoyment. || 9 ||
The commentary says: namely, by that nature of luminosity.
By means of the manifestation of its power of knowledge,
it perceives the supreme object, which is to be accomplished by all the causal factors.

Because it is the illuminator by virtue of that reality called *vidyā*, and because it manifests the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), [the object] is that which is to be accomplished by all the sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*) and the organs of action (*karmendriya*) according to their respective functions; it is the supreme, known as the "knowable" (*jñeya*), which is other than the object consisting of the agent—that is, other than the object consisting of an effect. Or, "supreme" (*param*) means that which is immediate.
The principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*) perceives—that is, knows—the object as being in close proximity due to its being reflected as an external object.

Indeed, by means of the instrument called *vidyā*, the intellect is apprehended in the form of an object of enjoyment, with external objects such as garlands and sandalwood paste reflected within it. As Kheṭakanandana has said: "The intellect takes the form of the object, consisting of pleasure and so forth."

In brief, they are objects of enjoyment. Likewise, even if the Great One (Mahat) is of the nature of light like the sun, nevertheless, because it is an object (karma), it is capable of making itself known only in dependence upon other instruments (karaṇas). Thus [ends verse 10].
1. The thirteenth verse in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*.
2. The immediately following verse in that same work. *Dīpikā*.
He explains the Sūtra beginning with "by that" (*tena*) as "by that which is called knowledge" (*vidyā*) and so forth.

Now, it was stated that one experiences enjoyments through the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties alone; that is incorrect, and thus he says "by that which manifests the power of cognition" (*jñāna-śakty-abhivyañjake*) and so forth, [referring] to the intellect’s perception of sense objects and those [faculties].

The meaning is that because it deviates when there is the cognition of an object through the intellect (*buddhi*), it is not the immediate cause; this is the point. For this very reason, he says "or else" (*yadvā*) and so forth.

This is the sense: that by which even the intellect—which is differentiated by the distinctions of determination (*adhyavasāya*), memory (*smṛti*), intuition (*pratibhā*), and conceptual cognition (*pratyaya*)—is itself known, that is *vidyā* (knowledge), and that is the supreme instrument (*karaṇa*); from that [instrument], the [intellect] is produced as its material cause (*prakṛti*).
Likewise, the intellect (*buddhi*) is not capable of making its own self— which has become the object (*grāhya*)— the instrument (*karaṇa*),

because as an object it is external. Furthermore, the group of sense organs (*buddhīndriya-vṛnda*), presided over by the mind (*citta*), presents the object of enjoyment (*bhogya vastu*) to knowledge (*vidyā*) as its domain.
And the Puruṣa perceives that which has been determined by the intellect (*buddhi*) through a process of reflection preceded by the activity of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).

As they say: "The Puruṣa is conscious of the object as it has been determined by the intellect. Therefore, the utility of the intellect and the other [faculties] lies in their capacity to present the object to be accomplished in its immediate proximity; but not...

By virtue of being the generator of consciousness. In that regard, *vidyā* (knowledge) is that by which one discriminates the object established therein through the various functions of the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and the senses; this is the accomplishment of knowledge (*vidyāsiddhi*).
And how knowledge serves as the instrumental cause [of liberation], he will establish in detail, preceded by a question, in the subsequent section.
"By the statement beginning with 'the existence of another manifestor' and so forth. || 10 ||
In order to reveal the true nature of passion (*rāga*), he says:
"The power of consciousness manifested as that [passion],
though its object is perceived, remains unsatiated."
That [seed] does not produce passion;
therefore, the Lord created it from that very [source]. || 11 ||

Because his power of knowledge has been manifested by that reality known as *vidyā*, the atom (*aṇu*), even when the object is perceived and thus thirsty—meaning its desire has not yet arisen—does not go, that is, it does not proceed to fetch objects of enjoyment.
Therefore, [the soul possesses] passion (*rāga*) which generates that desire; from that very [passion].
Ananteśanātha, whose nature is to manifest from the principle of Kalā, brought [the universe] forth. || 11 ||
The Lamp.

He explains the sūtra beginning with "tadabhivyaktā" (manifested by that) with the words "tena" (by that), etc. "Because of having the power of knowledge manifested" means because of having the power of knowledge established. "Precisely from that, the principle of *kalā*" refers to what was stated in the *Raurava*:
"From the principle of *kalā*, the two principles of *rāga* and *vidyā* came into being, as well as the unmanifest (*avyakta*)."

Therefore, this is the meaning: here, indeed, in every state, that which is observed as the desire for objects of enjoyment is not an inherent nature like [the soul's] consciousness (*jñatva*) or agency (*kartṛtva*), because it is not seen in the state of liberation.

Nor is it [inherent] through the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties, since those are established solely by their own effects; [if they were the cause], they would have to be the cause of some other effect.

And because there is a lack of valid evidence [for that]. Therefore, by whatever means it is logically established that one "possesses passion" (*sarāga*), the reality of passion (*rāgatattva*) is proven. If this is so, then let passion—which has the nature of deluding—exist within *māyā* as previously stated; what is the need for anything else? To this it is replied:
*Māyā* does not possess the quality of deluding directly.

There is no fault, as it occurs precisely through the medium of its effects (*kārya*). Furthermore, that [passion] is the colorer (*rañjaka*) only of that which is impure, and not of the pure ones such as the *Vidyeśvaras* and others. Now, you might object: "Like the Sāṃkhyas, you maintain that passion and the rest consist merely of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and thus they are attributes of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*), since—unlike the Naiyāyikas and others—you do not admit a separate latent impression belonging to a person (*puruṣa-vāsanā*)."

Since that [independent passion] also lacks a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), its capacity to color [the mind] must exist only in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*); thus, there is no establishment of a passion distinct from that [impression]. It is true that we shall explain that passion exists in the intellect (*buddhi*) in the very nature of a latent impression, like virtue (*dharma*) and other qualities; however, because it is a property of the intellect, it is just like any other cognition characterized by a modification (*vṛtti*) of that [intellect].
Through the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and by virtue of maturation, it becomes unified with the gross [mind] which consists of objective cognitions (*pratyaya*);

thus, it serves for the benefit of the *puruṣa*. Consequently, attachment (*rāga*), consisting of objective cognition, augmented by the effect of the attachment residing in the subject (*grāhaka*), is the cause of experience (*bhoga*). It is not [the cause] alone, because that would entail the impossibility of the existence of those free from attachment (*vītarāga*).

Nor is it of the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); for if the intellect were always joined with infinite latent impressions, it would follow that a person would simultaneously experience an infinite variety of contradictory cognitions. Thus, the existence of attachment as a distinct entity is established. [Objection: But surely karma itself will be the coloring agent. [Reply: That is not so, because its function is exhausted solely in the production of its fruit.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating numerous additional principles (*tattva*). Moreover, he will establish in the subsequent section that this passion residing in the subject (*grāhaka*) is not secondary, beginning with the words "passion is not figurative" (*rāgo na gauṇaḥ*). And these principles are [the categories] beginning with *kalā*, *vidyā*, and *rāga*.

It is stated in the *Mataṅga* and other scriptures that [these principles] exist even within the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) as the agents in the palaces of the King [of Consciousness], such as Mahāmāyā, Puruṣa, Viveka, Śiva, and so forth. And he will state precisely in the section on the paths (*adhvaprakaraṇa*):
"O Brahmin, in this way the principles (*tattva*), dispositions (*bhāva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and forms (*vapus*) [belong] to both the pure and impure paths."
These have been explained in brief. || 11 ||
1. "is produced" is the ellipsis.
2. "but rather" is the ellipsis.
3. "because of the impossibility of the apprehended object" is a variant reading.
4. There is a variant reading, *vyāpārāya*.
He, being delighted by that [work], desired even a sullied object of enjoyment (*bhogya*).
Even while eating, he does not take [it] up, nor does he attain detachment. || 12 ||

Colored by that passion and having generated attachment, he—desiring even this illusory object of enjoyment, though it be soiled—brings it forth. And while enjoying it in this manner, he does not become dispassionate;
for [the root] *spr̥h* belongs to the *cur*-class (the tenth class) and thus lacks the *aṇi*-affix. Therefore, "desiring" (*spṛhan*) is not faulty. || 12 ||
The commentary: Having thus engaged with the instruments for the purpose of defining the reality of time, he says:
"Thus engaged by the instruments..."
Having ascended to his duties along with the inhabitants of the celestial realms,
he enjoys the pleasures appropriate to the time in the lands of enjoyment.

In this manner, having been thus addressed, the person (puruṣa), possessing an agency sharpened by *kalā*, becomes active and intent upon enjoyment; he experiences enjoyments in the form of pleasure, pain, and so forth, in various spheres of experience that follow him in due course. As to with what he experiences them, the author says: "with the worlds," meaning together with bodies born of the worlds.

By means of the instruments—the organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), the organs of action (*karmendriya*), and the threefold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—there is a dependence upon the organs of action and the organs of cognition because of the impurity of the powers of action and knowledge. To the question "By what kind of instruments?", he says: "mounted upon their effects" (*kāryārūḍhaiḥ*). Because they are not all-pervading (*avibhu*), these [powers] lack a support.

Because of the impossibility of [the self] performing actions [itself], it is said that the existing [faculties], which have as their substratum the effects consisting of the gross elements and the subtle elements, bring about this effect through the ten types of instruments by entering into them; for they produce movement. And it has been stated by Kheṭakanandana: "This effect, having entered into the instruments, is made to move;
however, because they lack omnipresence, the instruments exert themselves by presiding over the effect. (13)
1. *Tattvasaṃgraha*, verse 4. *Dīpikā*:
He introduces the sūtra beginning with "thus engaged" (*iti pravṛttaḥ*), etc., [with the words] "the reality of time," etc., concerning that which has arisen from *māyā*.

"How is the determination of the true nature of time established here? To this he says, "In this manner," and so forth. The meaning is as follows: although the Self is indeed not limited by time, it is only through the experience of enjoyment produced by the threefold sheath of passion and the rest previously mentioned that it is fashioned by time. Therefore, time pervades all the effects of Māyā right here.

By virtue of its association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is stated to be that which is to be purified during initiation, just as [the soul] is situated above the unmanifest (*avyakta*) for the individual person (*puruṣa*).
This same principle should also be understood to apply to necessity (*niyati*). As he will state in the section on the paths (*adhvan*):
"The restrainer in the person, in necessity, and in time is the support of all the senses, all the bodies, and all the internal organs."
"He possesses the power of differentiation. Thus, in the venerable *Svāyaṃbhuva* and other scriptures, his purification is stated at the very place of origin.
What need is there for that here? For no other [scripture] is heard here. Nor is a difference in ritual action the cause of a contradiction between tantras;
rather, it is the difference in that [subject matter] itself. As it has been said: "Since a division of tantras is traditionally recorded according to the distinctions of ritual action and so forth."

Therefore, in that regard, one must act exactly as it has been stated, and not according to another system. Within the principle of the Puruṣa, time is conceived only as presided over by the power (śakti) of Īśvara; for it has already been declared that the engagement in activity belongs only to the insentient when it is presided over by the sentient. || 13 ||
1. The meaning is "of the division of the tantra" itself. [Commentary:
Now, what is this so-called "time," from where has it arisen, and what does it do? To this, it is said:
The object of cognitions such as "a moment" (truṭi) is time, which arises from Māyā;
it is that which measures [all things] until their emergence.
[He saw] the bound soul, determined by destiny. || 14 ||

Time is that which is the cause—the objective basis—for cognitions such as the moments of *truṭi*, *lava*, *nimeṣa*, and *muhūrta*. It is from this [time] that the continuous perception arises, such as "he remains for a *muhūrta*" or "he wanders for a *prahara*. This [time] has arisen from Māyā, conceiving the Self as being joined with the impurity (*mala*) of the state of a bound soul (*paśu*).

It is called *kāla* (time). As they say: "By means of activities resembling the forceful rotation of a water-wheel, that which impels (*kalayan*) is therefore designated by the name *kāla*. He explains what kind of *paśu* (bound soul) it impels:
"the *paśu* determined by *niyati* (destiny) until its emergence. This refers to the emergence from *niyati*.

Manifestation occurs from its own cause. From that point until the time of dissolution, this [Prakṛti] governs the bound soul (paśu) in the experience of pleasure and pain produced by karma. And this is not the function of Time (kāla), because its purpose is fulfilled merely through the act of measuring (kalana). || 14 ||
The *Dīpikā* connects the sūtra beginning with "truṭyādi" to the passage starting with "atha ko'sau. This is the intended meaning:
if this time which has been described by you is held to be all-pervading and eternal, as it is by the Naiyāyikas and others;

As for what they say: "They describe time as that which is eternal, one, all-pervading substance, the measure of things possessing action, and existing apart from activity"—that is incorrect. Because [the scripture] states, "It impels [the soul] immediately after the material cause, the principle of Māyā, which is produced from the knot and consists of *kalā* and *kāla*," that [definition of time] is untenable.

Because it is eternal and all-pervasive, and because it persists as far as the Śiva-tattva extends; furthermore, from the perspective of the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra), those who know time understand that time consists essentially of specific movements—such as the motion of the sun, planets, and stars—which they recognize as distinct according to their various cycles. Thus it is said: "Others, however, know time as consisting of specific actions, such as the movement of the sun, planets, and stars, which is differentiated by its various revolutions."

If it were thus, it would be formless and non-omnipresent, because it is a specific kind of action, like cooking and so forth. (Therefore, according to others, "form" is said to be a substance possessing dimension that is omnipresent. Consequently, because of its pervasiveness, its status as the impeller of all things below the principle of Māyā is again untenable. Now, from the perspective of the Vedāntins and the Buddhists:
Time is merely a construction of conventional usage; it is not said to be ultimately real. As some have stated:

"They declare that [time] is preceded by the synthesis of the intellect; or rather, the power inherent in cognition exists as something external yet unreal. Without relying upon the nature of time, conventional usage is impossible."
Nevertheless, the objection raised in the prima facie argument—that [the Lord] must be all-pervasive because [His existence] has been stated to extend as far as empirical usage—remains.
Furthermore, the reason for this is that, being of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is unreal, like a double moon; thus, His status as a prompter (*preraka*) is indeed untenable.
Now, the Sāṃkhyas claim that this [prompting] consists of the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), as they say: "Transformation..."

"Separation exists eternally according to the sequence of established states; it is perceived as the form of time, consisting of the past, future, and present. Even then, time is unstable, because it is impossible for transformation to exist as a mere action; thus, [this pertains] to the path below the principle of Māyā.

The impossibility of [the soul] being an impeller is precisely the point. Furthermore, because it is of the nature of non-cessation and is insentient, it is not possible for it to impel a *pudgala* as a sattva impels the intellect, the self, or God. Moreover, even by reasoning, time is understood to exist above the principle of *māyā*; yet, even there, [it cannot be an impeller] due to its connection with creation and dissolution.

"Because it is not so established. Furthermore, if passion (*rāga*) and the other [afflictions] were present, this would occur even during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). Otherwise, such a rule would be untenable. Now, if one objects that during the dissolution, because *māyā-tattva* exists entirely below [the level of *kalā*], it is impossible for *kāla* (Time) to act as an impeller, then setting all of this aside in order to resolve that difficulty:

He explains the sūtra beginning with *truṭi* and so forth. Regarding the word *kalayan*: it means "projecting" by means of the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of cognitions such as "slow" or "quick. As they have said: "Time is divided by the intellect. Furthermore, the intention here is this: first of all, time as it is accepted by the Sāṃkhyas is not tenable.
For, from the states of the body—such as childhood, youth, and so forth—which exists as the locus of the enjoyer’s experience, time is inferred as distinct from transformation (*pariṇati*).
As they say: "Until sixteen one is a child; thereafter one is considered young; until seventy..."

Regarding the term "old": for instance, if old age were caused solely by transformation (*pariṇati*), then because that [transformation] would be uniform everywhere and at all times, it could not serve as the cause for a specific state of old age. However, if it is caused by a specific transformation, one must explain from where this specific quality arises in it. For existence or non-existence that is eternal cannot be without a cause; as it has been stated: "Because [it would follow] that there is no cause," nor indeed...

[It does not arise] from its own continuum alone, because that [continuum] exists at all times. Nor does it arise from food, drink, cold, heat, or the like, because those too exist at all times without distinction. Nor does it arise from karma through a sequence of states, because [karma] would then have to exist eternally and invariably. Rather, its cause is that which produces the distinctions—such as birth, lifespan, and experience—just as karma is the cause of those specific factors.

"That is time. This has been stated: "That power called 'duration' (cirā), which is opposed to other powers, obstructs [other actions] and itself arises as something opposed. Thus, the fact that cognitions such as "slow" and "quick" serve as the inferential marks for the establishment of time applies to those things situated as prior and posterior.

In the case of a youth and an elder, even when they are spatially distant from one another, there arises the cognition of "remoteness" (paratva) in the youth and the cognition of "nearness" (aparatva) in the elder, despite the absence of spatial remoteness and nearness. This occurs because of the intention to convey the perception of a specific temporal distinction.
Furthermore, it is not logical that these two cognitions should arise from that same cause; therefore, that which is the cause of remoteness and nearness is Time.

Thus, this [time] is not of the nature of the transformation of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), nor is it of the nature of the movement of the sun and so forth; for, just like those, it cannot be logically established. This is the refutation of time as accepted by the Sāṃkhya, the astronomers, and the Vedāntins. Let it then be that time is exactly as accepted by the Naiyāyikas and others—distinct from action. True; however, it is not eternal.

Or, [time] is manifold because it is diverse in its various forms and because it is insentient. For if time were of a single nature, all things would always exist at one and the same time. Yet we observe that some entities are present, some are past, and some are yet to come. Therefore, time is manifold. As they say:

"Like darkness and light, its three paths are established; and within them, the states of entities arise sequentially. Now, the Naiyāyikas and others argue that because the action which serves as its limiting adjunct (upādhi) possesses forms such as the past and so forth, the distinction between the past and other times for that [time] is not ultimately real. That is incorrect.
Because that [action] lacks the existence or non-existence of pastness and so forth, its distinction as past and so on arises precisely from its connection with the times of the past and so on.

Otherwise, it would itself be time; thus, how could there be an establishment of time as something distinct from action? Therefore, since a distinction such as "past" and so on is impossible for the limiting adjunct (upādhi) by itself, it must belong to that which possesses the adjunct.
One must accept that time, like space or the self, possesses multiple forms through its distinctions such as past and so forth;

as it has been said: "For action, though distinct according to the divisions of present and so on, is manifested through the powers of *lava*, *kāṣṭhā*, and so forth, due to its connection with specific times. Therefore, regarding the time mentioned in the Itihāsas and other sources:

Presentness and so forth are accepted. As they say: "This day, which was the future and the past for a thousand yugas, has itself arrived as the present; thus people in the world desist [from their activities], thinking, 'The time has come. Time itself is threefold, like the world consisting of many types of beings situated in the eastern and western directions. Therefore...

Thus, the reality-status of the directions is not established apart from their spatial arrangement; however, the reality-status of time is established even apart from action, because it pervades the determination of all time. Furthermore, on the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan), just like the *kalās* and other categories, time exists indeed in its pure form. [Objection: But since time is impermanent, [how can it exist] until the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*)?
It was stated that there is no possibility of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). That is not so; for in that case, the power of Īśvara alone serves as the regulator.
Thus, everything is faultless. [Objection: If that is so, then let the power of Īśvara itself be time (*kāla*); what is the use of anything else?
As has been concluded by the sage Vyāsa from the words of the Blessed Nārāyaṇa: "I am Time."

Regarding the statement, "He is the one who has increased [the world] and brought about its destruction," we reply: If everything were to be ordained by the power of Īśvara alone, what would be the purpose of the principles (tattvas) such as earth and the rest? Yet, these are indeed observed.
Therefore, apart from his grace, the Lord performs other actions for the bound souls (paśus), such as their maintenance and so forth.

Because it is perceived that [the agent] acts only through the intervention of another category (tattvāntara), this too—being a part of that [category]—acts by depending on time, which consists of impulsion (preraṇātmaka), and not by power alone; thus, time is established.

Having thus described the nature of Time (*kāla*), he speaks of the nature of Necessity (*niyati*) preceded by a doubt, beginning with "of what kind," and so forth. "Manifestation from its own cause" means [manifestation] from that which consists of *māyā*. Furthermore, this Necessity is the regulator of the *sakala* (the embodied soul) alone; it is not [the regulator] of the *vijñānākala* or the *pralayākala*. Nor...

[This is] not due to the actions of *māyā*, because even in their absence, a restriction [of effects] is observed. Nor is it due to *kalā* and the rest, because they are themselves restricted by the power of the cause alone; thus he says: "The bound soul (*paśu*) in those born of karma," and so forth. Time alone restricts the bound soul. To the question, "By what necessity? he replies: "And this is not... and so forth. This is the intended meaning.
For if destiny did not exist, others would experience even the karmas acquired by others;

just as, in the absence of royal regulation, bandits might enjoy the fruits of agriculture and other labors. Consequently, there would be no undertaking at all of the scriptures concerning the performance of action, yet they have been undertaken. Therefore, for whomsoever...

There must exist some reality that acts as the regulator of the fruits and bodies appropriate to a person according to the actions they have performed; and that reality is what is called *niyati* (destiny). || 14 ||

1. Since time is the adjunct (*upādhi*) of all that is produced, the meaning is that [the dimension] belongs to those things possessing action. 2. The meaning is that whatever is expressed by the term "it impels" is what is logically possible therein. 3. There is a variant reading: *anityatvād avyāpakatvāc ca*.
4. "Because it is not all-pervasive" is a variant reading.
5. "Is established" is a variant reading.
6. "In the absence of passion and so forth" is a variant reading.
7. There is a variant reading: "the treatise is not even commenced.
8. "The treatise" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. [End of] the commentary (*vṛtti*).
Here, an objection is raised:
they have declared that experience, together with its means, is dependent upon karma.
Some [hold that] there is a determining karma which exceeds all others. || 15 ||

It has already been stated that the enjoyments and the means for those enjoyments must necessarily depend upon the karma of the enjoyer, because the diversity of enjoyment would otherwise be inexplicable in the absence of such dependence. Furthermore, it is that very [karma] which will serve as the regulator of those enjoyments. Consequently, any other principle postulated and called "Necessity" (*niyati*) is superfluous.

Because it is devoid of purpose, that [karma] becomes predominant. And so it has been said: "By whomsoever, by whatever means, in whatever manner, at whatever time, and whatever [karma]—whether auspicious or inauspicious—is one's own action; from that, by that, in that manner, at that time, as that, for that long, and in that place, it comes to pass under the power of the Ordainer. (15)
Commentary: Here is the resolution:
the purpose of all the principles (tattvas) is experience.
That [bondage] too is bound by karma;
let karma alone be the body and so forth—therefore, everything else is useless. (16)

Let it not be that [the principle of] necessity (niyatitattva) exists. Even those other principles that are the instruments of experience are themselves dependent upon karma; and since they necessarily depend on karma, let karma alone be the instrument of experience, as the others would be ineffective without it. This being the case:
There is the uselessness of everything, including the body, the sense organs, and the objects of the senses. || 16 ||
The *Dīpikā*:
He explains the sūtra beginning with "for the sake of enjoyment" (*bhogārtha*) with the words "let it not be," etc. This is the intended meaning:
because the capacity of karma lies solely in the production of a fruit, it does not [reside] even in the restriction thereof. To explain: it is not...
Karmic latency (*karmavāsanā*) alone establishes the relationship with the restriction of the agent, because it consists of karmic latency,

just like the karmic latencies of agriculture and so forth. Therefore, there must be another regulator, distinct from those respective actions, for the connection between the agent and the fruit of the action.

Because it establishes the relationship between the action, its fruit, and the agent—just like a visible king who regulates the relationship between the action, its fruit, and the agent in agriculture and other such activities. That which is the regulator is *niyati* (destiny); thus, *niyati* is established. Furthermore, its function pertains to the equilibrium of actions (*karmasāmya*).
It has indeed been stated in the section concerning the investigation of karma. || 16 ||
1. "Capacity" (sāmarthya) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. [This is] the commentary (vṛtti).
Now, that which depends upon the body and so forth...
Therefore, let action, which accomplishes the goals of man,
be the regulator, while depending upon necessity (niyati). || 17 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that action (*karman*), depending upon the body and so forth, is capable of accomplishing the human goal, but not by itself? For nothing single is a producer; rather, it is only the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) that produces an effect. To this it is replied: "Therefore, [action] depends upon *niyati*. If that is so, then just as [action] proceeds together with the body, senses, and so forth, which are engaged in their own respective functions...

Karma alone is capable of accomplishing the goals of human endeavor; thus, let it be that which governs [the results] by depending on the principle of necessity (niyati) that brings about its own effects—there is no fault whatsoever in this. || 17 ||
The commentary states: From that very [source], the principle of masculinity (puṃstattva) arose,
which is the basis for the cognition of "male."
The filling [of the body] proceeds from Pradhāna and the rest,
resting upon Rudra in the Bhuvana.

The meaning is that at the time of reabsorption (*saṃhāra*), that which was rested by Anantanātha emerged from that very *māyā-tattva* as the *puruṣa-tattva*. "The basis for the cognition of the *puruṣa*" means it is the cause of the perception of the *puruṣa*. By this [it is distinguished] from the *adhikāri-rudra-aṇus* residing within the womb of *māyā*.

And a distinction from those who dwell in the worlds has been stated, because for them there is no connection with the masculine suffix (*puṃ-pratyaya*). Furthermore, that masculine principle (*puṃstvam*) completes the collection of principles beginning with *pradhāna*, since *pradhāna* together with its effects is desired for the sake of the *puruṣa*. Thus, because study has students as its cause, the students are the teachers.

In such passages as these, the term "filling" (*āpūraka*) is to be understood. Furthermore, on the path of the phenomenal world (*bhauvana-adhvā*), that principle of the Person (*puruṣatattva*) has Rudra as its support. As it is stated in the venerable *Svacchanda-tantra*: "Therefore, learn from me the worlds within the principle of the Person; they are divine, [situated] amidst floods of water," and so forth. It is encapsulated by the *puruṣa* and *rāga* [mantras].
And this principle of Puruṣa is intended as the substratum of the Rudras, as stated in the *Kiraṇatantra*:
"Then Vāmadeva, Bhīma, Ugra, and he known as Bhava; Sarveśāna, Ekavīra, Pracaṇḍa, and the Lord Pumān; Umābhartṛ, Aja, Ananta, Eka, and Ekaśiva."

Established in the essence of passion (rāga-tattva) are these Rudras, fierce and possessed of intense power; in this very state, the Puruṣa is to be known as the protector of the primary grasper (pradhāna-graha). || 18 ||

The *Dīpikā* states: "Because of the necessity of the sequence, immediately following [the discussion of] the category of *paśu*, the designation of the name is given as 'masculinity' (*puṃstvam*) and so forth, since that which was established as eternally pervasive is [here] characterized by its nature as the individual soul (*nṛtatva*). Thus he says: "Dissolution," and so on.

This is what is meant: at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other rites, the one to be purified should be extracted from the *prakṛti-tattva* and from the world of Śrīkaṇṭha—which will be described later—and joined to the *puruṣa-tattva* in order to sever the impurity of the individual soul (*puṃs-mala*).
For the *puruṣa-tattva* is already conjoined with the five *tattvas* beginning with *kalā* and ending with *niyati* during initiation and other such occasions.
It attains the designation of "puruṣatva" (the state of being the individual soul). Therefore, in this state, the application [of the mantras] and so forth must be performed here.
Consequently, that is the reality (*tattva*) of the *sakala* (the embodied soul) alone, and not of the *vijñānākala* or the *pralayākala*. For this very reason, he says:
"And that is *puruṣatva*, etc. This is the meaning: the *aṇu* (individual soul) is augmented by the five principles beginning with *kalā*.

The person (puṃs), being joined with the error (viparyaya) of the non-self—the natural, worldly state characterized by desire for what is attainable within the sphere of primordial nature (prakṛti) and delusion—attains the designation of "personhood. And at that time, his distinction from primordial nature (pradhāna) does not manifest, as the venerable Patañjali said: "In regard to the impermanent, the impure, suffering, and the non-self..."
The notion of permanence, purity, pleasure, and self is ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, that very [ignorance] is joined here [to the soul].

Consequently, the state of being a person (*puṃstva*) with respect to what is actually suffering, non-self, and so forth, is purified through initiation (*dīkṣā*). Furthermore, because it is not a true principle (*tatva*), unlike other principles, it does not abide in its own place; rather, it exists according to the influence of karma.

The *puruṣatattva* indeed moves through every world. If this is so, then since the *puruṣatattva* is all-pervasive as it moves everywhere, it follows that it must be purified within the *pṛthivītattva* alone.

To this [we reply]: because the delusion concerning the sphere of *prakṛti* is gross, [the text] here [speaks of purification] in order to exclude the subtle delusions arising from the spheres of *kalā* and the rest.

Since pervasion has been stated, there is no contradiction. Thus it is said in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "O tiger among sages, that second principle called Puruṣa is pervaded by the three sheaths and gradually affected by Time."

"Embraced by *niyati*, he proceeds toward the state of a person (*pumbhāva*) existing within the Self. Likewise: "In those very enjoyments born thereof, [the soul] is augmented by the five *tattvas*. Since the *puṃstattva* has been described as being unchanging (*apariṇāmin*), there is no division of worlds (*bhuvanavibhāga*) therein; thus he says, "And in the *bhauvana*," and so forth, regarding initiation into the worlds (*bhuvanadīkṣā*).

The sense is that the impurity of that masculinity must be thoroughly purified by means of the presence of Rudra, who is designated as all the sense organs (*sarvendriya*). For this very reason, in order to demonstrate that wherever the worlds (*bhuvana*) are mentioned, it is the Rudras themselves who are to be purified there, the sequence of worlds recited in the *Śrīmatsvatantra* has been declared. Furthermore, he asks: "Where, then, do they reside? and says:

"Encased within *puṃrāga*, and so forth. This should be understood as referring precisely to those [categories] recited in the *Śrīmat-Svatantra* and other [Tantras]. Here, immediately after the primary world (*pradhāna-bhuvana*), each respective world is to be purified, because the world of *rāga* will be described as being above the world of *kāla*. In that regard, there is a distinction based on action (*kriyā*) and so forth.
And because of the acceptance [of the existence] of the worlds. || 18 ||
1. "If the category of *paśu* were established as being eternally pervasive, then there would be no specification of its regulator"—this is a variant reading.
2. "Like one principle from another principle" occurs in both manuscripts. — From the *Puṃstattvapaṭala*, verse 1½.
3. Those two verses. 4. Therein, the fourth verse.
5. The meaning is that it is recited in an independent scripture (*svatantrāgama*).
Then, from the principle of *kalā*, it produced the principle of *pradhāna*,
which is the cause of the seven knots.
That which is the cause of the secondary [nature]. || 19 ||

Thereafter, immediately following the emergence of the principle of Puruṣa from Māyā, the principle of the Unmanifest (Avyakta) arose from the principle of Kalā. To describe its nature, he says: "of the cause of the seven knots. This refers to Pradhāna, which is the source of the seven knots—namely, Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, and the five subtle elements (tanmātras).

The cause of the secondary reality (*gauṇatattva*) is the cause for the emergence of the sources of effects. For instance, the causal efficiencies (*arthakriyā*)— consisting of actions such as those of elephants, men, and horses, or ornaments such as bracelets and earrings— which occur at a later time regarding gold, jewels, and so forth, exist in the form of potentialities (*śakti*).

Thus, from the Unmanifest (avyakta) arises the principle of the Guṇas, which is the cause of the seven knots beginning with the subtle elements (tanmātra), which exist as their respective potencies and produce their own effects. || 19 ||

The *Dīpikā*: Now, in order to establish the principle of *prakṛti*, he explains the aphorism beginning with "tataḥ" (from that). "From that, from *māyā*" and so forth. "Due to the production of the *pums-tattva*" means: due to the direct [production] of the *kārya-kalā-tattva*.

Regarding the phrase "that which is pradhāna," and so forth: that which is the cause of the birth of this world—consisting of the principles from the *guṇas* down to the earth and comprising both the *tattvas* and the worlds—is called *pradhāna*. Now, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is simply the functions of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*.
That is incorrect, because they are multiple and lack consciousness (*acaitanya*).

Since objects such as jars must necessarily have a cause that exists in an undifferentiated state, that which is the cause is the *pradhāna*, which is distinct from *sattva* and the other *guṇas*. For this very reason, those who maintain the eternity of *sattva* are refuted; for even the *pradhāna*...

Because they are established as effects due to their multiplicity and their being restricted to each individual person, it has already been stated previously that there is no supreme liberation for those who have attained those respective levels of reality. And it is said in the venerable *Mataṅga*:
"Those whose state is fixed upon that which is neither higher nor lower than this, they are not liberated."
"O tiger among sages, they fall once again into a downward state. (19)
1. This means "the effect of illusion" (māyākārya).
2. This is the seventh verse in the section on the principle of primordial matter (pradhānatattvapaṭala).
3. "Facing downwards" (adhomukhā) is a variant reading.
Commentary:
Therefore, the material cause of the intellect and the other faculties is the secondary [form of] sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Their functions, such as illumination and the rest, are indeed well known for the most part. (20)

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (from that): from that primary principle (*pradhāna*), it produced a secondary principle (*gauṇaṃ tattvam*) consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, which is the cause for the emergence of the intellect (*buddhi*) accompanied by the mental states (*bhāva-pratyaya*) to be described hereafter; this is the connection with what precedes. And of those [qualities], *sattva* and the others, there are three functions characterized by illumination, activity, and restraint.
The mental modifications are not mentioned here because they are already widely known for their great abundance. || 20 ||

1. "Tat" (that) is the remainder [of the compound]. *Dīpikā*: And thus, it is indeed distinct from the principle of *prakṛti*, which is of the nature of the cause and characterized by non-differentiation.
In order to state that the reality of the qualities (*guṇatattva*) has the form of an effect (*kāryarūpa*), he then explains the sūtra beginning with "from that" (*tataḥ*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "from that" and so on: since the true nature (*sad-vṛtta*) of those qualities is known as manifested within their respective effects, from the intellect (*buddhi*) down to the earth, the reality of the qualities is [established] by means of the effects, starting with the intellect and so forth.

He says it is "specified" by the words "to be mentioned," and so forth. Consequently, the phrase "the cause of the arising of cognition" refers to the direct cause; the meaning is that for other [factors], it is an indirect cause, because the word "and so forth" in the expression "the material cause of cognition and so forth" includes all [of them].

This is also because it was indicated in the immediately following sūtra beginning with "the seven knots" (1.29). And it is said in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "O best of sages, when all [the elements] have become manifest, each respective principle of the qualities (*guṇatattva*) can be clearly described; not otherwise."
The Sāṃkhyas have also stated: "From primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat); from that, the I-maker (ahaṅkāra); from that, the group of sixteen;
from five among those sixteen, the five gross elements.
It is said that there are three [qualities] characterized by illumination, activity, and restraint because of their predominance, though this applies to the others as well.
Because of the possibility of virtuous qualities such as steadfastness, fortitude, and so forth; as it is said in the *Mataṅga*:

"Steadfastness, fortitude, as well as skill, gentleness, lightness, contentment, straightforwardness, purity, perseverance, as well as mindfulness, satisfaction, transcendence, patience, compassion, and generosity—these are always the virtues."
And eagerness— these are declared to be the functions of *sattva*. Cruelty, heroism, great energy, pride, malice, firmness, ruthlessness,
dissension, and hypocrisy— these are to be understood as the functions of *rajas* in this Pārameśvara Tantra.

"Discontent, dullness, dejection, malice, constant heaviness, excessive sleep, intoxication, laziness, suppression, and delusion—these are known as the functions of *tamas*, which manifest differently in all living beings. (20)
1. This means in the immediately preceding sūtra.
2. The sixteenth verse in the Guṇapaṭala.
3. The seventeenth verse in the Guṇapaṭala.
4. Regarding the variant reading *ghṛtir dākṣyam*, the distinction between *dhairya* (steadfastness) and *dhṛti* (fortitude) should be considered.
5. Regarding the variant reading *dambho rajo-guṇāḥ*. [End of] commentary (*vṛtti*).
Although there are three qualities (guṇas), they constitute a single reality because they are inseparable; thus,
each one of them is referred to as "the One."
It is based on the predominance of the function. || 21 ||

Although the qualities (guṇas) are three, they should be understood as a single principle of the qualities (guṇatattva) because they are never dissociated from one another. Now, an objection is raised: "Those states which are sāttvika, those which are rājasa, and those which are tāmasa"—in such passages, the effects of sattva and the other qualities are heard of as distinct. It is not the case that this principle is one simply because of their non-separation; thus he says:

"Each individual scripture," and so forth. Regarding those qualities for which there is an individual scripture—such as "this is Sāttvika," "this is Rājasa," and "this is Tāmasa"—the cause of this is the predominance of their respective functions (*vṛtti*).
An object is called *sāttvika* when its nature consists of a predominance of the function of *sattva*. In the same way, the *rājasa* and *tāmasa* categories are also to be understood. || 21 ||

The *Dīpikā* explains the sūtra beginning with "traya" (the triad), starting with the words "tritve 'pi" (even though there is a triad). As it was stated in that very same [text]: "And because of their equality, since a simultaneous activity of those qualities is not admitted."
O tiger among sages, although these [elements] arise from causes as described in this scripture, they are nevertheless celebrated individually because of their preeminent nature. || 21 ||
1. The meaning is "Matanga indeed.
2. "And mixed" (*vimiśrāśca*) is a variant reading. [End of] the commentary (*vṛtti*).
And thus:
there is no insentient thing whatsoever existing in this world.
That which is not pervaded by the qualities, nor in which there is even a single unmixed quality. || 22 ||

"There is nothing such" means that in this world there is not even a single insentient object that is not pervaded by the *guṇas*, nor is there any place where a single *guṇa*, such as *sattva* and the rest, exists unmixed and uncombined with others.
The intended meaning is that the entire world is endowed with the three *guṇas*—*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—which manifest in states of emergence and submergence and so forth. || 22 ||
1. "That object also does not exist"—this is the logical connection (*anvaya*).

Regarding the phrase "that does not exist" and so forth, he says "in this" (*asmin*) to indicate that the states of being *sāttvika* and so on are not being predicated here of conscious beings. *Dīpikā*: "That does not exist," etc. He states "in this" (*asmin*) to show that the qualities such as *sāttvika* and so forth are not being asserted here with respect to sentient beings.
"Jagati," etc. He states that by the words "yasmin" and so forth, the contact with the *guṇas* of conscious beings endowed with subtle bodies is described; thus he says "yatra ca," etc. (22).
Commentary: Having thus explained the principle of the qualities (*guṇatattva*), he speaks in order to explain the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*):
"The principle of the intellect is manifold from that."
This is the definition of the abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya):
it is that which is to be experienced by the Supreme Self, refined by the objects to be discussed hereafter. (23)

The principles such as *dharma* and so forth, whose characteristics will be described hereafter, as well as their opposites— ignorance, incapacity, and the rest— are the *pratyayas*. These very factors constitute the *liṅga*, the indicator of its existence,
for that supreme *buddhitattva* which is refined and colored by the objects to be described.

The "excellent" (prakṛṣṭa) is that which is immediate and directly accessible to the Self as an object of experience. Although external objects are also objects of experience, they are considered "inferior" (apakṛṣṭa) because they are not proximate to the Self, being merely reflected therein. And it has been stated by the venerable Sadyojyotiḥ: "In brief, the intellect takes the form of the objects [of perception] and consists of pleasure and so forth."
"They are objects of enjoyment. || 23 ||
1. The third verse in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* within the *Aṣṭaprakaraṇa*.
The *Dīpikā* explains the sūtra beginning with "the reality of cognition" (*buddhitattva*), etc., starting with the words "having the characteristics to be stated," etc.

"Arising from that," and so forth. The meaning is that dharma and the other factors themselves, having attained the state of being objects of enjoyment by way of their effects, are the "cognitions" (pratyaya). "They alone are the subtle body" (liṅga). This is the intended sense: actions such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, which consist of dharma and so on, when performed, do not yield results such as heaven immediately thereafter.

[They] produce [it]. Because they have their fruit in the next world and because they themselves appear as mere activities of the officiating priests and the sacrificer—having thus perished—they do not manifest; therefore, it cannot be said that the fruit follows the action, for that would contradict direct perception. Consequently, by means of those [actions], there arises a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) called the "unseen force" (*apūrva*), which is restricted to each individual self.

Even by others, it is accepted that [the self] acts because the declaration of the fruit (phalaśruti) would otherwise be inexplicable; yet that [action] is not possible in the Self, because it is changeless (avikāritva). Furthermore, it has been stated that since actions such as agriculture are seen to be for the purpose of purifying the self (ātmasaṃskāra), [action] belongs only to the insentient (jaḍa) wherein those [actions] reside.
They produce a mental impression (*saṃskāra*); that is the intellect (*buddhi*) endowed with the eight qualities beginning with *dharma*.

The same should be stated regarding the impressions of knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth. For it is by the power of those very impressions that a representation is observed even when the object is non-existent, as in dreams, creative imagination (*kṛti*), and intuitive flashes (*pratibhā*).
"Regarding that which will be stated, beginning with 'tadabhidhāsyamāna-': for this very reason, the intellect (*buddhi*) is established by the mark of determination (*adhyavasāya*).

For cognition is of two kinds: consisting of determination and having the form of non-determination. As they say: 'There exists a first, indeterminate cognition, which is mere observation (*ālocana*')."

"It arises from a pure object and is like the cognition of infants, the mute, and so forth. Furthermore, "that which is subsequently determined by the intellect through the properties of the object, such as genus (*jāti*) and the rest, is also accepted as being perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Of those two [types of perception], the former is always non-conceptual (*anadhyavasāyātmaka*) and appears solely in the form of the apprehender (*grāhakarūpa*).

It has been stated that [the self] is indeed of the nature of the self (*ātmasvabhāva*). However, that which consists of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), appearing as impermanent due to its arising and logical possibility, is not the nature of the person (*puruṣa*), because it is impossible for that which is eternal to have an impermanent nature. By this reasoning as well, their status as objects of conceptual determination is not possible.
But surely, let the Blessed One perform effects such as the intellect (*buddhi*) by means of the *guṇas* alone; what is the use of the intellect and the rest?

If this were so, then since the power of the Lord alone performs everything, what would be the use of the *guṇas* and the rest as well? Or, if it is said that he performs the effect only through the mediation of the *guṇas* and so forth—if this were so...
There is no contradiction whatsoever in [the Puruṣa] performing various effects such as determination through the superintendence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth.
1. There is a variant reading: *utpannopasthitena-avabhāsamānena*.
The "entities" (*bhāvāḥ*) are the qualities of the intellect (*buddhi-guṇāḥ*), namely *dharma*...
Those characterized by knowledge and dispassion are of the nature of goodness (sāttvika); those who have abandoned passion through the opposite process are of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).

Commentary: There are four dispositions (*bhāva*). The qualities of the intellect (*buddhi*) known as virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and power (*aiśvarya*) are to be understood by the designation "disposition" (*bhāva*). They are called "dispositions" because they bring about (*bhāvayanti*) the subtle body (*liṅga*) of the self.

These are to be understood as being of the nature of *sattva*. By way of reversal—that is, by contrast—when these same qualities are devoid of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and instead release passion (*rāga*), they become of the nature of *tamas*, consisting of unrighteousness (*adharma*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), and lack of mastery (*anaiśvarya*).
However, the state characterized by the absence of dispassion is of the nature of *rajas*. (24)
*The Lamp* (*Dīpikā*):

By the words "the entities" (*bhāvāḥ*) and so forth, he states that the entities are said to be dharma and the rest. Regarding the phrase "the four entities" and so forth, he explains the meaning of the word *bhāva* by saying: "they manifest their own mark (*liṅga*) in the intellect. In the intellect...
The meaning is that the eight states, beginning with dharma, exist as latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Regarding the phrase "these," and so forth:

the sense is that for that person whose sattvic and pure intellect has been activated, the four states beginning with dharma arise; the same should be understood for those who are rajasic and tamasic. || 24 ||
Commentary: He explains the suffixes. The suffixes have that [meaning] as their basis—
O Sage, six, nine, four times [four],
seven, and five are renowned as the groups beginning with Siddhi. (25)

Those factors, such as *dharma* and the rest, which are the material cause (*upādāna*)—that is, the cause of production—for those [entities], are accepted as the conditions (*pratyaya*) because they bring about the manifestation of the transmigrating soul (*saṃsāry-aṇu*). How many are there? He says: "eight, nine," and so forth.
There are eight kinds of accomplishment (*siddhi*) and nine kinds of contentment (*tuṣṭi*), whose characteristics will be described later. And it has been said by the Sāṃkhyas:

"Reasoning, oral instruction, study, the three-fold destruction of suffering, acquisition of friends, and charity—these are the eight accomplishments (siddhis). Likewise, there are four internal [accomplishments] called nature, means, time, and fortune; and nine [external ones] resulting from the cessation of external objects."
Thus it was said by Tuṣṭi. Four times seven makes twenty-eight;
incapacity (aśakti) is of that same number. There are eleven obstructions of the organs of action, the organs of perception, and the mind:
deafness, blindness, loss of smell, dumbness, and dullness of intellect; [and so forth].

Insanity, lameness, crookedness, impotence, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), and lameness—these, along with the previously mentioned destructions of the intellect (*buddhi-vadha*), which are the opposites of the contentments (*tuṣṭi*) and perfections (*siddhi*), constitute seventeen; thus, there are twenty-eight.
As the followers of Kapila have said: "The destructions of the eleven organs, together with the destructions of the intellect, are designated as incapacity (*aśakti*)."

There are seventeen divisions of the intellect (*buddhi*) consisting of the opposites of contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and attainment (*siddhi*). These five are well-known as the subdivisions of error (*viparyaya*), namely those called *tamas*, *moha*, *mahāmoha*, *tāmisra*, and *andhatāmisra*.
Furthermore, there are eight attainments, nine contentments, and twenty-eight incapacities (*aśakti*); thus they are grouped in order by category.
There are fifty conditions. || 25 ||

1. Deafness of the ear; blindness of the eye; loss of smell of the nose; muteness of speech; numbness of the tongue; insanity of the mind; leprosy of the skin; lameness of the hand; impotence of the generative organ; anal prolapse of the rectum; and lameness of the foot—this is the classification.
The sequence is not intended [to be significant] due to the requirements of the meter.
[The author of the] *Dīpikā* explains "the suffixes," etc., with "those very factors such as merit (*dharma*)," etc.; those very factors such as merit, and so forth.

The meaning is that the *pratyayas* (cognitions) have reached a state of excellence and, in their gross form, have entered the condition of being objects of experience (*bhogyadaśā*). He states this very point in the passage beginning with "of the transmigrating soul" (*saṃsāryaṇoḥ*) and so forth.

As it has been said: "They cause the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) to perceive [objects]; therefore they are remembered as *pratyayas*. Furthermore, "dharma" here is divided into the categories of *yama* and *niyama*.
It is divided into two types: for *yama* is the restraint of the mind, while *niyama* is the restraint of the senses. And it is said in the *Mataṅga*:
"Dharma is declared to be twofold: *yama* and the other, *niyama*. Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from guile—this *yama* is declared to be fivefold."

Now, the *niyamas* (observances) are also stated: "Freedom from anger, service to the teacher, purity, contentment, and straightforwardness—this is called *niyama*. Here, "service to the teacher" (*guru-śuśrūṣā*) is an illustration for other obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) duties; their characteristics have been explained in that very same place: "Giving, fasting, pilgrimages, recitation, and so forth are proclaimed [as *niyamas*]."

In that regard, it is stated: "The study of one's own recitation (*svādhyāya*) and the household where the sacred fire has been established. By the passage beginning with "the eightfold perfection" (*aṣṭavidhā siddhiḥ*), those fifty cognitive states (*pratyaya*) such as the perfections (*siddhi*) are shown here precisely as they are established in the Sāṃkhya system; they are not, however, the perfections established in our own [Tantric] tenets, for their definition is otherwise in the *Śrīmataṅga* and other such works.

And because its number is explicitly stated; for this very reason, the meaning intended by the author of the Sūtra is well-known from the Sāṃkhya system and others—this is the sense. The commentator (Vṛttikāra) has also spoken with reference to that [Sāṃkhya system], as in the passage beginning "and it is said by the Sāṃkhyas," and so forth. But what are the cognitive states (*pratyaya*) established in the Siddhānta? To this it is replied: therein, *dharma*...

It has been stated that [this] is divided tenfold according to the distinction between the *yamas* and *niyamas*. Furthermore, knowledge itself, when it has reached a state of excellence, is called *siddhi* (accomplishment). Among these, one *siddhi* is that knowledge which arises solely from the inference of one's own intellect (*svabuddhyūha*), without depending on the instruction of a teacher. As they say: "The *ṛṣis* are those who have directly perceived *dharma*..."
They came into being. They proclaimed the mantras by means of instruction to others who had not directly realized the Dharma;

thus, there was a conceptualization [of them] through the observation of the world by the Teacher himself, through the instruction of a guru, and through the destruction of the threefold internal suffering (ādhyātmika, etc.).

And for those whose selves have been cultivated through the attainment of friends, the practice of giving, and so forth—it is thus divided into eight types according to the differences in their causes. As it is said in the *Parākhya*: "Knowledge is that which is constantly practiced by one who has reasoned it out with his own intellect," and so on.
Here too, it will be stated: "The knowledge of the world arises from common sense, teachers, and scriptures; it is called 'disciplined' (*vainayika*)."

"Quality" (guṇa) refers to this. These should be understood as being illustrative of [the means] such as giving (dāna) and so forth. And it has been stated by the Sāṃkhyas: "Inference, verbal testimony, study, the three-fold removal of suffering, acquisition of friends, and giving—these are the eight perfections (siddhis). And these forms of knowledge [relate to] the Supreme Self, the Unmanifest, the qualities (guṇas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and mind (manas).

In the *Matanga* and other scriptures, it is shown that for those who hold the view that consciousness consists of the senses, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), or the gross elements (*bhūta*)—ranging from the Vedāntins down to the Cārvākas—these [levels] are to be known as the causes for attaining their respective states. Here too, it will be stated:

"The intellect (*buddhi*) which has the Puruṣa, Prakṛti, and so forth as its object—that is 'perfection' (*siddhi*) in this context. Consequently, they consist of the nature of those respective cognitions.

Success (*siddhi*), which is divided tenfold according to the differences in vision, is further divided eightfold for each [of those ten] due to the previously mentioned differences in causes. Thus, the total number becomes eighty.
Among these, the Sāṃkhyas have described the satisfactions (*tuṣṭi*) as being distinct from ignorance (*ajñāna*). As it has been said:
The internal [contentments] are four, known as those consisting of nature (prakṛti), means (upādāna), time (kāla), and fortune (bhāgya).

Nine contentments are declared to arise from the cessation of external objects. Thus, with respect to liberation through the gateway of the thirty principles, that [liberation] belongs to the Sāṃkhyas just as it does to them [the followers of the other systems].
For it is contentment itself; as they say: "One is satisfied with half [of what is required], one is satisfied with a quarter.

Here too, it will be said: "Contentment is the thought of one who has not achieved his goal, 'I have achieved my goal. Therefore, because this is the accomplishment of a goal for which no limit was set, it is called *siddhi* (accomplishment). This is the same in other cases as well.
All these have been described as varieties of *siddhi* (accomplishment), and thus there is no contradiction. What, then, are the *tuṣṭis* (contentments) in this context?

For one who possesses knowledge of the elements (*bhūtas*), the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), and so forth, there arise various types of contentment due to differences in the causes such as dispassion (*vairāgya*).
As it is stated in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*: "From that, from one or another [type of] knowledge, dispassion arises."
Thus: for here, indeed,
through the observation of living beings endowed with [the cycle of] exposition and so forth, there arises— due to the conjunction with the threefold suffering (ādhyātmika,

ādhibautika, and ādhidaivika)— weeping and the like from the pursuit of wealth and so forth, and from one's own passion (*rāga*) toward the body and so forth, as well as toward the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties.

And from the acceptance [of gifts], there arise ten forms of contentment based on the causes of detachment (*vairāgya*); these ten contentments, distinguished by their specific types of detachment, are: internal, external, celestial, natural, the non-weeping, the mocking, the desire-arousing, the intoxicated, the ascetic, and the forest-dweller. They occur sequentially through the causes of detachment.

[These] come into being. Through the attainment of this, the self indeed becomes satisfied; for as they say: "The man who delights only in the self and is satisfied with the self—he, liberated from all sins, goes to the eternal Brahman.
And that satisfaction is tenfold, according to the previously mentioned distinctions in philosophical systems.
For one endowed with knowledge of the elements (*bhūta*) and the rest, there arises [knowledge] for each one individually; thus, the number becomes one hundred.

Likewise, sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is eightfold, distinguished by the powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and so forth. Furthermore, that [sovereignty] belongs to those of divine origin, beginning from the Piśācas up to the Grandfather (Brahmā), and to those of the world of earth (*bhūloka*), according to the divisions of water and land.

Because there are two types [of each], in the eight desired stages beginning with that, there are sixty-four [subdivisions] through an increase of eight at each step in sequence. Thus, since a person's intellect proceeds toward the ten unrighteousnesses (*adharma*), which are the opposites of the previously mentioned restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), unrighteousness is divided tenfold.
Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is also fivefold, namely: *tamas*, *moha*, *mahāmoha*, *tāmisra*, and *andhatāmisra*.
Among these, due to *tamas*, the aforementioned perfections (*siddhi*s) do not manifest for the person.
Just as contentment arises from detachment (*vairāgya*), so too there are ten types of discontent (*atuṣṭi*s), which are distinct from the previously mentioned views and arise from non-detachment.
Since disgust and the other [afflictions] are causes of contentment, there is no differentiation [of contentment] based on their differentiation.
Just as the powers such as *aṇimā* arise from sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and so forth, the eightfold absence of *aṇimā* and the rest arises from the lack of sovereignty.
The incapacity of the body, the incapacity of the senses, and the incapacity of the mind and ego constitute ten types [of incapacity].

They number twenty-one. Since the forms of incapacity (*aśakti*), non-accomplishment (*asiddhi*), and dissatisfaction (*atuṣṭi*) are stated to be subdivisions of ignorance (*ajñāna*) and lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*), this is precisely a refutation of what was stated by the Sāṃkhya school.
For it is said: "Incapacity is defined as the eleven defects of the organs together with the defects of the intellect. Thus, these factors, beginning with virtue (*dharma*), [are established].
They number three hundred. And it was stated by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha:
"Dharma consists of ten divisions; knowledge of one hundred and eighty;
dispassion of sixty-four; sovereignty of ten; non-dharma, for that same reason, ignorance, and non-dispassion [each] of ten."

And non-sovereignty (anaiśvarya) is divided into twenty-one types. This differentiation of the suffixes denoting abstract states (bhāvapratyaya-bheda), as stated in brief, consists of three hundred [subdivisions]. Now, what indeed are these *tamas*, *moha*, and so forth? It is said:

here, that which is called *tamas* is so named because it is the cause of ten kinds of failure [regarding accomplishments] through such means as identifying the Self with the non-Self (*anātmany-ātmabhāva*).
It is of ten kinds. Delusion (*moha*) is of eight kinds, being the cause of non-comprehension regarding the powers such as *aṇimā*.

That which is the perception of superiority in objects such as sound—which are unworthy of being seen or heard—is the tenfold great delusion (*mahāmoha*). [This applies] to these ten, beginning with sound, and to the powers such as *aṇimā*.

And the eighteen-fold *tāmisra* is that fever which arises from seeing the non-attainment of the eight [powers] even when practicing according to the rules, or from the loss of those already attained; likewise,
when these eighteen previously mentioned [powers] are suppressed by another powerful yogin.

The suffering that arises is eighteenfold, known as *andhatāmisra*. Thus, through these internal subdivisions, these misconceptions (*viparyaya*) become sixty-four in number. And this has been stated in the venerable *Mataṅga* itself, beginning with the words: "That darkness [arises] from the onset of the power of *tamas*," and so forth. || 25 ||
1. Verse 18 in the Pauṣkara’s *Puṃstattvapaṭala*.
2. Verses 29 and 31 in the *Buddhipaṭala*.
3. Verse 47 in that same [chapter].
4. Furthermore, there is an additional reading in another manuscript: "And there is nothing else independently taught by the Sāṃkhyas regarding the elements.
5. This is the second verse in the section on the [eight] cognitive faculties (*pratyaya*) and so forth.
6. By the term "the uncreated" (akṛta), that world-realm of the principle of qualities (guṇatattva) bearing that name is described.

7. And those [faults] are: violence, theft, false speech, sexual intercourse with the teacher’s wife, retaliation for injury, constant abandonment of anger, impurity, discontent, and lack of straightforwardness.
8. In the Chapter on Intellect (Buddhipaṭala), the 175th verse. Commentary:
And those who have been thus enumerated and explained.
All phenomena are dependent; their characteristic is stated here as a mere summary. || 25½ ||
The *Dīpikā* explains the passage beginning with "entities possess causal conditions" (*bhāvāḥ sapratyayāḥ*), etc., starting from "and those which are thus," etc. (25½).
Commentary:
What is that? He says:
innate and acquired through discipline.
And the qualities of the individual soul are natural. || 26 ||
These entities, through the distinctions of being innate and so forth, become threefold for those in the cycle of transmigration. || 26 ||

The *Dīpikā* [commentary], preceded by a doubt regarding the definition of the states (*bhāva*), says: "What is that? and so forth. Furthermore, these states are to be understood as being innate (*sāṃsiddhika*) to Brahmā and the others. || 26 ||
Commentary: Now he explains the nature of those [qualities], beginning with the innate (*sāṃsiddhika*).
[It consists of] the refinement of specific attributes—
For those whose minds have been fully illuminated,
their innate quality shines forth even after the departure of the body, just as before.

For those whose minds have been perfectly kindled and inspired by the refinement of distinguished merit such as *iṣṭāpūrta* and other religious duties, that quality which shines forth— not only while joined with the body, but even upon the departure of the body, just as before— is to be understood as the one called *sāṃsiddhika* (innate). || 27 ||
Commentary: The quality of being well-disciplined shines forth from the world, common understanding, teachers, and scriptures.
The disciple has been purified by his mental, verbal, and physical conduct. || 28 ||

But he who has acquired [knowledge] from a teacher or from scripture according to the conventional understanding of the world shines and manifests as one trained (vainayika). Regarding the word "acquired" (samārjita): he is to be understood as one trained (vainayika) who has acquired it through pure activity by means of the movements of mind, speech, and body. || 24 ||
The *Dīpikā* explains the passage beginning with "lokadhiyā" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "yastu" and so on: "of one whose worldly cognition conforms to reality" means from the world;
and "of one possessing excellent wisdom" refers to [the influence of] spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and the like. And these [qualities] belong to those previously mentioned.

They should be understood as being indicative of generosity (*dāna*) and the other perfections as well. He says "yaḥ" and so forth [in verse 28], stating that by the words "well-acquired" (*samārjita*) and so on, the threefold nature of this very [merit] is described in another way.
The ordinary [consciousness] becomes manifest upon conjunction with the body, like the cognition of dreams and so forth. || 28½ ||

Furthermore, that which manifests as the very conjunction of the body with the forms of impressions (saṃskāra) present at the time one awakens from sleep, intoxication, or fainting— this is to be understood as the so-called "natural" (prākṛta) quality, even when the body has perished. || 28½ ||
Commentary: Now, in order to state the specific fruits resulting from these qualities, such as those that are innate (*sāṃsiddhika*) and so forth, he says:
"Heaven, liberation, and the non-obstruction of primordial nature."
The descent into a womb, the arrival in hell, and bondage; the attainment of objects among forms, both refined and common; and the gradual cessation of affliction—[these are the stages]. (29½)

In that regard, the purposes are successively accomplished and reach their stable state within the forms of both those to be disciplined and ordinary beings. What are they? He says: "Heaven. From dharma comes heaven; from knowledge, liberation;
from dispassion, dissolution into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*); and from power, non-obstruction—meaning the attainment of one's desires.
From unrighteousness comes birth in animal and other such wombs; from ignorance, the attainment of hell; from lack of dispassion, bondage;
and from lack of mastery, frustration. || 29½ ||

He connects the sūtra beginning with "svarga" [with the commentary] starting with "atha," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in forms" (*rūpeṣu*), the meaning is "in entities such as *dharma* and the like. The statement "liberation through knowledge" (*jñānānmukti*) means that for those who hold the views previously mentioned, liberation occurs up to the limit of each respective reality through its corresponding knowledge. As it was said: "The Buddhists are established in the principle of consciousness (*buddhitattva*)," and so on; however, it is not...
Supreme liberation (*parāmukti*). Since that is impossible without initiation (*dīkṣā*), as we shall explain later;
and "obstruction due to lack of sovereignty" refers to the aforementioned incapacity (*aśakti*). || 29½ ||
Commentary: Now, that which pertains to the innate (*sāṃsiddhika*) powers is being described.
Mastery and subjugation consist in the yoga of thorough knowledge thereof.
The absence of desire for enjoyments is the removal of the multitude of obstacles;
attachment to enjoyments, contempt, and the notion of "body" are obstacles to those [powers] that are spontaneously perfected.

Commentary: When the innate [powers] such as dharma and so forth exist, the connection with the preceding [verse] is that "this or that is accomplished. To the question "What? What?", he says: "subjugation" (vaśya), meaning mastery.
Movement results from merit that is spontaneously effective (*sāṃsiddhika-dharma*). Application to the thorough knowledge of that [movement] results from corresponding knowledge.

Lack of desire for enjoyments results from dispassion (*vairāgya*). The removal of the multitude of obstacles results from sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). Attachment to enjoyments results from demerit that is spontaneously effective (*sāṃsiddhika-adharma*). Humiliation is the act of being insulted.
From such ignorance [comes] the notion of a body; from a lack of dispassion [comes] attachment to the body; and from a lack of sovereignty [comes] obstruction in one's undertakings.
(Note: "dehalabdhiḥ" is an alternative reading.
Thus, in [this work] composed by Śrī Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, the son of Bhaṭṭa Vidyākaṇṭha...
The section on the exposition of the effects, beginning with the *kalās*, in the *Mṛgendravṛtti* is completed.
[From the] *Dīpikā*:
"Subjugation and conquest" (*vaśyākrānti*). This refers to the subjugation of the worlds (*lokas*) which are under one's own control, up to the limit of their respective principles (*svatattva*).

The locus (*sthāna*) is the application of the thorough knowledge of that; this means the attainment of the knowledge regarding its objects. And this has been stated in the *Bhoga-kārikās* as well, beginning with:
"Non-dharma and so forth are threefold, passion, and dharma and so forth are fourfold. Following this introduction:
