"For these, there is respectively downward rebirth, bondage, obstruction, and transmigration; [and then] heaven and liberation."

The results [of the practice] are: the natural state (*prakṛtibhāva*), non-obstruction (*avighāta*), and the fruits; then the fault of remaining in existence (*bhavasthānāparādha*), obstacle (*vighna*), and the non-transcendence of enjoyments (*bhogānatikrama*). The results consist of mastery (*vaśya*), abiding in the higher realms (*ūrdhvasthiti*), possessing right vision (*saddṛṣṭibhṛtva*), and the longing for enjoyment (*bhogaspṛhā*). Furthermore, the result in the form of the spontaneously accomplished (*sāṃsiddhika*) is the absence of obstacles regarding one's own thoughts; this is the case in the form that is innate (*vinayaprākṛte rūpe*).
The summary of the previously mentioned fruits has been stated up to this point [in] verse 57 on page 29.
Thus ends [the section] on the effects beginning with *kalā* in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā* composed by Aghoraśivācārya.

The tenth chapter, "An Inquiry into the Principle of Intellect" (*buddhitattvavicāraprakaraṇa*), is completed. Now begins the eleventh chapter, "On Cognition and the Like" (*pratyayādiprakaraṇa*). Commentary.
Having thus analyzed the entities, he now states another section that forms the remainder of the immediately preceding discussion in order to define the previously mentioned conditions: "Now,
of the groups beginning with the Siddhis..."
The general definition is stated only in brief, lest there be confusion regarding its various subdivisions. (1)

Immediately after the discussion on *bhāva* (the emotional states), the general definition of the groups beginning with the *siddhis* and *tuṣṭis*, which are associated with the *pratyayas*, is stated in brief. He asks: for what purpose? He replies: "So that there may be no confusion. This summary statement has been made according to their specific divisions (*prabhedaśaḥ*) or distinctions (*pravibhāgaśaḥ*).

Let there be no confusion or delusion of the intellect arising from that source. Eight and nine multiplied by four, and seven and five—by this much summary statement of the divisions, whatever confusion of the intellect might be feared is addressed;
for when the general characteristics have been thus summarized as "contentment is of such a kind" and "attainment is of such a kind," [the doubt is resolved].
The meaning is that this is for the purpose of [showing] that it does not exist. || 1 ||
1. The twenty-fifth verse in the section on *kalā* and so forth.
*Dīpikā*: Now begins the eleventh section, on *pratyaya* and so forth.

"Thus," and so forth. Since this [section] constitutes a supplement to the immediately preceding section, a separate pentad of relations need not be stated for it; the sense is that its establishment occurs through the very relation with the primary subject (*śeṣin*).
He now explains the sūtra beginning with "Now" (*atha*), starting with "Now," and so forth. But [one might object]: regarding the suffixes...

The general characteristic was already stated previously, namely that "the conditions (*pratyaya*) have those as their material cause (*upādāna*). For in that context, it was merely stated that all conditions arise from existence (*bhāva*). Here, however, there is no contradiction, as this refers to the individual nature of each of the groups, such as the *siddhis* and so forth. As for the question "For what purpose? and so on, the meaning is as follows: [there are] eight.

Since the number of the fifty accomplished states (*siddha-pratyaya*) based on the Sāṃkhya system has been shown in brief by the passage beginning with "nine," the definition of the essential nature of those accomplishments and so forth is likewise stated therein. [Regarding the statement:
"The general definition is stated for each [state] along with the understanding of the listeners," we shall provide the specific definitions.
This has already been demonstrated in the preceding section. || 1 ||
Commentary: Now that is being stated:
[the cognition] having as its object the soul, primordial matter, and so forth.
In this context, *buddhi* is that which is *siddhi* (accomplishment).
*Tuṣṭi* (contentment) is the thought of one who has not yet achieved his goal: "I have accomplished my purpose. || 2 ||

The intellect or discernment (*buddhi*) regarding the Spirit (*pums*), the Self (*ātman*), Nature (*prakṛti*), the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), and—by virtue of the inclusion of the word "etcetera"—the Manifest (*vyakta*), is called "perfection" (*siddhi*). However, the notion in a person whose purpose remains unfulfilled that "I have achieved my purpose" is "contentment" (*tuṣṭi*). || 2 ||

The *Dīpikā* explains the sūtra beginning with "puṃprakṛtyā" (by means of the soul and primordial matter), starting with "puṃsi" (in the soul) and so forth. By the inclusion of the word "ādi" (and so on), it is meant "and in the individualized manifestation.
This refers to those previously mentioned [categories] beginning with egoity (*ahaṅkāra*) and ending with the five elements. As it has been said:
"In the *Bhogakārikā*, it is said: 'The realization of the manifest and unmanifest, and the knowledge of the Knower, are now accomplished.

As for the words 'yātu' and so forth: because the sense of having fulfilled one's purpose (*kṛtārthatā*) has not yet vanished merely by attaining the aforementioned state produced through detachment (*vairāgya*) from those [lower levels], since supreme fulfillment belongs only to those who have attained ultimate liberation. For this very reason, it was stated previously."
Through dispassion, there is dissolution into prakṛti. || 2 ||
Commentary: Incapacity is the inability to produce a real effect when the causal factors are present.
When the mind apprehends something else in a manner that is only partially general, it is error (viparyaya). || 3 ||

Incapacity (*aśakti*) is the state of being unable to function even when an object is present, due to the impairment or destruction of the instruments— both internal and external organs— just as blindness or deafness prevents one from perceiving form, sound, and so forth. Misconception (*viparyaya*) is the cognition of something as being otherwise than it actually is, arising from some commonality with another object.
It is like the perception of water in a mirage. || 3 ||

*Dīpikā*: He states that incapacity (*aśakti*) and its opposite (*viparyaya*) are expressed by the sūtra beginning with "incapacity" (*aśakti*). [The phrase] "of the causal factors" (*kārakāṇām*), etc., is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes the body as well as the internal and external organs. As it is said in the *Mataṅga*:

"The effect does not come under [one's] control. For this very reason, since even the powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and the rest are produced by the body and the senses, their absence is also called "incapacity" (*aśakti*). As it is said in that same [text]: "The triad of sovereignty, beginning with *aṇimā*, is established through its effects; the five [powers] beginning with *prāpti* belong to the yogins."
"Born from the Cause" means, likewise, [the powers] such as *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, and so forth. || 3 ||
1. Chapter on Intellect (Buddhipaṭala), Verse 114:
The function [of intellect] is established as being that of illumination.
The [speech] of manifest beings and so forth arises from the nature of sattva;
and because it functions for the purpose of illumination,
it also originates from a portion of rajas.
Contentment, O Brahmin, is based on the quality of darkness (tamas), because its nature is false, even though it takes the form of happiness.
It is also determined to be of the sattvic nature. || 5 ||
Incapacity is characterized by a lack of activity and arises from the nature of suffering; it belongs to the quality of darkness (tamas).
Furthermore, a quality of passion (rajas) is also observed therein.
The effect depends upon the cause. || 6 ||
Its opposite is the womb of darkness,
and that [occurs] because of its false nature,
due to the appearance of mere generality.
One who is thus firmly resolved attains the state of a being (satva). || 7 ||

This very accomplishment (siddhi) is sattvic because it manifests the manifest and so forth, since *sattva* has the nature of luminosity (*prakāśa*). Furthermore, this accomplishment should be understood as arising from a portion of *rajas*, by virtue of its being motivated toward the purpose of manifestation; for it has been stated that the qualities (*guṇas*) do not produce effects in isolation.
The notion that "I have accomplished my purpose" in one who has not accomplished his purpose is called contentment (tuṣṭi).
Because it is of a false nature, this is characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas); yet, because it takes the form of pleasure, it is also determined to be of the nature of goodness (sattva).
Inactivity is said to be incapacity (aśakti), and for that reason it is of the nature of darkness; furthermore, because it is a cause of suffering, it is also of the nature of passion (rajas).

This is to be understood as follows: for whatever quality—whether of the nature of suffering known as incapacity regarding an effect, or of the nature of power—is present, it must necessarily have a cause; that is to say, it is produced by causes characterized as *rajas* and *tamas*.
Because error (*viparyaya*) is of the nature of falsehood, it originates from *tamas*. And that...
Because it reveals only the commonality of its opposite, it is also determined to consist of existence whose nature is luminosity. 4 = 5 = 6 = 7.
1. "On account of predominance" (*prādhānyāt*) is a variant reading. *Dīpikā*:
By the phrase "by way of illuminating," etc., he states that accomplishment (*siddhi*) and the other [attainments] are not distinct from the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "saiṣā" and so forth: since perfection (*siddhi*) has been described as being distinct according to the specific knowledge (*jñāna*), and since knowledge is characterized by *sattva*, one might ask how it can arise from a portion of *rajas*. To this, he says "nahi" and so forth. For it has been stated: "The singular mention of each of these [qualities] is based on the predominance of their respective functions. Furthermore, the *sāttvika* nature of knowledge is such that it is never unmixed.
"It transforms"—this should be understood in the same way regarding contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and the other [eight attainments]. 4 = 5 = 6 = 7.
Commentary: Concluding, he says:
"Thus, this is the illumination of the intellect."
Characterized by the suffix denoting abstract state (bhāvapratyaya),
it is called "awakening" (bodha) because it is the ground for the manifestation of awakening for the bound soul (paśu). || 8 ||

Thus, this manifestation of consciousness, characterized by the abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya), which has been explained, is designated by the term "awareness" (bodha) because it serves as the substratum for the manifestation of awareness in the bound soul (paśu), the transmigrating atom (aṇu). || 8 ||
The *Dīpikā* explains the sūtra beginning with "ityādi" as follows: "ityevam" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because they are the substrata for the manifestation of cognition":
even entities such as *dharma* and the rest, during the state of *saṃsāra*, [are objects] for the self by way of being objects of experience.
They become the causes for the manifestation of knowledge. As it has been said: "Experience for this [Purusha] is sensation characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth. This is the commentary.
Then, here the sage, under the guise of a Sāṃkhya, asks:
If the intellect (*buddhi*) is the cause of cognition,
then it must be distinct from that [cognition].
Even passion, when true dispassion is present,
being born of [mere] worldly artifice, what can it do?

According to the principle stated, if it is asserted that cognition lacks the nature of being an instrumental cause for itself, then knowledge (vidyā) would be rendered purposeless, since that too is accepted as a cause of cognition. Furthermore,
if it is accepted [as a cause] despite its being a general operation, then there would be an infinite regress.

Furthermore, even though the quality of *rāga* (attachment), characterized by non-detachment (*avairāgya*), exists as a property of the intellect (*buddhi*), what does the passion born of the *kalās* accomplish?
It accomplishes nothing at all, because its purpose is already fulfilled by the excellence of non-detachment itself.
Thus says the *Dīpikā*.

Regarding this, fearing that because of the consequence of [the term] "awakening" (*bodha*) and the consequence of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), the previously mentioned *vidyā* and *rāga* would be rendered purposeless, the Sage raises an objection with the words beginning "intellect" (*buddhi*). Thus he says: "Now, in this regard," and so forth.
Commentary:
Now follows the refutation of this [position]: when another manifestor exists...
If the manifestor is devoid of meaning,
then even when the mind, the deity, and the object exist, the cognition is likewise devoid of meaning. (10)
If that reality known as *vidyā*, which manifests consciousness (*bodha*),

were purposeless when another manifestor consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) exists, then for you, the follower of Kapila, the intellect would likewise be purposeless even when the mind and the objects characterized as sense-faculties exist. To explain:

When the mind—which is determined by the instruments such as the eye that grasp form and other objects—is already present as the manifestor, what purpose is served by another manifestor called "intellect" (buddhi)? For the accomplishment of each respective effect occurs through the sense organs alone when presided over by the mind. || 10 ||

The *Dīpikā* states that [the author] avoids the charge of the uselessness of knowledge (*vidyā*) by means of the passage beginning with "by another manifestor" (*vyañjakāntareṇa*), etc., and says "now this," etc. Regarding "that which manifests cognition": there are many factors, such as light and the proximity of the sense organ, involved in the apprehension of form and so forth.
The meaning is that the meaningfulness of manifestors is observed. || 10 ||
Now, some say this with the intention of expressing [the self] as an instrument:
"He too, together with the gods, with the mind as the sixth..."
The thesis is considered to be inconclusive. || 11 ||

Now, since it would follow that even the aforementioned cognition would be purposeless, one should not object by saying that if another manifestor exists, the manifestor [of that cognition] would likewise be rendered purposeless. Rather, some raise this objection with the intention of treating it as an instrument (*karaṇa*): namely, regarding that which is called "cognition" (*buddhi*).

Even if it were an instrument (*karaṇa*), what is the use of designating it as "knowledge" (*vidyā*)? As it has been said: "That [intellect] is knowledge; that is the supreme instrument. And here too it was stated: "He created the principle called knowledge, the supreme instrument of the Supreme Self. Yet this position is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the sense organs of cognition, of which the mind is the sixth. For instance: * *karaṇe satyapi kiṃ vidyābhidhānena karaṇena | yathoktam | sā vidyā tatparaṃ karaṇaṃ iti | ihāpyuktam tatvaṃ vidyākhyamasṛjat-karaṇaṃ paramātmanaḥ iti | so'pyayaṃ pakṣo manaṣṣaṣṭhaiḥ buddhīndriyairanaikāntikaḥ | tathāhi |* Even if it were an instrument, what is the use of designating it as "knowledge"? As it has been said: "That [intellect] is knowledge; that is the supreme instrument. And here too it was stated: "He created the principle called knowledge, the supreme instrument of the Supreme Self. Yet this position is also inconclusive with respect to the sense organs of cognition, of which the mind is the sixth. For instance: 1. *sā vidyā tatparaṃ karaṇam* (That is knowledge; that is the supreme instrument). 2. *tattvaṃ vidyākhyamasṛjat-karaṇaṃ paramātmanaḥ* (He created the principle called knowledge, the instrument of the Supreme Self). 3. *manaṣṣaṣṭhair buddhīndriyaiḥ* (By the sense organs of cognition, of which the mind is the sixth). 4. *anaikāntikaḥ* (Inconclusive). 5. *tathā hi* (For instance).

This argument— that the presence of another instrument renders an instrument redundant— is rendered inconclusive by the fact that the five sense organs, while being instruments in the act of grasping their respective objects, are accepted as having the mind (*manas*) as a sixth,
distinct instrument. On the contrary, it is precisely for one who depends upon another instrument [that such a further instrument is required].
Because an instrument (karaṇa) is observed in certain actions; as it is stated in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*:

"An instrument depends upon another instrument, like the rays of the sun in the sky. And just as these five [senses], beginning with hearing, are accepted by the proponents of the Self (*ātmavādin*) as having the status of instruments—even though they share the commonality of being instruments—with the mind (*manas*) as the sixth, so too [is the case here].
Even if the Buddha exists, there is no fault whatsoever, as the knowledge that apprehends him will be established. || 11 ||
1. The twelfth verse in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* of the *Aṣṭaprakaraṇa*.
2. The ninth verse in the *Kalādiprakaraṇa*.
The *Dīpikā*.
"This too is a [logical] position," and so forth; it is like the expression "he goes by means of a chariot, along a path, with a lamp," and so on. || 11 ||
Having thus supported the objection raised regarding both positions,
he speaks in order to refute it while raising a further doubt from another perspective: "Now, if there were a single application..."
In reality, [the self] is one;
therefore, let the ear, eye, hands, feet, and so forth be distinct entities for the sake of the person. || 12 ||

Indeed, that object which has a single application (viniyoga) is a single entity; another, while possessing that same single application, exceeds it or becomes redundant—just as a lamp is superfluous when there is light produced by a gem capable of destroying darkness. Consequently, [the three qualities] possess the nature of being the means for the experience of pleasure, pain, and delusion by the person.

The intellect alone is sufficient; therefore, fearing that the further pursuit of knowledge for its sake would be useless, this objection is refuted by the passage beginning with "the ear, sight, hand, foot," and so forth.
This is because, according to such an admission, the ear, sight, feet, hands, and other organs possess a single unified function.
The meaning is: "when one [of these] is admitted to be redundant. *Nuh* refers to the person (*pums*), the enjoyer who is connected with the state of being an animal (*paśutva*).

As was stated previously: "He does not enjoy objects of enjoyment that follow the course of time within the realms of experience. For that person (*nuh*), the ear, eye, and so forth, as well as the hand, foot, and so forth, must—according to your position—have distinct purposes, or else they would have a single object.

Let it not be so. But surely, who has said that the ear, the eye, and the other [senses] have a single object? For the eye does not grasp an object that is to be grasped by the ear, nor does the foot perform the function of the hand; this is because they possess distinct objects due to their individual natures. True; however, it was stated in this way with the intention of expressing that they are the sole means for experience (*bhoga*). For instance:
First, for the person who is the enjoyer, there arises an effort to seek mangoes and the like based on the experience of their fragrance;

then, upon hearing that "there are mangoes," one proceeds toward them; subsequently, there is the visual perception of them and the gustatory tasting of them by the tongue—thus, although the single functional application of the sense organs is being experienced, [it is not realized as such].

In your position, it is not logical to accept [a single, undifferentiated cause], for fear of its being purposeless. Therefore, according to your view, let the auditory organ, the visual organ, and so forth, as well as the hands, feet, and so forth, have distinct objects;
even though they share a non-differentiated object insofar as they are causes for the purpose of a person's enjoyment, let there nonetheless be distinct results. This is the meaning.
And it is not thus. 12.
1. There is a variant reading: "anubhavatv ity arthaḥ" (the meaning is "let him experience").
2. The word "asti" (is) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. [This is] the commentary (vṛtti).

Having thus refuted even this third manner of the opponent's objection, he says [the following] in order to reject the opponent’s intended notion that the *vidyā* and the *buddhi* have a single application:
"Nor do they have a single application."
And how is it that there is no [fault] regarding knowledge and cognition?
Through the medium of different applications, having multiple effects is not defective. (13)
Furthermore, there is no contradiction in knowledge (*vidyā*) and cognition (*buddhi*) being employed for a single purpose, because their objects are distinct;

and it is not defective for them to have multiple objectives when they proceed through different applications—that is, when they function by way of different "mouths" or modes of application. For example:

Since the act of cooking, which is accomplished by numerous means such as fuel, water, and a ladle, possesses distinct purposes, nothing is detracted from it by the admission of separate *kārakas*. || 13 ||

The Dīpikā says: But surely, even in the case of a single object such as fragrance, there would be the futility of the various sense organs due to their distinct functions of seeing, hearing, and so forth; yet, a difference in function is observed between knowledge (*vidyā*) and cognition (*buddhi*). To this, he replies:
"Thus," and so forth. || 13 ||
Commentary: Now, what is this difference in object between knowledge (*vidyā*) and cognition (*buddhi*)? He says:
Knowledge is the manifest power of the individual consciousness (*aṇu-cit-śakti*).
Having taken as their own object that which was intended by the person— the objects of the senses that have come within the range of the sense-orgons— [the cognitions arise]. (14)
Attachment is not different from the cognition of it, nor is it secondary because it possesses contrary properties;
and that [attachment] is either the state of being an object of enjoyment or this very [cognition].
Therefore, one who is free from passion is destroyed. || 15 ||

Knowledge (*vidyā*) is, first of all, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) of the individual soul (*aṇu*) made manifest; that by which the power of consciousness of the individual soul is made manifest—that is, ignited—is its sole function. Those whose senses (*akṣa*), meaning the organs of perception, have their lord—the mind (*manas*)—driven, impelled, and directed with focused attention, are of such a nature.

"Having accepted those as its domain and those as its objects. Regarding the phrase "employed by the person": since this very instrument called *vidyā* (knowledge), which exists as a direct benefactor to the Self itself and is intensely joined with the Person, becomes the object—that is, it attains the state of being grasped—therefore, the other [instrument] is far removed and distinct from *vidyā*.

Having thus refuted the futility of knowledge, the second objection is now dismissed: "Passion is not secondary because it possesses properties contrary to that. Passion does not arise from non-detachment, which is a quality of the intellect. Why? He says:
"Because it possesses properties contrary to that. This is because the secondary [passion] has properties different from the passion described in the scriptures.
The word *vidharma* (heterogeneous) has its nominal suffix elided; what is that heterogeneity? He says:

"And that is the state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*). A quality of the intellect (*buddhidharma*) characterized by the absence of dispassion (*avairāgya*), or an external object such as garlands, sandalwood, women, and so forth—which others accept as the very nature of passion—this alone is its heterogeneity.

That which constitutes the state of being an object of enjoyment must necessarily be accompanied by passion (*rāga*), which is the cause of attachment to enjoyment, as well as by an enjoyer. Furthermore, there can be no identity between the object of enjoyment and the cause of enjoyment. Or, if this very state of being an object of enjoyment is accepted as belonging to passion itself, then one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) would be destroyed; for from such an admission follows the undesirable consequence that no one could ever be free from passion.
When one does not admit that passion resides in the enjoyer,

but instead admits that passion takes the form of a specific object of enjoyment— such as an external beautiful woman— then everyone would possess passion toward objects of enjoyment such as women present before them, regardless of whether they are passionate or free from passion.

[He] attains [it]. For there would be no one here who is free from passion (*vītarāga*). In reality, even for those who are free from passion, it is accepted that they possess passion merely due to the proximity of specific objects of enjoyment. And it has been stated by Sadyojyotiḥpāda: "Regarding passion for specific objects of enjoyment, indeed no one would be free from passion."

Therefore, the cessation of passion resides only in the enjoyer; it does not reside in the specific objects of enjoyment such as form, taste, and so forth, nor in the nature of the mental states of non-detachment or momentary cognition. || 15 ||
1. The tenth verse in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* within the *Aṣṭaprakaraṇa*.
The *Dīpikā* explains the sūtra beginning with "vidyā" [as follows]: "First, as for 'vidyā'... and "the manifest atomic power of consciousness (*cicchakti*)."

It has been stated that the capacity of knowledge (*vidyā*) to establish the power of the knower is not possible without its [knowledge's] capacity for the perception of the intellect (*buddhi*). And this has already been explained above. With the words beginning with "attachment" (*rāga*), he refutes the uselessness of attachment; thus he says, "that much," and so forth. Furthermore, [he states] that it is a quality of the intellect characterized by the absence of dispassion (*avairāgya*).

It has been stated that [the intellect] in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) does not produce an effect. Furthermore, it will be stated immediately hereafter that even in the form of a mental modification (*pratyaya*), because it is an object of enjoyment, it is not the cause of desire. Now, one might ask: "Let the objects of the three *guṇas* alone be the cause of desire; what need is there for others? To this, he says: "A garland, sandalwood, a woman," and so forth; this too—
This has already been established in the preceding section: [it] brings about the state of being an object of enjoyment for both the objects and the self.
1. The sentence within the brackets [kuṇḍala] is to be considered. [Vṛtti: And for this reason.
Attachment is that desire for objects which does not exist in the two [other] categories;
action, however, must be postulated as all-pervasive.
Even when [the object] is imagined, that which exists elsewhere [remains].
As previously stated, attachment residing in the enjoyer is that longing for objects such as garlands and the like;

thus, the very cause of longing is expressed by the word "longing" itself. This is due to the metaphorical treatment of the effect as non-different from its instrument, as in the expression "clarified butter is life. And this cause of longing for objects, termed attachment, exists in two types of spheres: one being external.

In the case of honey, sandalwood, and so forth, it must be admitted that [passion] does not exist, because it would follow that those who are free from passion would still possess it. However, in the second case—that which is a quality of the intellect (*buddhi*) characterized by non-detachment—it lacks the status of being a cause for longing, because its nature is that of an object of enjoyment. This is because passion, which is the cause of longing, is produced by that [non-detachment].

This [entity], consisting of desire residing in the intellect (*buddhi*), takes the form of action and brings about the state of being an object of enjoyment; this is sufficient. Now, one might argue that action itself—manifesting as pleasure, pain, and so forth—will serve as the object of enjoyment by virtue of being the cause of longing.
To this he says: "Action must be postulated as all-pervasive. This refers to the two aforementioned objects.

Let it be that action (karman) is the pervading factor which establishes the states of being "with passion" (sarāga) and "free from passion" (vītarāga). Even if passion (rāga) is postulated as the cause for those [states], action must necessarily be admitted as the further postulate. Furthermore, action must be accepted as the cause even for that [passion]. Let that very [action] be the cause for the states of being with passion and free from passion, due to the diversity of its objective basis (vastu).
The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa). || 16 ||
Commentary: But the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that [the result] is stated to belong to the action alone.
The refutation applies only to those [feelings] that are fixed;
for hatred and passion, which are unequal, cannot coexist due to their mutual incompatibility. (17)
The refutation has already been shown regarding the view that action alone is established by necessity. Thus it has been said:
"Experience is the purpose of all principles, and that too is dependent on action;
let action alone [be the cause] for the body and so forth, therefore everything else is useless. Now, [if it is argued that action is] dependent on the body and so forth—
That [karma] accomplishes the goals of human existence; therefore, let it be that karma is the regulator which is dependent upon *niyati* (destiny).

Consequently, since its purpose is fulfilled solely through the diversity of the body, instruments, experiences, and so forth, and because there is no evidence for any other effect, karma does not produce the effects of passion (*rāga*); rather, it has the aforementioned purpose.
It is established that passion (*rāga*) is produced by the *kalās*. Furthermore, hatred (*dveṣa*) is not a distinct principle in the same way as passion;

for hatred and the other afflictions consist essentially in specific modes of activity generated by passion. Indeed, when some desired object is obstructed, hatred and the like arise in this [individual]. Now, [one might object] that they [the afflictions] exist through mutual suppression—

Since passion and hatred reside [in the same locus], it follows that there is the fault of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) in a single person; thus he says: "The fault is non-coexistence. What, then, is this fault of non-coexistence? If it means [their existence] at the same time, then this is not a defect; rather, it is indeed an ornament [to the system]. For when and where...

If you argue that there is attachment toward an object at one very moment and aversion toward that same [object] at another, or that there is attachment toward a certain enjoyer and aversion toward that same enjoyer, this is not tenable; that too is incorrect. For there is no contradiction between these two in their substratum, but rather in their objects.
Since attachment and aversion are not simultaneous, they do not operate with respect to the same object within a single substratum in a sequential manner.
There is no fault; for you yourself accept the co-inexistence [of light and darkness] that has been pointed out by us. || 17 ||
1. The sixteenth verse in the section on *kalā* and so forth.
2. There is a variant reading: *atulyabalatvena*.
[From] the *Dīpikā*.
He constructs an introductory framework (*pīṭhikā*) in order to explain the fragment of the sūtra beginning with "defect" (*doṣa*). [He says] "And not," etc.

If hatred were produced by attachment, then hatred would occur only in a person who possesses attachment; consequently, he states that there is the defect of their non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*). [He asks] "But surely," etc. He explains the passage beginning with "defect" as a response to this very point.
What, then, is it? || 17 ||
The commentary: For instance, [it is said that] for everyone, at all times, everything—
Engagement arises from the cognition of pleasure;
for one who has engaged, pleasure, pain, or even delusion arise. (18)
Following activity, there is aversion;
attachment arises prior to that. Furthermore, it [arises] by means of that which exists at the end of aversion.
Energy is the cause for the application [of practice]. || 19 ||
All worldly activity is undertaken for the sake of removing everything;

for one thus engaged, pleasure, pain, or delusion arises. Following the activity of eating and so forth, aversion arises toward that very same thing, while attachment arises at the time preceding it. Furthermore, after the period of aversion, at some point in time...
This is the statement regarding that: because whatever is more vigorous and more powerful is precisely the cause of the union produced by attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*) in yoga;
since this is so, and because passion is more powerful than hatred, the fault of their non-coexistence is not a fault. || 19 ||
The *Dīpikā* [comments]:
"That which is indeed vigorous," and so forth. It consists of passion (*rāga*). || 19 ||
Commentary: Having thus explained the incidental arising of the principle of *rāga* (attachment), he now describes the function of the principle of *ahaṅkāra* (ego).
Now, [regarding] the intellect (*buddhi*) from another manifest [principle]...
Pride became the instrument of the intellect,
by whose activity the five bodily winds exert themselves.

From the unmanifest (avyakta) arises the manifest (vyakta), which is the principle of the qualities (guṇatattva); from that [unmanifest] as its distinct cause arises the intellect (buddhi); from that [intellect] arises the ego (ahaṅkāra); and from the conscious self (cit/ātman) arises the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) characterized by the function of impulsion (saṃrambhavṛtti). Through the activity of which [internal organ], the five vital breaths (prāṇas) move within the body.
The winds move; they perform their respective functions. || 10 ||
The commentary says: Who are they? They are prāṇa, apāna, and so forth. But those...
The distinction is not real, but arises from the mode of application;
O Bharadvāja, listen to me as I describe that mode of application in brief. (21)

The five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa and apāna, are differentiated according to the distinctions in their functions (vṛtti), yet there is no real ontological difference between them, as they are indistinguishable in their nature as air. Now, he describes the distinction in their functions by means of a brief summary of their activity: "the function [is described] in brief. (21)
Commentary: Regarding that, he asks, "What is the function of the vital breath? He replies:
"Its function is called 'leading forth' (praṇayana)."
That which is called life—
that intellect of men wanders like one in blindness, searching for its way. 22.
That which performs this [function] is called *prāṇa*,
or rather, it is *prāṇa* by virtue of its connection with the vital breath,
within the conscious and subtle transportive power (*śakti*).
And the word *prāṇa* [is used] for the *kalās*. || 23 ||

Leading forth (*praṇayana*) means leading out intensely; it is the movement of the air residing within the body as far as the external *dvādaśānta*. This is the function or activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and this definition is indicated by its etymological derivation. That which is called "living" (*jīvana*) is indeed the function of the vital breath alone.
This is the intended meaning: according to the perspective of the *Nirukta*, the word "prāṇa" is indicated by its function as "leading forth" (*praṇayanāt*).
Furthermore, "prāṇana" means breathing or living (*prakarṣeṇānanam*); thus, it is called "prāṇa" because of that.
This is an etymological definition concerning its result, which is stated by way of its fruit, since it leads men to their goal.
Seeking [its object], the intellect wanders like one who is blind; that is indeed the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Reasoning (*ūha*) consists of deliberation (*vimarśa*), which is logic (*tarka*). In this regard, the impelling of this intellect is performed by the vital breath alone, for consciousness (*saṃvit*), mounted upon the chariot of the vital breath, performs its deliberation. Indeed, the vital breath is strength; through union with that, it is called "vital breath" (*prāṇa*).

It is said: because the term "prāṇa" should be understood as referring to consciousness (citi) and sentience (caitanya), to the subtle body (ātivāhika) consisting of the principles from kalā down to earth (kṣiti), to power (śakti) whose nature is strength, and to the kalās whose nature consists of the moon, the sun, and so forth. || 23 ||
1. *Prāpaṇam* is a variant reading. *Dīpikā*: [The word] "does" (*karoti*) is used here; the particle *eva* serves for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). Life (*jīvanam*) as well [is included].

He says that it is the function of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). "It is indicated by its result," and so forth; for when the vital breath exists, the body is said to live. He states another activity: "Of persons," and so forth. He provides another definition: "The vital breath indeed," and so forth. || 22 ||
1. This sentence, which has been arranged in a circle, is to be reflected upon. [The] commentary [states]:
He describes the function of the *apāna* [wind].
Likewise, by performing the removal of what has been eaten, drunk, feces, urine, and semen,
one acts under the designation of *apāna*.
It is sung by those who perceive reality. || 24 ||

Because it performs the removal—that is, the downward conveyance—of what has been eaten, drunk, excrement, urine, and semen, it is therefore designated by the term "apāna" (the downward-breath) by those who know reality. || 24 ||
Commentary: Now follows the description of the function of the two equal breaths (*samāna-vyāna*). [It consists in] the distribution of food and drink on all sides.
Because it performs dedication through equanimity, it is called *samāna*; because it bends the body, it is called *vyāna*. (25)

The state of being *samāna* belongs to the *samāna* wind because it regulates food and drink with equality everywhere; the state of being *vyāna* belongs to the *vyāna* wind because it pervades the body. (25)

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: "Due to the bending of the body," and so forth; this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the provocation of diseases and other such conditions. As it is said in the venerable *Kālottara*: "Vyāna bends the limbs; Vyāna is the provoker of disease."
Because it causes the destruction of pleasure through pervasion, it is called vyāna. Thus [ends the verse]. || 25 ||
Commentary: The function of udāna is now described;
it is preceded by the effort of the desire to speak.
By means of which, through the assistance of the organ of speech, the state of being phonemes is produced from the sound possessing the qualities of the space within the vocal cavity. (26)
If its location within this body is for the purpose of sustaining it,
then its fruit is mastery; the rest of the statement is to be supplied.
It was shifted onto another shoulder by her husband. || 27 ||

That which, preceded by the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*) and effort (*yatna*), performs the differentiation and diversification of that sound— which is of the nature of a quality belonging to the internal space (*vyoman*) or the cavity of the chest (*koṣṭha*)— by means of the organ of speech as its assistant, is [the *vāyu*] in this body.

The term *udāna* is to be understood [as the subject]. Furthermore, regarding whichever wind—such as *prāṇa* and the rest—the respective location and the mastery that results from its retention, along with the fruit arising from that mastery, all this must be explained; it has been indicated by the Blessed One in another section known as the *Yogapāda*. || 26–27 ||
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the Section on Cognition (*pratyayaprakaraṇa*), in the *Mṛgendravṛtti* composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, son of Bhaṭṭa Vidyākaṇṭha.
[The] Dīpikā.

He explains the phrase "the desire to speak" (*vivakṣā*) and so forth as "the wish to speak" (*vaktum icchā*) and so forth. As they have said: "The *nāda* (sound-potential), originating from space and air, emerging from the body and reaching the mouth, becomes differentiated in various places and attains the state of phonemes (*varṇa*); that is what is called 'speech' (*śabda*). This is merely an illustration.

Regarding the movement [of the breath] and so forth, it is stated in the venerable *Kālottara*: "The wind named udāna causes the lower face and limbs to throb with agitation and agitates the vital points (*marmāṇi*). These varieties have been shown here primarily; for there is also the possibility of others, such as Nāga and the rest, which are not predominant.

It is stated in that very same [text]: "Nāga is said to be in the upward belching; Kūrma resides in the opening of the eyes; Kṛkara is in hunger; Devadatta is in yawning; Dhanañjaya resides in nourishment and does not leave even the dead. And regarding the phrase "of which wind," etc., since the retention of the locations and so forth are limbs of yoga (yogāṅga), they are situated in that very place.

"They are to be seen. Therefore, as a secondary topic (*prasaṅga*) here, the divisions of the wind and the divisions of its functions have been shown precisely as supplementary to what was previously taught. As it has been said: "For whatever has a connection with something, that [connection] belongs to it, even if it is situated at a distance. The word *skandha* refers to those which will be discussed in the immediately following section.
It should be understood that [this] is in consideration of the aggregates of egoity (*ahaṅkāra-skandha*) and in terms of their actual meaning.
Thus ends the chapter on the investigation of cognition and so forth in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā* composed by Aghoraśivācārya.
Now begins the twelfth chapter, on the Faculties and so forth. Commentary:
Now, the threefold nature of the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), its effects, and an investigation thereof are introduced.
The commencement of another section. As before, the fivefold relationship should also be considered here.
Now, for the sake of establishing the meaning of the remainder, he [the author] proceeds from this very point regarding the aggregates (*skandhas*).

And so forth. || 2 ||

speech, hands, the generative organ, and the anus.

Speech, feet, hands, anus, and genitals are the five deities characterized by *rajas*.

Because their functions follow from that [quality] and they constitute the organs of action (*karmendriya*), the aggregate of ego (*ahaṅkāra-skandha*) known as the *vaikārika* is essentially abounding in *rajas*. || 4 ||

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: "Of these," and so forth. Even by means of the *vaikārika* [sattvika ego], the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is manifested through the medium of the organs of action. || 4 ||
Commentary:
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth.
The subtle elements (tanmātras), being indistinguishable from their qualities, are designated by the term "subtle element" (tanmātra). || 5 ||

Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—these qualities, being undifferentiated and having their specific distinctions unmanifested, are joined with that which consists merely of them, namely the nature of the elements; they are to be known by the term *tanmātra*.
Furthermore, because these are "merely" (*tāvat*) "measures" (*mātrā*), this word *tanmātra* is feminine in gender.

The non-distinction of their qualities is as follows: for example, in earth there is sound in the form of clattering and so forth, touch that is neither cold nor hot, color which is of many kinds, taste which is of six kinds, and smell which consists of fragrant and non-fragrant types. It is not thus [in the other elements].
The specific qualities residing in the earth-tanmātra, which is their cause, are not perceived;
rather, it is considered to be merely the five non-specific qualities, the earth-tanmātra itself. || 5 ||

The *Dīpikā* explains the sūtra beginning with "sound" (*śabda*). [It says] "sound, touch," and so forth. Even though the sense organs have been described, because they are not all-pervading (*avibhu*), these subtle elements (*tanmātra*)—sound and the rest—serve as their substrata.

It has been stated that the elements, such as space and the rest, are established. "This effect, having entered the tenfold organs, is made to exert activity; however, because they are not all-pervading, the organs exert activity by depending upon the effect," and so forth. Now, one might object: let the elements themselves, which are established by both disputants, serve as the substrata of the sense organs.
What is the use of the five *tanmātras* being included therein? To this he says: "Because they are unmanifest and without distinction," and so forth.
The meaning is that those substrates of the senses exist in both gross and subtle forms. As it is said in the *Mataṅga*:
"In this world, the *tanmātras* are like pots, and the great elements (*mahābhūtas*) are like their coatings. Furthermore, [this applies to] earth and the other elements.

The five elements (bhūtas) to be described hereafter are effects, like a jar and other such things, because their qualities are perceptible by external sense organs such as our own. Therefore, they must have a cause; and those which are the causes are the subtle elements (tanmātras). || 5 ||
1. The fourth verse in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* within the *Aṣṭaprakaraṇa*. Commentary:
And these are the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
Because they differ from the group that performs the function of illumination, they arise from *tamas*;
and because they are objects of illumination, they arise from *bhūtādi*.
Among those with ego-sense, he is characterized by tamas.

Because these [faculties] possess a distinctness—that is, a dissimilarity—from those two groups: the group characterized by the intellect (*buddhi*), the senses (*indriya*), and the mind (*manas*), which is luminous (*prakāśaka*) and of the nature of *sattva*; and the group of the organs of action (*karmendriya*), which is active in its operations due to being rajasic (*rājasa*).
Therefore, these [elements] arise from *tamas*; and because they are objects of illumination (*prakāśyatva*),

among these aggregates of *ahaṃkāra*, that which is the aggregate of *ahaṃkāra* beginning with the elements (*bhūtādi*) is to be illuminated, since its effects— consisting of the *tanmātras*— are [illuminated] by the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*).

Because it is perceived by yogis through the sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), this [ego] should be known as *tāmasa*. And it has been stated by the Sāṃkhyas: "From the *bhūtādi* [evolvent], the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) arise; they are *tāmasa*. (SK 25)
The *Dīpikā* explains the sūtra beginning with "prakāśaka" (the illuminator). It states "prakāśakṛt," etc.
Consequently, it is said that the dullness of the aforementioned powers of the sense organs is produced by the *ahaṅkāra* (ego) characterized by *tamas*.
In the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures: "Just as the impairment of the sense organs is observed in trees and the like.

Now, some Buddhists claim that trees are insentient (*acetana*). That is incorrect, because death is observed when the bark is stripped off entirely—as in the case of sheep and other animals—and because they are subject to seasonal changes. For [trees respond] through the embrace of a passionate woman, the sipping of water, and so forth.
The blossoming of the *kuravaka*, *vakula*, and other trees is observed; as they say:

"O *kuravaka* tree, you are deprived of the pleasure of the game of being struck by breasts; O *vakula* shrub, the sprinkling of wine from [her] mouth must be remembered by you; and since it is devoid of contact with feet, O *aśoka*, your state of sorrow remains."

Regarding the verse beginning with "Because of its manifest nature" (*prakāśyatvāt*) which was spoken by the wives of his enemies upon his abandonment of his own city, [the author] explains it with the words "In these...
(*eṣu ca*) and so forth. For this very reason, even through the direct perception of a yogin, those subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are not established. || 6 ||
Commentary: Now the function of the mind is described: it is that which impels the gods and moves swiftly.
And it has the nature of volition.
Hearing and the other senses are the perceivers of objects such as the mind, sound, and so forth. (7)

The "gods" (devas) are so called because they shine (dyotana); they are the sense-faculties (indriyas). The mind (manas) should be understood as that which sets them in motion, that which incites them, which is characterized by rapid movement, and which possesses the quality of volition (saṅkalpa). The ears and other [senses], however, are the gods insofar as they each grasp their respective objects, such as sound and the rest. || 7 ||

The *Dīpikā* [comments] on the term "impelling the gods" (*devapravartaka*) by stating the meaning of the word "god" (*deva*): "because of sporting (*devana*) or because of shining (*dyotana*)," and so forth;
that is, because of the illumination of objects. Regarding the phrase "of them," and so forth: and that [illumination] occurs through the internal mental resolve (*manassaṅkalpa*).
And it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga* that the mind is twofold by virtue of its presiding over the external senses:
"That mind, which brings about experience for the enjoyer, has two functions;
for it always acts as the external organs through its own appropriate capacity, while the power of the senses resides within the self by means of [the mind's] contraction."
Because it abides within, the internal organ is called *manas*. It is characterized by its nature of rapid movement;
this he will demonstrate immediately thereafter. And as for its having "volition" (*saṅkalpa*) as its quality:
volition means determination or one-pointedness. Neither purity nor the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is the cause of that [volition].

It has been stated that because they consist of action and lack the nature of cognition, these two—the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) and the cognition of the apprehender (*grāhaka-pratyaya*)—are the causes [of the mind].
Therefore, this so-called "attention" (*avadhāna*), which is of the nature of action and distinct from those two, that which is its cause is the mind (*manas*).
And this he will explain immediately thereafter with the words beginning "it is a different reality" (*tattvāntara*). Now, how is this so?
The sense-faculties are not accepted as having multiple objects, unlike the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. Therefore, he says: "But the ear and so forth," and so on;

this is the meaning. If there were only one sense-faculty, then sounds and other objects would be perceived by the eye alone, yet forms and other objects are not perceived by the ear and the rest. Therefore, it is not one, but rather many. || 7 ||

Nevertheless, it appears as if simultaneous,
except for its rapid movement.

for example, at the time of experiencing a form, there is no experience of touch, nor an experience of taste and so forth. Even though [an object] may be as beautiful as a sweet, fragrant, high-quality, crackling sound—like the moon—

nevertheless, those cognitions of taste and the rest are indeed successive, their subtle sequence being imperceptible like the piercing of a hundred lotus petals. And this [simultaneity] would not occur without the mind’s rapid movement.

And because it is manifold, the fact that the mind is an effect is established by this as well. || 11 ||
Commentary: With the intention of refuting the view that the sense organs are composed of the elements (bhautika), he states that they are derived from the ego-principle (ahaṅkārika).
The sense-faculties of a certain being belong to various species because they have fixed objects and because they manifest odors and so forth.
They also have that as their substratum. || 12 ||

The ear grasps sound alone, and the skin grasps touch alone; likewise, for certain proponents, other sense organs as well—being restricted to specific objects by virtue of being their causes—are perceived as having distinct origins. For if they were derived from the *ahaṃkāra*, they would not possess such restriction to specific objects.

Furthermore, because they manifest odors and so forth, the supports (ādhāra) or substrata (āśraya) of those odors and so forth—namely earth and the other elements—are composed of those very supports. For it is observed that only a substance consisting of earth manifests odor, and the olfactory organ is the perceiver of odor. Therefore, the olfactory organ is composed of earth.
The tongue is composed of water; the eye is composed of fire; and so it is for the others.
The *Dīpikā* states: "By means of the phrase 'because of having a fixed meaning' and so forth, the Sage [Dharmakīrti] raises an objection based on the perspective of the Vaiśeṣikas and others.
Regarding the phrase "that which perceives sound alone": this refers to "some proponent," namely the Vaiśeṣika and others. (12)
Commentary: Is this then correct or not? To this he says:
"Let it be so, provided that [the self] does not take [an object]."
The sense of touch is a causal factor possessing qualities; it perceives objects not currently in contact with it, while turning away from those that are already in contact. (13)
The visual organ perceives the substances of fire, water, and earth along with their forms;
therefore, that [cognition] would be born from three substances.
It is not accepted by others in that manner. || 14 ||

If each sense organ does not take up—that is, does not grasp—another cause accompanied by qualities that is distinct from its own cause, let it be so. The meaning is this: if the sense organ were to grasp a substance of the same genus as its own cause, as well as its qualities, then...

The restriction of objects is held to be the indicator of the restriction of their material causes (*prakṛti*). However, since the senses perceive other substances and their qualities as well, it is therefore not logical that the senses indicate their material causes by virtue of having unrestricted objects. Now, what [is the case]?

No thief whatsoever can seize the sound once it has reached the musical instrument.
Even if the sense organs have restricted objects, you must first answer this which I ask:

if every portion of space characterized by the apertures of the body is the manifester of the entire range of sound—that is, of sound in its many varieties—then let it be said that the other openings, such as the nostrils and so forth, are likewise [manifesters] because they possess that same nature. The apprehension of that [space] is being precluded. [It asks] "otherwise how? meaning: under the view that [the senses] are material (*bhautikatva*). He states that even the word [in the reason] contains an implication through the qualification "because it is sound" (*śabdatvāt*). Commentary: And even in those cases where reasoning (*yukti*) is not possible as a means of comprehension,
[one should rely on it] even when it is inaccessible to reasoning, by virtue of the words of the virtuous (*sadvākya*).
Cognition free from affliction is superior;
the wise hold that knowledge of the immeasurable is better than knowledge of the measurable. (18)
Even regarding an object that lacks logical possibility, the cognition—that is, the comprehension—arising from the teaching of the True Scripture (sad-āgama) is unimpeded.
Why is this so? He says: "Because its object is limited. This is because inference, by its dependence on a logical mark (liṅga), has a limited object;
whereas the knowledge of the All-Seeing One, which takes the form of scripture, has an unlimited object.
Those who know the scriptures [maintain] that seniority is [the determining factor]. || 18 ||

The *Dīpikā*: With the intention that this is also established by scripture (*āgama*), he states that the authority of the Śaiva Āgama is unavoidable, beginning with the words "And even where... and so forth. And therein [are mentioned] the sense organs and the mind.

It is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "The organs of action, being impelled, operate from their very own locations, producing activity within their respective domains; [this] is remote for the deities of the intellect, but proximate for those whose nature is action. (18)
1. The ninety-fifth verse of the Ahaṅkārapaṭala. Commentary:
He speaks in order to specify that which was introduced [earlier], namely, "from the *mātrās* comes the five elements."
The five elements are ether, air, fire, water, and earth;
they possess one, two, three, four, and five qualities respectively, beginning with sound.
It possesses the function of providing space and so forth. || 19 ||
The qualities indicative of shaking, burning, flooding,
and roughness are found in air and the other elements; sound is found in space.
They go toward sounds that correspond in phonetic quality. || 20 ||
Space, air, fire, water, and earth constitute the five elements (*bhūta-pañcaka*).

These possess an increasing number of qualities, beginning with sound. That which has sound and the others as its qualities in an ascending order is thus described; therefore, space has the single quality of sound, while air possesses the qualities of sound and touch.
Fire has the qualities of sound, touch, and form; water has the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste;
and earth has the five qualities beginning with sound. This should be understood as being endowed with the functions of space and so forth, which will be described later.
These qualities, such as sound and the rest, which exist in air and the other elements, indicate [their respective actions] such as shaking and burning.
Since the sound *śaka-śaka* indicates vibration in the wind, the sound *dhaka-dhaka* points to flaming in fire,
and likewise the sound *cala-cala* indicates flowing in water, while the sound *khaḍa-khaḍa* declares hardness in earth; and these sounds are produced by virtue of their mutual impact.

"In the sky," that is, in space (*ākāśa*), they sing a "consonant" (*savarṇa*), meaning a similar syllable, which is the echo; thus, they are "those who sing the consonant-echoes"—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. This has been stated in the *Bhogakārikās*: "Sound is produced by that substance [space] within the four distinct elements; it is a collection of echoes."
"Like the sun risen in the sky, so it is perceived by the wise. Thus [ends the commentary on verses] 19–20.
1. The Eleventh Verse. *Dīpikā*:
Now, in order to demonstrate the elements (*bhūta*), he explains the two sūtras beginning with "Space" (*vyoma*).

"Space has sound as its sole quality," and so forth. Now, [the Vaiśeṣikas argue that] sound is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) belonging to something possessing touch (*sparśavat*), because—while being perceptible to us—it is preceded by qualities of its own cause and does not persist as long as the substance itself, just like pleasure and other such qualities; thus, they maintain that sound is a specific quality of air and the like.

[The opponent claims: "It is indeed prohibited [to say that sound is a quality of tangible things]. That is incorrect, because it would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*). For we do not maintain that sound is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of tangible things; rather, by virtue of its existence in the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) of the primary elements (*bhūta*), it is only a general quality (*sāmānyaguṇa*).
Therefore, we are merely establishing that sound is not a quality of tangible things. Even in that case, if...
The phenomenon of an echo is a property (*dharma*); nevertheless, this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).

Since it has been stated that this [echo] is a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*), its being a quality of something possessing touch (*sparśavadguṇatva*) is already established; for it has been proven to possess specific qualities such as pleasure and pain. In that case as well, there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*). Therefore, by means of direct perception...
The properties of tangible things such as earth and so forth are perceived. This very point is stated:
"because words such as *śaka-śaka* [occur] in relation to air and so forth," and so on. The meaning is that the substratum (*āśraya*) of the echo (*pratiśabda*) is space alone. || 19 = 20 ||
1. The reading "vaiśeṣikoktā" (stated by the Vaiśeṣikas) exists [in some manuscripts]. Commentary:
"Possessing the functions of providing space and so forth" is the common characteristic (*sāmānya*) of the five elements.
In order to explain by way of analysis that which was stated as a qualification, he says: "Arrangement, providing space,
cooking, gathering, and supporting."
And the functions of air, ether, fire, water, and earth. || 21 ||

The arrangement or formation of wind is its function; the granting of space, that is, room, is the operation of ether (vyoman); cooking or ripening is the function of fire (tejas); the gathering or support is that of the waters (ap); and holding or sustaining is the function of the earth (dharaṇī). || 21 ||
The *Dīpikā* explains the sūtra beginning with "vyūha" (array). It states: "vyūha is arrangement," and so forth.
"Vyūha" refers to the joining together of parts. This is also an illustration [for other actions] such as trembling. As they have said:

"Air has touch, sound, support, and motion as its marks. Regarding "of space," and so forth, the meaning is that space is inferred by its effect, which is the nature of providing room (*avakāśa*). Now, some followers of Jaimini maintain that space is perceived because it is perceptible; as Maṇḍana [the Bhagavat] said: [text follows].
"How could the fixed location of a word be understood in isolation? For the division [of space] resulting from the senses and the contact with a location belong to that which is falling.
This is incorrect;

for that space would have to be established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as being of the nature of an opening (*avakāśa*) consisting in the absence of corporeal substances (*mūrtadravya*), and because it is formless (*arūpa*).

Therefore, the perceptibility of space is not established from a reason that is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*). What, then, is it that is seen here? It is simply the substance of light (*tejo-dravya*), known as illumination, which is all-pervading. Consequently, the conjunctions and disjunctions of birds [with this light] are established through perception. How, then, does the cognition "space provides room" arise?

It is established that [space] has the nature of the absence of corporeal substances, because sound exists as its substratum by way of being delimited by the space that consists in the absence of corporeal substances. Therefore, its apprehension in that form is due to error and not from the perspective of ultimate reality. For instance, sound, being a quality (*guṇa*), requires a substratum (*āśraya*), just like a variegated color.

[Such things as] cloth or walls; nor can space (avakāśa) be the substratum, because it consists of the absence of corporeal substances. Therefore, since sound is established as being qualified by space, space is understood to have sound as its quality. If this is so, then space must be eternal, because it is perceptible.

It might be so; but that is not correct. For it has been stated that [the ego-principle] is subtle only in relation to earth and the other elements, whereas because it is an effect of the *tanmātras*, it is gross in relation to them. Furthermore, it is not all-pervading (*asarvagata*). As they say: "Form (*mūrti*) is the dimension of a substance that is not all-pervading. Therefore, because it possesses form, and because its specific nature is restricted to each individual self (*pratyātman*), it is manifold.

Thus, its impermanence is indeed established; for even that which has a common form will be described as the support of the worlds (*bhuvana*), and it is impossible for the worlds—characterized by their specific arrangements—to be subject to destruction. As he will state: "The city and so forth, which are objects of experience, material, and subject to dissolution, are the maturation of fire."

Thus [it is said]. This is an illustration [applicable] to light and the rest as well. Consequently, the distinctions among fire—such as that produced from the earth or from a mine—and the further distinctions within terrestrial fire, such as the *āhavanīya* and others, are to be understood from the venerable *Mataṅga* and other [scriptures]. || 21 ||
1. The meaning is "how might it be?
2. "Space" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. This is the commentary (*vṛtti*).
Here the Sage questions by way of the Vaiśeṣika perspective:
"Sound is indeed a quality of space, because it is perceived elsewhere than that."
"O Blessed One, some say:
how can there be the qualities of all beings? (22)

"O Blessed One, since sound arises from such things as a drum, and because it is perceived elsewhere [than its source], it is a quality of space (*khaguṇa*). Thus, it is logically established that sound is indeed a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇa*), because it is perceived elsewhere than its substratum. The meaning is that it is not a specific quality of something possessing tangibility (*sparśavat*). Furthermore, how then can this be called a quality of all the elements (*sarvabhūtaguṇa*)? (22)

The *Dīpikā* says: "Again, [the author] objects to the view that sound is a quality of the five elements, stating 'here the Sage [says]... and so forth, beginning with 'sound is a quality of space' (*śabdaḥ khaguṇaḥ*). [He does so] because it is perceived elsewhere; that is, in the auditory faculty, in space, and so on. (22)
Commentary: To this it is said:
Where else [could it be] but in the space of hearing?
How else could that quality exist elsewhere?
For regarding the substratum desired by others, human experience alone is the determiner in that case. (23)

Regarding what was stated—that [the auditory organ] is distinct from its substratum because of its perception elsewhere—if it is intended that this "elsewhere" refers to the space of hearing (*śravaṇākāśa*), then how can it be said that "it and its quality exist elsewhere"? This is the underlying intention: the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to space (*ākāśa*). Thus, being a quality of that [space], it is perceived in the auditory space (*śrotrākāśa*).

How is it said that [the sound] is elsewhere? Now, if it is intended that [the sound arises] from another substratum (āśraya), that is not tenable. For in this case, experience is what determines the relationship for persons. Sound is perceived as having sound itself as its substratum; for instance, there is the cognition: "The sound is here on the drum," or "The sound is here on the lute. (23)
The *Dīpikā* explains the sūtra of the rebuttal, beginning with "from the substratum" (*āśrayāt*), etc. (23).
Commentary: If you then think that consciousness [resides] even at the root of the ear at certain times;
Let there be a transformation of this [intellect] as well, like the functioning of the auditory organ; what loss is there? || 24 ||
Now, you might think that consciousness (saṃvit) occurs even at the root of the ear. What follows from this?
Does the fact of its occurring there establish that sound has space as its sole quality?

[No,] for like the functioning of the auditory organ, this [sound] also reaches the vicinity of the ear through a process of transformation (pariṇāma), by way of a wave-like succession (vīcitaraṅga-vṛtti).

Perhaps there may be some apprehension [of the probans]; yet there is no harm in this. Furthermore, reasons that are contradicted by perception or scripture do not establish their intended object, because they are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). For example: "A human skull is pure because it is a part of a living being," or "Fire produces coldness because it is non-hot," and so forth. || 24 ||

The *Dīpikā* explains the prima facie objection beginning with "kadācit" (at some time) and so forth. It then explains the subsequent passage beginning with "atha" (now) as the refutation, and the passage beginning with "kiñcātaḥ" (what follows from this) and so forth.

Then he says that this reason—"because of being perceived elsewhere than its substratum"—is improper because it is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed), as it is contradicted by both perception and scripture; [this is expressed in the passage beginning with] "And not," etc. (24).
The commentary says:
"Contradicted by scripture and direct perception."
The experts in logic know that reasons do not establish the object [of proof], because they are fallacious due to the lapse of time (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa). || 25 ||

"By scripture" refers to such [scriptural passages] as "this is sound among the five [elements]," and so forth. Logicians maintain that those reasons which are subject to sublation by perception—consisting of the experience of touch as a specific quality—are not capable of establishing the object in question, because they are *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed). || 25 ||
Commentary:
Or, if it is argued that sound is a quality of space because it is perceived elsewhere than its substratum, then at that time:
Thus, this [quality] being established, let this odor also be a quality of space. || 25½ ||

The meaning is that this [absurd consequence] also follows. What is it? He says: "this odor. For it is perceived even when the *ketakī* flower and other such things have been removed. Since it is perceived elsewhere than its substrate, it must necessarily be established that this odor is also a quality of space (*ākāśa*). Because:

The fragrance of flowers such as the *ketakī* and *campaka* is perceived even when they are at a great distance; and the point is that just as this [fragrance] is not sublated by either perception or scripture, so too the previously mentioned reason—"because it is perceived elsewhere than its substrate"—is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). This is the intended meaning.
The *Dīpikā* states that [the author] raises another objection by means of the fragment of the sūtra beginning with "dūṣaṇāntaram api" and so forth. It says "yadivā" and so forth.
With "ayam" and so forth, he shows that very same point. With "āśrayād anyatra" and so forth, for this very reason, [he addresses] this logical reason (*hetu*).
He states that the sublation by perception is established, beginning with "And of this," etc. (25½).
Commentary: Concluding [the discussion], he states the specific qualities of the four elements:
"Thus, among these five, this is sound."
Tangibility resides in the four primary elements: earth and air possess non-cold and non-hot tangibility, while water and fire possess cold and hot tangibility. (26½)
In fire, color is radiant; in water, it is white; on earth, it is manifold, such as white and so forth.
Taste exists in all three, while [taste] is present in water alone.
Sweetness is of six kinds on earth. || 27½ ||
Odor on the earth is considered by the wise to be both unpleasant and pleasant. (28)

By this stated reasoning, this sound exists in all five elements; likewise, touch exists in these same [elements] excluding space—therein, in earth and air, it is neither cold nor hot; in water, it is only cold;
and in fire, it is only hot. As for "form in three," it exists only in earth, water, and fire; therein, in fire...

It is luminous and radiant in water, white in earth, and of many kinds such as white in other elements. Taste exists in earth and water; therein, it is sweet in water. In earth, there are pungent, sour, salty, bitter, acrid, and astringent tastes. Smell, in the form of fragrant and foul, exists in earth.
It is desired by the learned. || 26 = 28 ||
The *Dīpikā* explains that [the author] elaborates upon the fact that the elements possess one additional quality each, beginning with sound; thus he says: "By this," and so forth. || 28 ||
Commentary: Now, the manner in which these elements are situated within the body is described. In the body, there are bone, flesh, hair, and skin...
In the nails and teeth, the earth element is present;
in urine, blood, phlegm, sweat, semen, and so forth, water is established. (29)
[The fire] is in the heart, in the digestive [heat], and in the bile of the eyes, because its specific properties are observed therein,
through the various functions such as the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth.
The wind has already been mentioned by you. || 30 ||
Through the persistence of the functioning of pride,
[the breath] pervades the void within all the channels.

Earth is situated in the body as a derivative element (*bhautika*) within the bones, flesh, and so forth; water is in the urine, blood, and so forth; and the digestive fire (*audarya-tejas*) is in the region of the heart during the process of digestion, serving as the fuel for food and drink. It is also present in the bile of the eyes. This should be applied to each respective element based on the observation of its specific properties. In that regard, concerning the heart:

Because its property of heat is perceived in cooking, its property of ripening in digestion, and its light in the bile—manifesting as warmth, brilliance, and so forth—it is established as being composed of fire (*taijasa*). Just as air (*vāyu*) exists in various states through the distinctions of its functions such as *prāṇa* and *apāna*, so too has it been stated by you; thus the speaker [addresses] the listener.

This recalls the sage Bharadvāja, who stated previously: "That which is called activity (*vṛtti*) or leading forth (*praṇayana*) is termed 'life' (*jīvana*). Furthermore, in all the channels (*nāḍī*), space remains through the persistence of the function of the ego, that is, through the persistence of the operation of the *ahaṅkāra*. || 29 = 30 = 30½ ||
1. The twenty-second verse in the section on conditions (*pratyayaprakaraṇa*). *Dīpikā*:
Now, the stability of the external constituents of the body, such as the bones and so forth, is described starting with the words "deha" and so on.

Thus he says: "Now, as for these... and so forth. Here, the wind (*nabhasvān*) is mentioned in connection with the activity of ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), which follows upon the function of pride (*garva*). It should be explained that one's own space (*svam ākāśam*) abides within all the channels (*nāḍī*) by virtue of providing them with room.
But how is it that space [is affected] by the persistence of the activity of pride, and so forth? || 29 = 30 = 30½ ||
Commentary: Now, he speaks in order to describe the multitude of principles (tattvas) beginning with Kalā and ending with Earth as being the constituent causes of the subtle body.
From the agent down to the furthest reaches of the earth,
this subtle means for achieving one's purpose is restricted to the experience of each individual soul.
It is determined through its differentiation. || 31½ ||

It is called the *prayoktrī* (the impelling) *kalā* because it impels the person (*puruṣa*) by stimulating his power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). From that [kalā] down to the earth (*kṣiti*), this entire collection of principles (*tattva-vṛnda*) is the means for accomplishing the goals of the person; it is perceived as restricted and specific to each individual self due to the diversity of their experiences. If it were common [to all], [there would be no such distinction].
Because a distinction in experience would be untenable. But was it not said that action (*karman*) is the cause of the distinction in experience?

True; but not directly, rather through a succession of causes. For instance, action produces a distinction in the body of the self (*ātman*), and the variety of experience is produced by that distinction; thus there is no fault. And that distinction in experience—

Since the diversity of subtle bodies, distinguished by differences such as elephants, horses, and so forth, does not occur without [a cause], karma alone is the cause in this case as well; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. || 31½ ||
Commentary: And this is the subtle body (sūkṣma-śarīra).
Because its activity occurs simultaneously in all directions—
Because it does not arise [again], it does not go everywhere; even though they are of different classes, they have a single fruit, like the lamp, its wick, and the vessel. (32½)
If this [consciousness] were all-pervading and omnipresent, then its activity would arise simultaneously everywhere;

but it is not so. For its activity occurs only in a certain single location, characterized by the arising of the experience of the fruits of karma, consisting of various distinct types of manifold parts and so forth.

Furthermore, even though this [manifestation] arises from various factors, it has a single result; just as objects such as oil, a vessel, fire, and a wick— though produced by distinct causes— accomplish the single purpose of dispelling darkness,

so too should this fruit of the experience of karma be understood to arise from the subtle elements (tanmātra), the Great Principle (mahat), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and the limited portions (kalā), despite their diverse origins.
The *Dīpikā* states: "By the words beginning with 'sarvataḥ' (from all sides), its very omnipresence and its being the sole means for experience are expressed";
thus he says, "And this," and so forth. || 32½ ||
Commentary: Now, there is a verse for the purpose of concluding the explained subject matter and for introducing another section:
"Thus is this subtle body (ātivāhika) of this living being."

Since this [attainment] is not sufficient merely through a slight emergence from the interior of the dense forest of consciousness due to contact with consciousness, I shall describe the series of principles (tattvas) belonging to the world of beings (bhuvana), for the sake of the prosperity of the foundational body and its objects. 33½.

Thus, this subtle body (*ātivāhika-vapuḥ*) carries along the transmigrating being’s karma that must necessarily be experienced; this is what has been stated briefly by way of a summary—this is the remainder [of the sense]. And of what nature is it?
