It is consciousness (*cit*), due to its association with consciousness—that is, by virtue of its union with consciousness—even though it is insentient (*acid*), because it is never separated from sentience.

The meaning is "as if it were the nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpa*). "Gahana" means *māyā*; that which evolves within its womb and has that as its characteristic is "gahanagarbhavivarti. Since this much alone is not sufficient, I shall describe the series of *bhuvana-tattvas* which constitute the substratum of objects of enjoyment. He asks: for what purpose? He replies: "for the prosperity of the supporting body and its objects."

For the sake of that worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) which is the support of the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*), consisting of the enjoyment of objects such as garments, sandalwood paste, and so forth; or alternatively, for the sake of the supports— the gross bodies— which are the substrates, and the objects born of those worlds, namely the sense-objects (*indriyārtha*).

For their exaltation and arising, I shall describe the series of the Bhuvana-tattvas, since within that continuum of Tattvas and Bhuvanas—which serves as the substratum—the diversity of bodies and the diversity of enjoyments must necessarily be known during initiation; this is what is intended to be explained hereafter. (33½)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, on the Senses and so forth, in the *Mṛgendravṛtti* composed by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Vidyākaṇṭha.
[The] *Dīpikā*.
With the words "iti" and so forth, the conclusion is made regarding the uncommon creation of the principles (*tattva-sṛṣṭi*) which was previously described as the originator of the subtle body;
whereas the common [creation], consisting of the worlds (*bhuvana*), will be discussed in the immediately following section.

He says "it is proposed that the creation of reality (*tattvasṛṣṭi*) [is as follows]" and so forth. "In its womb" means within the womb of *māyā*, from *kalā* down to the earth (*kṣiti*). Therefore, the sense is that in all the worlds there is only the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*). "It is not sufficient" means—supplying the ellipsis—it is not sufficient for the variety of enjoyments and their means. "The elemental body" (*bhautiko dehaḥ*)... [refers to the gross body].
This is an illustration of the body born of the world (*bhuvanaja*). For this very reason, he states another interpretation beginning with "Or else" (*yadvā*), and so forth.
Furthermore, he explains that this section on the paths (*adhvan*) is useful for initiation (*dīkṣā*), beginning with "Since," and so forth.
Thus ends [the passage] in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā* composed by the teacher Aghoraśiva.
The twelfth chapter, the Investigation of the Faculties and so forth, is completed.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter, the Chapter on Time (adhvan). Commentary:
Now, with the words "for the sake of establishing the meaning already stated" and so forth, the description of the worlds and other elements is introduced;
this sets forth the connection and purpose indicated at the end of the preceding section:
"Now, for the sake of establishing the meaning already stated..."
Maheśvara created the worlds and so forth from the common sources, beginning with *kalā*.

Now, regarding the phrase "having spoken": immediately after the desire to emit the bodies, instruments, and worlds—which serve as the means for various experiences—in order to pacify the bonds of karma that obstruct the unsurpassed supreme good (*niratiśaya-śreyas*) for those of impure souls;
[it was] Maheśvara, the Lord Ananteśa. [He spoke] of the aforementioned matter concerning the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*), characterized by experience (*bhoga*).

For the sake of accomplishing and bringing to completion in its entirety, he fashioned the worlds from the common primary materials, beginning with *kalā*; and this fashioning of them is not a production of things previously non-existent, but rather occurs through their existence in the form of potentiality (*śakti*), as explained in the section on the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).
Manifestation is the becoming evident from its own cause by way of a specific individual form. || 1 ||
The Dīpikā: Now he introduces the section on the paths (*adhvan*), which constitutes the remainder of the category of the fetters (*pāśa*). Regarding the phrase "Now" (*atha*) and so forth:
its connection to the categories of reality is by way of being a category of the fetters; its connection to the context is precisely by way of being the section on knowledge (*vidyāpāda*).
The *pāṭalika* (chapter-section) has been shown at the end of the previous chapter. The connection according to the sūtra is indicated by the phrase "the net of bonds" (*pāśajāla*).

And that which consists of sentences is indicated by such statements as "engaged with the instruments, established in effects, together with the worlds" (*pravṛttaḥ karaṇaiḥ kāryarūḍhaissabhauvanaiḥ*). Regarding the phrase "of what has been stated," etc.: for the worlds (*bhuvana*) are indeed the substrata of experience (*bhoga*).
It has been stated that these are the causes of the various worlds, insentient bodies, and objects; and these [objects] belong to all selves in common, and so forth. || 1 ||
Those [mandalas], beginning with Kālānala and ending with Kalāprānta, are the maṇḍala;
thus know the reality of saṃsāra.
They declare it to be the place of enjoyment. || 2 ||

Commentary: These [realms] extend from the world of Kālāgni up to the worlds of Kalā. Those who know the ultimate reality describe this sphere of worldly existence as the locus of experience (*bhogasthāna*). By this, the state of being "with parts" (*sakalatva*) previously mentioned is established.
1. [The categories] possess those marks [of being effects] because they arise from sources such as *kalā* and so forth, but not from *māyā*.
For it is heard in the venerable *Svāyaṃbhuvatantra* and other texts that *māyā* is without parts (*akalā*).
Furthermore, if one were to admit that what possesses a configuration is an object of experience (*bhogya*), then for that which possesses a configuration and is an object of experience...

For fear of the consequence that [the world] would be non-eternal like a jar and so forth, it must necessarily be admitted that it is devoid of structure and is not an object of experience. Now, if Māyā is not an object of experience for the person (puruṣa), then since no other object of experience is possible apart from its effects, there would be nothing at all to be experienced; thus, the person would simply be a non-experiencer.

The Puruṣa is attached. It is true; however, that which exists in the form of manifestation (vyakti) is his object of enjoyment (bhogya), whereas this [Prakṛti] is not so, because she exists merely as power (śaktimātra)—this has been stated. || 2 ||
1. "The place of enjoyment" is the remainder [of the phrase].
*Dīpikā*: "Up to the worlds of Kalā" means up to the world of Gahaneśa situated at the summit of Kalā.
Immediately after this, he will state: "In Māyā as well, Gahaneśa and others are recited as the presiding lords.

In response to the inquiry, "Whose place of enjoyment is it?", he says: "That which was previously mentioned," and so forth. "Of that bearer of the mark" means of the Sakala who bears the mark of being possessed of kalās. However, it is not from Māyā; for even the worlds of Māyā are not... [the text continues].
They are manifested as abiding within Māyā; however, the meaning is that they reside at the limit of the Kalās which are the effects of that [Māyā]. || 2 ||
Commentary: Even if this were so, since those specific worlds are mentioned within that [Māyā-tattva],
and because it would be impossible for them to be "worlds" (*bhuvana*) without possessing a particular spatial arrangement, the *māyā-tattva* must also [be admitted].
He says that [the objection] that there would be the consequence of having a spatial arrangement [is not valid]:
"Even in Māyā, lords such as Gahaneśa and others are recited."
And the purification of reality (tattvaśuddhi) in initiation— all that is at the beginning of its performance.
It is understood from the scriptural declarations of eternality, omnipresence, and so forth;
that which is perceived as an object of experience, such as the city and the like, [is not the ultimate reality].
That which possesses form is subject to the law of destruction.
Although in the Māyātattva, Rudras such as Maṇḍaleśvara and Gahaneśvara are recited as inhabitants of the worlds— as it will be stated: "Ananta, Trikala, Goptṛ,
Kṣemīśa, Brahmaṇaḥpati, Dhruva, Tejo'dhipa, the two Rudras, Gahaneśa, and Sarvarāj."

The Rudras who preside over Māyā are the lords of the mandalas. Although it will be stated in the Kriyāpāda that even during initiation (dīkṣā) there is purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi) by virtue of [the soul] abiding in the principle of Māyā, nevertheless, that [purification] does not bring about a specific spatial arrangement for it; rather, it refers to those worlds which are said to reside therein.

And those residing there, as well as the lords of the mandalas—all this is to be known as being at the summit of *kalā*, which is the effect produced by that [Māyā]. The meaning is that *kalā* is the first manifestation of Māyā in the form of *śakti*, and all of this is situated upon its head. To the question, "How is this known? he says:

Regarding "eternality, pervasiveness, and so forth": for its eternality and pervasiveness have been established previously and are heard of in the scriptures (*āgama*). Furthermore, if it were to contain the worlds within itself, then it would possess a specific configuration; and if that were the case, it would be non-pervasive and subject to destruction. He states the reason for this as well.

"Whatever has been seen before," etc. This means that for whatever reason, whatever is seen or currently being perceived— such as cities, walls, and so forth— which is corporeal and subject to dissolution while possessing the quality of being an object of experience (*bhogya*),

and within whose womb these worlds with their specific arrangements reside— if its status as an object of experience is accepted directly [as belonging to the Self], [then it follows that the Self is subject to change].

In that case, it would follow that [the cause] possesses corporeality and perishability; therefore, there is no fault whatsoever provided that it is precisely its effect—such as *kalā* and the rest, which exists in a manifest form—that is joined with the worlds. (3–4)
1. There is a variant reading, *rūpabhuvane*.
The *Dīpikā* states that in order to demonstrate this very point, he raises a doubt regarding the two sūtras beginning with "in Māyā" (*māyāyām*).
"If it is thus," and so forth. "The purification of reality" (*tattvaśuddhi*) is an elliptical expression that includes the purification of the worlds (*bhuvanaśuddhi*).
He summarizes the points already explained with the words "And of this," and so forth. And within those worlds, Śiva exists precisely in the state of presiding authority (*adhikārāvastha*). (3–4)
The commentary states: This very same principle should also be followed in the case of the pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā) known as Mahāmāyā. Thus he says:
Even in the pure path (śuddhādhvan), those who are the lords of the supreme Māyā are also recited within that [pure path].
They too [placed it] upon the crown of his head. || 5 ||
On the pure path, that which consists of supreme *śuddhavidyā* is designated as *māyā*.

Thus it is stated in the *Raurava*: "Above *māyā* is *mahāmāyā*. In that regard, those who are authorized for their respective tasks to be performed within their own domains must also carry out that work at its head, according to the sequence taught in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures.
They are to be understood as established. || 5 ||

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: It states that the worlds beginning with Indhika are also included within these, saying "this very same principle," and so forth. [This refers to] Mahāmāyā, which consists of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), and not to that which is its effect.

As it has been said: "The supreme is the Vāgīśvarī-vidyā; Māyā is remembered as the lower vidyā. And the previous word *kṛti* refers to the one who holds authority (*adhikārī*). Regarding this, he says "therein," and so forth. Within those worlds, Śiva himself, while remaining in the state of possessing authority, is designated by various names according to the distinctions of his limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and is thus called the Lord of those respective worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*). As for the worlds themselves...
He will state that the ultimate division consists of the state of the *bindu*.
He says, "in the sequence taught in the venerable *Matanga* and other scriptures," because it has been stated even in the *Matanga* and elsewhere:
"He may be an initiate (*adhikārī*), an enjoyer (*bhogī*), or one intent on absorption (*layī*), according to figurative usage. And here, those who are initiated...

By the word "presiding" (*adhikṛta*), he makes this known: through the word "Lord" (*pati*) found in the Sūtra, the worlds in their state of presiding are indicated; because it is precisely those [worlds] that possess a specific arrangement, his abiding upon their summit is stated. And for this very reason, [he is the Lord] of *Śuddhavidyā* and so forth, which constitute the material cause (*upādāna*) of the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*).

The accomplishment of Mahāmāyā is to be understood. Consequently, even the bodies of the Vidyās, Vidyeśvaras, and others are not composed of Māyā, because they have transcended Māyā and are devoid of karma and the like. That which is the material cause of their worlds and their bodies is that Mahāmāyā known as Kuṇḍalinī. || 5 ||
1. If it is established that [the word] has the sense of "introduction" (*adhikāra*), then it is correct. Commentary:
Now, the height and breadth of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) situated below on this path shall be described.
And in order to state the measurement of the worlds contained therein, he describes the measurement in *yojanas* by means of the sequence beginning with the atom (*paramāṇu*).
Dust is seen transversely.
At the third station, which possesses sixty-four qualities, there would be the tip of a hair [of the sun's rays] permeated by a net.
A nit, a louse, and likewise a barley grain— these multiplied threefold constitute a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
A cubit (*pāṇi*) is multiplied by those same [fingers].
The bow is marked by those [four] and the Vedas [four].
A *daṇḍa* should be known as two *dhanus*; a *krośa* consists of two thousand of those;
they say that two *krośas* make a *gavyūti*.
And two gavyūtis make one yojana.
The *kapāla* hell is as vast as the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) in its thickness, measuring many *yojanas*.

When the most subtle dust particle visible to the eye is seen entering through the interstices of a lattice in the light of the sun, that measure should be multiplied by eight, and that result again multiplied by eight,
until at the third stage the measure named *kācāgra* (hair-tip) is reached. And it has been said:

In the illustrious *Svatantra*, it is said: "When there is a conjunction of eight atoms (*paramāṇu*), that is called a *trasareṇu*; it is also termed a 'lotus-dust' (*padmarajas*). O Goddess, eight *trasareṇus* constitute a hair-tip (*vālāgra*);
by that same rule, eight hair-tips make a nit (*likṣā*), and eight of those make a louse (*yūkā*)."

By those eight [units], a barley-corn (*yava*) is to be known. "In this way" means that eight barley-corns constitute one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). A cubit (*pāṇi*) is multiplied by those very [fingers] tripled;
that is, a cubit is formed when those same [fingers]—multiplied by three, thus twenty-four finger-breadths—are further multiplied [to form the measure].
Since the word "Veda" indicates the number four, one should understand that the measurement known as a *dhanus* (bow) is marked by those four cubits (*pāṇi*). Two *dhanus* make a *daṇḍa* (staff);
two thousand *daṇḍas* make a *krośa*; two *krośas* make a *gavyūti*; and two of those make a *yojana*.
The shell of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍakapāla) should be known to extend for ten million yojanas, forming an arbuda of these [yojanas]. (6–8½)
1. "Of the subtle atoms situated in the rays of the sun through a lattice" is the meaning.
*Dīpikā*: [The commentary] connects the three and a half sūtras beginning with "rajas" (dust) etc. "Now," etc. || 6–8½ ||
Within it is a golden abode;
for it is indeed the very same as that of the Fire of Time.
There dwells the God, surrounded by Rudras of such a kind, possessing the sharp-rayed brilliance of the fire at the end of time.
He is renowned as Kālāgni.
In whomsoever his radiant power is aroused, fear arises by that power in all beings existing throughout the three times.
And when urged by the Destroyer, O Lord... || 11 ||

"Of that" refers to the interior of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). Within it is the golden abode of Kālāgni, measuring ten million [yojanas]. In that abode dwells Kālāgni, surrounded by numerous Rudras possessing a brilliance equal to ten million suns at the end of a kalpa;
he whose splendor is kindled when he is impelled toward dissolution by the supreme Lord’s power known as Saṃhartrī.
Terror arises in all beings existing throughout the entire course of time. || 11 ||
The *Dīpikā* states: "By the words 'of that' (*tasya*) and so forth, the worlds contained within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) are described along with their measurements.
Thus he says: "Of that," and so on. (11)
From its very nature, ten crores of flames issued forth,
extending for half a yojana.
The smoke was thick and most terrible.
Commentary: By its very nature, those flames are ten crores in measure; the smoke is five crores, thick, dense, formidable, and unbearable.
1. There is a variant reading: *kālādhvavartibhūtānām*. 2. This means "measuring ten million yojanas.
3. This means "five times ten million yojanas."
Then there are thirty-three *puṭas*,
each measuring ten lakhs less than a crore;
the intervals between them are thirty-two.
Hundreds of thousands of evil-souled ones. || 13 ||
These places were created by the Ordainer of Time as causes for torment.

Commentary: Immediately following that, there are thirty-three compartments (puṭas) consisting of the expansion of the hells, each measuring ninety lakhs [yojanas], with thirty-two intermediate spaces between them, each measuring one lakh. These are as follows:
"It was created by Adhva-vedhas for the purpose of tormenting the wicked"—that is to say, by Ananteśa, the creator of the path of the worlds. || 13½ ||
I shall declare those [names] to you by their names;
listen to me, O foremost of the twice-born.
Raurava, Dhvānta, Śīta, Uṣṇa,
Santāpa, Abja, Mahāmbuja— these,
with Kālasūtra as the eighth, are indeed [the hells].
They are known as the hells. || 15 ||
Commentary: Now, the names of the eight great hells:
[the first] is called Sūcyāsya (Needle-mouth), and [the second] Kālakhaṅga (Black-sword).
O Sage, there are those with razor-edged garments, and those who suffer from the intense heat of burning glowing coals. (16)
There arise eight [beings] most loathsome, following upon great sounds and words. || 16½ ||
1. And there exists the reading "aṣṭau ca bhībhatsāḥ. [The] commentary [states]: "Extremely loathsome; exceedingly terrifying. The word for 'great' is hell (naraka)."
The meaning is that those which possess a form corresponding to this designation are known as the "Great Hells. [End of] commentary.
Now follows the group of eight kings of the hells.
They were smeared with lac, devourers of flesh, and they breathed out without breathing in. || 17 ||
1. Yugma, Adri, Śālmalī, Loha,
Pradīpta, Kṣutpipāsaka,
and the Heap of Worms (Kṛmīṇāṃ Nicaya).
These are proclaimed to be kings. || 18 ||
1. There is a variant reading: *yugmārdra*.
Now, by means of the passage beginning with "the iron pillar" (*lohastambha*), the eight names known as the *Rājarājeśvarāṣṭaka* are stated:
the iron pillar, then feces and urine...
Likewise, there is the river Vaitaraṇī;
and Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Kumbhīpāka, and Raurava. || 19 ||
The Avīci hell is followed by Mahāpadānu;
these are remembered as the lords of the kings of kings. || 19½ ||
Now, in order to determine the number of these layers along with the intervening spaces, he says: "The number of yojanas for these layers together with the hells... (20).
There are thirty-two million and two hundred thousand, O best of the twice-born. (20½)
Thirty koṭis and two lakhs is the measure of the thirty-three sections together with their intervening spaces;
from that, thirty thousand [are subtracted].
Having abandoned the earth, she became like fresh lac.
It consists of iron in its eastern half and gold in its western half.
Immediately after that, having left aside thirty thousand yojanas, the earth measuring nine hundred thousand [yojanas] consists of gold in its eastern half, while the other half consists of iron;
this is its lower layer.
And half of that [mass] is of clay, and half is of iron. || 22 ||
There, the lord of these thirty-two hells is stationed;
he is renowned as Kūśmāṇḍa.
Possessing the brilliance of the fire of the sun at the time of universal dissolution. || 23 ||
With a terrifying face, enraged, with round, hollow eyes,
and a chisel in his hand, he was likewise accompanied by such beings.
He is enveloped by increasingly numerous elements. || 24 ||
Below the golden enclosure of the earth consisting of nine layers mentioned immediately above, there is an iron enclosure;
half of that is of clay and half is of iron. Therein reside the thirty-two previously mentioned hells, over which the lord named Kūśmāṇḍa presides.
He remains surrounded by such beings, distinguished by attributes such as having a terrifying mouth;
he is one whose hollows are rounded in their interiors and whose eyes are shaped like shallow bowls (*śarāva*). Thus, the *ṭaṅka* mentioned previously is a battle-axe (*paraśu*). || 24 ||

The *Dīpikā* states: Thus, together with the lower wall of the *maṇḍala*, the seventeen crores [of *yojanas*] extending from the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*) down to the end of Smoke constitute the extent of the hells; these are the intervening forms, along with the upper and lower chambers.

There are thirty-three. Here, thirty-two hells, beginning with Raurava, are shown as the primary ones, because their total number is one hundred and forty. As it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*: "One hundred and forty is proclaimed to be their number."
"Regarding the thirty-two kings therein," and so forth, "and among these...

The point is this: since their lord is included within the world-sphere (*bhuvana*) of Kūṣmāṇḍa, during the initiation (*dīkṣā*) pertaining to the world-spheres, those hells are purified precisely through the purification of him. || 24 ||
Above the layer of iron and gold, this is the eighth earth;
it consists of six thousand [yojanas] each, while the middle one is [four thousand].
She is free from the three crores of Arka-lakṣas.
The Vasatīs consist of nine thousand;
beyond them is the Daśasahasrakī.
Thus, seven of these [groups] are established by the virtuous.
The seven netherworlds (pātāla) are thus renowned. || 26 ||
1. There is also a clear variant reading: "sāṣṭādaśalakṣadvikoṭikī.
Following that which was mentioned as the two layers of gold and iron, this earth is the eighth, upon which we are situated.
Beyond this, there are six other stages (*bhūmi*) measuring one thousand [kalpas];
among these six, that which occurs in the middle is the seventh stage, the "Middle" (*madhyā*). It measures twelve hundred and eighty-eight million [kalpas].
The meaning is "lakṣas" (hundreds of thousands). In the intervals between these eight levels (*bhūmi*) are the dwellings (*vasatayaḥ*), which are abodes (*āspadāni*).
Each measures nine thousand [yojanas]. Regarding the phrase "the one above":
it refers to the dwelling situated above, which will be described as having golden abodes measuring one thousand *yojanas*, belonging to Hāṭakeśāna.
That [earth] serves as the foundation for ten thousand [yojanas]; and seven of these dwellings are called the "Seven Pātālas" by the learned. || 26 ||
The *Dīpikā* explains the passage beginning with "ayorukma" (iron-gold) and so forth, starting with "kāñcana" (golden) and so forth. This is the meaning:
[it refers to] the first earth, measuring one thousand [yojanas], and the seventh earth.
In the midst of this eighth earth, which measures three hundred million *koṭis* of *arcalakṣas* and whose intervals between each of its six dwellings measure nine thousand *yojanas*,
there resides that which is the lower portion of this earth and serves as the seat of Hāṭakeśa.

Together with the dwelling measuring ten thousand [yojanas], there are seven garments. Its upper portion is the surface of the earth measuring eight thousand yojanas. Thus, from the surface of the earth to the end of the hells, it is two koṭis and ninety-eight lakhs of yojanas.

As for the measurement of the hells together with the intermediate spaces, they total fifty crores: thirty crores plus the seventeen previously mentioned ending with Dhūma, making two hundred and thirty-seven crores. And this measurement is the same in all the scriptures; even where there is a difference in the intermediate measurements, it is still the same.
The inclusion of some [categories] within others occurs for certain reasons; thus, there is no contradiction. || 26 ||
Understand that which is being described according to its name and its presiding deity: the manifestation known as Paratāla.
And Nitala and Gabhastimat. || 27 ||
Mahātala, Rasātala, and Pātāla— these are the seven netherworlds, O Sage.
Commentary: Having thus spoken by name, he now describes the presiding deities. Among these seven, O Lord of Daityas—
The serpents and the night-stalking demons. || 28 ||
Seven groups of seven have been enumerated; now, learn them from me as well. || 28½ ||
In each of these, seven Daityas, seven Nāgas, and seven Rākṣasas are said to reside;
understand them as they are being described. || 28½ ||
The Daitya Śaṅkhaśravas was formerly Prahlāda, and [the Daitya] Śiśupālaka was [formerly] Śiśupāla. || 29 ||
Karkanduka, Hiraṇyākṣa, Bṛhadgarbha, and likewise Bali. || 29½ ||
Thus ends the group of seven Daityas within the seven [groups]. || 29½ ||
The commentary says: He speaks of the Nāgas:
the Kādraveyas, Kuṭilaka, and so forth.
Vāsuki and likewise Kambala. || 30 ||
Then Kārkoṭaka, Kālāṅga, Durdarśa, and Takṣaka. || 30½ ||
The offspring of Kadrū are the Kādraveyas. || 30½ ||
Commentary: Now follows the group of seven Rākṣasas introduced immediately after the Nāgas:
Vikaṭa and Lohitākṣa.
The one named Yamaka has a hideous face. || 31 ||
Karāla, Bhīmanihrāda, and Piṅgala—these were the Rākṣasas. || 31½ ||
Commentary: Now follows the world of Hāṭakeśvara—
above them all, without exception.
The sovereign lord of the netherworld.
Residing in the golden orb of the thousandfold abode, he who stands in gold is praised for the attainment of what is dear.
Just as by the ornaments of ascetics. || 33 ||
The wives of the Daityas, Yakṣas, Suras, and lords of the Nagas [sang] with graceful words. || 33½ ||
Above those netherworlds (pātālas) resides their lord, Hāṭakeśa.

The wives of the Dānavas, Guhyakas, Devas, and Nāgas praise that Blessed One with beautiful words of hymn. Describing who they are, he says: "restrained" (yatāḥ), meaning self-controlled. With what kind of words do they praise him?

"With ornaments of pauses" (yativibhūṣaṇaiḥ) means: a pause (yati) is a sequence consisting of quick, medium, and slow tempos; those words of praise which have that very [pause] as their ornament—with such [words], meaning with flattering verses devoted to song, they propitiate [the Lord].
For what purpose? "For the attainment of the beloved," because they are under the sway of desire. || 33½ ||

The *Dīpikā*: Now, in order to show that the seven netherworlds (*pātāla*)— which are included within the world of Hāṭakeśvara— are to be purified specifically during the initiation into the worlds (*bhuvanadīkṣā*), their subordination to that [Hāṭakeśvara] is stated by the passage beginning with "above them" (*teṣām upari*).
Thus he said, beginning with "of those netherworlds," and so forth. || 33½ ||
Then the earth, the refuge of various people, [measured] one hundred crores [of yojanas]. || 34 ||
Adorned with continents, mountains, rivers, oceans, and the circle of treasures. || 34½ ||
Commentary: Immediately following that, the earth—abounding with various types of people and adorned by the multitude of continents and oceans to be described hereafter—[is established]. 34½.
Dīpikā:
Having thus stated the measurement from the surface of the earth upwards, [the author] now describes the transverse measurement of the Brahmāṇḍa in this region as well.
In order to demonstrate that its measurement is one hundred *koṭi*s of *yojanas*, he explains "a hundred *koṭi*s" and so forth.
Regarding "immediately after that" and so on: it is called an *aṇḍa* (egg/cosmic shell) precisely because of its egg-like form.
This is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*: "This cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is said to have a shape identical to that of a hen's egg. (34½)
The commentary states the measurements and names of the continents:
Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, and Krauñca.
Śālmala, Gomeda, and Puṣkara; these islands, each double the size of the preceding one starting from Lakṣa, are surrounded by oceans beginning with the Salt Ocean. || 35½ ||

As will be described later, the seven continents, beginning with Jambūdvīpa, each double the size of the preceding one and are surrounded by oceans— such as the salt ocean and the milk ocean— that are equal in measure to those continents.
Commentary: Beyond that is the golden earth and the Lokāloka mountain.
Beyond that is the darkness, then the Garbhoda ocean, and the shell of the world-egg; such is the surface of the earth.

Below that is the ground consisting of gold, then the mountain known as Lokāloka; beyond that is darkness, and then the ocean called Garbhoda, and finally the shell of the cosmic egg—this constitutes the terrestrial plane.
Commentary: Now, desiring to know this classification in detail, the Sage asks:
"O mountain, river, and elephant..."
O Śakra, I wish to hear in detail about the blessed Earth, adorned with forests and oceans.
O Lord of Gods, while you— the witness of all things directly— speak,
the instruction on the final goal has been drawn forth.
My mind runs toward the sacred revelation (Śruti). || 38½ ||

I desire to hear in detail how the world is adorned with various forests, mountains, rivers, islands, groves, and oceans; for my mind, seized by an insatiable curiosity for knowledge, runs toward you—the teacher who perceives everything directly—in order to hear it from you. (38½)
Commentary:
"I shall expound"—this is the speech of Indra.
"O best of the twice-born, I shall expound."
Like the body of the speech currently presented,
listen with a one-pointed mind to the islands, rivers, and forest regions. (39½)

From this point onward, because the subsequent portion of the text is easy to understand, it will be explained by means of a commentary in certain places. I shall proceed; I shall speak, following the sequence of the body of the discourse currently under discussion. || 39½ ||
Jambūdvīpa is the navel of the earth; it is circular, measuring one hundred thousand yojanas,
and is surrounded by the salt ocean.
By that much [of the cycle] having been completed. || 40½ ||
"Extending so far" means measuring one hundred thousand [yojanas].
In its center stands the golden mountain, the king of mountains.
The mountain Meru, frequented by the gods, eclipses the splendor of the sun. || 41½ ||
In the midst of that [ocean] stands Meru, the king of mountains, frequented by the gods, made of gold, and surpassing the splendor of the sun; it is situated there. (41½)
He, having descended sixteen thousand [yojanas] from the surface of the earth into the ground, was one hundred thousand [yojanas] high, less that amount.
At the base, it is sixteen [units] in width. || 42½ ||
It has entered sixteen thousand yojanas into the earth;

starting from the surface of the ground, it rises eighty-four thousand yojanas upward, and at its base, it is sixteen thousand yojanas in width. Its shape above is like a shallow bowl (*śarāva*), with its width doubling as it ascends.
And it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda-tantra*: "One thousand and sixteen [yojanas] is its extent at the base;
at its root, its width shall be that same amount, and above, it is double that. O Goddess, Meru, the king of mountains and the refuge of the gods, has the shape of a shallow bowl. (42½)
In his three intervals between the feet, at the joints increased by four [fingers], || 43 ||
The rims, shaped like bracelets,
emerged most brilliantly;
one was ten thousand [yojanas] long.
The supreme [power] consists of a thousand humans. || 44 ||
The ridge near the summit that serves as the refuge of the world-protectors is called the Cakravāṭa.
[She who possesses] the radiance of all jewels. || 45 ||
Commentary: In those [mountains] which have an interval of twenty-five thousand [yojanas], consisting of a quarter of the height of this Meru,
and which increase by four thousand [yojanas] in each successive stage;
At the joints of the sections, three rims shaped like bracelets, well-luminous and serving as girdles, protrude.
It is precisely at these three places that he demonstrates the fourfold increase, beginning with "one ten-thousand," and so forth.
The first is ten thousand units in measure; the second is one thousand units in measure.

It measures fourteen thousand [yojanas]. Because of the statement regarding a fourfold increase, the third [circle] is eighteen thousand [yojanas] in extent. That which is the rim (*nemi*) near the summit, serving as the support for the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), and which is radiant with the luster of various inlaid jewels—that, according to those who know the scriptures, is what is referred to by the term *cakravāṭa*.

And thus, of Meru, which has the previously mentioned height of eighty-four thousand yojanas, three mountains measure seventy-five thousand [yojanas]. As for the three terraces, they are nine thousand [yojanas] high, because each one measures three thousand; such is the traditional teaching (āgama). (43–45)
The *Dīpikā* explains the passage beginning with "in the three intervals between the quarters" and so forth, starting with "of this Meru" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "increased by four thousand": this increase in measurement is horizontal across the directions; it does not refer to the height.
Because it will be explained later. Here he says: "The first [rims] are ten thousand in measure," and so forth.
This means that three rims, each ten thousand in width, have protruded.
Regarding these [rims], which are separated by intervals, their height from the surface of the earth is stated in other scriptures as follows:

He says that it should be known: "And thus," and so forth. "The three joints" (*parvatrayam*)—here, by the word *parva*, the three intervening spaces from the surface of the earth up to the Cakravāṭa mountain range are denoted. "And the three rims" (*kaṭakatrayam*) means the three felloes (*nemi*). (43–45)
Below that, on its joints, reside the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Maruts;
on its eight peaks, they likewise dwell.
The eight cities are situated together. || 46 ||
Learn from me their names according to the directions, beginning with the east, starting with Indra.

The meaning is: among the three regions mentioned as situated below the Cakravāṭa, it refers to that which is the abode of the Siddhas and others, namely the upper girdle called the Cakravāṭa. The rest is clear. || 46–46½ ||
Dīpikā: For this very reason, he explains the sūtra beginning with "siddha" and so forth, starting with "situated beneath the Cakravāṭa mountain range," and so on. 46.
A web of light from various jewels.
Adorned with circles, frequented by Siddhas, Sādhyas, and Maruts, Amarāvatī has a ground of gold and belongs to Hari.

Commentary: Adorned by a surrounding halo of the combined luster of various jewels, frequented by Siddhas and others, and possessing a ground of gold, there is in the east the city of Indra named Amarāvatī. 47½.
Vahni’s Tejovatī is characterized by red and yellow jewels,
with golden walls and gate-towers.
Vahni—
It is frequented by beings of equal status. || 48½ ||

Commentary: A *gopura* is a gate-pavilion. *Saṃyaminī*, the city of Death, is frequented by spirits (*bhūtas*) whose power is equal to fire—that is, possessing a brilliance similar to it—and is lofty.
It has a circular enclosure of iron walls and is frequented by Kālapāśa, Pitṛvyādhi, Pretas, and Mārīs. || 49½ ||

Commentary: In the southern direction lies the city of Yama named Saṃyaminī, which is exceedingly lofty, surrounded by a multitude of iron walls, and inhabited by the noose of Time and other such instruments. A portent named Mārī is a calamity that causes the simultaneous destruction of many worlds.
He is presided over by a distinguished deity; and that deity, commanded by the Lord of the Pretas, performs her work wherever it may be. || 49½ ||
Dark like the abode of Death, the lord of the Daityas, it was frequented by demons and possessed a mass of radiance like blue jewels.
Adorned with an excellent canopy. || 50½ ||

Commentary: Adorned with excellent canopies possessing masses of luster like lapis lazuli and sapphire, the city of Nirṛti, inhabited by Daityas, is dark-hued like the city of Yama; it is known as Kṛṣṇā. || 50½ ||
The Śuddhavatī, belonging to the Lord of Waters,
is constructed of crystal stone;
it is like white clouds— by those [waves]...
She shines with her splendors, having been served [by them]. || 51½ ||

Commentary: There is a city named Śuddhavatī, the city of Varuṇa. Constructed of crystal slabs and frequented by sea-monsters, tortoises, and other creatures, it shines with houses as bright as white copper. || 51½ ||
But for Vāyu, it is fragrant, filled with lofty white and yellow banners,
and inhabited by powerful spirits.
She is fashioned from all kinds of jewels. || 52½ ||
The city of Vāyu, named Gandhavatī, is adorned with white and yellow banners, fashioned with various jewels, and inhabited by powerful beings. 52½.
The great and auspicious white [image] of the Moon, fashioned from pearls and other gems,
shines forth, praised by the assembly of the twice-born.
With houses possessing the splendor of the Snowy Mountain.
Commentary: To the north of Soma is the white city named Mahodayā;
by the inclusion of the phrase "constructed of pearls and so forth," it is understood that it may also be made of moonstone or rock-crystal. And it is praised by hosts of Brahmins.
It shines with palaces possessing the luster of frost and other such things. || 53½ ||
The city of Yaśovatī, which bore the fame of having burnt the God of Love and Death with the blazing eye on its forehead— entirely...
Born of jewels, she is served by Rudra. || 54½ ||
Commentary:

It was fashioned from all kinds of jewels for Īśāna, who by his blazing third eye burnt Kāma and Kāla, and who, for that very reason, bears the glory of having destroyed all the enemies of the entire world.
The city named Yaśovatī, inhabited by Rudras, is situated in the northeastern direction. || 54½ ||
Thus, these eight cities, which provide comfort in all seasons, are half the extent of the Cakravāḍa mountain range and are shaken by the wind.
Reddish-brown due to the dust that has settled upon them. || 55½ ||
These [worlds], created by the Ordainer for those who follow the wheel of world-protection,
are called "heaven" for the sake of prosperity.
They are sung by poets upon the earth. || 56½ ||
1. There is a variant reading: *smarasyeśasya śobhitā*.
Commentary: They are called "givers of the pleasure of all seasons" (*sarvartusukhadāḥ*) because they bestow the happiness and sorrow associated with all the seasons. Likewise...
These cities— measuring nine thousand yojanas each, extending for half the distance of Mount Akravāṭa, following the circles of the world-protectors (Lokapālas),

and existing for the welfare and prosperity of those who worship Indra and the other deities— are celebrated by poets as "Heaven" (Svarga). Because of the brilliance of the nectar from the flowers of the Pārijāta— the specific celestial tree— and its other qualities, [it is so designated].
It is appropriate that these possess loveliness. || 56½ ||
Commentary: Now, the city of Brahmā measures fourteen thousand [yojanas].
In the center of the self-existent Svayambhū, there is a city named Manovatī, which is worshipped by the lords of the world. (57½)
She who, with her great splendor, made the paths of the sky intensely red,
as if vying with Sāvitrī.
She who transcends those desiring heaven. || 58½ ||
Commentary:

"Mahāśrī" means possessing immense splendor. "Svargakāmātivartinī" means that those who desire heaven (svargakāmāḥ) turn away from it; thus, she transcends those who seek heaven. This is precisely because of her possession of such extraordinary brilliance.
And because it is the cause for attaining the state of Brahman, it seems as if it were vying with the Sāvitrī mantra itself. || 58½ ||
In that [city], the gods and sages of great luster worship the Lord of Great Yoga for the sake of spiritual perfection.
[He saw] the Creator of beings, [surrounded] by Yama and the others. || 59½ ||

Commentary: In that [state], the gods and great sages, whose powers are unequal [to his], worship and serve the Creator— the object of meditation even for great yogins— for the sake of spiritual perfection, by means of restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and so forth.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the restraints (yamas).
Purity, contentment, straightforwardness, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (niyamas). 59½.
In the eastern direction of that mountain,
there is a peak resembling the sun;
they call it Jyotiṣka.
It is always dear to Paśupati. || 60½ ||
Commentary: In that city of Brahman, situated in the northeastern direction, is the exceedingly radiant peak of Meru, beloved by the Supreme Lord, known as Jyotiṣka.
The *Dīpikā* [comments]: "Of the Supreme Lord" refers to Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, the disciple of Ananta, who resides above Satyaloka. As it is stated in the *Mataṅga*: "In the north-eastern direction..."

"The great, luminous Śiśira [abode]—there, O tiger among sages, I have established my residence for the sake of favoring the worlds. Furthermore, in other scriptures, it is heard that even Viṣṇu has a station on the summit of Meru;
as stated in the *Kiraṇa-tantra*, beginning with "the excellent mountain in the middle of Meru," it is described as being endowed with three peaks.
"Born of silver, gold, and jewels: Kṛṣṇa’s horn is of silver, Brahmā’s is considered to be of gold, and Śiva’s station is born of jewels; beneath that dwell the immortals. Thus it is said.
Also in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*: "Upon its summit stand the horns of the Gaṇas, and the hair [of the Lord], proud of its sovereignty."
Established upon its golden peaks, variegated with jewels, were Skanda, Nandi, Mahākāla, and others.
Gaṇeśa and the other foremost of the Gaṇas. || 61 ||
The abode of the Teacher, the God of gods, the enemy of Tripura,
is frequented by tens of thousands of Rudra-hosts.
And by Brahmā and the other supreme gods.
Commentary: On the level plains of that Jyotiṣka [world],
there are the subordinate lords of the Gaṇas (gaṇeśvaras), such as Skanda, Nandīśa, and others, who are inferior to the supreme Sadāśiva-tattva because they will be described below.
This is the abode of the Lord himself, the teacher and guide of Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods;
it is served by Rudras in countless numbers and by the deities headed by Brahmā. (61½–62½)
Thus, below this Meru are the other mountains situated in the various directions; the remaining [portions] are the nine continents.
Learn from me the number of years in this [kalpa].

Commentary: Thus Meru has been described. Below it, there are four supporting mountains (*viṣkambha-śaila*) which will be mentioned later, situated in the directions starting from the east; excluding those, there are nine continents (*dvīpa*) and regions (*varṣa*) here.
Understand this in Jambūdvīpa. || 63 ||
Commentary: Regarding that, he first states the mountains by way of division: Niṣadha and Hemakūṭa.
And Himavat, the best of mountains, is to the south of Meru; Nīla and Śvetaśṛṅgin are to its north. || 64½ ||
With a diameter of two thousand [yojanas], a height of ten, and nine intermediate spaces,
these well-jointed [mountains] extend toward the east.
They have reached the millions of oceans. || 65½ ||
Commentary: To the south of Mount Meru are Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat; to the north are the boundary mountains named Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgavat. These have a width of two thousand yojanas.

They are ten thousand [yojanas] in height and separated by nine thousand [yojanas], with their boundaries touching the salt-water ocean on the eastern and western sides. "Suparvāṇaḥ" means those whose joints (*parvaṇi*)—that is, the intermediate regions (*varṣāṇi*) to be described later—are very beautiful (*su-śobhana*). 64½–65½.
Mālyavat and Gandhamādana, which extend from south to north and east to west, have a width equal to half of that [distance].
The two inner [distances] from Meru are as follows: || 66½ ||

Commentary: Taking half the measurement of the Niṣadha and other mountains as their width—that is, with a width of one thousand [yojanas] each—they extend from south to north. To the east and west of Meru are Mālyavat and Gandhamādana.

"The interval between them" means that the distance between these two, measured from south to north, is exactly the same as the remaining interval— thirty-four thousand [yojanas] in extent— which lies between the Niṣadha and other mountain ranges situated in the four directions. || 66½ ||
Commentary: He speaks in order to define that very [region] by means of its mountain divisions:
"To the east of Mālyavat..."
From Mount Gandhamādana to the north of Ilāvṛta, and from Mount Nīla to the south of Niṣadha. || 67½ ||
Commentary: To the west of Mount Mālyavat, to the east of Mount Gandhamādana,
to the south of Mount Nīla, and to the north of Mount Niṣadha lies the region of Celāvṛta.
Situated in the center of Jambūdvīpa. || 67½ ||

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: "By the mountains of division," and so forth. This refers to the interval of Mount Meru, bounded by the four mountains of division situated in the four directions, beginning with Niṣadha. || 67½ ||
To the east of Mālyavat lies the region of Bhadrāśva, crowded with auspicious people;
[to its west are] Suketana and Ketumāla.
From Gandhamādana in the west. || 68½ ||
Commentary: To the east of Mālyavat lies the region of Bhadrāśva; to the west of Gandhamādana is the region named Ketumāla, which possesses beautiful dwellings. (68½)
That which lies to the south of Niṣadha and to the east of Hemakūṭa is known by the name Kimpuruṣavarṣa.
Bhārata is from the Himavat mountain. || 69½ ||
The region called Ramyaka lies to the north of the Nīla mountain; Hiraṇya lies between the Śveta mountain and that which is to the north of Śṛṅgavat.
That is called Kuruvarṣa. || 70½ ||
Commentary: To the south of Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himādri are the regions (varṣas) known as Hari, Kimpuruṣa, and Bhārata. Likewise, to the north of Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgavat [are the others].
Ramya, Hiraṇyavat, and Kuru-varṣa. || 70½ ||
The Creator fashioned four supporting mountains,
fifty thousand leagues in height, for the stability of Meru.
To the east of them is Mount Mandara. || 71½ ||
Śveta, resembling yellow pigment, is to the south;
Gandhamādana is to the west; and Vipula, which is blue, is to the north.
From Supārśva comes Saumya, and from him Aruṇa. || 72½ ||
In them stand wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadrumas) one thousand yojanas in height—
kadamba, jambu, and aśvattha.
The Nyagrodhīyas and the Uttarāntikas. || 73½ ||

Commentary: For the sake of the stability of Meru, there are supporting mountains (viṣkambha) named Mandara, Gandhamādana, Vipula, and Supārśva, which are white, yellow, blue, and reddish-brown in color, located in the directions starting from the east.
They were created with a height of fifty thousand [yojanas], in which stand the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa) such as the Kadamba and the Jambu, rising one thousand yojanas high. (71½–73½)
The river produced from the juice of jambū fruits, having circled Mount Meru,
entered right into its very root.
Having turned that earth into gold. || 74½ ||
Having drunk it, birds, serpents, mice, wild animals, forest-dwellers,
and others became golden.
Beings have made rafts upon it. || 75½ ||
Commentary: "Having gone around" means having circumambulated. "Of this" refers to Meru. "Branch-dwellers" are monkeys;
by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," elephants, horses, and so forth are meant. (74½–75½)
Jambū was the island-banner among the trees of the kalpa-epoch, renowned for its preeminent power despite the existence of other such trees.
This is Jambūdvīpa, following that. || 76½ ||
Commentary: The banner (*ketu*) or flag (*dhvaja*) of the islands is "Island-banner" (*dvīpaketu*). || 76½ ||
Commentary: Now the lakes and groves of the boundary mountains (viṣkambhaśaila) are described. Among them, [the first is] on the eastern boundary mountain.
At its base is the Caitraratha grove;
there is a lake named Aruṇodaka, adorned with golden lotuses.
This is clear:
at the foot of the southern mountain, it is surrounded by Gandharvas,
Suras, Siddhas, and Apsarases.
There is the Nandana grove and the Mānasa lake, which steals away the mind’s tranquility.
Commentary: To the south, at the foot of the Viṣkambha mountain, is a grove named Nandana, and here is a charming lake called Mānasa. (78½)
At the base of Vaipula is Vaimrāja,
and there is Sitoda, the best of lakes;
it is frequented by the gods and remains concealed.
With lotuses possessing the radiance of the sun. || 79½ ||
Commentary: At the foot of the mountain named Vipula is a forest called Vabhrāja, and there is a lake of white water,
adorned with lotuses possessing the brilliance of the sun, which is frequented by the gods.
Near Saupārśva is the forest named Dhṛtimat and the auspicious lake covered with fragrant lotuses.
It is always served by the ancestors. || 80½ ||
Commentary: At the foot of Supārśva is a forest named Dhṛtimat; there is also a lake called Bhadraka. (80½) Commentary.
Description of the food, lifespan, complexion, and so forth of the people dwelling in the continents beginning with Ilāvṛta at the present time—
lifespan of thirteen thousand [years].
In the region surrounded by the Sutvigila mountains, people subsist on the juice of jambu fruits and perceive objects through the light of Mount Meru. 81½.
By the light of that Meru, the object was perceived as "O, you are a hero! He possesses the luster of a beloved,
a lifespan of ten thousand years, the brilliance of a blue lotus, and feeds on the essence of the jackfruit tree.
In Ketumāla, the people possess divine bodies and are happy and strong. || 82½ ||

He whose lifespan is ten thousand times ten thousand years—that is, one hundred million years—is such a person. Likewise, he is called "the consumer of the essence of the panasa fruits" because he consumes the essence, meaning the refined extract, of those fruits known as *panasa*. 82½.
In Bhadravājini, the one who eats the blue lotus has the luster of the moon’s orb;
his lifespan is ten thousand years.
He is abandoned by suffering, grief, and fear. || 83½ ||
In the region of Bhadrāśva, there is [the land] called Bhadravājinī;
there, the lifespan is thirty thousand years, and people subsist on the fruits of wish-fulfilling trees.
In the Kuru region, there will be births of twins, and the people will have the luster of the *śyāmā* flower. || 84½ ||

Commentary: "Kāmādi" means one whose eating of tree fruits is according to desire; the meaning is that he creates and eats tree fruits as he pleases. "In the Kurus" means in the region of Kuruvarṣa. "Yugmaprasūtiḥ" means born simultaneously.
There are two girls; Śyāmā has the luster of a priyaṅgu flower, while [the other] possesses a complexion that is mostly fair.
Commentary: Now, within this very region, the two islands of Candradvīpa and Bhadrākaradvīpa, situated in close proximity, are described.
Two thousand Bhūtas,
marked by the junction of the single direction,
have Soma and Vāyu as their abodes; they are Siddhas.
They were frequented by sages and celestial bards. || 85½ ||
The two continents are Candrabhadra and Ākara; their inhabitants have the complexions of the moon and the red lotus;
and their food is Ailāvṛta. || 86½ ||
Their inclusion [in the measurement] is stated due to their proximity within the ocean of Kuru;
thus, in the salt ocean situated at the edge of Kuru-varṣa, there are forty-five thousand yojanas.
Situated at the junction of the northern and northwestern directions, visible as they stand encircling [the world] with one common boundary,

and inhabited by Siddhas and others, the two islands known as Candradvīpa and Bhadrākara are to be understood. Among them, the people of Candradvīpa possess the luster of the moon, while those dwelling in Bhadrākara have the radiance of red lotuses.

The lifespan and food—consisting of fruits and roots—spoken of by Celāvṛka; and that which is located in the ocean at a distance of one thousand times the number of elements (eighty-four thousand) yojanas: the locative case here is used in a non-co-referential sense (*vyadhikaraṇa*) to mean "while staying in that place.
[The word] *sānnidhyāt* means "by proximity. || 87½ ||
*Dīpikā*: Following the description of Kuru-varṣa, the two sub-continents are mentioned here in connection with the context; thus he says, "Now, right here," and so forth.
The lifespan of the people of Hiraṇmatī, who possess the luster of the moon, is always twelve thousand five hundred years.
It is like one who, while questioning, bites into the fruit of the lakuca tree. || 88 ||
In the region named Hiraṇyavatsa, the lifespan of the people, who subsist on Likuca fruits and possess moon-like luster, is twelve thousand five hundred years. || 88 ||
In Ramyaka, the lifespan of people who are as delightful as blue lotuses is twelve thousand years.
For one who eats the fruit of the nyagrodha tree. || 89 ||
In the region named Ramyaka, the lifespan of people who have the luster of blue lotuses and subsist on banyan fruits is twelve thousand years. (89)
The people of Ikṣvāku have the luster of silver and a lifespan of ten thousand years; those of Kiṃpuruṣa are golden and [dwell] at the Plakṣa tree.
The lifespan of one who eats [only] once every ten thousand years is ten thousand years. || 90 ||

In Harivarṣa, the people have the luster of silver; their lifespan is as previously stated, and they eat sugarcane alone as their food on all sides, thus they are called *Ikṣvādas*, a people whose sole nourishment is that. In Kimpuruṣavarṣa, however, the people have a golden luster, eat the fruit of the *plakṣa* tree, and live for ten thousand years.
Thus have the regions beginning with Kiṃpuruṣa been described to you;
in them, there is no distinction of stages of life.
In the *vivarti* [kalpa] and those beginning with the *kṛta* [yuga], || 91 ||
Possessing wisdom, splendor, strength, wealth, and progeny appropriate for the age,
he was one who ate only what was cultivated, yet remained subject to suffering.
The people in Bhārata are afflicted by the three [miseries]. || 92 ||
What desired goal would a single quality, when applied with diligence, not accomplish? For it is the ground of all fruits.
For the field of action is the cause. || 93 ||
In these regions such as Kiṃpuruṣa and the others thus mentioned, there is no variation in conditions even through the cycles of the Yugas.

But in this Bhārata-varṣa, a person is characterized by such things as intellect, lifespan, radiance, vigor, wealth, and offspring, which correspond to the Kṛta and other Yugas. These are the intellect and the rest.
The meaning is that in the Kṛta and subsequent ages, [the lifespan and other qualities] of people diminish accordingly.

Here, "people" refers to those afflicted by the threefold suffering—pertaining to the self (ādhyātmika), pertaining to the divine/supernatural (ādhidaivika), and pertaining to external beings (ādhibhautika)—who subsist on both cultivated and uncultivated produce. However, there is this one quality [of the Kṛta age]: that effort is successful.
How much more, then, would it not accomplish? The meaning is that it is capable of accomplishing everything. Why is this so? He says:

"of all," because this [earth] is the field of action (*karmabhūmi*) and the cause for all fields of fruition (*phalabhūmi*). As it has been said: "O Brahmin, this is the field of action; beyond this is the field of fruition. Whatever action is performed here..."
That is experienced in another world; the expression "of all" is a hyperbole (atiśayokti), because it is impossible otherwise. || 93 ||
1. There is a variant reading: *tuṃ īśayati iti yāvat*.
[The author of] the *Dīpikā* explains this, preceded by the raising of a doubt: "Of all the grounds of fruition (*phalabhūmi*), from what [source]... [He asks: "Why?"
"Thus he said," and so forth. This is stated because there is an abundance of fruits in those [other worlds] and an abundance of karma in this one;

for even here, it is precisely the fruit of karma that is experienced. Furthermore, in those [other worlds], the good and evil deeds of Indra and others are heard of, as in the case of Nahuṣa and Yayāti. Therefore, the statement that "this is a land of action" (*karmabhūmi*) and so on is indeed logically justified as an indicator.
In the stream of the nine oceans, there are islands situated on ground half the size of those [oceans],
beginning with Indradvīpa and the rest.
Learn from me their names.

In this land of Bhārata-varṣa, which is joined by nine streams from the ocean, "arghakāni" refers to those regions where half is water; that is, in such a place where the land is covered by water for half its extent. As it is stated in the venerable Kiraṇa-tantra: "Water is five [parts] and land is five"—in such a Bhārata-varṣa.
Understand that the nine islands, beginning with Indradvīpa, are being designated here by name. 94.
Commentary: Now he says that: Indradvīpa and Kaśeru.
Tāmravarṇa, Gabhastimān, Nāgadvīpa, Cāndramasa,
Gāndharva, and likewise Vāruṇa.
The ninth is called Kumārikā; it contains various mountains and rivers,
and is crowded with people of various castes.
They are celebrated as being in the land called Bhārata. || 96 ||

These nine islands, crowded with various types of peoples and nations, are described as being within the region named Bhārata. The word *dvīpa* should be understood as masculine as well, due to its inclusion in the list of words ending in *-a*. (96)
1. The meaning is that it is read in the neuter gender because of its optional nature (*vaikalpikatayā*).
*Dīpikā*: [This refers to] the nine [islands], such as Indradvīpa and others, and the ocean currents situated between them.
The authoritative measurement is stated in the venerable *Svacchanda-tantra*: "For each individual island, a thousand [yojanas] is proclaimed;

five hundred should be known as land, and likewise five hundred as water. Thus, the division of the number for Bhārata, consisting of nine thousand [yojanas], is established. And so it is for Indradvīpa and the others.
Starting from the southern ocean, it is situated on the island known as Ṣaṭkumārikā. || 96 ||
The king named Āgnīdhra was the lord of Jambūdvīpa in the lineage of Manu;
by the names of the kings born from him, [the land was known].
The Bhārata and other such works are so called. || 97 ||

The son of Manu's lineage, named Āgnīdhra, was the sovereign of Jambūdvīpa and had nine sons, beginning with Bharata. The nine regions of Jambūdvīpa ruled by them became famous under the names of Bhārata and the others. || 17 ||
Now, the seven continents separated by the seven oceans are described:
[they are surrounded] by waters of salt, milk, curd, clarified butter, sugarcane juice, wine, and nectar.
The continents, beginning with Jambūdvīpa, are double in size [successively], starting from one hundred thousand [yojanas], and they are circular. || 98 ||

The seven islands, beginning with Jambūdvīpa, should be understood as being separated by the seven oceans, beginning with the Salt Ocean and the Milk Ocean, which have dimensions doubling from one hundred thousand [yojanas] onwards. The reason for the name Jambūdvīpa was previously stated in the passage beginning, "Jambū was the tree that became the banner of the island."
1. This is the seventy-sixth verse in this section.
Now, he explains the etymological significance of the names of the two-legged beings, such as the Śākas, according to their own designations:
"In the Śāka [continent], the Śāka tree is lofty."
The golden whip became known as "vegetable" (śāka) when the Self-born One desired to perform a sacrifice at Kauśa. (99)

In Śākadvīpa, there is a lofty tree called Śāka, which is the cause for its being named Śāka. When Brahmā desired to perform a sacrifice, golden *kuśa* grass appeared; this is the reason for the name Kauśadvīpa. || 99 ||
On Mount Krauñca, in the golden cave, the Daitya Krauñca was slain by Skanda after he had pursued him for a very long time.
The master of wondrous illusions, with his excellent power of illusion. || 100 ||
That mountain, on account of its act of providing an opening for that Daitya, became known as his banner.
It is called Krauñca by name. || 101 ||

In Krauñca-dvīpa, on the mountain Krauñca with its golden caves, the Daitya named Krauñca was slain by Kārttikeya while he was fighting; thus, it is designated as Krauñca-dvīpa because it is characterized by that Krauñca mountain. 101.
On Śālmala is the Śālmali tree, made of gold, a thousand yojanas high, with the brilliance of the sun;
it is the beloved banner of the immortals.
That is the basis for its designation. || 102 ||
In Śālmalidvīpa, there is a Śālmalī tree, one thousand yojanas in height and possessing the brilliance of the sun; it is the basis for the name of that [continent]. 102.
On Gomeda Island, there was a king named Gopati who was intent on performing the Gosava sacrifice;
he became the patron (yājya) of those who were like Agni himself.
In the lineage of Manu, among those characterized by gentleness. || 103 ||
While they were engaged in the sacrifice to Hari, Gautama, out of anger, chose the Bhṛgus as his officiating priests.
He cursed Soga, saying, "Go to destruction! || 104 ||
In his sacrificial enclosure, those cows were burnt by the sage’s fire of wrath;
the earth was covered with their fat.
From him, Gomeda was born. || 105 ||
Gopati, born of the lineage of Manu, performed the sacrifice known as Gosava;

he became the patron (yājya) of the descendants of Utathya, who were as radiant as fire. When those descendants of Utathya had gone away for the sake of performing a sacrifice to Indra, Gopati chose the Bhrigus to serve as his officiating priests (gurus).

Out of anger, Gautama cursed him; he went to his destruction, and the cows that had entered his sacrificial enclosure were consumed by the fire of Gautama's wrath. Because the surface of the earth was covered with their fat, the island is known as Gomedha. || 105 ||
The river named Puṣkariṇī is adorned with golden lotuses;
by it, that Puṣkaradvīpa [is characterized].
It has been proclaimed and is served by the gods. || 106 ||
Commentary: Puṣkaradvīpa, frequented by the gods, is characterized by a river named Puṣkariṇī, which is like a lotus-born stream,
just as [it is described] among the Kiṃpuruṣas and others.
The people there are always established in their state;
likewise, they subsist on food made of milk and other substances in Śāktadvīpa and the other islands. 107.
Having the luster of snow, the moon, a blue lotus, a young sprout, and crystal,
he has a lifespan of ten thousand years.
He for whom the sole thorn of suffering has been destroyed. || 108 ||

Just as in the regions such as Kiṃpuruṣa and others, and likewise in the ages such as Tretā and the rest, people abide in the state of the Kṛta Yuga; so too in the islands such as Śāka and others, they respectively subsist on milk and other foods,
possess a luster like that of snow or the moon, live for ten thousand years, and are free from the great sorrow known as suffering.
This is to be known. || 107 – 108 ||
Within the seventh ocean,
there are two crores, three and a half million, and fifty thousand [yojanas].
From the ear, which contains a golden mountain within it. || 109 ||
"Prior to the seventh enclosure" means starting from the interior—that is, from the central part—of that very Meru, facing toward Meru itself.

"From the corner" means from the intermediate space between the supporting mountains (*viṣkambha-śaila*), following the sequence of corners produced by the region of Ilāvṛta. The two ends [of the diagonal] are formed by the triangle.
The measurement of its petals is fifty-three lakhs, one thousand, and fifty-five crores. || 109 ||

The *Dīpikā* summarizes the meaning explained for the term "the place of half" (*ardhakasthalam*) with the words: "fifty-three lakhs. And this [refers to] that which is surrounded by Jambūdvīpa, measuring two crores and so forth.

Since this salt ocean measures fifty thousand [yojanas], and since each of the six continents beyond it successively doubles in size starting from one hundred thousand, it follows by implication that the six oceans beginning with the Milk Ocean have those same respective measurements. || 109 ||
Then a golden ground, with mountains and trees made of various jewels,
was created by the Creator for the sake of sport.
The [retinue] of the gods consists of one hundred million. || 110 ||
The Creator fashioned for the sporting of the gods a golden ground, ten million yojanas in extent, upon which there are various jewels, trees, and mountains. (110)
Outside of that [mountain] is Lokāloka, the regulator of light and darkness,
with a width of ten thousand yojanas.
Adorned with lofty peaks. || 111 ||
It is called the "Regulator of Light and Darkness" (*lokālokaniyāmaka*) because it regulates the world situated within it and the light situated outside it;

the meaning is that there is no world beyond that [mountain]. Regarding the phrase "having a diameter of ten thousand *yojanas*": its width is ten thousand [yojanas], and it is surrounded by exceedingly lofty peaks. || 111 ||
On whose horns the rays of the sun, though intensely hot, do not cause distress due to their distance, resembling the light of the moon.
O Sage, these are the abodes of those who uphold their hopes.

Because Mount Lokāloka is exceedingly high, the pleasure-palaces of the world-protectors situated upon its peaks are not scorched by the rays of the sun; due to the great distance, those rays serve merely as a source of moonlight-like illumination.
Beyond that is dense darkness,
measuring nineteen hundred thousand and forty thousand [yojanas].
And thirty-five crores. || 113 ||
The king of the oceans consists of twenty-seven lakhs and one koṭi [yojanas];
the golden shell (kaṭāhaka) is one koṭi [yojanas].
"From the womb," that is, from all sides. || 114 ||

Outside of Lokāloka is a dense darkness measuring thirty-five crores, nineteen lakhs, and forty thousand [yojanas]. Beyond that, however, is the king of oceans called Garbhoda, which is twenty-seven lakhs and ten million [yojanas] in extent. Of that too—
The golden cauldron outside measures one koṭi [yojanas] in extent; thus is the division into hundreds of koṭis. || 114 ||
The *Dīpikā* states:
"The division into one hundred crores" refers to forty-seven crores, forty-six lakhs, and one thousand [yojanas], including the shell of the cosmic egg up to the golden ground (*hemabhūmi*).

And its measurement is fifty [crores]. Within that, from the seventh ocean to the center of Meru, there are two crores, five million, and fifty thousand; thus, on one side there are fifty crores of *yojanas*, and likewise on the other side, making it one hundred crores in extent.
"Thus, the Egg of Brahmā. || 114 ||
Commentary: Having thus stated the measurement of the extent of the world of Bhūrloka, he now states the measurement of the height of the six worlds beginning with Bhuvarloka.
The Bhuvarloka extends from the surface of the earth to the limit of Dhruva for a distance of one hundred thousand yojanas (tithi-lakṣa);
the Svarloka is one crore (ten million) yojanas less than that.
The refuge of the most excellent among the celestial beings. || 115 ||
There, where twenty million people reside,
dwells the assembly of sages beginning with Marīci,
surrounded by eighty million common folk.
The refuge of the people born of Pitṛ and Jahnu. || 116 ||
Where the great yogi Sanandana, as well as Ṛbhu and Sanatkumāra, reside at the peak of ascetic power;
And Sanaka, who was possessed of great austerity. || 117 ||
Beyond that is the abode of the Self-Existent One, the world of truth (Satyaloka),
which is endowed with an abundance of supreme desire.
Nine and seven crores. || 118 ||
There Sāvitrī resides in embodied form, as do the Vedas along with their followers. || 119 ||
1. *Samāśraya* is a variant reading. [The] commentary [states]:
"From the surface of the earth—that is, from the ground—up to the limit of the Pole Star (*dhruva*)."

The Bhuvarloka extends for fifteen hundred thousand [yojanas] up to the Pole Star (Dhruva), which serves as the support for the circle of luminaries (jyotiścakra). The Svarloka, the abode of the foremost among the celestial beings and the principal inhabitants of heaven, has an elevation of eighty-five hundred thousand [yojanas]. The Maharloka, the station of the multitude of sages beginning with Marīci, measures two crores [of yojanas].

Janaloka is delimited by eighty million [yojanas] and is the abode of the Pitṛs, such as Jahnu, and of sages. Tapoloka is twelve crores in height; it is the refuge of Sanandana, Ṛbhu, Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, and others. Immediately beyond that, because their intellect is fixed solely upon the Truth—

The abode of Brahmā, who has attained mastery over the Kalpas, is Satyaloka, which possesses the perfection of all sovereign powers and rises sixteen crores [of yojanas] high; therein reside Sāvitrī in embodied form, as well as the Vedas and the Upavedas. (119)
The *Dīpikā* [commentary] states:

By the verse beginning with "tithilakṣa" (one hundred and fifty thousand yojanas), he describes the height starting from the surface of the earth, which serves as a supplement to what was previously stated. This is indicated by the phrase "evam" (thus) and so forth. || 119 ||
Then, there are four and six [verses] respectively for Madhu and Tripuravidviṣ,
in the Jyotiṣmatī and Citrā meters.
The skull-bowl is the pinnacle. || 120 ||
"Extending for a hundred koṭis" refers to the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍagolaka);
this [world] is indeed almost equal to that.
In all streams [of consciousness], it is by way of conceit. || 121 ||
Above that is the radiant abode of Viṣṇu, the enemy of Madhu, extending for four koṭis;
and that of Śambhu, the enemy of Tripura, is of the same kind, with a height of six koṭis.
The shell of the cosmic egg (aṇḍakaṭāhaka) is one koṭi. Thus, [this measurement is] from below the Bhūrloka.
Just as there are fifty crores of *yojanas* [downwards], so too above that is another fifty;

thus the mass of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is one hundred crores in both its breadth and height. And this [egg] is, for the most part, of a uniform shape in all its upward, eastern, southern, western, and northern currents.
Śakra protects its eastern quarter; Agni protects the southeastern;
and the Destroyer of Beings protects the southern.
The Rākṣasa [wind] blows toward the south-west. || 122 ||
The god Varuṇa [presides over] the western direction;
Nabhasvān, the northwestern;
Soma, the northern; and Yakṣeśa—
The Viśvedevas [are worshipped] in the north-eastern direction. 123.
Hari is the Brahman above, and he is always intent upon all things below.

The guardians of the directions of that Brahmāṇḍa, beginning with Indra, are as follows: in the north are Soma and Vaiśravaṇa; above, Brahmā stands as the protector; and below is Viṣṇu. These remain eternally attentive with their whole being.
The Rudras, ten by ten, stand as the controllers even of these;
they too are possessed of prosperity, yet [they remain under the control] of those [higher beings].
They do not step forward from fear. || 124½ ||
Surrounded by those of great heroism, possessing various forms and a radiance like that of the rising sun,
who wielded diverse weapons.
Learn their names from me.

Of these world-protectors (lokapālas), the Rudras are the presiding deities, stationed ten by ten in every direction; out of fear of them, even though they possess great sovereignty, these [world-protectors] do not abandon their respective stations in their capacity as guardians. These...
And they were surrounded by attendants of various forms, bearing diverse weapons, possessed of great strength, and radiant like the rising sun.
The *Dīpikā* explains the sūtra beginning with "of these also" (*eṣām apīti*). It says: "of these guardians of the world" (*eṣāṃ lokapālānām*), and so forth.
Precisely because they are the presiding deities over them, in the worship of the pavilion and other rites to be described, the hundred Rudras [are worshipped] by way of Indra and the others.
The sense is that they are indeed worthy of worship; for in the scripture of the Supreme Lord, neither bound souls (paśus) nor fetters (pāśas) are worshipped.
Commentary: Now he states their names—
Budhnavajraśarīrāja.
The crusher of Kapālin’s curse; the manifestation of power, the imperishable teacher, the wielder of the Pināka bow, and the lord of the thirty gods. || 126½ ||
These are the restrainers of Śakra. || 126 ||
Now, for Agni:
Bhasman, Kṣayāntaka,
Hara, Jvalana, Agni, and Hutāśana.
Piṅgala, Khādaka, Babhru, and Dahana are situated in the direction of Agni (the southeast). || 127½ ||
The ordainer, the sustainer, and the creator; the one who separates from Yama and death; the lord of dharma and adharma, and the one who joins [beings] with them.
And the Haras have Yama as their leader. || 128½ ||
He spoke of the lords of Nirṛti:
"Nirṛti is the slayer, the killer,
with cruel eyes, smoke-colored and blood-red."
The gods of the forest were terrifying with their upright phalli, three eyes, and fangs.
One who eats flesh (*māṃsa*) is a *palāda*, a flesh-eating *rākṣasa* or *niṛti*; those who protect him are the *palādapās*. || 129½ ||
Then he spoke to Varuṇa and Īśāna: "Balā, Atibalā, Pāśāṅkuśa, Śvetabhadra, and Jalāntaka."
The monkeys possessed great strength and long arms, and their roars were like the sound of thunderclouds. || 130½ ||
The sound of thunder is *meghanāda*. Those who protect (*pānti*) or guard (*rakṣanti*) the water (*kaṃ*) are called *kapās*.
Furthermore, the lords of the wind are described as having the speed of a light and swift breeze.
Sūkṣma, Tīkṣṇa, Kṣaya, and Antaka; Kapardī, Abda, Īśa, Pañcānta, and Pañcacūḍa are the Vāyus. (131½)
O fortunate ones, possessing forms like the lords of treasures, wearing matted locks of gentle fortune,
and bearing jewels of abundant splendor—
And the Prasādas, Indus, and Yakṣas [are located there]. || 132½ ||
Regarding "Indu and Yakṣapā": these are the lords of Indu and Yakṣa, who were previously mentioned as the guardians of the northern direction.
[They are] Vidyeśa, Sarvavit, Jñānin, Vedavit, and Jyeṣṭhavedaga.
Vidyā, Vidhātṛ, Bhūteśa, Balipriya, and Sukhādhipa. || 133½ ||
Commentary: In the location of the northeastern direction (īśāna), these [deities] beginning with Vidyeśa are the controllers.
Then, those above are mentioned:
1. Sarvavidyeśa, Sarvajñajñānin, Jyeṣṭheśa, Vedagā, Balipriya, Sureśāna, Bhūteśa, and Darśanāyaka—thus is the variation in the reading.
Śambhu, Vibhu, the presiding lord of the qualities, the three-eyed one, and the sovereign of the thirty gods;
the wise one who desires to touch the sky—
And they have intermarried with the Mūrdhanas. || 134½ ||
The ten Rudras, beginning with Śambhu, abide as presiding deities over the head [of the body] within Brahman.
The word *vāha*, preceded by *sam* and *vi*, denotes the two acts of *saṃvāha* (union) and *vivāha* (marriage) of the Rudras. || 134½ ||
In order to describe the Rudras residing below the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), he says:
"Krodhana, Anilabhuja, Bhogin, Grasana, and Udumbarēśvara."
Viṣa, Viṣadhara, Ananta, Vajra, Daṃṣṭrin, and Viṣṇupā. || 135½ ||
Then, water and the other elements are the planes of enjoyment; established within them are five groups of eight for those who experience them.
The glory of the fruit obtained from the field [of merit]. || 136½ ||

Immediately above the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), in their respective locations, are the expanses of water and other elements; therein reside five groups of eight Rudras, numbering eight each. As to what they are like, he says: "They are the appointers [of fate], possessing the glory of the fruits obtained from the field (*kṣetra*)."

The meaning is that for those who employ— the ones who bring about— the glory of the fruit obtained from the field, that is, the site occupied by [the deity], the perfection of the fruit of each respective occupied field bears result solely through his grace. || 136½ ||
1. The reading is *tryakṣaścaṇḍāmarasstutā*.

2. From the verse beginning with *budhnavajra* up to the verse ending with *krodha no'nile*, there are many variant readings (*pāṭhabheda*) in these stanzas; they have been included here because they do not result in a contradiction of the meaning (*arthavaiṣamya*).
The *Dīpikā* explains the passage beginning with "Then, water and so forth" with the words "Immediately thereafter," and so on.
Furthermore, the proof for these qualities, such as being authoritative (*āpta*), has not been stated here; it should be understood from the venerable *Mataṅga* and other sources.
As it is stated there: "Therefore, water is ten times [the size] of fire; from water, air;
and from air, space—in this *Pārameśvara* scripture. From space, the ego (*ahaṅkāra*);
beyond that, the Great One (*mahat*). Beyond the Great One, O Sage, the triad of qualities (*guṇas*) is to be known."

The principle called Pradhāna, arising from the three qualities (guṇas), possesses ten times their power; the remaining principles taught in the scripture are said to possess a hundred times that power. The principles ending with Māyā are thus [increased], but above them, up to the Sādāśiva-tattva, they exist in a thousandfold manner, while the supreme one beyond that exists in a hundred-thousandfold manner. This is the group of four.
"Then, beyond that, is the immeasurable Supreme Śiva, who is the limit of peace. This means that there is the attainment of the fruits of the respective fields presided over by Him;
