that is to say, through the worship of the respective lords of the worlds (bhuvaneśvara), there is the attainment of those respective worlds.
1. The fortieth verse in the Chapter on Valid Cognition (Pramāṇapaṭala). Commentary:
Therefore, he states their names:
Bhārabhūti, Āṣāḍha, Ḍiṇḍi, Lākulya, Amarapuṣkara,
Prabhāsa, and Naimiṣa.
This is the secret octad in the water. || 137½ ||
This secret group of eight exists in its true nature as water. 137½.

Dīpikā: These five groups of eight locations, beginning with Bhārabhūti, should be understood as existing even within Bhāratavarṣa under those respective names for the purpose of attaining those particular worlds. As it is said in the Mataṅga:

For the sake of the welfare of human beings in the holy land of Bhārata, the Creator formerly established those [sites] as signs, in which Hara is ever present, through the attainment of which [welfare is gained]. (167½)
Śrīśaila, Jalpa, Kedāra, Bhairava, Āmrātakeśvara, Hariścandra, Mahākāla—
In the case of the *madhyāsātipada* [meter], there is a brilliance [of form]. || 138½ ||
Regarding "the stations of mindfulness" (*satipadā*): they exist together with the "transcendent step" (*atipada*), meaning that this is the group of eight great secrets.
Regarding "in the will" (*rucau*): the meaning is that they are established in the principle of fire (*tejas*). || 138½ ||
Mahendra, Bhīma, Vimala, Kurukṣetra, Gayā, Khalā, Sanāpada, Uttara, and Sāṭṭa—
The letters *hā*, *sā*, *na*, and *kha* are located in the bird. 139½.
"Sanāpadottarāḥ": that which exists together with *nāpada* is *sanāpada*; "uttara" means the last, which is expressed by the word *khala*.

Those for whom Rudra is [the first]—namely Mahendra and the others—are the *sanākhalas*. In *kha*, meaning the sky or the element of wind (*vāyu-tattva*), this is the eightfold secret of secrets. || 139½ ||
1. The meaning is "more secret. *Dīpikā*:
The group of eight situated in the element of air is the group of eight more secret than the secret. (139½)
Sthāṇu, Svarṇākṣa, Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Mahālaya,
Vastrāpada, and the one called Avimukta.
Ten million Rudras in the circle of the sky. || 140½ ||
They call this the Pavitrāṣṭaka.
Regarding "the lunar mandala": they say that within the principle of space (ākāśa-tattva) lies this group of eight purifiers (pavitrāṣṭaka). || 140½ ||
O best of the twice-born, I shall describe to you by name the eight Sthāṇus located within the belly of the senses of pride. || 141½ ||
"Consisting of pride, the subtle elements, and the senses" means [the principles] beginning with ego (ahaṅkāra), the subtle elements (tanmātra), and the sense organs (indriya).
The eight [entities] beginning with Ākoṭa and ending with Sthāṇu, which will be described later, are situated there. 141½.

The *Dīpikā*: Now he explains the passage beginning with "Then pride" (*atha garva*). Regarding "Then pride," etc.: [one might object] that in the venerable *Mataṅga*, by the passage beginning "Now those Rudras who are endowed with the qualities of yogic sovereignty in the subtle elements" (*tanmātreṣvatha ye rudrā yogaiśvaryaguṇānvitāḥ*), [pride] is mentioned even in relation to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
The worlds (*bhuvana*) of the Viśvedevas are enumerated [elsewhere].

How then is it said that only an octad exists within the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *ahaṅkāra* and ending with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*)? For this very reason, those [worlds] also, in the initiation regarding the worlds (*bhuvanadīkṣā*), are to be purified here as being included within this very octad.
There is no contradiction in [the statement] "in order to make known. || 141½ ||
Commentary: He states their names:
Mākoṭamaṇḍaleśāna—
Dviraṇḍa and Chagalaṇḍaka;
Sthaleśvara and Sthūleśvara; as well as Śaṅkukarṇa and Kālāñjana. (142½)
Commentary: Now he describes the eight worlds situated within the principle of intellect (*buddhi*).
There are eight subtle cities of the gods.
In the intellect (buddhi), beginning from the first, are the Paiśāca,
the Rākṣasa, the Yākṣa, the Gāndharva, and the Māhendra [tanmātras], which possess great power. 143½.
It was gentle, presided over by Prajāpati, belonging to Brahmā,
and blazing with supreme splendor.
Within the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) is the subtle group of eight worlds. Among them, the Paiśāca world comes first;

that is, beginning with Paiśāca and ending with Brāhma, following Rākṣasa and the others. It is "blazing with supreme splendor," meaning it possesses a radiance even greater than that of Mahendra, who is himself endowed with great prosperity. 144.

The *Dīpikā* states: "In the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), there is a subtle group of eight worlds. This group of eight divine origins is subtle because the gross divine origins are situated within the Egg (*aṇḍa*). As the followers of Sāṃkhya say:
The divine creation is of eight kinds, that of the animal womb is fivefold, and the human is of one kind; such, in brief, is the elemental creation. || 144 ||
Commentary: Now he describes the eight worlds of those who possess the reality-level of the qualities (guṇatattva). In the realm of the qualities (gauṇe) are the abodes of the lords of yogis.
The uncreated [system] is Kṛtabhairava;
[the others are] Brāhma, Vaiṣṇava, Kaumāra, Sauma, and Śrīkaṇṭha is the last. 145.
[The mantra] of Vīrabhadra, praised by the best of yogis, which consists of radiant flames,
situated in authority beneath its own feet.
Possessing a glory superior to all the Rudras. || 146 ||
The world of that Vīrabhadra— who possesses a glory superior to those established in lower positions because he is directly favored by the Supreme Lord—
is radiant and praised by yogis; and here indeed, these Rudras reside at the summit of the principle of *guṇatattva*.
They remained. || 146 ||
*Dīpikā*:

Regarding the phrase "having performed the Bhairava [rite]," this means that which is both performed (*kṛta*) and [the rite dedicated to] Bhairava (*bhairava*). He explains the passage beginning with "of Vīrabhadra" by saying "from his own station," and so forth. For this very reason, Bhārabhūti and the others are lords of the worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*).
They are indeed appointed by Ananta. Furthermore, it has been stated that these inhabitants of the Guṇatattva are also impelled by Śrīkaṇṭha:
"All those authorized by Śrīkaṇṭha are unfailing and powerful.
This is because he too is appointed by Śiva. Therefore, [the region] above the Guṇatattva and below the Pradhāna—

The world of Vīrabhadra has been described for the purpose of its persistence even during the intermediate dissolution (*madhyamapralaya*) at the end of the *guṇatattva*. As he will state: "Then the hundred Rudras, along with the illustrious Vīra and Śrīkaṇṭha, the lords of *pradhāna*, having pervaded with their power the subtle universe and the conscious subtle bodies—the latent dispositions situated within *prakṛti*..."

"They await the time that marks the end of his sleep. For this very reason, in the Mataṅga-tantra, the world of Śrīkaṇṭha is said to begin from the level of Pradhāna onwards. However, during the period of this [world's] stability, Vīrabhadra’s domain, like that of the hundred Rudras, is also strictly above the cosmic egg (aṇḍa). His authority likewise extends only up to that limit; it does not, however—
It should be understood that this extends up to the Guṇatattva, just as in the case of Śrīkaṇṭha. As it is stated in the Raurava:
"The hundred Rudras and others, headed by Vīrabhadra, are known to be presided over by Śrīkaṇṭha.
It is also stated elsewhere: "Those headed by Vīrabhadra are indeed the supports of the cosmic egg (aṇḍa). And therefore:

The Gurus maintain that the world of Śrīkaṇṭha is to be purified in that very same location as the world of Guṇatattva. However, Vāmadeva and others state that the thirteen Rudras are situated precisely at the summit of Guṇatattva, below Vīrabhadra;
this is expressed in the passage beginning with "atraiva ca" and so forth. (146)
1. "They are indeed appointed to infinity" is the connection with what precedes.
To the question "Who are they?", he says:
Vāmadeva, Bhava, and Ananta.
Bhīma, Māpatya, and Īśvara;
Sarveśāna and Īśvara, known as Eka-vīra and Eka-śiva. || 147 ||
Fierce, with a blazing gaze, the Lord stands at the summit of all qualities,
to be worshipped through profound austerity.
Anger and the other [passions], having attained the state of being heavy. || 148 ||
In the injunction regarding their own respective offices, the Rudras are fierce, possessing the vision and action directed toward all objects. || 148½ ||

Having propitiated the lords of wrath (Krodheśas) and others situated above through great austerity, they attained the status of Gurus and the quality of being bestowers of grace. These Rudras are fierce in the performance of their own respective duties, and they are skilled in the yoga of knowledge and action regarding all matters. || 148½ ||
The *Dīpikā* [comments]: "For one who is engaged in the activity of knowing all objects" refers specifically to the domain limited by one's own [perceptual] capacity. || 148½ ||
Hear now of the ten times more glorious principal lords from among them:
Krodheśa Caṇḍasaṃvarta—
The Jyotis, Piṅgala, and Śūra gaṇas.
Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, and Śikheda—these are remembered as such. || 150 ||
Those whose glory is ten times greater than that of Vāmadeva and the others previously mentioned are these Krodheśas and other principal lords (pradhānādhipas). || 150 ||

The *Dīpikā* explains the passage beginning with "from them" (*tebhyaḥ*) as "from Vāmadeva and the others," and so forth. "Caṇḍasaṃvartaka" is the name of a single [deity]. It has been stated that these eight, beginning with Krodheśa, are indeed appointed by Śiva.
He is the support of all the senses, of all bodies, and of all internal organs;
he is the controller within the person and in destiny.
In time, he possesses the power of differentiation. || 151 ||

Commentary: In the world situated within the principle of the Person (puruṣatattva), Rudra is the presiding deity, characterized by the attributes of possessing all the senses and so forth. As was stated previously during the exposition of the principle of the Person, in the *Bhauvana* [section].
"Taking refuge in Rudra. Thus, he abides as the one known as the "Restrainer" within Niyati, and as the possessor of the power of reckoning within Kāla. || 151 ||
1. The eighteenth verse in the section on *kalā* and so forth. *Dīpikā*:
"Residing in the principle of *puruṣa*" and so on. And this world-sphere (*bhuvana*) is situated above *pradhāna*.

It has been stated that [the soul] resides only in the lower portion of the worlds of passion (rāga) and so forth, because it is impossible for the person (puruṣa) to be the support of the worlds. This very point is made known by the words "that which was said," etc. (verse 151).
Bhuvaneśa, Mahādeva, Vāmadeva, Bhavodbhava,
Ekapiṅgeśa, and Īśāna—
And they are thumb-sized and radiant. || 152 ||
Resembling the Supreme Lord, within the womb of Passion (rāga) and Knowledge (vidyā), in the stage of Limited Agency (kalā),
[there are] sixty-four great cities.
In the mandala, there are the lords of the mandalas. || 153 ||

In whichever world of *kalā*— within the womb of passion and ignorance (*rāga-vidyā*)— the sixty-four great cities (*mahāpura*) are situated according to the previously mentioned method and the sequence of eight groups of eight as taught by the venerable Mataṅga and others, there reside these lords of the worlds (*bhuvaneśa*) and so forth.

The lords of the maṇḍalas remain possessed of great splendor because they possess power comparable to that of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara). Why, then, is the arrangement of the sixty-four maṇḍalas not mentioned here? It should be understood as described in the venerable Mataṅga-tantra and other such scriptures. || 153 ||

Dīpikā: In the phrase "in that world of *kalā*," the word *bhuvana* (world) here denotes a location; the meaning is "the path beginning with *rāga* and ending with *kalā*. In that [path], these are the lords of the worlds (*bhuvaneśas*) and so forth. Therefore...
The sense is that by this very purification, their purification also occurs during initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Because they possess powers comparable to those of the Supreme Lord, they are "of beautiful luster" (*sukāntayaḥ*). Therefore, these [deities] such as Krodheśa and the others are also *maṇḍalins* who are indeed favored by Śiva; they are not, however, appointed by Ananta like Gahaneśa and the others. How so?
Furthermore, he will state immediately thereafter that Gahaneśa and the others are the sovereign lords of the mandalas;
thus, there is no contradiction, as their status as impellers is asserted merely by virtue of their residing in the upper worlds. || 153 ||
Commentary: Now he states the sovereign lords of those [elements] as well:
Ananta, the protector of the three times.
Kṣemīśa and Brahmaṇaspati; the two Rudras, Dhruva and Tejo'dhipa; and Gahaneśa and Viśvarāj. || 154 ||
The Rudras who preside over Māyā are the lords of the mandalas;
they are mounted upon the wheel of saṃsāra—
They are the causes of the dissolution of the collection of beings. || 155 ||
This entire ground of existence for all beings is indeed so terrible,
that in it the ignorant sink down.
Like weak cows in the mud. || 156 ||

These eight Rudras, beginning with Ananteśa, who are the presiding deities of *māyā*, are the transformers of the multitude of beings mounted upon the wheel (*cakra*) of perpetual wandering within transmigratory existence itself; they are the agents of worldly life.
This much indeed is the terrible and inauspicious ground for all beings, wherein the ignorant [are lost].
Like oxen stuck in the mud, they fall into despair. || 156 ||
The Dīpikā:
He states "only this much," and so forth, to show that the path of Māyā (māyīya-śuddhādhvan) is exactly this much. || 156 ||
Now, the Vidyārājñīs residing in the world of Vidyā are described:
Bhṛguṇī, Brahmavetālī, Sthāṇumatī, Ambikā, and Parā.
Rūpiṇī, Nandinī, and Jvālā—these are the seven lords of each of the seven arbudas. || 157 ||
The Vidyārājñīs, praised by Rudra, have been described within this Vidyā. || 157½ ||
These seven Vidyārājñīs, praised by Rudra as the sovereigns of the mandala just described, are the mistresses of seventy million mantras. || 157½ ||
The *Dīpikā* states: "By the words beginning with 'bhṛguṇī', the worlds of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) are described"; thus he says "atha" and so forth.
Above those [worlds] is Dīptaśrī—
The Lord of Mantras, the sovereign of knowledge, is established there, permeated by consciousness and followed by the eightfold assembly of Rudras. || 158½ ||
The Ucchuṣmas, the Ābaras, the Caṇḍas, those of great heroism, the Padadruhas,
the Rudras, the Gaṇas, and the guardians of the quarters.
The scriptures remain as their masters.
And those beginning with Ananta have already been described by name;
and their essential nature, O Brahmin, has also been told.
Previously, [this was] by way of a connection to the questions. || 160 ||

Above the Vidyārājñīs, beginning with Bhṛguṇī and others, stands Rudra, known as the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyādhipa), possessing radiant splendor and endowed with the perfection of unsurpassed knowledge and action. To the question "Of what nature is he?", it is said: "The Lord of Mantras" (Mantreśa); that is, the venerable Lord Īśvara, who acts as the impeller of the Lords of Mantras, such as Ananta and the rest.
Those Rudras whose vision and action (*dṛkkriyā*) are intensified by being permeated by that [consciousness]—the eightfold array (*vyūhāṣṭaka*) belonging to them follows him;

thus he is "followed by the eightfold array. The meaning is that those Rudras who reside therein are impelled by Īśvara. And it has been said: "Īśvara impels the lords of the lower vidyās and the individual souls (*aṇu*). Therefore...

As soon as they are impelled, they create the lower world. Herein are the Rudras such as Ucchuṣma and others, the Gaṇas, and the deities beginning with Devī, Skanda, Caṇḍeśa, and Vṛṣa; the lords of the directions beginning with Indra;
the scriptures such as the Niśvāsakārikā and others; and the Lords beginning with Ananta who reside there. They...
Furthermore, Ananta and the others have already been described previously according to their names, their essential natures, and the sequence of questions. || 160½ ||
The *Dīpikā* explains the passage beginning with "above them" and so forth, starting with "of Bhṛguṇī and the others. Here, however,
the group of eight Rudras is to be purified as being situated within the world of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyādhipa*).
The teachers maintain, however, that Ucchuṣma and the others, who reside within the worlds of the Vidyeśvaras such as Ananta and the rest, are those to be purified.

For this very reason, he says "of the Mantreśas," and so forth. Among Ananta and the others, the venerable Lord Īśvara is indeed Ananta himself who acts as the impeller; all the others situated below him are his impelled subjects, as has already been stated previously.

"Gaṇas and so forth here," etc. These, beginning with Gaṇeśvara, are those who will be described as objects of worship among the Gaṇeśas and others in the section on ritual action (kriyākāṇḍa). "And the scriptures": the meaning is that the scriptures have attained the nature of philosophical systems (darśana). "And the lords, Ananta and the rest, are situated": and of these...

Because it exists above the worlds of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyādhipati-bhuvana) whose functions have been withdrawn within the path of Mahāmāyā itself, and because Ananta is denoted by the word "Īśvara," this group of eight worlds should be known as situated within the principle of Īśvara.
As he will state: "Beyond Īśāna, up to the end of Śānta, that is remembered as the Sādāśiva principle."
In the venerable Parākhyatantra as well, it is stated: "Likewise, [the one] named Ananta and Īśvara. (160½)
In Sadāśiva is the Pavitrāga,
with its entire retinue beginning with Sakala;
the god Sadāśiva [resides] in the Bindu.
Nivṛtti and the other Kalas are the Lords (Īśvaras). || 161½ ||
The Lord resides in the sound of the *nāda* within the power (*śakti*), he who is the best among all possessors of power; he is the source of the universe and the mistress of speech.
Beyond the Lords is Śiva. || 162½ ||

In the realm of Sadāśiva are the purificatory Brahmans beginning with Sadyojāta, as well as the ancillary mantras (aṅgas). The Lord Sadāśiva resides there, he whose divisions and retinue consist of the eight Rudras—Jvālinī and the others—who are both manifest and unmanifest (sakala-niṣkala). However, in the Bindu-abode, [resides] Nivṛtti.

The four lords of the *kalās* known as *Pratiṣṭhā*, *Vidyā*, and *Śānti*: in the world of *Nāda* resides the Lord of Sound (*Dhvanipati*), namely Nādeśvara. As it is stated in the *Śrīmat-Svatantra* in the section on *Nāda*: "In the *Suṣumnā*, there resides Suṣumneśa, whose luster is like ten million moons."

"Ten-armed and three-eyed, seated upon a white lotus throne, with the moon as his crest-jewel, the glorious one, five-faced and of great body. Regarding "in Śakti": in the refuge of Śakti, the Supreme Lord, the most excellent among all possessors of power, resides; and in this very place is the source of the universe, and so forth.
The power known as Kuṇḍalinī, which is the cause of the origin of the entire universe through the sequence of Nāda, Bindu, and so forth, is established there.

As it is stated in the venerable *Svacchanda Tantra*: "There, the power Kuṇḍalinī follows Māyā and Karma; the effects such as Nāda and Bindu belong to her—thus is the stability of the world. And: "The lords of speech [are her manifestations]."

They reside in this very place as the Lords of the Worlds (*bhuvaneśvaras*). As it is said in that same [text]: "And for the lords of the worlds and those who dwell therein, O Dear One, He is the cause. Beyond that is Śiva.
The nature of Supreme Śiva (*paraśiva*) is to be known as partless (*niṣkala*) and transcending all causes. For instance:
It is stated in the illustrious *Svatantra* itself: "O fair-faced one, that which transcends those is the supreme reality, free from affliction. (162½) [Note:
There is a variant reading *daya* for *dayā*.
*Dīpikā*.

He explains "in Sadāśiva" and so forth with "in the world of Sadāśiva" and so forth. The inclusion of the limbs of Brahmā occurs precisely within the category of powers (*śakti*) such as *sakala* (with parts) and *niṣkala* (without parts). As stated by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha in the *Śivabhedāṣṭakaprakaraṇa* in his commentary on the *Kālottara*: "The *sakala*, the *niṣkala*, and the *śūnya*..."
"Kalāḍhya, Khamala, Kṛta, Kṣapaṇakṣama, Antastha, Kaṇṭhoṣṭha, and the eighth is remembered as [the ninth]," and so forth;
having thus established the eightfold division of the Prāsāda mantra, in the commentary on the concluding aphorism: "Those mantras..."

Because it establishes the differentiation of the powers presiding over the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara), these very differentiations are designated [as such], just like the limbs of Brahmā and so forth. If this is so, how can it be said that there are "eight Rudras"? There is no contradiction, as this is a figurative designation (upacāra) based on the eightfold nature of Rudra, who is Śiva. As for the differentiation into Dhvanipati and the others—

Just as there are distinctions in the states of Sadāśiva, it is spoken of metaphorically as belonging to Śiva alone by virtue of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that preside over those worlds. As he will state: "Beyond Īśāna and up to the end of Śānta, the principle is known as Sādāśiva; the worlds [therein] are also the *kalās* beginning with Nāda, and nothing else."

"Because the Lord is Śiva. For this very reason, since Śiva possesses a body of power (śākta-śarīra), these [deities] are also metaphorically described as his retinue by virtue of being presided over by him;
however, those who dwell in their respective worlds [attain their state] either through the worship of the condition of the respective lords of those worlds or through initiation (dīkṣā).

For those who are engaged in that [practice] and whose selves are to be refined, there exists indeed an ultimate distinction as well as a conjunction with the body of *bindu*. Now, one might object: since the principles (*tattva*) of Śakti and Śiva are also heard of in other scriptures, how is it that the Sādāśiva principle is traditionally defined as extending from Īśāna up to Śānta?
Because the justification for the statement about to be explained follows from this, he says: "In the *vindu*," and so forth.
It is logical that the transformation of the power of grasping (*parigraha-śakti*), known as Mahāmāyā, through the divisions of *nāda*, *bindu*, and so on, is indeed ultimate (*pāramārthika*).
In that regard, the fourfold set of *kalās*—*nivṛtti* and the others—which constitute the locus of Śiva’s enjoyment, is called the *Śakti-tattva*.

Thus it is said in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "That which consists of the four forms, which is radiant, and which is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*), in that [state] the enjoyment of the Lord of the universe is always declared. He states "the world of Nāda" to indicate that the worlds beginning with Indhikā, which will be described hereafter, are characterized by the Lord of Sound (*dhvanipati*) and are included within the Śiva-tattva.

And here, the first expansion of the power of Mahāmāyā is the *nāda*, which consists of the worlds. However, when Mahāmāyā has withdrawn her effects, Śiva remains eternally as the support in his partless (*niṣkala*) state; thus he says "in the power," and so forth. Furthermore, this very [power] possesses a specific state that is the cause for the production of sound.

He states that what is called *kuṇḍalinī* in other treatises is included here within the *śivatattva* itself, beginning with the words "And in this very [tattva]," etc. (In this context, by the word "universe," it is meant that it is not of one nature or the other). Furthermore, the term "Lords of Speech" (*vāgīśāḥ*) refers to Śiva himself—the producer of sound through the sequence of *nāda*, *bindu*, and so forth—who is designated thus metaphorically due to the differentiation of his effects.

And because these possess qualities identical to those of the Lords of the Worlds (Bhuvaneśvaras), such as Nāda, Bindu, and so forth, they are referred to by the term "Lords of the Worlds" in other scriptures; thus he says, "In this very [text]," and so on. Consequently, since Mahāmāyā is insentient, she lacks the capacity to produce effects such as sound and the like without being presided over by Śiva.

The proponents of the doctrine of *śabdabrahman* (the Word-Brahman) have been refuted. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate in the opening of the *Kriyāpāda* that the status of sound as an effect is established, stating: "From power (*śakti*) arises resonance (*nāda*), from that the point (*bindu*), and from that the imperishable *mātṛkā*. And by the statement "Śiva is beyond that," [it is shown] that Śiva is superior to all who possess power, as was previously stated.
It is said that the ultimate abode of Paramaśiva lies precisely beyond such Great Māyā; thus he says, "beyond all causes," and so forth. || 162½ ||
1. Root Text | Commentary: Now, in order to raise this objection, the Sage poses a question.
The state of the individual soul (aṇu) is conceived as existing within the path that begins with Sadāśiva and ends with Śiva;
it is the repose in the transcendence of all things.
How is it that there are lords above that? || 163½ ||

Beyond the principle of Sadāśiva, extending as far as Śivanātha, the existence of the bodies of the individual souls (aṇus), the lords of the Kalās such as Nivṛtti and the others, and the lords of sound (dhvanipatis) and so forth, is conceived as their union with divine bodies. And within that principle of Sadāśiva lies the repose of all excellence; indeed, there is nothing beyond it.
Apart from the principle of Niṣkala Śiva, there is nothing whatsoever that transcends it. And so, how can lords be said to exist above it? || 163 ||
Dīpikā: Here, the Sage, being doubtful due to the concise statement, raises an objection; thus he says, "Now, this... and so forth. Vṛtti: [The commentary follows].
In this regard, the established conclusion is as follows:
the reality that begins with Īśāna and ends with Śāntātīta is known as Sādāśiva.
Even the worlds, as well as the principles beginning with Nāda, are not other than Śiva, the Lord. || 164 ||

Commentary: Having transcended the principle of Īśvara, which is characterized by Ananteśa and the other Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), one should know the principle of Sadāśiva, which extends up to the partless (niṣkala) principle. And here, the very digits (kalās) such as Nāda and Bindu are to be understood as the worlds (bhuvanas).

And here, Śivabhaṭṭāraka alone is the sovereign of all the principles (tattvas); there is no other whatsoever. Consequently, there is no room for the objection: "How can there be lords above him? || 164½ ||
The Dīpikā explains the Siddhāntasūtra beginning with "Ananteśa" and so forth; for this very reason, in this scripture,
during the initiation into the principles (tattvadīkṣā), the principles of Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śiva [are established] by means of a single ritual application alone.
"Purity is to be understood here," and so forth; and this has already been demonstrated previously. || 164½ ||

Commentary: If this is so, then how is it that the distinction between the Lords—which was stated in the verse beginning "If thus [He is] not [the Lord], then the Lord of Sound is the best among all possessors of power"—is maintained? To this, he says:
However, that distinction of the Lord (pati-bheda) which exists here [in this system] is like the distinction of powers (śakti-bheda) [in other systems],
being a metaphorical designation for a distinction of functions (kṛtya-bheda).
Its differentiation arises from the differentiation of its locus. || 165½ ||

There is no lord here other than the venerable Śiva; however, as for the distinction among the lords of the kalās such as Nivṛtti and the rest that appears in this scripture, it should be understood as being caused by differences in location and produced by differences in function— just as a single power is designated as distinct through the metaphorical application of different functions, such as being divided into Vāmā and so forth.

To demonstrate that very distinction of effects, he first states the common nature of the four lords of the kalās— Nivṛtti and the rest— who reside in the Bindu and the worlds, with the words: "That by which [he] brings about the unfolding..."
These are the Śaktis of Naratejas;
they are the sovereign lords of the worlds known by the names Nivṛtti and the others.

Commentary: Those powers by which the Lord effects the manifestation of the light of the individual soul— which consists of omniscience and omnipotence— are indeed the powers known by the names Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, and so forth.
They are described as the sovereigns of the worlds; such is their common essential nature. || 166½ ||
Commentary:
Now he states its uncommonness:
it causes the elements to cease.
By that [power], she is his "reverser";
"reversion" (nivṛtti) is her station, and the Lord there is likewise possessed of reversion.
That power by which [the Lord] brings about the fourteenfold creation of beings, and by generating dispassion toward saṃsāra, leads them toward liberation—
that is the power of the Blessed One, which performs the activity of turning back worldly existence. And that is the locus presided over by Him.

That [level] is designated as Nivṛtti, and its presiding lord is Parameśvara, who possesses Nivṛtti; thus, this distinction is said to be figurative (bhākta) due to the difference in location and the difference in function. The same should be understood for Pratiṣṭhā and the others as well. || 167½ ||

The *Dīpikā* explains the sūtra beginning with "nivartayati" (it turns back) with the words "yayā" and so forth. The phrase "the fourteen-fold creation of beings" (*caturdaśavidhaṃ bhūtasargam*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those who are bound; and in this context, it refers exclusively to...
The teachers maintain that the Blessed Lord is to be meditated upon as having the form of Sadyojāta by those desiring to attain that state (*tatpada*).

Likewise, in the worlds of Pratiṣṭhā, Vidya, and Śānti, He is to be meditated upon respectively in the forms of Vāmadeva, Aghora, and Tatpuruṣa alone; such is the case for the inhabitants of those respective worlds.
It has been stated that for those who worship the state of the respective lords of the worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*), the union with the body of *bindu* is indeed real.

As he will say immediately thereafter: "Even those who have attained that state through the yoga of Śiva-practice, having obtained the bliss that lasts until the end of that state, proceed to the supreme state. (167½)
Commentary: For instance, the movement of one who has desisted [from worldly activity] occurs once again.
That by which the characteristic of movement is negated is "stability" (pratiṣṭhā);
that is the "abode" (sthāna), and its possessor is the "Lord of that" (tatpati). || 168½ ||

The Śiva-power known as *Pratiṣṭhā* is that which, because it is the cause for the cessation of movement, prevents the downward course characterized by transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) for the individual soul (*aṇu*) who has been favored by meditative reflection (*anudhyāna*) and is oriented upward. Its station is the world-sphere (*bhuvana*) of Pratiṣṭhā, and its lord is [the deity] thereof.
He should be known as the one designated as the Lord of the Foundation. || 168½ ||
That by which one bestows knowledge upon the individual soul, having abandoned the objects accessible to the senses,
is Vidyā; this is also its locus.
And Vidyeśa is its lord. || 169½ ||

Excluding the knowledge of verbal testimony— which has as its object that which is authoritative— and inferential knowledge— which has as its object that which is to be inferred— the Supreme Lord manifests through a certain power the entire collection of objects directly perceived by the atomic self; that power is called *vidyā*, and that [is what is meant].
The world known as Vidyā and its Lord, known by the name Vidyeśvara, are to be understood [in this manner].
That by which Hara effects the pacification of all his sufferings is peace (śānti), and that is the state (pada).
Performing that, he too becomes empowered.
[This is] the commentary (*vṛtti*). By means of which power Lord Śiva effects the pacification of all suffering for this self.
That is peace, that is power, and that place is called Peace; and he who effects that is also called the Lord Possessing Peace. || 170½ ||
Having thus described the fourfold division of the *bindu*, he speaks for the purpose of describing the *nāda*-kalā:
"That which is the perception of objects above and below,
which is both great and even greater..."
And by those [meditations], the Greatest (mahattama) is performed for one who is liberated from consciousness. || 171½ ||
Those [deities] beginning with Indhikā, their location, and their lord exist in all three [worlds]. (172)

Liberation (*vimukti*) is release, the departure from bondage. The form [of the word] is "one who desires liberation for oneself. And thus, for the man seeking liberation who is being liberated, a great light—illumination—pertaining to the upper and lower realms is provided by *indhikā*; and that very same [light] is produced as even greater under the name *dīpikā*.

However, by means of *rocikā*, that very same [deity] is made most great; these are their respective positions, designated as *indhikā* and so forth. In all three of these digits (*kalā*), the presiding lord should be understood as being possessed of them and characterized by *indhikā* and the others. || 171½ – 172 ||

The *Dīpikā* explains the passage beginning with "above and below" by means of the passage beginning with "liberation," and so forth. Furthermore, these worlds such as Indhika and the others are illustrative examples of those mentioned in other scriptures.

It should be understood that these include the world of Śāntyatīta as well as the worlds beginning with Anāśrita. However, even in those cases where only the single world of Śāntyatīta is mentioned, it should be known that these [other worlds] are included therein. Furthermore, these worlds of the Śiva-tattva exist in the form of the power (śakti) of Mahāmāyā.
Because it is impossible for it to be the support of the worlds, it is said that [the powers] reside at the summit of the cessation of its effects.
Commentary: Now, he describes the function of both Mocikā and Ūrdhvagā as previously stated:
"Even when there is the conjunction with omniscience and so forth..."
The state of being subject to injunction arises from a portion of impurity;
that [knowledge] by which one wipes it away is the liberator, and its locus is that very state. (173)
The *mocaka* (liberator) and the one who performs its action— whomever he makes the Lord (*īśāna*), he [becomes];
and that upward-moving one [attains] his state.
And its Lord is the Master of the upward-moving [breath]. || 174 ||

Although those who hold office as Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) possess qualities such as omniscience, they remain subject to being impelled due to the persistence of a residue of impurity (mala). That power by which the Lord causes this state of being impelled to cease for the self is His power known as the "Liberator" (mocikā). Furthermore, there is its location and that which performs its function.
The Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) is designated by the name Mocikā for all of this. That power (śakti) which brings about the state of the Lord as one who has bestowed grace is called Ūrdhvagā;
that place is called Ūrdhvaga, and its presiding lord is called the Lord of Ūrdhvagā (Ūrdhvagādhipati). || 173–174 ||
Even those who have attained that state through the yoga of Śaiva practice experience bliss until the end of that duration.
Having attained it, they go to the supreme state. || 175 ||
And they do not perform creation and so forth,
because they are established solely in their own self-interest.

Because they are endowed with the Śaiva and Pārameśvara means of accomplishment known as *jñāna*— consisting of various types of instructions to be described— and that known as *dīkṣā*, which consists of the arrangement of many kinds of worlds, those individual souls (*aṇu*s) partake of that state, [experiencing] unsurpassed bliss consisting of the nature of that state until the end of its duration.

Having attained enjoyment, they go to the supreme state and become equal to Śiva; yet they do not perform the tasks of creation, maintenance, and so forth like the Supreme Lord, because their final rest and fulfillment lie solely in their own self, characterized by the attainment of liberation (nirvāṇa). Beyond that—

Since no other object to be attained is possible and since the state of being impelled has ceased, they do not perform the functions of creation, maintenance, and so forth; such is the meaning. || 175–175½ ||
The commentary: Concluding, he says:
"Thus is the principle (tattva) ending with Sadāśiva."
This has been explained to you in brief. || 176 ||
"But even slightly, that is from you"—this was said by the inquirer, the sage Bharadvāja. (176)

The commentary: Having stated that "the reality beyond Īśāna up to the end of Śānta is known as Sādāśiva," he extends this principle by implication to state that its power-reality (*śakti-tattva*) is likewise included within it.
1. The reading is "saṃkṣepatas tv eti.
Even when [the capacity] exists, it is thus;
this [is so] because of the connection with all that is to be done.
The ritual action has that [state] and so forth as its object; otherwise, one who is partless is always [so].

Power (*śakti*) should likewise be understood as all-pervasive. Thus, according to the manner described, this Lord Sadāśiva, by virtue of his *kṛtya*— that is, through the influence of his activities such as maintenance (*sthiti*) and so forth— is "with parts" (*sakala*),
being accompanied by the thirty-eight *kalās* associated with the five Brahmans, beginning with Tārā.

The form [of the deity] was commenced with the mantras beginning with *sutārātaraṇī*, as previously stated. That body [was formed] by means of five mantras useful for the fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtya*): *Īśa*, *Tatpuruṣa*, *Aghora*, *Vāmadeva*, and *Sadyojāta*, [assigned] to the head and so forth. And that [assignment] pertains to those respective locations.
The meaning is that the object of which [the Lord] is the beginning—namely, the first [act]—is the accomplishment of the fivefold activity solely by His will. Regarding the phrase "elsewhere":

whether there is no engagement in [the acts of] maintenance and so forth, or when they have ceased, the Supreme Lord is at all times indeed partless (niṣkala), because He assumes a form fashioned by *kalā* for the sake of His effects. || 177 ||

The *Dīpikā* [comments]: By the passage beginning with "Thus, the principle of Sadāśiva," having concluded that Śiva is the direct presiding deity of the worlds of Sadāśiva and the others, [the author] states "it is the same for Śakti as well."

He says "that power-principle also," etc., concluding that even that power possesses the state of presiding over those respective worlds. Here, it is the partless (niṣkala) power alone that is called the "power-principle" (śakti-tattva), and not that which consists of the effects of Mahāmāyā mentioned previously. "This is Lord Sadāśiva," and so forth.

He is called *sakala* (with parts) because he is engaged in the world of Sadāśiva; he is called *sakalāniṣkala* (both with and without parts) because he is intent on activity in the worlds of Nivṛtti and the others; and he is called *niṣkala* (without parts) because he is engaged in the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*). As it has been said:
"The agent is threefold—capable, intent, and engaged"—and "his function concerns that [Supreme] and so forth."
By that word, through the force of the meaning, the principle of Śakti, which is the effect of Mahāmāyā, is expressed. || 177 ||
In the knots (*granthi*) predominant in the [spiritual] stages (*bhūmi*), and in the *vidyā*, *bindu*, *kalā*, and so forth,
the multipliers (*guṇakāra*) for the periods (*daśā*) and other units shall be ten and so on.
O Sage, below the tip of the nāda. || 178 ||
The "ground" (*bhūmi*) is the earth; the "primal matter" (*pradhāna*) is the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti*); and the "knot" (*granthi*) is *māyā*.

In these—the principles of the ground, primal matter, and knot—as well as in *vidyā* (pure knowledge), in *śuddhavidyā*, and in the ninefold [set] of *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*, there are the multipliers of qualities. These are the locations where the qualities are bound.

The meaning is that they exist. In that regard, within the three principles (tattva) consisting of earth, primordial matter (prakṛti), and illusion (māyā), there are bonds (pāśa)—that is, fetters—which consist of the qualities (guṇa) and abound in sattva, rajas, and tamas. The meaning is that here the triad of qualities beginning with sattva exists as bondage. Even though sattva excels in its luminosity (prakāśa) relative to rajas and tamas...

Because it is impossible for *rajas* and *tamas* to be completely separated from it, their status as fetters (*pāśa*) is established. Thus it has been said by the Siddha Guru: "The impure bondage of worldly beings, which is the experience delimited by the quality of *sattva*, arises from the qualities of the mind; it is to be consumed by the fire of the realization of the Lord. Regarding *vidyā*:

In the group of nine consisting of Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā, there is the middle Kalā called Rocikā, which is the creator of the unsurpassed, most great light of the qualities such as omniscience, contentment, and beginningless awakening;
below that are the two Kalās of Nāda and the four Kalās of Bindu, which are Śuddhavidyā and the Unmanifest (avyakta).
And the earth and the *kārās* exist as obstacles; for this very reason, he said:

"The ten and so forth are below the limit (*koṭi*) of the *nāda*. That which is the limit of the *nāda*—the end of the digit (*kalā*) called "upward-moving"—below that are these ten, as previously stated, consisting of the nine digits of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*.
And the principle of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā)— this group of ten,
because they are locations that obstruct the supreme Lord’s qualities such as unsurpassed omniscience and contentment,
are the "first" or primary *kārās*, the grounds of bondage; whereas the others are the ground of primordial nature (*prādhānika*).

They explain it in this way, intending the reading "granthiḥ" (the knot) as a non-compound: namely, that the ground of the knot is the primary locus of pervasion for the impure qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—belonging to *pradhāna*—which is like a knot in a noose. [This occurs] within the *vidyā* [tattva], in the group of nine consisting of *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*.

In this manner, within the ten primary locations, there are cities; however, those other pure beings, such as the *satvas* and so forth, having brought about their respective worlds, come into existence for the purpose of performing specific functions.
As it is stated in another scripture: "Above the two cosmic eggs—the elemental (*pārthiva*) and the primal (*prākṛta*)—there are two other eggs."

"Pure [principles] such as *sattva* and the rest exist within the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*. Regarding this, it should not be objected that their status as *kāra* (causes) is untenable precisely because they are pure; for even those [pure principles], being causes of obstruction to supreme liberation (*kaivalya*), do not lose their nature as *pāśa* (bonds). And it has been said: "Up to *samanā*, O fair-limbed one..."
"The net of snares is endless. || 178 ||
Dīpikā: Having thus concluded the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan), which is useful for the initiation into the worlds,
[the author now proceeds] with the inclusion [of the worlds] within the five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, for the initiation into the kalās that is about to be described.

In order to demonstrate that everything, consisting of both pure and impure aspects, is to be purified, the locations of their pervasion are shown by the passage beginning with "the earth is predominant" (*bhūmiprādhānika*), as he says:
"The earth," and so forth. Here, "earth" refers to the *pṛthvī-tattva*, which is to be purified by being included within the *nivṛtti-kalā*.

This group of principles beginning with *pradhāna* and extending up to the principle of *prakṛti*, including the *aptattva* and so forth, is included within the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*. The collection of principles beginning with *puruṣa* and ending with *māyā*, characterized by the *granthi*, is included within the *vidyā-kalā*. And that which is characterized by *vidyā*—namely, those called *śuddhavidyā*, *īśvara*, and *sadāśiva*—[is included within the *śānti-kalā*].

The three principles (*tattvatraya*) are included within the *śāntikalā*, while the ninefold [principles] of *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā* are also included within the *śāntyatītā*. Now, how is it that these serve as the locus for the bondage of the qualities (*guṇabandhana*)? To this he says:

"In that regard," and so forth. Consequently, starting from the earth element (*kṣmādi*) and extending up to *māyā* by way of the body, the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest come into existence.

Regarding the phrase "in the Vidyā, in the ninefold [set] of Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā," and so forth—the word "and" (ca) implies that the aforementioned qualities such as omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) and others constitute the locus of bondage; this is the remainder of the sense. Therefore, it should be understood that here the term *guṇakāra* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), whereas previously it was a descriptive compound (*karmadhāraya*).

[Objection: But has it not been shown that because omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) and the other [perfections] have already been manifested by *Rocikā* alone, how can there be their "bondage" (*bandha*) in those aforementioned locations? To this he says: "That which belongs to the unsurpassed," and so forth. [Objection: If this is so, why was it stated, "in the group of nine consisting of *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*"? [Reply: It is said: in the locations such as *Rocikā*...

Even when endowed with omniscience and other such qualities, the state of being subject to injunctions persists due to a portion of impurity; this is because the remaining trace of impurity characterized by the lack of autonomy (apreryatā) is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "tadyathā. Thus, until the purification of the power of concealment (tirodhāna-śakti), there remains the quality consisting of supreme sovereignty.
It has been stated that there is an obstruction, and we shall explain this further in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Therefore, because the ninefold [principles] consisting of *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā* serve as indicators for the triad of principles beginning with *vidyā*, their primacy arises from the power of the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* which constitute the nature of impurity (*mala*). This is expressed in the passage beginning with "the ten and so forth" (*daśādyāḥ*), as he says: "Therefore..."
"Thus he says," and so forth. However, the explanation beginning with "But others" is improper because it lacks coherence between what precedes and what follows;

rather, it serves to demonstrate the pervasion (vyāpti) that is useful for the initiation (dīkṣā) by means of the Kalās, which will be discussed later. Furthermore, regarding the two-fold pervasiveness, it is stated in other scriptures that there are pure qualities such as *sattva* and the rest; however, that is precisely what has already been stated here.
This is because, even in the pure path (śuddhādhvan), the subtle kalās and so forth will be discussed later. || 178 ||
Commentary: Now, in order to state that which was not previously mentioned— namely, the extent of the domain of Gahaneśa and the others who were mentioned earlier— he says:
Above Kalā and below Vidyā,
the lords of the Gahana are heard;
the interval between them is this much—
In this case, the function of indication (lakṣaṇā) arises from the exclusion of other meanings (diti). || 179 ||

In this context, the word *vidyā* should be understood as *māyā*. As it has been stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*: "Māyā is remembered as the supreme *vidyā*. Below this [level] and above *kalā*, the Rudras such as Gahaneśa and others are heard of in the scriptures. Among them:

The extent of that interval between those two—Māyā and Kalā—is defined here by the intellect (*buddhi*) alone through its characteristic measure; however, no further means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is stated for this, because of the scriptural revelation of the infinity of the *māyā-tattva*. Thus it has been said by the venerable Bṛhaspati:
Even the words of all perfected beings (*siddhas*), uttered over a long period of time, would be exhausted;
for because of the infinity of *māyā*, the number of its streams cannot be told.

The *Dīpikā* introduces the sūtra beginning with "ūrdhvam" (above) and so forth with the words "idānīm" (now) and so forth. [An objection: But this sūtra is irrelevant here; therefore, it must be construed as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with what was stated previously, beginning with "anaṃtaḥ trikalaḥ" (the infinite has three times).
This must be explained. Why, then, is it not recited in that very place? Because of the maxim: "The sūtras are like Vedic meters.
For it is recited thus: "It leads to prosperity. Here, the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) arises from intelligence (*buddhi*);
the meaning is that the vision characterized by that [intelligence] is knowledge (*jñāna*), which is inference (*ūha*). || 179 ||
The commentary says:
"In this way, for both paths as well... [to conclude].
For those engaged in sequential generation,
dissolution occurs in reverse order,
extending as far as the two principles of Śakti.

In the manner thus described, the dissolution occurs through the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), which is the reverse of the sequence of emission (*sarga*), for both the pure and the impure paths that possess such an emission. The meaning is that whatever originates from a particular source, its reabsorption occurs back into that very source. This process extends as far as the two principles of *Śakti*.
For the pure [soul], it extends up to the supreme power (parā-śakti); for the impure, it extends up to the power of māyā. || 180 ||

The *Dīpikā* says "in order to conclude" (*upasaṃhartum āha*), which is an elliptical expression [referring to the state] during dissolution (*pralaya*). Furthermore, dissolution here is of two kinds: that pertaining to the specific creation (*asādhāraṇa-sarga*) and that pertaining to the general creation (*sādhāraṇa-sarga*). Among these—

The first [type of liberation], consisting of the dissolution of the body, is twofold. In that regard, one pertains to the gross body due to the exhaustion of certain karma that bestows birth, lifespan, and experience; the other pertains to the subtle body even during its period of persistence, due to the exhaustion of all karma through knowledge, yoga, renunciation, or the experiencing [of results].

It occurs; however, at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), it is for all [beings], and thus that alone is the dissolution of the uncommon path of reality (*tattvamārga*). The second, however, is due to the withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*) of the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ; that alone is the dissolution referred to here by the words "in reverse order" (*prātilomyena*) and so forth. As it is said in the *Mataṅga*: "Time (*kāla*) is [the cause] of human beings..."
Dissolution is of two kinds: one is due to the exhaustion of experience and the observation of the end of the body;
the other dissolution is observed through the destruction of the three worlds. "Ending with the Supreme Power" means ending with the power of Kuṇḍalinī. (180)
Commentary: Desiring to know specifically the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama) which was indicated with extreme brevity, the sage asks a question.
O Blessed One, how and to what extent does the dissolution of the individual and the collective occur on the path of reality?
Speak, O you who perceive all things!
Since you, O Blessed One, perceive the meaning of all the scriptures, therefore instruct us:

how, by what means, in what sequence, and over what period of time does the dissolution—the withdrawal—of the path of the principles (tattvādhvan), from the individual soul (prādhānika) separately up to the principle of Power (śakti-tattva) collectively, take place? This is the meaning of the question. || 181 ||
The *Dīpikā* explains the introductory question-sūtra beginning with "of the individual" (*vyastasya*), starting with "since" (*yataḥ*).

Regarding "of the individual [world] consisting of Pradhāna and so forth": this refers to the world consisting of Pradhāna, beginning from earth and ending with the principles (*tattva*) of the qualities (*guṇa*). From the word "and so forth" (*ādi*),...
The meaning is that there may sometimes be a dissolution of the three worlds. || 181 ||
Commentary: Now, here is the reply: [it applies] to the entire [universe] during the Great Sleep.
The intermediate dissolution of the differentiated [universe] and likewise the period of its maintenance— let this duration as it is being described be understood. (182)

The power of the *māyā-tattva*, which has been diminished by the production of bodies, instruments, worlds, and so forth— the means for the enjoyment of infinite beings— has been incessantly expended; now, for the sake of providing rest to transmigrating souls weary from wandering in saṃsāra, it is withdrawn in order to re-activate its various powers capable of accomplishing those same effects once again.

The dissolution of the path beginning with Pradhāna is the withdrawal of the entire path into the "Great Sleep" (mahāsvāpa), which is characterized by the reabsorption of all forms, from Sadāśiva downwards, as assumed according to one's own will. As to what that [sleep] is and of what nature it is, so it shall be explained further on.
He will clarify that creation is likewise [of two kinds], by way of being both distinct and collective.
For it is distinct insofar as it is produced by various presiding deities such as Parā, Aparā, Vidyeśvara, and others;
yet it is collective insofar as it takes the form of Ananta and the rest, impelled by the will of the Supreme Lord. Thus, regarding this distinct [creation]...
The question asked—namely, "When does the dissolution of the entire path occur?"—has been answered by this much.

Now, regarding the answer to the question, "How long [does it last]?", that is, for how much time does that dissolution endure: since dissolution is preceded by persistence, let the duration of that persistence be heard as it is being described, beginning with the words "The time of persistence," and so forth. || 182 ||
The *Dīpikā* explains the aphorism of the established doctrine (*siddhāntasūtra*) beginning with "uninterruptedly" (*anavaratam*).

The phrase "of the *māyā*-principle" (*māyātattvasya*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), intended to include *prakṛti* and the other principles as well, for it is precisely for the sake of stimulating them that the intermediate dissolution (*madhyamapralaya*) occurs.
"Of the individual [universe]," and so forth. The dissolution of the path beginning with Pradhāna occurs first; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
As for the dissolution of the three worlds (*trailokya-pralaya*), it will become clear in the immediately following sūtra, where it is well-known. "For instance," and so forth.

At the conclusion of the intermediate dissolution (*madhyama-pralaya*), because the creation of the principles (*tattva*) such as the Guṇas is performed by Ananta, there follows the creation of the worlds (*bhuvana*).

The commentary states that the differentiated creation (vyastasarga) is accomplished by various authorities because the creation of the body and so forth is the work of Śrīkaṇṭha, whereas the creation of Brahmā and others is the work of different agents;
the integrated creation (samastasarga), however, occurs at the end of the Great Dissolution (mahālaya) through the infinite gateways impelled by the will of the Supreme Lord.
He asks, "What is this? and says:
"A day of the one born from the golden egg lasts for a thousand cycles of four yugas."
The night lasts for as long as the day, according to the measure of a day and night, during that half of a kalpa.
This dissolution occurs in reverse order;
[the process] beginning with primordial nature (prakṛti) is thereby excluded.

A day belonging to Brahmā, who was born from the golden egg, consists of a duration of four thousand cycles of the four yugas, beginning with Kṛta; his night is of exactly the same length. By this measure of day and night, in a year numbering three hundred and sixty [such days], according to the calculation of tens, hundreds, thousands, and so forth—

When the number of years reaches a *parārdha* through a calculation beginning from one thousand, then there occurs the dissolution (*vilaya*) of the inverted path of primordial matter (*prādhānika*). And this occurs "in reverse order," meaning by way of the opposite sequence to that of creation;
for while the emission (*sarga*) of the inverted path occurs later, the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) of the elements occurs first—such is the reversal. And at that time:
That which is the material cause of creation—such as *prakṛti*, *pradhāna*, and so forth—is here refuted;
rather, its activity is withdrawn by those who have authority over it. (183½)

The *Dīpikā* explains the sūtra beginning with "caturyuga" by means of the passage beginning with "kṛtādi. The measurement of these yugas is not stated here; it should be understood from other *saṃhitās* and similar sources. As it is said in the *Mataṅga*: "That which is called a *truṭi*..."

A *kalā* is subtle; twice that is known as a *lava*. Two *lavas* are a *nimeṣa*, and fifteen of those constitute a *kāṣṭhā*. Thirty *kāṣṭhās* make up a *vāha*, and thirty *vāhas* are called a *muhūrta* in this world. O observer of noble vows, thirty of those *muhūrtas* are declared to be a day and night (*ahorātra*).
In this supreme Shaiva Tantra, a fortnight (pakṣa) is to be understood as consisting of fifteen units within the cycle of day and night.

Two fortnights are recorded as a month; two months are called a season (ṛtu). O best of sages, three seasons constitute a solstice (ayana), and two solstices are defined as a year. This is the solar reckoning for the human race.
According to the perspective of the Tantras, three hundred and sixty years of the celestial dwellers are said to constitute one divine year.

Four thousand such divine years make up the Kṛta Yuga; its dawn and its twilight each last for as many hundreds of years. The other ages, beginning with Tretā, are each reduced by one thousand [divine] years.

The periods consisting of the twilights (*saṃdhyā*) and twilight-portions (*saṃdhyāṃśa*), as well as those established by *kalpas*, are all declared hereafter to constitute a *caturyuga* of years. Furthermore, a *manvantara* consists of twelve thousand [years] of these;
it should be understood by those seeking calculation that seventy-one *caturyugas* make up one day of Brahmā. Thus ends the section concerning the day of Brahmā.

The duration of the stability of the three worlds is equal to that very length of night; this constitutes the time of its dissolution. As it is stated in that same place regarding the lifespan of the Indras appointed to their respective duties: "The lifespan of each one shall be seventy-one *yugas*. By fourteen such lifespans of Śakra, there is one day of the Lotus-born One."

This existence of the three worlds has been described by you in brief. Likewise, O Sage, the night is of such a duration that during it the three worlds go to destruction when darkness arrives at the onset of day. Then Brahmā, having arisen from his bed, enters [the world] through the nature of the instruments (karaṇātmanā), and by the power of Rudra’s energy, he again pierces through [the veil] so that the world emerges.

He states the measure of time for everything from the earth up to the qualities (guṇas), ending with the intermediate dissolution (madhyamapralaya), beginning with the words "by this" and so forth. This very same measure also applies to the duration of that dissolution. Furthermore, it is stated in other scriptures that this constitutes the full lifespan of Brahmā, who is born from the golden egg, and is one day and night for Śrīkaṇṭha. || 183½ ||
