Then, O hero, the hundred Rudras and Śrīkaṇṭha, the lords of the primary principles (pradhāna), having pervaded the subtle universe with their power (śakti),...
And the subtle bodies endowed with consciousness. || 184½ ||
Those whose dispositions remain in their natural state wait for that time which marks the end of their sleep.
And at that time, the hundred Rudras, Śrīkaṇṭha and Vīrabhadra,
Krodheśa, Caṇḍa, Saṃvarta, and others who are the primary presiding deities, remain until the end of the dissolution of Prakṛti, because the world they govern then exists in the form of Śakti.

Abiding in their own power, they remain presiding over the subtle bodies composed of the principles beginning with earth and ending with kalā, which are initiated by the latent impressions of karma residing in prakṛti, and over the individual souls endowed with consciousness.
Immediately after that:
impelled by the bearer of the Śiva-īṣṭa mantra,
they are sent forth by the Lord of the Maṇḍala.
Having brought forth the world at the proper time, they exercise their own authority. || 186 ||

Furthermore, at the beginning of each intermediate creation, impelled by the will of the Supreme Lord and urged by the Vidyeśvaras such as Ananta and others, they are set in motion by the presiding Rudras known as Maṇḍalādhipatis; having fashioned the world at that time, they exercise their respective offices. || 186 ||
Commentary: Here, the Sage, being doubtful because of the scriptural statement regarding the latent dispositions residing in the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), asks:
"What is that *karman*, such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth?"
Since it is established that a quality resides within the possessor of the quality,
how can it be said that the quality does not depart from its substrate? (187)

It has been stated that action, which consists of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), exists as a quality (*guṇa*) of the intellect (*buddhi*), according to the passage beginning with "the states are qualities of the intellect: virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and power. For the departure of a quality from its substratum is never observed; indeed, whiteness does not depart from a cloth.

Or is it possible to separate the sweetness from sugar and the like? Therefore, the meaning of the question is: how can there be a scriptural statement regarding the latent tendencies (āśaya) residing in the primordial nature (prakṛti)? || 187 ||
The *Dīpikā*: In this context, he states "here," etc., to show that the question of the Sage arises as a consequence (*prasaṅga*). || 187 ||
Commentary: As for the established conclusion (siddhānta):
it is true that action is a quality of the intellect (buddhi).
The quality of one who possesses qualities does not depart;
it is only through their residence within the body, the senses, the fruits [of action], and the stages of existence that the quality is metaphorically attributed to them.

Indeed, it possesses the quality of being an attribute of the intellect (*buddhi*), according to the manner previously stated; for there is no departure of an attribute from its substrate, namely action whose nature consists of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). However, in that case, it is figuratively said that "that action resides in *prakṛti*. He asks: "From what seed of figurative usage [is this said]? and replies: "Of the body, the senses, the fruits, and the ground..."

Because they reside therein. Since the bodies, senses, objects, and the spheres of experience for the enjoyers reside only within *prakṛti*, karma is also said to reside therein by virtue of being situated there. Although the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) resides in the intellect (*buddhi*), because the intellect itself resides in *prakṛti*, it is stated that the selves have their deposits situated in *prakṛti*; thus, there is no contradiction. || 188 ||
Commentary: Furthermore, various metaphorical applications of words are observed, based on seeds of metaphor such as "being located therein" (*tātsthya*).
For instance:
"In the case of a substratum, a cause, an effect, that which is proximate, and that which is beneficial..."
And the wise have declared that there is also metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) when there is an imitation of qualities such as dharma. || 189 ||

The wise who know that [subject] have declared that *lakṣaṇā* (indication) brings about the cognition of a secondary meaning because the following of the primary meaning is untenable. Where and where? He says: "In the locus," and so forth. First, regarding the locus (*ādhāra*), for example:
"The platforms are crying. For here, the platforms—which are the substratum—[are indicated by those who are upon them].

Because it does not follow from the literal meaning—namely, the act of crying characterized by weeping—and because it would be purposeless, the "wailing" belonging to the children situated there is attributed to them through a *lakṣaṇā* based on their location (*tātsthyātma*).
As for *lakṣaṇā* in the sense of a cause (*kāraṇe*), it is as in the example: "It has rained on the rice. For here, [the rain is attributed to the rice].

In its primary sense, the meaning of "the rice has rained" (*śālivarṣaṇa*) is incoherent; therefore, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it refers to a timely and abundant rainfall which is the cause of rice. Since there is no possibility of obstacles or deficiencies [in that cause], the effect characterized as rice is figuratively attributed [to the cause] as being already accomplished. Alternatively, it is like the expression "clarified butter is life" (*āyur ghṛtam*).

In the expression "clarified butter for longevity" (*āyuṣkāraṇe ghṛte*), there is a figurative application (*upacāra*) of the term "longevity" to its effect [the health resulting from it]. Likewise, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is possible even with respect to an effect, as in the case of "wool is clothing" (*ūrṇāḥ prāvaraṇāḥ*) or "cotton is clothing" (*tūlaṃ vāsaḥ*). Here, indeed, since wool and cotton have not yet undergone transformation into the state of cloth through the form of yarn (*sūtra*), they cannot be designated by the primary sense [of "clothing"].

Covering by means of the function [of the material] is not possible, because that effect is established as having the nature of the woolen blanket or the cloth itself. Consequently, the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the terms "wool" and "cotton" is made with respect to the blanket and the cloth.
An example of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on proximity is: "A hamlet on the Ganges. For here, by the primary function (*mukhyā vṛtti*), [the word "Ganges"]...

If the word "Ganges" were to denote, by way of its primary function (*vṛtti*), either the stream in the form of flowing water or some specific feature thereof, then its location in a village would be entirely impossible; therefore, by implication, its proximity is established as the basis for secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Secondary indication is also seen in the case of that which is beneficial, as in the example: "Alms..."
They cause him to dwell—this is what is meant by "the teacher causes [the pupil] to study" (*kārīṣo'dhyāpayati*).

In this context, it is said that they do not merely prevent his departure by seizing his alms-bowl and upper garment with their hands; nor do they stop him from leaving the place altogether by means of affectionate words such as "you must not go. Rather, [they cause him to dwell].
Abundant food and condiments, because they cause satisfaction,

are metaphorically designated as the "instigators" (prayojaka) by virtue of being conceived as contributing to the act of sitting down [to eat]. Likewise, one does not teach a young student while saying, "O son, study with cow-dung fuel," nor does one enter into his body.
He makes him recite as if he were being taught by spirits, vetālas, and the like.

By serving as a cause for the removal of cold, it possesses conformity (*ānukūlya*) through its assistance to the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayanavidhi*); thus, it is figuratively designated as the "prompter" (*prayojaka*) of that [study]. Furthermore, by the inclusion of the phrase "in the imitation of qualities (*dharma*) and so forth," there is either an imitation of form (*ākāra*) or an imitation of genus (*jāti*). Among these, regarding the imitation of qualities, for example, [the word] "lion" [is applied to a man].

"The young brahmin is a *gaurvāhīka*. In this case, it is said that the word "lion" is applied to the young brahmin in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) for the purpose of imitating the qualities of a lion, such as courage and so forth, by means of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because its primary sense (*mukhyā vṛttiḥ*)—namely, being a lion—is impossible in his case. As for "the *vāhīka*," [it refers to] a male.

Since it is impossible for [the word] to denote one who carries on his back, the word *go* (cow) is employed with a figurative application (*upacaritavṛtti*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in order to imitate the properties found in a bull, such as standing while eating, walking, urinating, and so forth; for such a connection does not occur through the primary application (*mukhyā vṛtti*). Such is the nature of the form...

Regarding *kṛti* (imitation), as in the example: "by darknesses pierceable by needles. For here, since darkness is formless (*amūrta*), its being "pierceable by a needle" is not applicable to darkness in its primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*); therefore, in order to express its extreme density (*atinibiḍatva*) through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the generic form (*ākṛti*) is imitated by means of "pierceability by a needle. Thus, the darknesses are indeed dense.
The meaning is that, like clothing and other such things, it is possible to effect a division of these [atoms] by means of a needle or similar instrument. || 189 ||
1. "Clothing" is the meaning. *Dīpikā*:
This is stated to show that the various types of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) are being explained by way of digression following the main topic.
He introduces the foundational sūtra with the words: "And they are seen," and so forth. || 189 ||
Commentary: Having thus illustrated the incidental seed of metaphorical usage, he speaks again, following the sequence for concluding the present topic.
In this way, at the end of a parārdha of creations such as the qualities (guṇas), Māyā, which is the cause of the qualities, consumes the kalā; the kalā consumes the kalā.
She has turned her back on her own office. || 190 ||
Upon its cessation, the gods who hold office therein also cease,
because [the world] consists of creation, maintenance, and so forth.
The qualification has that [attainment] as its basis. || 191 ||

When a period of time known as a *parārdha*— measured by the previously stated duration of the creations of the *guṇas* and so forth— has elapsed, the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is the cause of the *guṇas*, withdraws the *kalā* into its own self. Then Māyā, turning away from her office and desiring to withdraw her own activity, likewise withdraws that *kalā* from her domain.
He withdraws [all things] into his own self alone. And upon the cessation of that office of Māyā, all those who were appointed to it cease;
they remain with their activities desisted. Since their entire office—consisting of creation, maintenance, and so forth—is based upon Māyā, how could they [continue] when that has ceased?
There may be a cessation [of the creation].
190 – *Dīpikā*: He explains the two sūtras beginning with "guṇādisargāṇām" and so forth. Here...

The inclusion of the unmanifest (avyakta) and time (kāla) should be understood as indicative of the inclusion of attachment (rāga) and the other [afflictions] as well, by virtue of their own causes being included. Regarding the phrase "of that" and so forth:
therein, the supreme Mantra-Īśvaras possess supreme liberation due to the relinquishing of their office; others, however...
According to their fitness for the state of Bhuvaneśvara, they become either *pralayakevalins*, *vijñānakevalins*, or liberated souls (*muktas*). || 190–191 ||
Commentary: Thus, the reabsorption (*pratisañcara*) in the impure path has been described. Now, he speaks in order to describe [it] in the pure path.
Thus, among the twenty principal lords of mantras,
he always eats the desired state, which is the reality of the Vidyā.
The drop of that [Bindu] is the Bindu-sound (baindava-dhvani). || 192 ||
The supreme power devours the sound; Hara himself rules over that power.

In this very sequence, when the Mantramaheśvaras—Ananta and the others—who have fulfilled their office and desire to attain supreme liberation (parakaivalya), are present, the Vidyā-tattva withdraws its sovereign power into the Sadāśiva-tattva. That [Sadāśiva-tattva] dissolves into the Bindu; and the Bindu also dissolves into the nature of Nāda.
Even Nāda [dissolves] into the Supreme Śakti; however, the Supreme Lord, having directly withdrawn that Śakti into His own self, does not produce the Kalās.

The *Dīpikā*: Now, demonstrating that at the very time of the withdrawal of *māyā*, there is also the withdrawal of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), he explains the sūtra beginning with "In this way" (*evam*) and so forth. [He says] "By this very [means]" and so on; [and] "in the supreme power" (*parasyāṃ śaktau*).

It has been stated that she consists of Mahāmāyā. Having withdrawn [the universe] into her own self, she does not bring forth further creative powers (kalās); the meaning is that she presides over it. || 192 ||
Commentary: And when this has been done, the Supreme Lord [acts] thus for the rest of living beings.
And Paraśiva, having perceived Māyā through the power of his own vision, proceeds toward emanation from his state of sleep. (193½)

By means of His own power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), for the sake of the repose— meaning the state of non-activity— of the material cause called *māyā*, whose power has been diminished through the production of various effects such as bodies, organs, and worlds suitable for the experiences of transmigrating beings exhausted by wandering in *saṃsāra*; by this much [the Lord's nature is described].

In due time, these beings come to rest; and once their capacity has been accumulated, the causal principle called Māyā becomes capable of further creation. Having thus reflected, the Supreme Lord proceeds for the sake of creation as before.
Commentary: Just as these have been described as dissolving into their own respective causes, he says that other things are likewise:
"In this way, the principles (tattvas) and the entities (bhāvas)."
O Brahmin, the worlds and the forms belonging to both the pure and impure paths have been explained in brief. || 194½ ||

In this very sequence, whatever else exists within the white and black paths—whether it be principles (tattva), states of being (bhāva), worlds (bhuvana), or anything else—it should be understood that it has dissolved into its own cause; thus, it is explained in brief. || 194½ ||

The *Dīpikā* explains [the passage] beginning with "In this way, the principles" (*evaṃ tattvāni*) and so forth, starting with "By this very sequence" (*anenaiva krameṇa*). The intended meaning is as follows:
just like the previously mentioned impure, real body, the pure subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) is also...

If it is asked: "Since that which consists of *mahāmāyā* exists as the essence of reality (*tattva*) in the form of a specific state of power (*śakti*), for what reason is this pure subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*) postulated? [The answer is:
It is for the sake of utility in initiation (*dīkṣā*). For, because the Self (*ātman*) is all-pervading, in initiation...

Regarding the statement that "seizing and so forth are not possible," just as on the path of illusion (*māyīya-adhvan*) one performs establishment, gathering, conjunction, and so on by means of the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), likewise on the pure path (*śuddha-adhvan*) one performs conjunction,
seizing, and so forth in their respective locations by means of the subtle body consisting of the power of speech (*vākśakti*).

Because it is said "it is performed," and because they share the same designation as the previously mentioned principles such as Time (Kāla), there is no consequence of their being distinct from those principles; for this very reason, the term "in the impure" (*aśuddhau*) is used here, just as in the case of the Māyīya path. 194½.
Commentary: Here the Sage asks:
"And what is the body of the five atoms of knowledge?"
The drop (bindu), the resonance (nāda), and then the cause;
the five aggregates (skandhas) are the supreme path—wherein do the phenomena (bhāvas) and conditions (pratyayas) abide? || 195½ ||

Regarding that which was taught by the Blessed One to us— that there is such a dissolution (*pratisañcara*) within its own cause of the pure and impure paths, consisting of the principles (*tattva*), states of being (*bhāva*), elements (*bhūta*), and worlds (*bhuvana*)— in that [dissolution], [the path] takes the form of Vidyā, Sadāśiva, Bindu, Nāda, and the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*).
The meaning of the question is: "In what locations do the entities (bhāvas) exist as causal conditions (pratyayas) within the pure path?
The *Dīpikā* states that the Sage poses this inquiry, asking: "In which specific places do which principles (tattvas) abide in a subtle form?"

"Regarding 'here' and so forth: 'the entities (bhāva) are established as conditions (pratyaya)' means that the intellect (buddhi), which is the primary cause of the entities, and the other principles (tattva) characterized by it [are meant]. || 195½ ||
Commentary: Herein is the established conclusion (siddhānta): Sound is subtle; it is the digit (kalā) and time (kāla).
O Sage, when the pair of passion (rāga) is accompanied by the Puruṣa, the gross sound (nāda) consists of five kalās and rests upon the five principles (tattvas).
The four knots beginning with *pradhāna* are the treasure; the *bindu* consists of four parts.
Within the *garva*, the gods have the mind (*manas*) as their foremost.
Existence and the other categories reside within the intellect. || 197½ ||
O God, the body of the five mantras is situated in the pentad of subtle elements;
the lords of the mantras reside in the subtle elements.
The mantras reside within the gross elements. || 198½ ||

The essential point here is this: the impure path is established as being pervaded by this pure path of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). And therein, because the *bindu-tattva*—which possesses a specific pervasion as will be described—is included within it, [the impure path is subsumed].

There is no contradiction whatsoever in the persistence of the suffixes denoting abstract states (*bhāvapratyaya*). For instance, the subtle supreme *nāda* is called "a part" (*kalā*); because it is pervaded by the *kalās*, it is spoken of through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) as being in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *kalā*.
Or, for example, by accepting all objects of knowledge such as *nāda* and *bindu*, its cause [is designated] accordingly.
The nature of *paranāda* remains thus established as the state of the *kalās* through the inclusion of the entire path of the non-white (*asitādhva*);

therefore, it is figuratively designated by that [state]. In the "pair of Time" (*kālayugma*), which consists of *niyati* and *kāla*; in the "pair of Passion" (*rāgayugma*), which consists of the natures of *vidyā* and *rāga*; and "together with *puruṣa*" (*sapūruṣa*), meaning accompanied by the *puruṣa*-tattva—these five *tattvas* are the substratum.

That [Nāda] has as its support the five principles (*pañcatattva*) and is the gross sound (*sthūlanāda*) consisting of the five kalās. And by this very sequence, it contains within itself— that is, it is the treasury (*nidhi*)— of the fourfold group of knots (*granthi*), which are the *prakṛtis* in the form of fetters (*pāśa*), characterized by *pradhāna*, *guṇa*, *mahat*, and *ahaṅkāra*.

The *bindu* should be understood as consisting of the four *kalās*, beginning with *nivṛtti*, mentioned previously. Within this [bindu], within the *garva* (pride), which is the principle of *ahaṅkāra* (ego), the ten instruments along with the mind are situated; in the *buddhi* (intellect), however, the states such as *dharma* (virtue) and so forth, as well as their material causes—the aforementioned *pratyayas*—are established. And thus:

Sadāśivanātha, whose body consists of the five mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, presides over the pentad of subtle elements (tanmātra) starting with earth; thus he abides as the pentad of subtle elements. Furthermore, the pervasion of the Lords of Mantras (mantreśas) extends to the subtle elements—the specific types of matter that constitute the subtle body—and to the mantras themselves.

Regarding gross entities such as earth and so forth, although [the Self] is pure, there is no fault in its remaining in this state by encompassing these objects of knowledge within non-duality. || 197½ ||
1. The reading is *vyāpakatvāt*.
The *Dīpikā* explains the Siddhānta-sūtra beginning with "This here," etc., [referring to] the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*) which is the pervaded (*vyāpya*).

The meaning is that as many divisions as there are, so many subtle forms reside even within this pure path consisting of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). In that regard, he shows which principles (*tattva*) they are by saying "for instance" (*tathāhi*), and so forth:
"characterized by the primary matter (*pradhāna*), the qualities (*guṇa*), the great one (*mahat*), and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*)," etc. And because these are the sources of effects (*kāryayoni*).
The meaning is that it is expressed by the word "knot" (granthi). || 198½ ||
1. *Skandhāni* is a variant reading.
[This is] the commentary (*vṛtti*). Now, for the purpose of concluding the explained meaning, [there follows] the section on action (*kriyāpāda*) of that which is to be explained.
And there is a verse for the purpose of introduction:

Thus: that vast net of bonds, consisting of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), the subtle atoms, the obstructing darkness, the seed-syllables, and so forth, which is traversed by those whose vision follows the way of the fettered (*paśu*);
for the purpose of its pacification, [it arises] from the ritual action to be described hereafter.
The perfection of the Śāmbhava mantra possesses a radiant and unimpeded power.

Thus ends the Vidyāpāda in the illustrious Mṛgendra-tantra. In the manner thus described, that which necessarily obstructs the individual souls (aṇu)— the bound beings (paśu)— is the "obstructor of the individual soul" (aṇunirodhi),
consisting of the impurity (mala), karma, and māyā, as well as the powers of obstruction belonging to the Great Lord (Maheśvara), such as the seed of darkness (dhvāntabīja) and so forth.

Because it possesses manifold powers due to its nature as the concealer of the infinite [Self], it is "exceedingly abundant" (*su-bhūyas*), meaning most extensive. By those whose vision—meaning knowledge—is "strayed" (*sṛtā*) or diffused among the non-theistic scriptures of the Paśupatas, it remains unseen and uncomprehended. It is like a "net" (*jālam*) because, as the cause of bondage, it pertains to the fetters (*pāśas*).

The prosperity of the Śiva-mantra, blazing with unimpeded power, arises precisely from the cause of the ritual action and so forth to be described hereafter for the purpose of pacifying that [affliction]. This is the intended meaning:
by means of the prosperity of the mantra, whose innate capacity has been intensified through the sequence of the ritual of initiation (dīkṣā) to be explained.
Since it serves as the cause for the pacification of the bonds of ritual actions such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) and leads to spiritual elevation,

the power of mantras— which possess inconceivable and incomparable majesty— is unimpeded even in severing the bonds of impurity (*mala*), karma, and *māyā*, just as it is in the removal of poison and the like. Thus it has been said:

Regarding the occasion for defining the essential nature and function of the mantra, the Siddha Sadyojyotiḥ stated: "Like poison, it swiftly cuts away the impurity (mala), karma, the womb (yoni), and the effects (kārya) of the bound soul (paśu); yet, when propitiated, it bestows various supernatural powers (siddhi) upon the foremost of practitioners."
1. In the *Tattvasaṃgraha* within the *Aṣṭaprakaraṇa*, the thirty-fifth verse states:
Whatever may be useless, and whatever irrelevant matter concerning an object of knowledge (*prameya*) one may address—that is certainly not fruitless thundering.

Nevertheless, may the appreciation of those who know it flourish here, through this investigation of the subject matter at hand as presented by the King of Beasts, which is appropriate for the present occasion.
Having received grace from the venerable Vidyākaṇṭha, whose throat was Śaṅkara,
Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha [composed] this.
His son composed a commentary upon it.
Thus ends the section on the Path of the Worlds (*bhuvanādhvaprakaraṇa*) in the *Mṛgendravṛtti*, composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Vidyākaṇṭha.
|| It is finished ||
The Vidyāpāda is completed.
[The author] explains the verse beginning with "dīpikā" by means of the words "ity evam" and so forth; therein, by the words "kriyātaḥ" and so on...

A general introduction to the section on ritual action (*kriyāpāda*) is now made; by the term "perfection of mantra," the extraction of mantras—which will be discussed there as the primary subject—is indicated. May it be auspicious!

He who, himself skilled in grammar, lexicography, and logic, composed the *Pāṣaṇḍāpajaya*, the *Sakāvyatilaka*, the *Bhaktaprakāśa*, and other works— this very one is the illustrious Aghoraśiva, a crest-jewel among Brahmins, a treasury of sacred learning, and a venerable Śiva.
In this chapter, he composed the *Dīpikā* titled *Vidyā* for the commentary on the *Mṛgendra*.
Thus ends the section on the Paths (*adhvaprakaraṇa*) in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā* composed by the teacher Aghoraśiva.
The Vidyāpāda is completed. Śrī.
Now follows the Yoga-pāda (accompanied by the commentary composed by Śrīmannārāyaṇakaṇṭha).
Herein, first of all: "From this extensive bondage, which obstructs the state of the Supreme, initiation alone..."

Because of the scriptural statement that "it liberates [the soul] and leads it upward to the abode of Śiva," initiation alone is the cause for attaining unsurpassed liberation (kaivalya); and because of that [initiation], which— by means of the method for defining the nature of the bound soul (paśu), the fetters (pāśa), and the Lord (īśvara)— demonstrates the pervasion of the entire path (adhvan).

Since it is impossible to accomplish [the goal] without the knowledge that determines the majesty of the mantras, the lords of mantras, and so forth, that very knowledge— the Vidyāpāda along with its appendages—
is stated first for the purpose of defining the nature of the bound soul (paśu), the fetters (pāśa), and the Lord (īśvara). Thereafter—

The section on ritual action (*kriyāpāda*) has also been taught for the purpose of demonstrating the various methods of initiation (*dīkṣā*) along with their auxiliary components. However, at present,

even one who knows the sequence of knowledge and action— such as an initiate (*sādhaka*) or a spiritual son (*putraka*)— being ignorant of the self due to a lack of practice in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and so forth, [remains in this state].
Since it is not possible to accomplish the performance of one's respective duties as they have been taught [in the previous section],
there follows the commencement of the *Yogapāda* for the sake of making known Yoga, accompanied by its ancillaries such as breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). And here,
the intended meaning is the manifestation of the Supreme Lord’s own nature within the individual soul (*aṇu*) whose bonds have been destroyed.

The relationship has been established by means of the three subjects of the treatise, characterized as the bound soul (paśu), the fetter (pāśa), and the Lord (īśvara). And its purpose should be understood as that which has been set forth. The relationship pertaining to the sūtra is also obtained from the introductory statement of the enumerative sūtra, "consisting of three categories and four feet"; and it is of the nature of a sentence.

By such statements as "the application [of the ritual] will be explained through the sections on Conduct (caryā), Yoga, and Action (kriyā)," it has been stated that this section on Yoga is necessarily useful for the *samayin*, the *putraka*, and for the *sādhaka* and *ācārya* who have received initiation, even though it belongs to the general context (*prākaraṇika*). As for the topical sequence (*pāṭalika*), however, it will be mentioned at the end of the subsequent chapter and section.
This is introduced by the phrase "frequented by the supreme yogins."
Then, considering that their own duty is extremely difficult for those who lack self-mastery,
those who possess self-mastery should strive [to fulfill it].
The teachers and others who desire victory. || 1 ||

Those who possess the Self are "possessors of the Self" (*ātmavantaḥ*), because they are engaged in delighting in the Self and have directly realized the nature of the Self; the suffix *matup* here denotes a permanent connection. Furthermore, for such individuals—the sons of the teacher (*deśika-putra*), the initiates (*samayin*), and the practitioners (*sādhaka*)—it is difficult to accomplish their respective duties.

Having understood this, those beginning with the preceptor (diśika), desiring victory over the successive stages, should strive—that is, they should be diligent—for that purpose; here the optative suffix (*liṅ*) indicates an injunction.
Now, he asks: what indeed is this so-called "self-possession" (*ātmavattva*)? He says:
Then, for one who has conquered the senses, the state of being a yogi— characterized by self-mastery—
is attained through the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other disciplines.
One should gradually attain mastery over the senses. || 2 ||

The yogi is necessarily engaged through the manifestation of his own true nature, which is characterized by Śiva-hood; the state of being such a yogi (yogitva) is inseparable from the state of being the Self (ātmavatva). For this very reason, the word *yoga* should be understood as derived from the verbal root *yuj* (to join), and not from *yuj* in the sense of "meditative absorption" (*samādhi*). This...

Because it is intended as a constituent part of that [practice]. And this belongs to one who has conquered the senses; for one who has brought the collection of the sense organs under control accomplishes other tasks as well—how much more so the state of being a yogi? Thus they have said: "A wise person who practices self-restraint should exert effort over the senses as they roam among alluring objects, just as a charioteer does with his horses."

For one who has conquered the senses, the attainment of one's true nature occurs very quickly. And it was said by Sanaka: "Having restrained the senses, the objects of the senses, the subtle elements (tanmātras), and likewise the mind, one whose movement and volition are stilled merges into the Supreme Self. He now explains how that state of having conquered the senses is achieved:
"From the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth.

Through the cultivation of the seven ancillaries beginning with breath control, whose characteristics will be described later, mastery over the senses occurs gradually and in due course. The second occurrence of the word "gradually" (śanaiḥ) refers to the domain of practice.
Prāṇāyāma and the other practices should be performed gradually, according to the sequence of increasing the duration as it will be described;

for if they are practiced excessively, defects such as abdominal tumors (vātagulma), upward movement of wind in the rectum (gudodāvarta), upward breath (ūrdhvaśvāsa), insanity (unmāda), and loss of memory (smṛtimoṣa) arise, which are causes of obstacles to yoga.
They would arise. || 2 ||
Now, in order to teach yoga along with its ancillaries (sāṅga), he says: breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra),
concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and contemplation (vīkṣaṇa).
Concentration on the recitation is the limb; yoga itself is the eighth, being the possessor of limbs. || 3 ||

The seven limbs are breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the rest; yoga itself, however, is to be understood as the eighth, being the principal (aṅgin). Now he states the definitions of these [limbs], beginning with breath control:
"Prāṇa" is the wind that has been previously described.
Its extension consists of sweating;
characterized by stimulation, drawing, and restraint, it removes defects of the sacrificial rite.

Although the wind is one, it possesses fivefold divisions such as prāṇa, apāna, and so forth, due to the differences in its functions like breathing; and these functions have been demonstrated in the Vidyāpāda.
The "exhaustion" (khedana) of such a wind occurs predominantly externally because of the state of [the yogin's] autonomy (svātantryabhāva).

Impulsion; likewise, its internal drawing back, restraint, and the state of being held (kumbhīkaraṇa), as well as exhalation, inhalation, and cessation—this exhaustion of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, characterized in this way, is prāṇāyāma. By the word "kratu," the sense organs or volition are meant; their defects [are what are restrained].
It is called "the remover of those defects" because it dispels—that is, pacifies—the faults caused by the non-performance of prescribed duties and the performance of prohibited ones.

For it has been said: "Just as the impurities of metallic ores are burnt away when they are being smelted, so too are the defects within the range of the senses stilled by breath-control (prāṇāyāma). (4)
Now, the definition of withdrawal (pratyāhāra):
"Then, when their mind is occupied with the tasting of fragments of pleasure,"
Withdrawal must be practiced;
it is the turning away from everything.

Then, immediately after the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) should be performed. To explain what its nature is, he says "of those": regarding the savoring of that minute fragment of pleasure—that slight trace of bliss—pertaining to the objects of those [senses], for the mind that is engaged in and intent upon it, [withdrawal is superior] to all [other means].
In this way, the withdrawal of the senses from their objects is to be practiced as pratyāhāra. || 5 ||
To the question, "What would happen if this were practiced in this way? he says:
"By that, the mind's perception [arises] from the cessation of contact between the senses and their objects."
It attains the state of being fit for retention within a word imagined according to one's own will.

By that withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), because the mind (*citta*) has been withdrawn from its conjunction with the objects of the senses, there occurs a cessation—the desisting from its own activity; through this cessation which serves as the cause, the intellect (*mati*) attains the fitness for the concentration (*dhāraṇā*) to be described later, in a state fashioned according to one's own will. And here, "intellect" (*mati*) does not mean the faculty of cognition (*buddhi*), but rather—
Reflection (*manana*) is the mental activity of the mind known as conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*), for it is that very [activity] which is heard of as "retention" (*dhāraṇā*).
As Patañjali said: "Retention is the fixing of the mind upon the body," and likewise, "the fitness of the mind for retentions. (6)
To explain meditation (dhyāna), he says: "Meditation is the thought directed toward that [object], and it is prescribed to be practiced repeatedly. (6½)

Dhyāna is that reflection upon the mind restrained by dhāraṇā, which has as its object forms such as the three eyes and five faces; and this has been taught repeatedly on various occasions in passages such as, "The four lotus-faces possessing the luster of gold, bees, snow, and gems," and so forth. || 6½ ||
Now, the definition of concentration (samādhi):
when that [mind] attains one-pointedness, it is designated as concentration. || 7 ||

When that meditation reaches a state of one-pointedness, wherein there is the appearance of only the object of meditation, it is then designated as "samādhi" in the treatises; as Patañjali has said: "That very [meditation], when it appears as the object alone and is as if empty of its own form, is samādhi. (7)
Commentary: He states the definition of *japa*:
"Japa is the recitation of that [mantra] while meditating upon it."
The manifestation [of the truth] before the Sage. || 7½ ||

Japa is said to be the repetition performed for the purpose of bringing the object of meditation (dhyeya) into presence; this includes mental recitation in the form of internal discourse, that which is designated as whispered (upāṃśu), the commentary (bhāṣya) consisting of a subtle sound perceptible only to oneself, and the audible mantra. || 7½ ||
1. The twenty-second verse in the section on conditions (*pratyaya*) and so forth.
Now, in order to define *ūha* (inferential modification), he says: *Ūha* is the contemplation of an object.
It arises immediately after conceptual construction. || 8 ||

That which is the "ūha" (inference/reasoning) of men, which wanders like one lost in the dark while searching for a path—that is called *prāṇa*. By this [statement], because of the subtlety of the wind known as *prāṇa* in the *vidyāpāda*, it is being inferred (*takṣyan*) as "ūhan" (inferring); thus, what was stated there proceeds as its "anūha" (non-inference/non-reasoning). Furthermore, it is said likewise in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "its *anūha* proceeds."

Thus, that *ūha* (deliberation), which consists of investigation, should be understood as having arisen immediately after the conceptualization caused by dissatisfaction with the object obtained through the attainment of various stages (*bhūmikā*). || 8 ||
Now, for what purpose is this modification (ūha) useful to the yogin? He says:
"When he knows the state to be abandoned and that to be accepted, [by virtue of] its stability..."
That which nourishes it, its opposite, and that which further nourishes the latter.

Because of that stability and abiding of that joy (*uha*), for that reason, in due order—that is, for which cause—the yogi, as he arises, understands through the method of perceiving all things as they truly exist:
the state to be abandoned (*heya-pada*), that which nourishes it, its opposite (*vipakṣa*), and that which nourishes the opposite. For example:

One knows what is to be adopted, what nourishes that [adoption], what is the opposite, and what nourishes the opposite; for this very reason, it is an excellent limb of yoga. As it is said in the *Mālinīvijaya*: "Even though [all] limbs of yoga are equal, reasoning (*tarka*) is the supreme limb of yoga, for the purpose of discerning what is to be abandoned and so forth. This is also stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*.
The yogi should perceive that reality which sets in motion the accomplishment of yoga, which brings about cessation, and which is established in manifold ways. || 9 ||
Having thus described the limbs of yoga, he speaks in order to state their fruit:
"For the yogi who has exerted effort in these [limbs], whether taken individually or collectively..."
The powers shine forth, pervading the universe like the rays of the sun. || 10 ||
No man, nor Rākṣasas, nor Dānavas, nor gods,
can overcome him as he shines with intense brilliance, surpassing all these.
By the light of vision, action, and vital breath. || 11 ||

In those limbs such as breath-control (prāṇāyāma), whether practiced individually or collectively, when the yogin has perfected his practice, all powers shine forth and blaze, pervading the universe like the rays of the sun;
the meaning is that he shall possess unimpeded capacity in all undertakings. And because of his exceedingly fierce splendor, no one can surpass him.

No one whatsoever can assail him while he remains thus resplendent, surpassing and transcending the Rākṣasas, Dānavas, gods, and humans, because he stands having gone beyond them by means of his preeminent knowledge, action, vigor, and splendor. The word *rorucānam* (shining intensely) serves as the reason expressed through the medium of this epithet. (10–11)
Regarding this, the Sage asks: "What is the cause for the withdrawal of the mind? It is the exhaustion of the vital breath resulting from sensory contact."
The cessation of concentration (dhāraṇā) and the other [limbs] is the root of everything; therefore, it [cessation] is the source of all.
O best of gods, [I shall explain] in detail that which is remote and established,
as well as whatever other means there may be.
And let the perfection of yoga be explained. || 12-13 ||

The cessation of the mind from contact with the objects of the senses is indeed held to have breath-control (prāṇāyāma) as its cause; for through mastery over the vital breaths and so forth, the mind comes under control. And that cessation of the mind from the objects of the senses is the cause of concentration (dhāraṇā) and the other stages; therefore, for that reason, the exhaustion of the breaths [is necessary].

Since it is the root of everything, beginning with concentration (*dhāraṇā*), let it be explained in detail. Furthermore, whatever other means for the attainment of yoga remains established as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) or a primary member (*aṅgin*)—such as eating food that is wholesome, moderate, and well-digested; staying in an unobstructed place and maintaining a proper posture; or practicing purity (*śauca*) and so forth—that too [should be explained].
"O Blessed One, O Lord of the Immortals, let it be told to us," such was the question of the Sage. (12–13)
Now, the reply to this is as follows: it is not possible to explain this in detail for fear of prolixity regarding the ritual injunction.
Nevertheless, the enumeration is stated because the question must necessarily be addressed. || 14 ||

Because it figuratively indicates the injunction, the term "injunction" is also applied to the treatise. If the subject matter were to be stated in full detail, it would result in excessive prolixity for the treatise; therefore, it is inappropriate to state the subject matter in full detail at this stage, for listeners are generally averse to excessive elaboration.
Nevertheless, because the question must necessarily be addressed, a brief presentation of the entire procedure is now set forth. || 14 ||
Regarding that, he speaks briefly to explain purity (*śauca*), which stands as the first limb [of the practice]:
"Having discharged urine and so forth according to the rule, with one, half, ten, and seven [applications of earth]."
One should purify the linga, the anus, and both hands with earth.
Having drunk water twice and thrice, one who observes the vow should wipe his mouth twice and touch the crown of the head,
the arms, the navel, and the heart.
Having rinsed his lips two or three times. || 16 ||

"Having performed the voiding of feces and urine according to rule" means having done so without transgressing the injunctions of the general scriptures. As it is stated in the *Vāsiṣṭha*: "With his head covered, having made the ground separated from [the earth] by grass unfit for sacrifice, he should void urine and feces; facing north during the day, and facing south at night. Thereafter—

One should purify the penis, the anus, the left hand, and both hands respectively with one, fifteen, seven, and seven applications of earth. Regarding the phrase "twice for the practitioner" (*dvir vratī*):
it will be explained in the *Caryāpāda* that the status of being a "practitioner" (*vratī*) applies to all four, including the *samayin*, the *putraka*, and so forth.
Therefore, this rule of purification applies to those who are not under a vow (*avratin*). One who is under a vow (*vratī*), however, should perform that same act twice:

having drunk water three times, having sipped it (*ācamya*), and having wiped the mouth twice, he should touch the sense-orifices (*khāni*)—the apertures of the senses—as well as the arms, the navel, the heart, and the head. He should likewise touch his lower lip two or three times.
One should wash it. || 15–16 ||
And immediately thereafter:
one who is healthy, having eaten wholesome and digested food, in a house enclosed by three walls;
Or, in a forest or similar place free from disturbances, seated upon one's own seat and facing north; || 17 ||
Having paid homage to Maheśāna, Umā, Skanda, and the lords of the Gaṇas, [the practitioner] should keep the neck,
head, and chest straight.
With the two eyes fixed on the tip of the nose. || 18 ||
Protecting the testicles with his heels,
not touching his teeth with his teeth,
and with his body braced, [he should place] the weight on the tips of his teeth.
Having taken hold of the tongue, he remains well-established.
One should retain the breath through the nostril until it reaches the limit of one's capacity. || 19½ ||
One whose food is beneficial—meaning free from harm—and which is digested upon reaching its final transformation, is thus described.

Being healthy for that very reason, through the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and so forth; in a house enclosed by three walls or ramparts, or in a quiet place such as a forest or a mountain cave, it is "excellent" (*suṣṭhu śobhane*) because it serves as a cause for dwelling in comfort and being free from disturbance.

Seated upon a seat such as a rug or cloth covered with a garment of bark or deerskin— or, by virtue of practice, established in a yogic posture (yogāsana) taught in other scriptures, characterized by stability and comfort, such as the lotus, the cross-legged (svastika), or the half-moon (ardhacandra)— he is "seated in his own seat" (svāsanastha). Facing the northern direction, [he meditates upon] the Supreme Lord and the Goddess.
Having bowed to Guha and Gaṇeśa, with his throat, head, and chest clearly aligned,
his gaze fixed on the tip of his nose, the rows of his upper and lower teeth slightly separated,
pressing his testicles with his heels to prevent upward jumping during the force of the *udghāta*, and keeping his body unbent, he remains well-established.

Placing the tongue against the edge of the teeth, one should exhale—cast the breath outward through the right nostril according to one's ability—in order to purify the channels within the body. || 19½ ||
Through that practice of exhalation (recaka),
one gradually attains proficiency in the various actions of piercing (vedha) and dispersal (vikṣipta).
Even in the case of objects situated at a distance. || 20½ ||

Through the practice of *recaka* characterized as previously described, the yogi gradually attains mastery over even distant objects, over acts of piercing (*vedha*), and over scattered activities that take the form of causes for dissolution. || 20½ ||
Now, the characteristic of *pūraka* (inhalation): it is the filling of the form with external air according to one's capacity.
Through the practice of this inhalation (pūraka), one should draw up even that which is very heavy.
Pūraka is the forceful filling of the body with external air according to one's capacity.
When this is well-practiced, one becomes capable of attracting even the heaviest objects, such as stones and the like. || 21½ ||
To explain *kumbhaka*, he says: "Having abandoned both emission and retention, cessation is known as *kumbhaka*."
Through the practice of that, the power of obstruction attains manifestation without hindrance. || 22½ ||

Having abandoned emission, which consists of expulsion, and retention, which is of the nature of filling, *kumbhaka* (the "pot-like" breath) results from the restraint of the internal air. Through its practice, the power of unimpeded restraint is manifested, as is the capacity to paralyze desired objects. || 22½ ||
As he thus moves along the paths of the Moon, the Sun, and Śiva, the wise one,
perceiving his fitness for that dharma, [proceeds].
The yogi should accomplish the intended goal. || 23½ ||
Through the practice of that [meditation], the yogi who knows the movement of this circulating wind as it is subject to control determines,

in accordance with the desired object, whether among the movements in the central, left, or right channels— such as "for this action, the wind moving in the right is best," or for that, the middle, or for this, however...
Thinking that what is gentle is indeed praiseworthy, the yogi should accomplish his desired goal. || 23½ ||
For instance: one should practice inhalation (pūraka) or retention (kumbhaka) while [the breath] remains on the path of the moon.
For the sake of nourishment or for the purpose of conquering death, one should perform exhalation (recaka) for oneself or for another. 24½.
In the absence of fire, the withering of trees, the destruction of seeds, and the arousal of paralysis, madness, and poison.
In the mouths... [perform] the exhalation (recaka). || 25½ ||
In meditation, worship, recitation, and other such practices,
as well as in the renunciation of the body for Śiva,
the kumbhaka breath-retention is the most excellent, surpassing even the recaka exhalation.
And also at the conclusion of the initiation rites. || 26½ ||

When the vital air is situated in the left channel, one should perform *kumbhaka* (retention) and *pūraka* (inhalation) for the sake of nourishing oneself, for the sake of refreshing oneself, and for the sake of [practices] such as *mṛtyuñjaya* (the conquest of death); this is understood from the inclusion of the phrase "and so forth.
As it has been said: "Or, for the sake of nourishing another and so on, one should employ exhalation (*recaka*) while staying in the left [channel]."

However, when one desires to perform actions such as igniting fire, causing trees to wither, rendering them seedless, paralyzing, intoxicating, or inflaming poison, then one should perform *recaka* (exhalation) while the breath is situated on the solar path (*sauramārga*).
"Paralyzing" (*stobha*) refers to the intensification of a small amount of fiery poison or similar substances, according to the tradition of Śaṅkara.

Regarding that meditation, worship, recitation, and so forth, as well as the departure of the soul (*utkrānti*), which are prescribed as duties during the equinox (*viṣuvat*) situated on the *suṣumṇā* path—the locus of Śiva—in that context, the two [practices] of *kumbhaka* (retention) and *recaka* (exhalation) are employed for the establishment (*saṃsthāpana*) of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Establishment means the act of consecration (*pratiṣṭhāpana*). || 26½ ||
Now, in order to state the rule regarding the duration of time for the practice of these [breath-controls], such as exhalation (recaka) and so forth,
he says: "The shortest, the middling, and the longest."
With twelve *tāla*s and so forth; the knee has a circumference of twelve *tāla*s. (27½)

The duration of time required for the hand to circle the kneecap once is to be known as one *tāla*, consisting of twelve such units of time. With twelve such *tālas* constitutes the lowest (*kaniṣṭha*) breath control (*prāṇāyāma*); with twenty-four, the middling (*madhyama*).

The best [practice] consists of forty-eight [breaths]. Thus it is said in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*: "The twelve-finger [span] breath-restraint (*prāṇāyāma*) is to be known as the lowest; the middling is with twenty-four [fingers], and the best should be double that. (27½)
Thus, that prāṇāyāma which consists of the aggregate of regulated exhalation (recaka), retention (kumbhaka), and inhalation (pūraka),
is also accompanied by meditation (dhyāna) and recitation (japa).
Another [type of meditation] is with an object (sagarbha), while the other is devoid of it (tadujjhita). Just as that which has an object leads to steadiness of mind, the other does not. || 28½ ||

This breath control (prāṇāyāma) as well, when joined with meditation (dhyāna) and recitation (japa), is to be known by the name "with the embryo" (sagarbha). That which is performed without meditation and recitation is "without the embryo" (nirgarbha). And just as the state of being a cause for the steadiness of the mind belongs to the "with-embryo" type, it does not belong to the "without-embryo" type in that same way.
The intended meaning is that practice should be performed for the sake of *prāṇāyāma* with its internal retention (*sagarbha*). || 28½ ||
Sin committed at night is [cleansed] in the morning, and that committed during the day is [cleansed] at the end of the day. || 29 ||
This breath control (prāṇāyāma) performed at dawn, along with its internal retention (sagarbha), destroys the sin committed during the night;
however, when performed at the end of the day, it destroys the sin committed during the day—this is the connection for the householder. || 29 ||
Thus, there is a purpose for breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) even when it is somewhat "ungarbed" (*nirgarbha*). To the question, "What then is the use of that [garbed one]?", he says:
"Even the ungarbed [breath control] destroys the gods..."
The state of being in motion for those who are running forward. || 29½ ||

For the senses of the gods, which—driven by beginningless ignorance—run excessively toward their objects, this "childless" (nirgarbha) prāṇāyāma, when practiced continuously, destroys their restlessness and excessive velocity; that is to say, it effects mastery over the senses. || 29½ ||
Moreover:
He becomes one who has bathed in sacred fords and is consecrated in all sacrifices.
The son should always perform this [rite] for his ancestors together with those still in the womb. || 30½ ||

But he who, being duly appointed, practices this "pregnant" (sagarbha) [mantra] joined with recitation and meditation, obtains the fruit of one who has bathed in all sacred fords and been initiated into all sacrifices. And he becomes a boat and a raft for the ancestors to cross over the ocean of worldly existence; by his grace, they too [cross] the ocean of becoming.
The meaning is "they cross over. || 30½ ||
In order to explain the state of being pregnant with the embryo (sagarbhatā), he says:
"One should meditate upon the God who is the destroyer of the path of darkness,
and one should always recite that which expresses Him."
Alternatively, the principles beginning with earth were fashioned as having that very form.

By means of the reason that he is the presiding lord of all, one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord—who dwells at the limit of the paths and transcends all causes—as the ultimate reality. Furthermore, one should mutter His mantra, which is the signifier;
the meaning is that during the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should effect the non-separation of sound and its referent. Or else:
One who desires the fruit of *dhāraṇā* should meditate upon the elements, beginning with earth, as having the Supreme Lord as their essential substratum;
for the Blessed One is eternally and everywhere present as the presiding controller of all sentient and insentient beings.
Now, [the author] asks: "In the meditation on the principles (tattvas) such as earth and so forth, what is the purpose of the contemplation of the Lord (bhagavad-bhāvanā)? He replies:
"Because an insentient principle, even if perfected, cannot be beneficial."
One should meditate on the body as Śiva;
whatever is desired is granted by that. || 32½ ||

For it is said that the collection of objects such as earth and so forth, being inherently insentient, cannot be beneficial even if perfected through the practice of meditation without the presiding presence of the nature of Śiva;
therefore, one should meditate on all this as the very body of the Supreme Lord. Thus, whatever is intended—
One should meditate upon even an object that has an acidic nature. || 32½ ||

And since this is so, therefore—for the sake of accomplishing the meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) and the other mental states (*vṛtti*), as well as the vital breath (*anila*)— [The following verse should be supplied: *sthirasukham āsanam* || 2.46 || A posture (*āsana*) is that which is steady and comfortable. || 2.46 || [And further: *tato dvandvānabhighātaḥ* || 2.48 || From that [posture], there is no affliction by the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*). || 2.48 || [And: *tataḥ svābhyāsapūrvakaṃ prāṇāyāmam abhyaset* || Thereafter, one should practice breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) preceded by its own mastery.
