is destroyed. || 2.52 || [And: *tato 'pi cittaprasādanam* || 2.53 || From that also comes the clarification of the mind (*citta-prasādana*). || 2.53 || [And: *tataḥ punaḥ śvāsapraśvāsayorgativicchedaḥ prāṇāyāmaḥ* || 2.49 || Furthermore, breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is the interruption of the flow of inhalation and exhalation. || 2.49 || [And: *tataḥ kṣīyate prakāśāvaraṇam* || 2.52 || From that, the veil over the light [of knowledge] is destroyed. || 2.52 || [And: *tato 'pi cittaprasādanam* || 2.53 || From that also comes the clarification of the mind (*citta-prasādana*). || 2.53 || [And: *tataḥ punaḥ śvāsapraśvāsayorgativicchedaḥ prāṇāyāmaḥ* || 2.49 || Furthermore, breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is the interruption of the flow of inhalation and exhalation. || 2.49 || [And: *tataḥ kṣīyate prakāśāvaraṇam* || 2.52 || From that, the veil over the light [of knowledge] is destroyed. || 2.52 || [And: *tato 'pi cittaprasādanam* || 2.53 || From that also comes
The wise man, with an undistracted mind, should practice the sagarbha kumbhaka.

For the sake of accomplishing the previously mentioned limbs of yoga, such as the dhāraṇās, as well as the functions of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth which serve purposes like directing [the breath], one should practice *kumbhaka* with its internal content (*sagarbha*), remaining with an undisturbed mind; that is, one should perform it. || 33½ ||
One who has established mental stability for a period of time equal to the duration of the sun's rays attains the designation of "dhāraṇā" (concentration).
Because it bestows the perfection of the dhāraṇīs. || 34½ ||

This *sagarbha* (with seed) *kumbhaka*, when performed for twelvefold the duration by means of the cessation of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛttinirodha*), receives the designation of *dhāraṇā*. Why? He says: "Because it bestows the attainment of *dhāraṇā*";
that is, being practiced in such a manner, it grants the success associated with *dhāraṇā*. || 34½ ||
The word *dhāraṇā* has the sense of "abiding," and it also has the sense of "place" by way of metaphorical usage. || 35 ||
These, beginning with the forest, are the abodes for a beginner, and no others. || 35½ ||

For the beginner, who has just begun the practice and is ascending, the elements such as earth and so forth constitute the locus of practice, and not any other collection of principles such as the unperceived (avyakta), mahat, or ego (ahaṅkāra); for the practice of each subsequent stage is indeed easy once it is preceded by the practice of the perceptible elements like earth that are already being experienced.
This is the sequence of instruction found in all the Yoga treatises. || 35 ||
Now he declares their forms, shapes, purposes, and marks: "In terms of color, they are gold, snow, light, black, and transparent."
But [the mandalas] have the shapes of a half-vedī, a triangle, a circle, and a lotus. || 36½ ||
The vajra, lotus, and flame arise for the attainment of stability, nourishment, burning away, impelling, and emptiness.
But they are endowed with the bindu and the void. || 37½ ||

Those five elements, beginning with earth, are respectively yellow, white, blazing [red], black, and transparent in color; and in shape, they are square, a half-moon, a triangle, circular, and lotus-shaped; and they are characterized by the sequence of the vajra, the lotus, the flame, the drop, and the void.
They become marked for the sake of stability and so forth; the meaning is that they become effective means for achieving those [qualities]. || 37 ||
And having understood those [persons] as being hostile, compliant, or neutral;
The yogi should maintain them both individually and collectively for the sake of attaining the desired goal. || 38½ ||

Having understood the elements beginning with earth—both individually and collectively—as being friendly, hostile, or neutral, the yogi should fix his mind upon them for the sake of accomplishing desired tasks. || 38½ ||
Then, desiring to know the nature of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and its fruit, the sage asks:
"In what place should the form of concentration be meditated upon by the wise man?"
Moreover, O Lord of the Gods, tell us the fruit of these [practices] both individually and collectively.

The meaning of the question is as follows: "In which place should that form, which has been taught in the *dhāraṇās* through its qualities such as being golden, snowy, luminous, black, or transparent, be contemplated by one who knows it? And what is the fruit of these *dhāraṇās*, both taken individually and collectively? O Lord of the Gods, please instruct us. (39½)
The reply is as follows:
when the heart— that is, the mind— is distracted,
the knower of the goal should fix his attention on the earth.
Thirsty, he drinks water;
with weak digestive fire, there is heat in his stomach. (40½)

For the sake of establishing the functions of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, one should direct the wind to the heart, throat, and other locations; in cases of being overcome by poison and the like, one should direct it to space (vyoma).
Among those, [the rule applies] where there is utility. 41½.

When there should be distraction of the mind, then the yogi who knows the purpose should maintain the earth-element concentration (pārthivī dhāraṇā), which is said to be the cause of stability, in the region of the heart. But when he is afflicted by an irresistible thirst, then he should sustain the water-element concentration (vāruṇī dhāraṇā) in the throat.

Because it is taught for the purpose of nourishing that [fire], one should bind the previously mentioned Āgneyī [mudrā] within the stomach when the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni) is weak, in order to kindle it;
and for the sake of accomplishing the functions of the vital breaths (prāṇa), etc., which were previously described, such as leading [the breath] and so forth.

When one has attained mastery, one should maintain the wind-element (vāyavī) in the previously mentioned locations, such as the heart and throat, in order to accomplish those respective fruits. However, one who is being overcome by poison, insanity, disease, or similar afflictions should fix the meditation on space (vyomadhāraṇā) upon any one of those aforementioned sites, such as the heart, from among them. Or else, wherever [it may be].
One should hold it upon that limb which is free from afflictions such as poison and which is suitable for practices such as *dhāraṇā*, so that it serves a purpose. || 41 ||
Now, while discerning the mutual states of enmity and friendship among these elements beginning with earth, he first speaks in order to state the universal commonality of space:
"Space [is common] to all beings."
Air, water, fire, and earth; water and fire, earth and air, and water and earth, as well as fire and air. (42)
Having understood that the neutral, enemy, and friendly planets are situated in pairs within each of the four quarters, the wise man [should proceed].
One should apply [this] for the sake of attaining one's desired goal. || 43 ||

First, space (*ākāśa*) should be known as their friend because of its pervasiveness and because it provides room for all things by being situated within them. Regarding the triads of four— wind, water, fire, and earth— one should understand that within each respective tetrad, they occur in pairs according to their sequence (that is, two by two).

These should be understood as neutral, enemy, and friend respectively. For instance, in the first group of four—wind, water, fire, and earth—there is neither mutual friendship nor enmity between water and wind, nor between earth and fire; thus, their status as neutral should be understood. [Likewise for] water and fire...

Regarding "earth and wind": here too, within this middle group of four, these four exist in a state of mutual relationship as the sublated and the sublator; thus, their *arātitva* (enmity) is their state of being enemies. Regarding "water and earth" and "fire and wind": however, in this third group of four, between earth and water, and between wind and fire—

Having thus fully understood and realized that friendship arises from being a supporter, the wise yogi should employ these [means] as a means of accomplishment, either in such a manner or at such a time as is appropriate, for the sake of attaining his desired goal. || 42-43 ||

Now, in the section concerning the investigation of the *pratyayas* and so forth included within the *Vidyāpāda*, it was stated: "The location for each [of the winds] during their retention, their mastery, and the remaining results have been proclaimed by the Lord in the *Skandha*. Following that, the common locations of the functions (*vṛtti*) of the *prāṇa* and other [winds] are as follows:
And the Sage asks in order to know the result:
"What are the locations within this little body for the functions of the vital breaths and so forth?"
"O best of gods, tell me: what would happen if they were conquered? (44)

The meaning of the question is: "O Blessed Indra, tell us what are the locations for the functions of the prāṇa, apāna, and so forth—such as leading forward and leading away—in which their mastery must be achieved; and when those functions of the prāṇa and others have been mastered, what fruit will result within this body?"
The suffix *ka* is employed to indicate that even though the self (*ātman*) is all-pervading (*vyāpaka*), it has become non-pervasive or contemptible due to that [state]. || 44 ||
To this, the reply is:
because of its retention in the regions of the heart, throat, navel, and back.
The mastery of the functions such as inhalation and so forth shall belong to the yogin. || 45 ||

By the restraint of that aforementioned wind— which exists in the form of prāṇa and so forth— at the five locations beginning with the heart and ending with the back, the yogi achieves mastery over the functions of prāṇa and the others, such as leading [the breath] (praṇayana) and so forth. || 45 ||
One who has conquered passion assumes a body for himself according to his own will;
one who has conquered misconduct partakes of food [only as required].
He does not discharge feces and the like. || 46 ||
One whose vision is victorious attains qualities such as mastery over speech through the conquest of the equalized state of existence.
He shall become a self-controlled one, free from old age. || 47 ||
Mastery over the body and its movements arises when the mind is conquered;
there is no clinging to mud, water, or thorns.
His energy is inexhaustible and marvelous. || 48 ||

The yogi who has conquered that which is called "leading forward"—namely, the function of the *prāṇa*—is one who maintains his own body for as long as he desires, according to his own will. This is because the function known as "leading forward" is described as being the very nature of life (*jīvana*). Likewise, he is one by whom that which is called "leading away"—namely, the function of the *apāna*—has been conquered.
A yogi of this kind, even while eating, becomes pure-bodied. For, through mastery over the *apāna* breath, his food and drink do not transform into excrement, urine, or other impurities;

rather, they transform solely into the essence of the nutrient-fluid (*rasa-dhātu*). Thus, he becomes entirely free from internal impurities such as feces and the like—this is the case for all embodied beings.

For it is through the state of being the essence of the nutrient fluid (*rasa-mala-dhātu*) that the transformation of food and drink occurs. He by whom the function of giving known as upward-looking (*unnayana*) has been conquered attains qualities such as mastery over speech in the form of poetic composition and eloquence. But he by whom the equalizing function (*samāna-vṛtti*) has been conquered is forever free from old age and is all-enduring.

The entire body becomes [under one's control]. Having achieved mastery over the function of the pervasive movement (vyāna) known as "bending" (vinamana), one wanders through the body at will. The meaning is that one becomes capable of sending forth or drawing back the vital air (marut) through the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) or the openings of the ears and so forth. Likewise:
Even when sitting upon mud, water, thorns, or similar things, he remains in a state of non-contact with them; moreover, his strength becomes indestructible. || 48 ||
Thus, immediately following this incidental exchange of questions and answers, the subject at hand is now described:
meditation consists of twelve types of concentration (dhāraṇās) and bestows the manifestation of divine light.
Concentration is the cause of these twelve, beginning with the power of atomization (aṇimā). || 49 ||
Retention (*dhāraṇā*) was previously described as consisting of twelve *kumbhakas* performed together with breath-holding.

Those twelve are to be known as meditation (*dhyāna*). And because that [meditation] bestows the manifestation of light—the arising of a divine, stainless, supramundane illumination—it is called "bestowing the arising of divine light"; thus the fruit of its practice has been stated.
These twelve meditations are called *samādhi*;
they are the cause for the divine perfections (*siddhis*) such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
For one who possesses such *samādhi*, there will be the manifestation of *aṇimā* and the other powers. || 49 ||
Even without breath control (prāṇāyāma), one who has thus mastered the self and remains established in the mind attains [perfection] through constant practice.
Immediately after [the discussion of] the qualities (guṇas), [the following are] stated. || 50 ||

In this manner, by being constantly disciplined in this way toward the self, the yogi whose mind is mastered— without even the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma)— while remaining with the fluctuations of the mind (cittavṛtti) restrained in any location whatsoever,
practices that [concentration] and thereby attains these qualities, beginning with atomization (aṇimā), in uninterrupted succession. || 50 ||
Furthermore:
whatever object is attained according to the sequence as it has been prescribed;
In each of those instances, his manifestation of consciousness would have as its object the pervasion by that [consciousness]. || 51 ||
Thus, having perceived everything situated externally with the eye as it were,
and having abandoned all objects, one remains.
One should practice the Śiva-tattva thoroughly. || 52 ||

Through the practice according to the sequence described, whatever reality— from earth up to Śiva— the yogi attains and internalizes by means of *dhāraṇā* (concentration) and other methods, in each of those instances there arises for this yogin a manifestation of his own self-awareness whose object is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that [reality]. For instance, first, regarding the principles (*tattva*) beginning with earth:

By means of the seven possessors of power— namely Śiva, Mantra-Maheśvara, Mantreśvara, Mantra-Vijñānākala, Pralayākala, and Sakala— and by as many powers as there are, each one of the elements beginning with earth possesses fifteen modes in its own nature, such as the waking state and so forth, and the forms of being situated in the body and so forth.

Regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*), it has been stated as follows: "The principle of earth (*dharātattva*) is differentiated by means of the various forms of the glorious power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).
Together with its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), that [principle] should be known to consist of fifteen [categories].
Those beginning with Śiva, whose essence is the *sakala* (the embodied), are proclaimed to be the possessors of power (*śaktimant*); their powers (*tacchaktayaḥ*) are also to be known."

In the same way, it has been taught by the wise: "Thus, this great multitude of principles (tattvas), from water down to the root [Prakṛti], is divided by these various distinctions," and so forth. Thus, for the yogin who possesses that pervasive realization, consciousness transcends [the limited state]; this is heard in the venerable Kāmika-tantra: "When that which is external remains [as such]..."

Having realized that every object has come within the range of one's own vision, one should abandon all those entities—such as *vidyā* and the rest—which are distinct from Śiva, because they are the means for attaining the state of Śiva that exists at the end of all paths; instead, one should practice the reality of Śiva (*śivatattva*) and remain solely devoted to it. These [other things] are to be abandoned.
In the reading "having completely abandoned the objects of the senses" (padārthān santyajya), the meaning is indeed clear. || 52 ||
That living being who, while practicing the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and other such rites that contain the essence of Śiva, gives up his life-breaths, [attains liberation].
He attains the state of Śiva. || 53 ||

Let alone the manifestation of knowledge regarding the scope of pervasion; even without the absolute affirmation (ekāntavidhi) that will be described hereafter, any living being who performs breath-control (prāṇāyāma) consisting of meditation on and recitation of the Supreme Lord, when he casts off his vital breaths, attains the state of Śiva—meaning, he is liberated. || 53 ||
Then the sage said:
"The supreme form of Maheśa can never be meditated upon."
Since the imagined [world] arises from diversity for the sake of delusion, how can the mind find stability therein? (54)

Regarding the nature of the Blessed One, who is essentially partless (*niṣkala*): since his essential nature is formless and lacks materiality, it cannot be meditated upon. As they have said: "You, possessing form, must necessarily be worshipped; for the intellect does not reach an object that is formless. Now, even though his form is non-existent from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), [the following applies]...
For those who meditate, the conceptualization of specific forms that serve as the basis for the mind’s fluctuations results in this imagined form;
due to its variety—such as white, yellow, red, and so forth—it would lead to delusion. How, then, can there be a mental abiding or stability therein?
For how can the mind, which is by nature fickle, be restrained when its object is an unreal form produced by imagination?
The Question: 54.
Now, regarding this, the meditative concentration is as follows:
when the earth and water elements are marked with various signs,
then they are not to be focused upon during the practice of dhāraṇā.
Nevertheless, yogins are heard of as being established through those two by way of appearance.
It is true that the nature of the formless Blessed One cannot be meditated upon according to the sequence previously described;

however, the attainment of His true nature will occur through the sequence of instruction on the objectless (*nirālambana*). As for the statement that "that which is imagined due to diversity leads to delusion," that is not tenable in the case of what is taught in the scriptures (*āgama*).
Because meditation cannot be conceptual in nature if it is to be considered the ultimate reality;

for if one were to admit that the performance of the various diverse rites taught therein is optional, then since initiation and the like would also become unreal, they would be rendered purposeless—thus, what is the use of scripture? Furthermore, the object of meditation [is established] due to its manifold variety.
Let us set aside for now the claim that meditation is impossible;

even in the contemplation of the form of the Supreme Lord, these two well-known *dhāraṇās* (concentrations) called "the Earthly" and "the Watery," which are established in all general yoga treatises, are clearly present, as they too are characterized by various forms and marked by the thunderbolt (*vajra*).

Furthermore, because it is marked by snow, water, and blue lotuses, it cannot be meditated upon as an object of meditation. Nor is such an admission appropriate here, since it is heard that for yogis who have practiced those two concentrations on earth and water, many supernatural powers (*siddhi*) arise despite the diversity of their respective forms.

Likewise, even when there exists this realization of the fruit of dhāraṇā— which is taught in the scriptures and obtained by a yogi through the practice of many treatises— [it may still not be firm]. || 55 ||
How can there be stability of mind for one whose mind is overwhelmed by enjoyments?
[The Buddha] did not teach this with reference to those beings who are excessively attached.
Hara spoke this means of accomplishment. || 56 ||

Now it is asked: how can there be stability—that is, the abiding of the extremely flickering mind through the complete cessation of all its fluctuations—for those whose minds have been distracted by the habitual practice of various enjoyments undertaken over thousands of births? As it has been said:
In the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā: "For the mind, O Kṛṣṇa, is restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate;

I consider its restraint to be as difficult as that of the wind. And likewise: "Yet it is possible to block the flow [of the mind] from sense objects, even as that of the great ocean whose waves are tossed by a fierce fire."
"Not by the mind"—this is not correct. For the Supreme Lord did not prescribe this means called Yoga for beings who are not dispassionate;
rather, it was for those whose stains of longing for worldly enjoyment have been washed away by the cascading streams of abundant dispassion. They alone [are the ones] in this way.

Those who feel revulsion for the enjoyment of saṃsāra—which has long since arisen and is devoid of essence—regard this [state] as supreme. Furthermore, for those possessed of such practice, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain, even in this visible world. 56.
And for this reason— it is possible to gradually make even the entire world an object [of one's realization].
What wonder is there in a body that is self-controlled and characterized by the practice of dispassion? (57)

Those who possess dispassion and practice— meaning they shine through dispassion, lack of desire, and the repeated cultivation of that [practice]— and who are self-controlled, endowed with tranquility; by such yogis, the entire world is gradually pervaded through the process of *dhāraṇā*.
If even that can be made an object of perception, how much more so the manifold, supreme form of the Lord, which is the object of meditation? || 57 ||
Having thus taught the yoga with an object, he prepares the ground to teach the superior objectless [yoga]:
"What indeed is this measure of form?"
They are practitioners endowed with all empowerments;
at all times, they provide assistance to all beings in every possible way. || 58 ||
Having mentally conceived the location, form, and dimensions,
[one should meditate] where the mind comes to rest.
That very object of meditation should be contemplated again and again. || 59 ||

Alternatively, for the Supreme Lord, who is the yogin of all substrates, this very form—with its white and other colors, ten arms, five faces, and so forth—is simply to be meditated upon; what restriction could there be regarding such a form? The meaning is that there is none whatsoever, as He manifests His expansive majesty.

Indeed, worshiping the Blessed One at a limited location is certainly improper. Therefore, with a mind unwavering whether externally or internally, having conceptualized the place, form, dimensions, and appearance,
one should repeatedly [direct the mind] wherever the mind finds peace— whether in a mental body (*bhāva-śarīra*) or a physical body (*bhūta-śarīra*).
One who possesses effort and has mastered the methods obtained through the instruction of the Guru should meditate. And it is said in the *Pārameśvara*:

"Neither the senses, nor the vital breath, nor the mind, nor the intellect, nor desire exists; I am not, nor is there another; therefore, there is the dissolution of the mind. The destruction of the mind is the attainment of the Supreme—this is the truth, O Mother of the Gaṇas. (58–59)
Now he states the fruit of this very [practice]:
"By that, there arises in his mind a stability characterized by distinguished qualities, gradually..."
Having destroyed the obstacles, the refinement of yoga arises once it has been opened.

Regarding that which was previously questioned— how there can be stability of the mind— this [verse] is for that purpose. By means of this aforementioned yoga, for this yogi who is free from obstacles, the steadiness of the mind— that is, its lack of wavering— is produced, which is utterly distinct from resting in any other form.

He asks, "What kind of stability is that? and replies: "Possessing special qualities (*saviśeṣaguṇam*)," meaning that in which the previously mentioned special qualities—namely the *aṇimā* and so forth—are present with their respective degrees of excellence (*sātiśaya*). Having done what is this produced? He says:
"Having gradually revealed its true nature through the refinement of yoga (*yogasaṃskāra*)," because it is established upon those latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
The meaning is that for one who remains established in that conventional practice and is free from obstacles, stability of mind arises in that very state.
For one who abides thus correctly,
without even the conceptualization of forms,
and whose mind is devoid of anything whatsoever—
One's own form unfolds. || 61 ||
That which consists of the form of all-pervading vision and action, which is composed of bliss and is imperishable—
having attained which, one does not experience suffering again.
Having attained a yoga that brings about inauspiciousness. || 62 ||

Thus, for the yogi who practices this previously described method of yoga correctly through the power of excellence in pure practice— even without the conceptualization of forms— and whose mind is "nothing-at-all" (akiñcicca), not thinking of anything whatsoever, [the mind] dissolves into its own self through the cessation of the mind.

The meaning is that for one who abides in the tranquility of the great ocean free from waves, one's own innate form unfolds, blossoms, and becomes immeasurable; it expands and becomes one's own nature, free from all veils. To the question of what kind of innate form unfolds, he says: "having the nature of the vision and action of all objects," and so forth. All objects...

Vision is the knowledge of all objects, and action is its functional form; since these two constitute His very nature, knowledge and action are declared in the scriptures to belong to Śiva—the supreme, stainless one who is present in all things.
That which is taught in the Āgamas as the nature of Śiva is accordingly delightful, beautiful, and imperishable.

And for this yogin who practices in this manner, that which is imperishable becomes manifest; and having attained it, he does not enter—that is, he does not reach—the "bringer of inauspiciousness" (*aśivāvaha*), characterized by *saṃsāra*, which brings about birth, death, and other forms of misfortune, namely, the conjunction with suffering. And it has been said by the venerable teacher Avadhūta: "Just as [it was] led..."
"Just as metals are reduced to the state of gold by the best of elixirs so that they do not return [to their former state], so too those impelled by the teaching of the Mata [do not return]. (62)
In this regard, preceded by a praise of its own nature, he says the following in order to declare that it must not be revealed to anyone because of its extreme secrecy:
"Of all these secrets..."
This secret [teaching], praised by the Siddhas and the Immortals, is the direct perception of Śambhu;
it is the supreme means for generating passion. 63.
This should not be given to one who has resided [here] for only a short time, nor to one who is excessively negligent, nor to one who lacks intelligence, nor to one who is devoid of austerity.
And whoever does not worship Śiva. || 64 ||

Since this is more intensely to be concealed than even all other secrets, because it is the cause for attaining unsurpassed supreme bliss, it is for that very reason praised by the Siddhas and the immortals;
and because it directly illuminates the splendor of the Supreme Lord, it is most excellent and purifying.

This is the cause of purification; therefore, it is not for one who has resided [in the lineage] for a short time. Because he has been initiated for too brief a period, it is not for a disciple whose unsurpassed yoga of faith and action is unknown, nor for one who is excessively negligent, because for such a negligent person, both knowledge and yoga cannot be protected; nor is it for one who lacks austerity and is devoid of discipline.

Furthermore, although one who performs the worship of the Supreme Lord is free from negligence and is not dull-witted, he lacks qualification due to the absence of austerity and the lack of devotion. || 64 ||

Thus, the fruit of this yoga-vidhi— characterized by both worldly enjoyment (bhukti) and liberation (mukti)— is to be understood; this verse serves both as a conclusion to this section and as an introduction to the Caryāpāda, which will be discussed further on.
Through the practice of this, shining brilliantly with networks of rays that possess divine powers, he wanders through the auspicious worlds;
then, at the proper time, having cast off his body which is free from outflows (anāsrava), he abides [in liberation].
He dwells in his own self alone as the abode of wondrous conduct. || 65 ||

The practice of this objectless yoga is its repeated cultivation; from that [practice arise] the sixty-four divine, supramundane qualities, which are the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth. Those who possess these are "possessors of divine powers. With their "networks of rays," which are the expansions of power, he is "shining intensely," being resplendent due to his mass of diffused light.

"Having wandered at will through the desired worlds"— that is, having completed their wandering characterized by play (*krīḍā*) in those worlds such as heaven and so forth; [the senses] which were previously inclined toward the exclusive grasping of external objects and averse to the perception of the inner self, now "flow," meaning they move outward with independence.

The meaning is that because the senses are denoted by the word *āsrava* (influx), he— having become free from that influx by abandoning external functioning— is always inward-turned with his entire collection of senses; and having abandoned even the divine body at any time as desired, he remains established in his own true nature alone, becoming blissful.

To explain what kind [of being] he is, he says: "the abode of wondrous conduct. That conduct is characterized by wonder because it is exceedingly marvelous; it is the state of being the agent of the fivefold activity, such as maintenance (*sthiti*) and so forth.
He is the abode, that is, the locus, of that [conduct], wherein the fivefold [activity] is accomplished by mere will, just like the Supreme Lord.

Even though he is capable of the activities of maintenance and so forth, he remains within his own self because there is nothing further to be done; this has been explained almost entirely in the Vidyāpāda itself.
This concise statement shines forth, expanding the object of knowledge in its full extent;
through the investigation of the sequence of what precedes and follows, there is no tautology whatsoever.
There is no over-extension because it speaks of the subject at hand, nor is there any under-extension in this manner.
The yoga with its constituent limbs, as proclaimed in this venerable Mṛgendrāgama, is victorious.
Thus ends the Yoga-pāda in the Mṛgendra-vṛtti composed by Śrī Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, son of Śrī Bhaṭṭa Vidyākaṇṭha. May there be auspiciousness!
